fields.title: After His Heart
fields.subtitle: Spiritual Leadership in the Way of Jesus
fields.description: A book on spiritual leadership for the whole Church: pastors and elders, house-church leaders, deacons, teachers, parents and believers who lead at work. Fifty chapters in ten parts teach the leader’s call, heart and life with God; shepherding the flock; leading together; vision and mission; the dangers that bring leaders down; leading through hardship; home, work and accountability; and finishing well. Each chapter is full of Scripture, tells the story of leaders from church history and the global Church, and ends with questions and a step for the week.
fields.about_html:
“I will give you shepherds who are after my own heart,” God promised through Jeremiah, “and they will shepherd you with knowledge and insight.” This book is about that kind of leader. It is not a book of techniques. It begins with the heart, because the Lord looks at the heart, and it holds up Jesus, the Good Shepherd, as the pattern for everyone who leads His people, whether a congregation, a house church, a class of children, a family or a team at work.

Fifty chapters move through ten parts: The Call; The Leader’s Heart; The Leader with God; Shepherding the Flock; Leading Together; Vision and Mission; Dangers on the Road, from pride, money and sexual sin to the abuse of power and envy; Leading Through Hardship, from loneliness and burnout to failure, persecution and the hidden years; The Leader’s Life, at home, single, at work and under accountability; and Finishing Well. A conclusion gathers the portrait of a shepherd after God’s heart.

Every chapter is full of Scripture and lets leaders from across the centuries and around the world speak: Polycarp and Gregory the Great, Richard Baxter and John Wesley, Samuel Ajayi Crowther and Pandita Ramabai, Amy Carmichael and Mary Slessor, Hudson Taylor, Watchman Nee, Josephine Bakhita and the leaders of the East African Revival, among many others. Each ends with questions for reflection and one step for the week. Where faithful Christians differ, on church government or women in church office for example, the book sets out the main views fairly. Three appendices explain how churches are led, offer a leader’s self-examination and give plans for training leaders, and a glossary explains the words a new leader may not know. Scripture is quoted from the Open Word Bible (OWB), Balanced edition, which is dedicated to the public domain.

qa.question: What is After His Heart about?
qa.answer: It is a book on spiritual leadership in the way of Jesus. Its title comes from God’s promise in Jeremiah 3:15: “I will give you shepherds who are after my own heart.” It teaches what kind of person a Christian leader must be, how to care for God’s people, the dangers to watch for, and how to finish well.

qa.question: Who is After His Heart written for?
qa.answer: For anyone who leads God’s people in any way: pastors, elders and deacons, house-church and small-group leaders, Sunday school, youth and women’s leaders, missionaries, parents, and believers who lead at work or in society. It was written with the fast-growing churches of Africa, Asia and Latin America in mind, and for new leaders as well as experienced ones.

qa.question: Is this book suitable for a new leader?
qa.answer: Yes. The Introduction suggests where a new leader can start, the language is kept plain, discussions of questions on which Christians differ are marked “Going deeper” and can wait, and the glossary at the end explains unfamiliar words.

qa.question: How is each chapter laid out?
qa.answer: Each chapter opens with a key Scripture, teaches from many passages of the Bible, lets one or more leaders from church history or the global Church speak in their own words, and ends with questions for reflection and one practical step for the week ahead.

qa.question: Can After His Heart be used to train leaders in a group?
qa.answer: Yes. Appendix C gives two plans: a ten-session course built on key chapters, and a fifty-week plan through the whole book, with guidance on leading a session and on training others to lead groups in turn. Appendix B offers self-examination questions for each of the ten parts.

qa.question: How does the book handle questions on which Christians disagree?
qa.answer: Where faithful Christians differ, on church government, the baptism in the Spirit, revival, or women in church office for example, it presents the main views fairly and then lands on the common ground all share. Appendix A sets out the episcopal, presbyterian and congregational forms of church government without taking sides.

qa.question: Which Bible translation does it use?
qa.answer: Every Scripture is quoted from the Open Word Bible (OWB), Balanced edition, a translation from the Hebrew and Greek that is dedicated to the public domain.

fields.title: Introduction: After His Heart
fields.body_html:
“I will give you shepherds who are after my own heart, and they will shepherd you with knowledge and insight.”

— Jeremiah 3:15 (OWB)

Somewhere today a woman is opening her small house for a Bible study. A young man is standing in front of a youth group for the first time, his hands shaking. A farmer who is also an elder is walking to visit a sick neighbour before the sun is hot. A pastor with no salary is sweeping the floor of a church made of iron sheets. A mother is praying with her children before school. A believer in an office is deciding whether to sign a report she knows is false. Each one of them is a leader. Each one of them is shaping other people’s lives, for good or for harm.

This book is for them. It is for pastors and elders, deacons and teachers, missionaries and youth leaders, cell group leaders and Sunday school teachers. It is also for parents, and for believers who lead in a business, a school, a hospital or a government office. If someone follows you, listens to you or learns from you, you are a leader, and God cares how you lead.

Why another book on leadership?

There are many books on leadership. Most of them are written for business. They teach useful things: how to plan, how to manage time, how to build a team. But they usually measure a leader by results. Did the company grow? Did the numbers go up? Did people do what you wanted?

The Bible measures leaders in another way. When God rejected Saul as king of Israel, Samuel told him, “The LORD has looked for a man after his own heart” (1 Samuel 13:14). When Samuel went to anoint the next king, he was impressed by the tallest of Jesse’s sons. But God told him, “The LORD does not see in the way a person sees. A person looks at what is there for the eyes, but the LORD looks at the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). The man God chose was the youngest son, who was out looking after the sheep.

Centuries later, when God’s people had been led badly for a long time, He made them a promise through the prophet Jeremiah: “I will give you shepherds who are after my own heart, and they will shepherd you with knowledge and insight” (Jeremiah 3:15). That promise gives this book its name. God does not first look for leaders who are clever, strong or popular. He looks for leaders whose hearts are shaped like His heart. Knowledge and skill matter, and this book will teach many practical things. But they grow out of the heart. A leader with great skill and a wrong heart can do great harm. A leader with a right heart and little skill can learn, and God will use them.

A book for the whole Church

Most of the world’s Christians now live in Africa, Asia and Latin America. Many of their churches are led by pastors and elders who have never been to a Bible college. Many of them work another job during the week to feed their families. Many of them lead in places where Christians are poor, or few, or persecuted. They do not need a book that assumes a large building, a paid staff and a big budget. They need the Bible, and the wisdom of Christians who have walked this road before them.

So this book draws on the whole Church, across the centuries and across the world. You will meet Gregory, a bishop of Rome around AD 600, who wrote one of the first books on caring for souls. You will meet Augustine of North Africa, Chrysostom of Antioch, and Polycarp, who learned from the apostle John. You will meet Samuel Ajayi Crowther, a Yoruba boy rescued from a slave ship who became the first African bishop of the Anglican Church. You will meet Pandita Ramabai of India, the revival leaders of East Africa, pastors in China, and the founders of the first Black churches in America. Many of their own books and letters are free to read on Ochorus. When we quote them, we will tell you where to find them.

We also want this book to be easy to translate, because it is written for the whole Church in many languages. So we have tried to write plainly, in short sentences, and to explain any word that a new reader may not know. A Glossary at the end of the book (Chapter 56) explains words such as elder, overseer, deacon and ordination.

The journey ahead

The book has ten parts, with five chapters in each.

  • Part One: The Call asks what spiritual leadership is, and who calls us to it. We look at Jesus the Chief Shepherd, at how God calls leaders, at the towel and basin of servant leadership, and at the kind of authority a spiritual leader holds.
  • Part Two: The Leader’s Heart looks at character: humility, integrity, watching over your own soul, love and courage.
  • Part Three: The Leader with God turns to the hidden life that feeds the public one: prayer, the Word, the Holy Spirit, rest, and seeking God’s guidance.
  • Part Four: Shepherding the Flock covers the daily work of caring for people: teaching, knowing each person, seeking the lost, correcting and restoring, and comforting those who suffer.
  • Part Five: Leading Together shows that nobody should lead alone. It covers shared leadership, training new leaders, unity, handling conflict, and men and women serving together.
  • Part Six: Vision and Mission looks outward: seeing what God sees, planning with wisdom, reaching the nations, caring for the poor, and leading in times of revival and change.
  • Part Seven: Dangers on the Road names the temptations that ruin leaders: pride, money, sexual sin, the abuse of power, and envy and favouritism.
  • Part Eight: Leading Through Hardship walks through loneliness, burnout, failure, persecution and the hidden years of waiting.
  • Part Nine: The Leader’s Life turns to the leader’s home, to singleness, to caring for your own body and time, to leading at work, and to accountability.
  • Part Ten: Finishing Well looks to the end: handing on the work, leaving a legacy, growing old in the work, giving account to Christ, and the day when the Chief Shepherd appears.

After the Conclusion there are three appendices. Appendix A (Chapter 53) sets out the main ways churches are led and governed. Appendix B (Chapter 54) offers questions for a leader to examine their own life. Appendix C (Chapter 55) shows how to use this book to train a group of leaders. The Glossary (Chapter 56) comes last.

How to read this book

Each chapter follows the same pattern. It opens with a verse of Scripture. It teaches from the Bible under a few headings. It then tells the story of one man or woman of God, or shares part of a letter they wrote, under the heading “A voice from the Church”. It ends with questions for reflection and one practical step for the week ahead.

You can read this book in three ways.

  • Alone. Read one chapter a week, slowly. Look up the Bible passages. Write down your answers to the questions. Take the step for the week.
  • With a mentor. Ask an older, wiser Christian to read it with you. Meet once a week to talk about one chapter. Be honest with them about the questions that are hard for you.
  • In a group of leaders. Many churches can use this book to train their elders, deacons and group leaders together. Each chapter is short enough for one meeting. Appendix C (Chapter 55) gives a plan for a ten-week course and for a whole year.

Some chapters include a short section called “Going deeper”. These sections deal with questions on which faithful Christians disagree, such as how a church should be governed. We set out the main views as fairly as we can. If you are new to leading, you may skip these sections and come back to them later.

New to leading? Start here

Perhaps you have just been asked to lead something for the first time. Perhaps you are not sure you are ready. That is a good place to begin, because nobody is ready on their own. If you do not know where to start, read these four chapters first.

  1. Chapter 2, What Makes Leadership Spiritual. It explains what this book means by leadership, and why every believer leads someone.
  2. Chapter 5, The Towel and the Basin. It shows how Jesus led, by serving.
  3. Chapter 7, Humility. It explains the attitude that keeps a leader safe.
  4. Chapter 12, Prayer First. It shows where a leader’s strength comes from.

Then come back and read the book from the beginning. Do not worry if some chapters seem to be about work much bigger than yours. The same Shepherd leads a village house church and a city cathedral, and the same principles apply to both.

A short map of church history

You will meet people from many centuries in this book. This short map will help you to place them.

  • The early Church (about AD 30 to 500). The apostles and the first leaders after them, such as Clement of Rome, Ignatius of Antioch and Polycarp of Smyrna. Later, the great teachers of North Africa and the Mediterranean, such as Cyprian, Athanasius, Augustine and John Chrysostom. Much of the Church was persecuted until the early 300s.
  • The medieval Church (about 500 to 1500). Leaders such as Gregory the Great, Bernard of Clairvaux and Catherine of Siena. Monasteries kept the Scriptures alive and sent out missionaries.
  • The Reformation (the 1500s). Martin Luther, John Calvin and others called the Church back to the Bible and to salvation by grace through faith.
  • The Puritans and the revivals (the 1600s and 1700s). Pastors such as Richard Baxter, and preachers such as John Wesley and George Whitefield, through whom many thousands came to faith.
  • The age of world mission (the 1800s and early 1900s). Missionaries such as William Carey and Hudson Taylor, and, just as important, the first great leaders of the churches they helped to plant, such as Samuel Ajayi Crowther in Nigeria and Pandita Ramabai in India.
  • The global Church today. From the East African Revival to the house churches of China, the centre of the Christian world has moved south and east. The Church is now truly a family from every nation.

Grace first

One more thing before we begin. This book will challenge you. It will ask hard questions about your heart, your motives, your home, your money and your use of power. Some chapters may make you feel that you are not fit to lead at all.

If you feel that, remember this: no leader in the Bible was fit in themselves. Moses had killed a man. David committed adultery and murder. Peter denied Jesus three times. Paul had persecuted the Church. Each of them was a sinner saved by grace and kept by grace. Paul wrote, “Our fitness comes from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5).

Spiritual leadership does not begin with what we do for God. It begins with what God has done for us in Jesus Christ. He is the good shepherd who laid down His life for the sheep (John 10:11). Every one of us was once a lost sheep that He carried home. We lead others only because He first led us, and we lead well only as we keep following Him.

Questions for reflection

  • Who are the people you lead, at home, at church, at work or in your community? Write down their names.
  • Think of a leader who helped you to know God better. What was it about them that made the difference?
  • When you hear the word “leader”, what picture comes into your mind? How does it compare with the shepherds God promised, “after my own heart” (Jeremiah 3:15)?
  • Which of the ten parts of this book do you most need right now, and why?
  • Do you feel ready to lead, or not ready? What does 2 Corinthians 3:5 say to you?

A step for this week

Write the names of the people you lead on a small piece of paper, even if there are only two or three. Keep it in your Bible. Each day this week, pray for each person by name. Ask God to give you a heart like His for them. At the end of the week, notice whether praying for them has changed the way you see them.

study_questions.question: What does it mean to be a shepherd after God’s own heart?
study_questions.answer: It means leading as God Himself leads His people: with love, truth and care, not for our own gain. God promised, “I will give you shepherds who are after my own heart, and they will shepherd you with knowledge and insight” (Jeremiah 3:15). The heart comes first, because “the LORD does not see in the way a person sees” (1 Samuel 16:7).

study_questions.question: Who is this book on spiritual leadership written for?
study_questions.answer: For anyone who leads God’s people in any way: pastors and elders, house-church leaders, deacons, Sunday school teachers, youth and women’s leaders, parents, and believers who lead at work. It was written for the whole worldwide Church, with new leaders given a shorter path through the book to start with.

study_questions.question: Do I have to be gifted or experienced to lead in the church?
study_questions.answer: No. Leadership begins with God’s grace, not our ability. Paul wrote, “Our fitness comes from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5). God calls ordinary people, shapes their hearts and gives them what they need, so a new leader can begin by depending on Him.

fields.title: What Makes Leadership Spiritual
fields.body_html:
“With you it must be different. If any of you wants to become great, that one must serve the rest of you.”

— Matthew 20:26 (OWB)

Picture two leaders in the same town. The first is the most powerful man in the district. People stand when he enters a room. Nobody argues with him. When he wants something done, it is done quickly, because people are afraid of what will happen if it is not. The second is an old woman who leads a small prayer group in her home. She has no title and no money. But when young mothers are in trouble, they go to her. When a quarrel breaks out in the church, people ask what she thinks. When she prays, people believe God hears.

Which of the two is a leader? In a sense, both are. Each one shapes the lives of other people. But only one of them leads in the way Jesus taught. This chapter asks what makes leadership spiritual. The answer is not a title, a building or a crowd. It is something deeper.

What is leadership?

At its simplest, leadership is influence. A leader is someone whose words, choices and example move other people. Some leaders have a title: pastor, elder, bishop, director, chief. Many do not. A father leads his children. An older sister leads her younger brothers. A worker who refuses to cheat leads the people who work beside her, whether she knows it or not.

This means that almost every Christian leads someone. You may not lead a church, but you may lead a family, a class, a team in a shop or a field, or a group of friends. The question is not whether you will influence other people. You already do. The question is where you are leading them, and how.

The Bible treats leading as a gift from God. When Paul lists some of the gifts God gives to His people, he writes, “the one who leads, with eagerness” (Romans 12:8). He also says, “anyone who wants to be an overseer is setting their heart on a good work” (1 Timothy 3:1). It is not wrong to want to lead. It is a good work. But because it is a good work, it must be done in God’s way.

“With you it must be different”

One day the mother of James and John came to Jesus with her two sons. She asked Him to give them the two best seats in His kingdom, one on His right and one on His left. When the other ten disciples heard about it, they were angry. Perhaps they were angry because they wanted those seats themselves.

Jesus called them all together and said: “You know that among the Gentiles, rulers act as lords over their people, and the powerful wield their authority over them. With you it must be different. If any of you wants to become great, that one must serve the rest of you. And if any of you wants to be first, that one must be your slave” (Matthew 20:25-27).

Jesus did not deny that the disciples would lead. He was training them to lead His Church. But He drew a clear line between two kinds of leadership. In the first kind, the leader is at the top and the people exist to serve the leader. In the second kind, the leader exists to serve the people. Jesus said, “With you it must be different.” That word “different” is the heart of this whole book.

Then Jesus pointed to Himself: “It is the same with the Son of Man. He did not come so that others would wait on him. He came to serve them, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:28). The greatest leader who ever lived did not demand that others serve Him. He served them, all the way to the cross.

Four marks of spiritual leadership

What, then, makes leadership spiritual? It is not enough that the leader is a Christian, or that the work happens in a church. A pastor can lead in a worldly way, and a believer in a business can lead in a spiritual way. Here are four marks.

1. Its source is God. Spiritual leadership begins with God’s call and God’s gifts, not with our own ambition. Jesus told His disciples, “You did not choose me; I chose you. I appointed you for this: to go and bear fruit, and for your fruit to remain” (John 15:16). A spiritual leader knows that they lead because God has placed them there, and that they can only lead well with the strength God gives. Peter wrote, “Whoever serves must serve in the strength God supplies” (1 Peter 4:11). We will look at God’s call in Chapter 4.

2. Its aim is God’s purpose. A worldly leader asks, “How can I get people to do what I want?” A spiritual leader asks, “How can I help people to become what God wants?” Paul described his aim like this: “We warn every person and teach every person with all wisdom, so that we may bring every person before God mature in Christ” (Colossians 1:28). The goal is not a bigger group, a famous name or a successful project. Those things may come, but the goal is people who know God, love God and become like Christ.

3. Its means are God’s ways. A spiritual leader does not use any method that works. They do not lie, threaten, flatter or manipulate, even for a good cause. They lead by serving, by telling the truth in love, by example, by prayer and by depending on the Holy Spirit. Peter told the elders of the churches, “Do not rule harshly over the people given into your charge; set an example for the flock instead” (1 Peter 5:3). The way we lead matters to God as much as where we lead.

4. It is done before God’s face. A spiritual leader knows that they will give account to God for the people they lead. The letter to the Hebrews says that leaders “stay awake watching over your souls, as people who will have to answer for them” (Hebrews 13:17). This is a sobering thought, but it is also freeing. A leader who lives before God does not need to please everyone. They need to be faithful to the One who called them. We will come back to this in Chapter 50, Giving Account.

Two kinds of leader

It may help to set the two kinds of leadership side by side. These are not rules, but pictures to help you see the difference.

  • A worldly leader is driven by ambition. A spiritual leader is moved by God’s call.
  • A worldly leader trusts their own gifts. A spiritual leader depends on God.
  • A worldly leader wants to be served. A spiritual leader wants to serve.
  • A worldly leader uses people to reach a goal. A spiritual leader sees people as the goal.
  • A worldly leader wants to be noticed. A spiritual leader wants Christ to be noticed.
  • A worldly leader makes people depend on them. A spiritual leader helps people depend on God, and trains others to lead.
  • A worldly leader answers to the crowd. A spiritual leader answers to God.

Be honest as you read this list. Most of us see something of both kinds of leader in ourselves. That is why we need the grace of God, and why spiritual leadership is a life of growing, not a place we arrive at once and for all.

An honest heart and skilful hands

The Bible often compares leaders to shepherds. This is a picture that people in many parts of the world still understand well. A shepherd lives with the sheep. They lead them to grass and water. They protect them from wild animals. They search for the ones that are lost. They carry the weak ones. It is humble, tiring and often lonely work.

King David began his life as a shepherd. One of the psalms describes how God took him from looking after sheep to look after a nation: “He cared for them as a shepherd with an honest heart and led them with skillful hands” (Psalm 78:72).

Notice the two things in that verse: an honest heart and skilful hands. Both matter. A leader with a good heart but no skill may love people but lead them badly. They may never plan, never teach clearly, never deal with problems, and the flock suffers. A leader with great skill but a dishonest heart is even more dangerous. They may build something impressive, but they will use people and in the end they will hurt them.

God wants both. That is why this book has chapters on character and prayer, and also chapters on teaching, planning, teams and handling conflict. But notice the order. The heart comes first. Skills can be learned in a few months or years. A heart after God’s heart is formed over a lifetime of walking with Him.

A voice from the Church: Gregory the Great

In the year 590 a man named Gregory was chosen to be bishop of Rome. Rome at that time was a broken city. Floods had destroyed food stores. A plague had killed the last bishop. Enemy armies threatened the city, and the people were poor and afraid. Gregory did not want the job. He had given away his family’s wealth to found monasteries, and he wanted to spend his life in prayer and study. He even wrote to the emperor asking him not to confirm the choice. But the people insisted, and Gregory accepted.

Soon afterwards, another bishop wrote to Gregory and gently rebuked him for trying to avoid the office. Gregory answered with a book, which became known as The Book of Pastoral Rule. It is one of the first books ever written on how to lead and care for God’s people, and for centuries afterwards bishops in many parts of Europe were given a copy when they began their work. It opens with these words:

“No one presumes to teach an art till he has first, with intent meditation, learnt it. What rashness is it, then, for the unskilful to assume pastoral authority, since the government of souls is the art of arts! For who can be ignorant that the sores of the thoughts of men are more occult than the sores of the bowels?”

— Gregory the Great, The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part 1

In plainer words, Gregory is saying this: nobody tries to teach a craft before they have learned it. So it is foolish for anyone to take charge of other people’s souls without preparation, because caring for souls is the greatest craft of all. The wounds of the heart are more hidden than the wounds of the body. A doctor who does not know medicine would be ashamed to treat a sick body. How much more careful should we be with a sick soul?

Gregory led the church in Rome for fourteen years. He fed the poor of the city from the church’s farms. He sent missionaries to the distant island of Britain. He wrote hundreds of letters. And he chose for himself a title that many church leaders have used since: “servant of the servants of God”. He understood what Jesus meant when He said, “With you it must be different.”

Thirteen centuries later, an American pastor named E. M. Bounds put the same truth in a different way. In his book Power Through Prayer he wrote: “Men are God’s method. The Church is looking for better methods; God is looking for better men.” Bounds used the language of his time, but what he said is true of women and men alike. God’s plan to reach the world does not rest first on programmes, buildings or money. It rests on people whose hearts belong to Him.

Why this matters

Leaders matter because people follow them. “Keep in mind those who led you, who brought you the word of God. Look closely at where their way of life led them, and follow the example of their faith” (Hebrews 13:7). People copy what leaders do far more than what they say. A church will rarely pray more than its leaders pray, or give more generously than its leaders give, or forgive more freely than its leaders forgive.

Leaders also matter because their influence lasts. A father who walks with God can shape his grandchildren. A pastor who teaches the Bible faithfully can shape a church for a generation. A leader who abuses their power can damage people’s faith for the rest of their lives. That is why God takes leadership so seriously, and why He promises to give His people “shepherds who are after my own heart” (Jeremiah 3:15).

If you are a leader of any kind, God has trusted you with something precious: other people. They do not belong to you. They belong to Him. In the next chapter we will meet the One who owns the flock, and who is the model for every leader: Jesus, the Chief Shepherd.

Questions for reflection

  • In what places do you have influence over other people? Include your home, your work and your church.
  • Read Matthew 20:20-28. Why do you think the disciples were so concerned about who would be greatest? Where do you see the same desire in yourself?
  • Which of the four marks of spiritual leadership (its source, its aim, its means, and living before God’s face) is strongest in your life? Which is weakest?
  • Look at the list of “two kinds of leader”. Which line challenges you most, and why?
  • Gregory said that caring for souls is “the art of arts”. What do you need to learn to care for people better?
  • Think of the people who follow your example. What are they learning from the way you live?

A step for this week

This week, do one task for the people you lead that no one will notice or thank you for. Clean something, carry something, or help someone quietly. Do not tell anyone. While you do it, pray, “Lord Jesus, You came not to be served but to serve. Make my leadership like Yours.” At the end of the week, ask yourself what you learned about your own heart from doing it.

study_questions.question: What makes Christian leadership different from leadership in the world?
study_questions.answer: Jesus said the rulers of the nations lord it over their people, but “With you it must be different. If any of you wants to become great, that one must serve the rest of you” (Matthew 20:26). Spiritual leadership is service, given by God and done in His strength, for the good of others.

study_questions.question: Is it wrong to want to be a leader in the church?
study_questions.answer: Not when the desire is for the work rather than the honour. Paul wrote that “anyone who wants to be an overseer is setting their heart on a good work” (1 Timothy 3:1). The test is whether we want to serve, as Jesus “came to serve them”, or to be served.

study_questions.question: Where does a spiritual leader’s strength come from?
study_questions.answer: From God, not from talent or position. Peter wrote, “Whoever serves must serve in the strength God supplies” (1 Peter 4:11). A spiritual leader is chosen and sent by Christ, who said, “You did not choose me; I chose you” (John 15:16).

fields.title: Jesus, the Chief Shepherd
fields.body_html:
“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”

— John 10:11 (OWB)

In many parts of the world, shepherds still lead their flocks in the old way. A herder walks out in the morning, and the animals follow, because they know the voice that calls them. In the evening the herder counts them as they come home. If one is missing, they go back out to look for it, even in the dark. People who have watched this every day of their lives understand at once why the Bible speaks of God as a shepherd.

In the last chapter we saw that spiritual leadership is different from the leadership of the world. In this chapter we meet the One who shows us what that difference looks like. Every Christian leader is a shepherd of some kind. But there is only one Chief Shepherd. Before we can lead others, we need to know Him, follow Him and learn from Him.

The Shepherd of Israel

Long before Jesus was born, God’s people knew Him as their shepherd. David, who had once looked after sheep himself, wrote the best-known song in the Bible: “The LORD is my shepherd; I will never be in need. He settles me down in meadows of fresh green grass; he leads me gently to water where I can rest” (Psalm 23:1-2).

The prophet Isaiah described God’s tender care in the same way: “Like a shepherd he will pasture his flock. He will gather the lambs into his arm and carry them close against his chest, and he will lead the nursing ewes with care” (Isaiah 40:11). God is strong, but He is not rough. He carries the little ones. He does not drive the weak ones too hard.

But the people of Israel also had human shepherds: their kings, priests and prophets. Many of them led badly. Through the prophet Ezekiel, God spoke strong words against them: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel who have been taking care of themselves! Should not shepherds take care of the flock? You eat the fat, you dress in the wool, and you slaughter the best animals, but you do not take care of the flock. You have not strengthened the weak or healed the sick or bandaged the injured. You have not brought back the strays or gone looking for the lost. You have ruled them with force and cruelty instead” (Ezekiel 34:2-4).

These are some of the most serious words in the Bible for anyone who leads. The bad shepherds used the flock for their own comfort. They took the best food and the best clothes. They did not care for the weak or search for the lost. And they ruled by force. We will come back to these words in Part Seven, when we look at the abuse of power.

Then God made a wonderful promise: “I myself will search for my flock and look after them” (Ezekiel 34:11). “I will search for the lost and bring back the strays. I will bandage the injured and strengthen the sick” (Ezekiel 34:16). And He said, “I will set over them one shepherd, my servant David, and he will take care of them” (Ezekiel 34:23). David had died long before. God was promising a new David, a King from David’s family who would be the true shepherd of His people.

The Good Shepherd has come

When Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11), the people who heard Him knew these promises. Jesus was saying that He was the One they had been waiting for. In John 10 He describes what a good shepherd does. Each part of His description is a lesson for every leader.

He knows His sheep by name. “He calls each of his own sheep by name and leads them out” (John 10:3). “I know those who are mine, and those who are mine know me” (John 10:14). Jesus does not see a crowd. He sees each person. He knows their name, their story and their needs.

He goes ahead of them. “Once he has brought all his own sheep out, he walks on ahead, and the sheep follow him because they know his voice” (John 10:4). A good shepherd does not drive the sheep from behind with a stick. He walks in front, and they follow. He never asks them to go where He has not gone first.

He gives them life. “I came so that they may have life, and have it in overflowing measure” (John 10:10). The thief comes to take. The shepherd comes to give.

He lays down His life for them. “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). Here is the deepest difference between Jesus and every bad shepherd. The bad shepherds of Ezekiel 34 ate the sheep. The Good Shepherd let Himself be killed to save them.

He does not run away. Jesus compared Himself with a hired man: “A hired man is no shepherd, and the sheep are not his own. So when he sees the wolf coming, he leaves the sheep and flees” (John 10:12). Then He explained why: “He flees because he works only for pay, and the sheep mean nothing to him” (John 10:13). A hired man is in it for what he gets. When danger comes, he protects himself.

He gathers other sheep too. “I have other sheep as well, which are not of this fold. I must bring them too, and they will listen to my voice, and they will become one flock with one shepherd” (John 10:16). The heart of Jesus reaches beyond Israel to people of every nation. His flock today speaks thousands of languages.

The Gospels show that this was not only teaching. It was how Jesus lived. “When Jesus came ashore, he saw a great crowd. He felt deep pity for them, for they were like sheep with no shepherd, and he began to teach them at length” (Mark 6:34). He was tired. He had gone there to rest. But when He saw the people, He felt their need, and He fed them, first with the Word and then with bread.

The Chief Shepherd and His under-shepherds

After Jesus rose from the dead and returned to heaven, He did not leave His flock without shepherds. He gave the Church leaders to care for it. But He did not hand His flock over to them. He remains its Shepherd.

The apostle Peter understood this well. Near the end of his life he wrote to the elders of the churches: “I am an elder with you, a witness of the sufferings of Christ ... Tend God’s flock among you as shepherds do” (1 Peter 5:1-2). Notice two things. First, Peter does not write as a great apostle giving orders from above. He writes as “an elder with you”, a fellow worker. Second, he calls it “God’s flock”. It does not belong to the elders. Then he looks ahead: “Then when the Chief Shepherd is revealed, you will be given a crown of glory that will never wither” (1 Peter 5:4).

So every Christian leader is an under-shepherd. Jesus is the Chief Shepherd. This simple truth changes everything about how we lead.

The flock is not ours. Paul told the elders of Ephesus to “shepherd the church of God, which he won for himself through his own blood” (Acts 20:28). The people we lead were bought with the blood of Jesus. We must never speak or act as if they were our property. A leader who says “my church” or “my people” must remember that they are only looking after someone else’s treasure. One day we will hand it back.

We follow His pattern. If Jesus is the Chief Shepherd, then His way of shepherding is the pattern for ours. We know people by name. We go ahead and set an example. We give life rather than take it. We do not run when danger comes. We reach out to those who are not yet in the flock.

We are not alone. The work of caring for people is too heavy for any human being. But the Chief Shepherd has not left the work to us. The letter to the Hebrews ends with a prayer: “May the God of peace, who led our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, up from the dead through the blood of an eternal covenant, make you ready in every good thing for doing his will” (Hebrews 13:20-21). The Shepherd who rose from the dead still leads His flock, and He gives His under-shepherds what they need.

We answer to Him. One day the Chief Shepherd will appear. He will ask how we cared for His sheep. That should make us careful. It should also give us hope, because He promises a crown that will never wither to those who served Him faithfully.

Shepherds are sheep too

There is one more truth that every leader needs to hear. Before we were shepherds, we were lost sheep. Peter wrote, “For you used to wander like lost sheep, but now you have come back to the shepherd who watches over your souls” (1 Peter 2:25).

A leader never stops being one of the sheep. We still need to hear the Shepherd’s voice. We still need to be fed, corrected, carried and forgiven. The leader who forgets this becomes proud and lonely. They begin to think they must have all the answers. They stop listening. They stop confessing their sins. They stop being fed themselves. Many leaders have fallen because they forgot that they were sheep.

A voice from the Church: Augustine of Hippo

Augustine was a bishop in the town of Hippo, on the coast of North Africa, in what is now Algeria. He lived from AD 354 to 430. He was one of the greatest thinkers the Church has ever known, but he never forgot that he was a sheep before he was a shepherd. On the anniversary of the day he became bishop, he would preach to his people about what it meant. In one of these sermons, known today as Sermon 340, he said something that leaders have quoted ever since. In plain English, his words were these:

“What I am for you frightens me. What I am with you comforts me. For you I am a bishop; with you I am a Christian. The first is the name of an office I have been given. The second is the name of grace. The first is a danger. The second is salvation.”

— Augustine, Sermon 340

Augustine felt the weight of being a leader. He knew he would answer to God for his people, and that frightened him. But he found comfort in remembering that he was also one of them, a forgiven sinner, a member of the same flock, under the same Shepherd. His office was a heavy responsibility. His salvation was a free gift. He did not confuse the two.

Every leader needs to hold both truths together. For your people, you are a leader, and you must take that seriously. With your people, you are a brother or a sister in Christ, saved by the same grace. If you forget the first, you will become careless. If you forget the second, you will become proud.

Do you love Me?

The most moving picture of the Chief Shepherd and His under-shepherds comes at the end of John’s Gospel. Peter had denied Jesus three times on the night He was arrested. After the resurrection, Jesus met Peter by the lake and asked him three times, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” Each time Peter said yes. And each time Jesus gave him a task: “Feed my lambs.” “Shepherd my sheep.” “Feed my sheep” (John 21:15-17).

Notice what Jesus did not ask. He did not ask, “Peter, are you clever enough? Are you strong enough? Will you never fail again?” He asked, “Do you love me?” Love for Jesus is the first qualification for caring for His people. A leader may have many gifts, but if they do not love the Shepherd, they will not truly love the sheep.

Notice also what Jesus said when the conversation ended. He told Peter that one day he too would die for his faith, and then He said, “Follow me” (John 21:19). Jesus had called Peter with the same words by the same lake, three years before (Mark 1:17). Leadership did not replace following. The shepherd of the sheep was still a follower of the Shepherd.

That is where all spiritual leadership begins. We love Him because He first loved us. We follow Him, and as we follow, we feed His sheep. In the next chapter we will ask how He calls people to this work.

Questions for reflection

  • Read Psalm 23 slowly. Which picture of the Shepherd means most to you today? How could it shape the way you lead others?
  • Read Ezekiel 34:1-6. Which of the failures of the bad shepherds do you think is most common among leaders today?
  • Jesus knows His sheep by name. How well do you know the people you lead? What could you do to know them better?
  • Do you ever think of the people you lead as “yours”? What changes when you remember that they are God’s flock, bought with His blood?
  • Augustine said, “For you I am a bishop; with you I am a Christian.” Which of these two truths do you find easier to forget?
  • If Jesus asked you today, “Do you love me?”, what would you say? How does your love for Him show in the way you lead?

A step for this week

Each day this week, read a few verses from John 10:1-18. Then choose one person you lead and do one thing for them that a good shepherd would do: call them by name, ask how they really are, visit them, help them, or pray with them. At the end of the week, thank the Chief Shepherd that He has never stopped caring for you.

study_questions.question: Why is Jesus called the Good Shepherd?
study_questions.answer: Because He gives His own life for His people. He said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). He fulfils God’s promise in Ezekiel: “I myself will search for my flock and look after them” (Ezekiel 34:11).

study_questions.question: What did God say to the bad shepherds of Israel?
study_questions.answer: He condemned leaders who served themselves: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel who have been taking care of themselves! Should not shepherds take care of the flock?” (Ezekiel 34:2). Then He promised to do the work Himself: “I will search for the lost and bring back the strays. I will bandage the injured and strengthen the sick” (Ezekiel 34:16).

study_questions.question: How should church leaders see themselves in relation to Jesus?
study_questions.answer: As under-shepherds who serve under the Chief Shepherd, and as sheep who need His care themselves. The flock belongs to Christ, not to the leader, and every leader must first follow Him, as the psalm says, “The LORD is my shepherd; I will never be in need” (Psalm 23:1).

fields.title: The Call of God
fields.body_html:
“Then I heard the voice of the Lord asking, ‘Whom am I to send? Who will go on our behalf?’ I answered, ‘I am ready. Send me.’”

— Isaiah 6:8 (OWB)

“How do I know if God is calling me to lead?” Few questions trouble young Christians more. Some wait for years for a voice from heaven that never comes. Others rush ahead because they enjoy being in front, and never stop to ask whether God sent them. Some feel a deep desire to serve but are told they are too young, too poor or too uneducated. Others are pushed into leadership by their church before they are ready, and are crushed by it.

The Bible does not give us a simple formula. But it does show us how God has called His servants through the centuries, and it gives us ways to recognise His call. This chapter looks at both.

Two kinds of calling

First, we need to see that the Bible speaks of calling in two ways.

The first and most important call comes to every Christian. It is the call to follow Jesus. Paul wrote to the church in Corinth, “Just look at your own calling, brothers and sisters. When God called you, not many of you were wise as people measure wisdom, not many held power, not many came from leading families” (1 Corinthians 1:26). God called them to belong to Christ, to become holy, and to serve Him with their whole lives. That call is for every believer, whether they lead or not.

The second kind of call is to a particular task or role among God’s people. God called Moses to lead Israel out of Egypt. He called Jeremiah to be a prophet. Jesus called twelve disciples to be apostles. The Holy Spirit called Barnabas and Saul to a missionary journey. Today God still calls people to be pastors, elders, deacons, evangelists, missionaries, teachers and leaders of many kinds.

The first call always comes before the second. Nobody can lead others to Christ who has not first come to Christ. And the second call never replaces the first. A pastor is a disciple first and a pastor second. If you are not sure about a call to lead, make sure first of your call to follow.

How God has called His servants

The Bible is full of stories of God calling people. No two stories are exactly the same, but some patterns appear again and again.

God takes the first step. Moses was not looking for a mission when God spoke from the burning bush. He was looking after his father-in-law’s sheep. Isaiah was worshipping in the temple when he saw the Lord. Amos said, “I am a herdsman, and I take care of sycamore-fig trees. But the LORD took me from tending the flock and told me, ‘Go and prophesy to my people Israel’” (Amos 7:14-15). Jesus told His disciples, “You did not choose me; I chose you” (John 15:16). Spiritual leadership begins with God’s initiative, not ours.

God often calls people in the middle of ordinary work. Moses was keeping sheep. Gideon was threshing wheat. Elisha was ploughing a field with twelve pairs of oxen when Elijah threw his cloak over him (1 Kings 19:19). Peter and Andrew were throwing a net into the lake (Mark 1:16). God does not usually call people who are sitting still waiting to be called. He calls people who are being faithful where they are.

God calls unlikely people. Moses said he could not speak well. Jeremiah said he was too young. Gideon said his family was the weakest in his tribe. Peter said, “Lord, leave me! I am a man full of sin” (Luke 5:8). Paul had persecuted the Church. God seems to delight in choosing people the world would overlook. “God chose what the world counts weak, to put the strong to shame ... so that no human being could ever boast in God’s presence” (1 Corinthians 1:27-29).

God’s call often meets reluctance. When God told Moses to go to Pharaoh, Moses asked, “Who am I?” (Exodus 3:11). He made one excuse after another, until at last he said, “Please, Lord, send someone else” (Exodus 4:13). Jeremiah protested, “I do not know how to speak; I am a mere youth” (Jeremiah 1:6). A sense of weakness is not a sign that God has not called you. It is often a sign that you understand how big the task is.

God’s call comes with God’s presence. God did not answer Moses by telling him how gifted he was. He said, “I will be with you” (Exodus 3:12). He told Jeremiah, “Have no fear of them, for I am with you to rescue you” (Jeremiah 1:8). The strength of the one who is called is not in themselves but in the One who calls.

God’s call often begins with a meeting with His holiness. Isaiah saw the Lord “sitting on a throne, high and towering” (Isaiah 6:1). His first response was not “Send me!” but “Woe to me! I am finished. My lips are unclean” (Isaiah 6:5). Only after God had cleansed him did he hear the call and answer, “I am ready. Send me” (Isaiah 6:8). Those who have seen how holy God is, and how gracious He is to forgive, make humble and willing servants.

Three ways to recognise a call

Most leaders today do not hear God speak from a burning bush. How, then, can we know whether God is calling us to a task? Christians through the centuries have looked for three things working together. Think of them as three strands of a rope. One strand alone is weak. Three together are strong.

1. An inward desire and burden. Paul says that “anyone who wants to be an overseer is setting their heart on a good work” (1 Timothy 3:1). God often begins His call by placing a desire in the heart: a love for His people, a burden for the lost, a longing to teach His Word. Jeremiah described it as “a fire burning in my heart, shut up inside my bones” (Jeremiah 20:9). Paul said, “It will go hard with me if I do not preach the gospel!” (1 Corinthians 9:16).

But we must test this desire. Is it a desire to serve, or a desire to be important? Is it a burden for people, or a wish for a platform? A real call from God usually grows stronger with time and prayer. It survives hardship and disappointment. Ambition tends to fade when there is no reward.

2. The confirmation of the Church. In the Bible, God’s call to lead was almost always recognised by others. When the apostles needed helpers to care for widows, they asked the church to “look among yourselves for seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and of wisdom” (Acts 6:3). When God called Barnabas and Saul, He spoke to the whole group of leaders at Antioch, and “after more fasting and prayer, they laid their hands on the two men and let them go” (Acts 13:3). Paul reminded Timothy of the gift given to him “when the elders laid their hands on you” (1 Timothy 4:14).

This protects us. Our hearts can deceive us. We may think we are called when we are only ambitious. Or we may think we are not called when we are only afraid. Wise, godly people who know us well can often see what we cannot. If you believe God is calling you to lead, share it with mature believers and leaders in your church. Ask them to pray and to tell you honestly what they see. Be willing to wait for their confirmation.

3. The gifts and character to do the work. God equips those He calls. When Paul describes the leaders of the church, he lists their character far more than their abilities. An overseer must be “clear-headed, self-controlled, respected, welcoming to guests, able to teach, not a heavy drinker, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not someone who loves money” (1 Timothy 3:2-3). Only one item on that list, “able to teach”, is a skill. The rest describe a person whose life has been changed by Christ.

So ask: has God given me the gifts this task needs? And is my life showing the fruit of the Spirit? Look for evidence in what you are already doing. If God is calling you to teach, has your teaching already helped people? If God is calling you to lead a group, do people already come to you for help? God usually calls people to more after they have been faithful with less.

Sometimes there is a fourth strand: God opens a door. A need appears that you are able to meet. A church invites you. A way is made where there was none. But open doors alone are not enough to show a call, because not every open door comes from God. Look for the open door together with the other three strands.

Two dangers

When it comes to God’s call, people tend to fall into one of two dangers.

The first danger is running toward a platform. Some people want to lead because they want to be seen, respected or paid. They push themselves forward. They are impatient with the slow process of testing. Paul warns that a leader “must not be a recent convert, or he may become proud and fall under the same judgment as the devil” (1 Timothy 3:6). Leadership given too soon can destroy a young believer. If you find that you want a title more than you want to serve, stop and examine your heart. God is not in a hurry.

The second danger is running away from a real call. Others hear God’s call clearly but refuse it. They are afraid of failure, or of criticism, or of the cost. Jonah “got up to run away to Tarshish, out of the presence of the LORD” (Jonah 1:3). Moses made so many excuses that “the LORD became angry with Moses” (Exodus 4:14). False humility can be a form of disobedience. If God has called you, and the Church has confirmed it, saying no is not humble. It is simply saying no to God.

Some of the greatest leaders in church history felt both dangers at once. Gregory of Nazianzus, a bishop in what is now Turkey in the 300s, ran away after he was made a priest against his will. Later he came back and wrote a long explanation of why the work had frightened him so much. A generation later, John Chrysostom tricked his own closest friend, Basil, into being ordained while he himself escaped. Then he wrote a book, On the Priesthood, to explain why he had done it. Both of them later became great leaders. Their fear came from a true sense of how serious the work was. But in the end they had to obey.

Going deeper: Who may be called?

Christians agree that God calls both men and women to serve Him, and gives His gifts to both. But they disagree about whether some offices in the church, such as pastor or elder, are open to women. Some churches believe the Bible keeps these offices for men. Others believe they are open to all whom God gifts and calls. We will look at the main views fairly in Chapter 26, Men and Women in the Work of God.

Christians also use the word “ordination” in different ways. In some churches it is a sacred act that sets a person apart for life. In others it is a simple recognition by the congregation. What all agree on is the pattern of Acts 13: God calls, the church prays, and the church sends. Appendix A (Chapter 53) sets out the main ways that churches recognise and appoint their leaders.

Finally, a call to ministry is not the same as a salary. Many of the world’s pastors work at another job to feed their families, as Paul himself made tents. Their calling is no less real. We will look at this in Chapter 45, Leaders at Work and in Society.

A voice from the Church: Samuel Ajayi Crowther

When Samuel Ajayi Crowther was about thirteen years old, raiders burned his town in what is now Nigeria. They tied a rope around his neck and led him away. He was sold six times. At last he was chained on a ship bound for the Americas. That same evening a British warship stopped the slave ship and set the captives free. Crowther was taken to Sierra Leone, where he learned to read, came to faith in Christ and was baptised.

He became a teacher, then a pastor, then a missionary to his own Yoruba people. He translated the Bible into Yoruba. He travelled up the great Niger River, often in danger, planting churches led by Africans. By 1864 he had been a minister for more than twenty years.

That year Henry Venn, the leader of the missionary society Crowther worked with, made a bold plan. He wanted Crowther to become a bishop, the first African bishop of the Anglican Church. Some European missionaries were against it. But the strongest objection came from Crowther himself. Many years later his son told the story. Crowther came to the committee in London in an old coat with brass buttons, and some members laughed at him. When Venn told him the plan, he refused. “I am not worthy,” he said. “No, sir, I am their servant in the field; I cannot accept it.”

Venn prayed with him and sent him away for two days to think and pray. When he came back, he refused again. At last, the family remembered, the old man appealed to him one more time. Crowther answered with the words of Eli in 1 Samuel 3:18: “It is the Lord; let Him do what seemeth Him good.” The two men knelt together to pray, and Venn wept.

We should hold this family story a little lightly, because it was told many years later. But it fits everything we know about Crowther. As a bishop he asked to be called “Right Reverend Bishop, and never as My Lord.” He knew that the eyes of many would be on him, and that “any false step taken by me will be injurious to all the Native Churches.” He did not want the office. He accepted it because he believed God and the Church were calling him to it. And he served in it for nearly thirty years, as he had said, as a servant in the field.

Crowther’s story shows all three strands of a call. He had a deep love for his people and a burden to reach them. The Church saw God’s hand on him and confirmed it. And his long, faithful service had already shown the gifts and the character the work required. His reluctance was not disobedience. It was the right kind of fear, the kind that drove him to his knees.

The One who calls is faithful

If you are wondering whether God is calling you, do not be anxious. Keep following Jesus. Be faithful where you are. Serve in small ways. Pray. Talk to wise believers. Let the Church test you. If God is calling you, He will make it clear in His time, and He will give you what you need to obey.

And if God has already called you, take heart. Whatever your weakness, the answer He gave to Moses is His answer to you: “I will be with you” (Exodus 3:12).

Questions for reflection

  • Are you sure of your first call, the call to follow Jesus? How did it come to you?
  • Which Bible story of a call (Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos, Elisha, Peter or Paul) is most like your own experience? Why?
  • Think about the three strands of a call: an inward desire, the confirmation of the Church, and the gifts and character for the work. Which of these can you see in your own life? Which is missing?
  • Are you more in danger of running toward a platform, or of running away from a real call? Be honest.
  • Who are the mature believers who could help you test your sense of calling? Have you asked them?
  • Crowther said, “I am their servant in the field.” What would it look like for you to see your role in that way?

A step for this week

Choose one mature believer or leader you trust. This week, ask to meet them. Tell them honestly what you sense God may be calling you to do, or what you are already doing. Ask them three questions: “Do you see a desire to serve in me, or a desire to be important? What gifts do you see in me? What in my character needs to grow before I can carry more?” Listen without defending yourself. Then pray about what they say.

study_questions.question: How do I know if God is calling me to lead?
study_questions.answer: The chapter gives three marks to look for together: an inner sense that God is calling, the gifts and character to do the work, and the confirmation of the church. Isaiah’s answer, “I am ready. Send me!”, came after he had met God (Isaiah 6:8).

study_questions.question: Does God only call educated or important people?
study_questions.answer: No. Paul wrote, “Just look at your own calling, brothers and sisters. When God called you, not many of you were wise as people measure wisdom” (1 Corinthians 1:26). Amos was a herdsman: “the LORD took me from tending the flock” (Amos 7:15). God chooses the weak so that no one can boast.

study_questions.question: What should I do if I feel unworthy of God’s call?
study_questions.answer: You are in good company. Moses asked, “Who am I?” (Exodus 3:11), and Peter said, “Lord, leave me! I am a man full of sin” (Luke 5:8). God’s answer is not that we are worthy, but that He goes with us and is faithful to the work He gives.

fields.title: The Towel and the Basin
fields.body_html:
“The Son of Man himself came, not so that others would serve him, but to serve them and to give his life as the ransom price for many.”

— Mark 10:45 (OWB)

In the time of Jesus, people walked everywhere on dusty roads in open sandals. When guests arrived at a house for a meal, someone washed their feet. It was not a pleasant job. It was usually done by the lowest servant in the house. No respected teacher would ever do it for his students. In many cultures today there are still tasks like this: jobs that nobody of any standing would be seen doing.

On the night before He died, Jesus did one of those jobs. He knelt on the floor with a towel and a basin of water, and washed His disciples’ feet. Then He told them to do the same for each other. In that simple act, Jesus gave His Church a picture of leadership that it has never been able to forget. This chapter looks at what it means.

What Jesus knew

John begins the story in a surprising way: “Jesus knew that the Father had put everything into his hands. He knew too that he had come out from God and was on his way back to God. He got up from the meal, put aside his outer garments, took a towel and tied it around his waist” (John 13:3-4).

Notice the order. Jesus knew who He was. He knew that all authority had been given to Him. He knew where He had come from and where He was going. And because He knew these things, He was free to take the towel.

This is the secret of servant leadership. Many leaders cannot serve because they are insecure. They are afraid that if they do humble work, people will stop respecting them. They need their title, their seat at the front and their special treatment, because without these things they do not know who they are. Jesus did not need any of these things. His identity was secure in His Father. So He could kneel on the floor without losing anything.

The same is true for us. A leader who knows that they are loved by God, accepted in Christ and sent by Him does not need to prove their importance. They are free to serve. The more secure we are in God, the lower we can bend.

The towel and the basin

John also tells us why Jesus did it: “He had loved his own who were in the world, and he loved them to the end” (John 13:1). The towel was an act of love. Jesus was not performing a ceremony. He was caring for His friends.

Peter could not accept it. “Lord, are you going to wash my feet?” he asked. “You are never going to wash my feet, not ever!” (John 13:6, 8). Peter knew this was the wrong way round. The Master should not serve the disciple. But Jesus answered, “If I do not wash you, you can have no share with me” (John 13:8). Before we can serve others, we must let Jesus serve us. We must accept His cleansing, His forgiveness and His care. Proud people find this hard. They would rather serve than be served, because being served makes them feel weak.

When He had finished, Jesus sat down and explained: “You call me ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord,’ and you are right, because that is what I am. So if I, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, then you too have a duty to wash each other’s feet. What I gave you was an example, so that you also would do as I have done for you” (John 13:13-15). And then: “Now you know these things; you are blessed if you act on them” (John 13:17).

Notice that Jesus did not stop being Teacher and Lord when He washed their feet. He said, “you are right, because that is what I am.” Servant leadership does not mean that the leader stops leading. It means that the leader leads by serving.

A quarrel at the table

Luke tells us something sad about that same evening. At the very meal where Jesus washed their feet, “A quarrel also broke out among them over which of them was to be thought the greatest” (Luke 22:24). Even after three years with Jesus, the disciples were still competing for position.

Jesus answered them patiently: “The kings of the Gentiles act as lords over their people, and those who hold power over them are given the title ‘Benefactor’. With you it must not be this way. Instead, the greatest among you must become like the youngest, and the one in charge like the one who waits on others. Think about it: who is greater, the guest who lies at the table, or the one who serves the meal? Surely the one at the table. Yet here I am among you as the one who serves” (Luke 22:25-27).

Notice the word “Benefactor”. Rulers in those days liked to be called benefactors, people who do good to others. They used power over people and then expected people to thank them for it. Leaders can do the same today. They control people, and then remind them how much they have done for them. Jesus said, “With you it must not be this way.”

The mind of Christ

Paul gives us the deepest picture of servant leadership in his letter to the Philippians. He tells the believers, “Do not act out of rivalry or out of a craving for empty glory. Instead, be humble, and regard each other as standing above yourselves” (Philippians 2:3). Then he points to Jesus: “Among yourselves, think in the way that Christ Jesus also thought, who, being in the form of God, did not treat being equal with God as something to exploit for himself. Rather, he emptied himself, taking on the form of a servant and coming to share the likeness of human beings. And when he was found in outward form as a human being, he humbled himself, becoming obedient all the way to death, death on a cross” (Philippians 2:5-8).

The towel in the upper room was a small picture of something far greater. The Son of God came down from heaven, became a human being, lived as a servant and died on a cross. That is the shape of His whole life: down, and down, and down again, for our sake.

And then Paul writes, “That is why God has exalted him far above all” (Philippians 2:9). The way up in God’s kingdom is the way down. Jesus taught this again and again: “Those who lift themselves up will be brought low, and those who make themselves low will be lifted up” (Matthew 23:12). Peter learned the lesson and passed it on: “Humble yourselves, then, under God’s powerful hand, so that he may raise you up when the time is right” (1 Peter 5:6). A servant leader does not try to lift themselves up. They leave that to God.

What servant leadership is not

The phrase “servant leadership” is used so often today that it can lose its meaning. So it helps to say what it is not.

It is not weakness. Jesus washed feet, but He also drove the money-changers out of the temple. He was gentle with the broken, but He spoke strongly to proud religious leaders. A servant leader can be firm, can say hard things and can make difficult decisions. The question is whose good they are seeking.

It is not doing whatever people want. Jesus served people’s needs, not always their wishes. When the crowds wanted to make Him king by force, “he went back up into the hills, alone” (John 6:15). When the people of one town wanted Him to stay, He said, “Let us move on to the market towns nearby, so that I can proclaim the message there as well” (Mark 1:38). A servant leader listens to people, but serves God’s purpose for them, even when they do not understand it yet.

It is not refusing to lead. Some people use humility as an excuse to avoid responsibility. They never make decisions, never correct anyone and never give direction. That is not serving. A flock without a shepherd scatters. Sometimes the most loving thing a leader can do is to lead clearly.

It is not doing everything yourself. A servant leader does not have to do every task in the church. Jesus trained others and sent them out. Moses learned to share the work with others. Serving the people well often means training and trusting others to serve with you. We will look at this in Part Five.

What servant leadership is

Positively, servant leadership means at least these things.

  • Using power for others. Every leader has some power, whether it is the power to decide, to speak, to include or to exclude. A servant leader asks, “How can I use this power for the good of the people I lead?”
  • Seeing needs. Jesus noticed the dirty feet that everyone else ignored. A servant leader notices the person who is lonely, the family that is hungry and the young believer who is struggling.
  • Being willing to do humble tasks. No job is beneath a servant leader. They will sweep the floor, set out the chairs, visit the sick at night and sit with the dying. They do not do this to be seen, but because it needs doing.
  • Making others great. A worldly leader wants to be the most important person in the room. A servant leader wants others to grow, to use their gifts and even to do better than them.
  • Leading by example. Jesus said, “What I gave you was an example” (John 13:15). A servant leader never asks others to do what they will not do themselves.
  • Giving themselves, not only their work. Paul told the believers in Thessalonica, “we gladly gave you not only the gospel of God but ourselves too, for you had become dear to us” (1 Thessalonians 2:8).

Titles and honour

In many cultures, leaders are given great honour. People stand when they enter. They are given the best seat and the best food. They are called by grand titles. Is this wrong?

The Bible does teach that leaders should be respected. Paul told the believers in Thessalonica to “recognize those who work hard among you, who lead you in the Lord” and to “think of them with the highest respect and love because of the work they do” (1 Thessalonians 5:12-13). It is good for a church to honour its faithful leaders, and it is good for a leader to receive that honour graciously.

But there is a great difference between receiving honour and demanding it. Jesus warned His disciples against loving titles: “But as for you, do not let anyone call you ‘Rabbi.’ There is one who is your teacher, and all of you are brothers and sisters together” (Matthew 23:8). The danger is not the title itself. The danger is a heart that needs it. A good test is this: how do you feel when you are not given the honour you expect? If you feel angry or hurt, your heart may be resting on your position rather than on Christ.

We have already met two leaders who understood this. Gregory, the bishop of Rome, called himself “servant of the servants of God” (Chapter 2). Samuel Ajayi Crowther asked to be called “Right Reverend Bishop, and never as My Lord” (Chapter 4). Both held high office. Both refused to let it go to their heads.

A voice from the Church: Hudson Taylor and William Burns

In 1855 a young English missionary named Hudson Taylor was working in China. He was only twenty-three. Foreign missionaries at that time wore European clothes, lived in foreign areas of the coastal cities and travelled with crowds following them, staring at their strange appearance. Taylor found that the crowds made it hard to preach and hard to be welcomed into people’s homes.

So he made a decision that shocked many of his fellow Europeans. He put on Chinese clothes and lived as much as possible in the way the people around him lived. He did not do it to look clever. He did it to remove a barrier between himself and the people he had come to serve. In his short book A Retrospect, he wrote simply: “Much benefit was found to result from this change of costume; and I, and most of those associated with me, have continued to use native dress.” Years later, the China Inland Mission which he founded asked all its missionaries to do the same.

Soon afterwards Taylor travelled for several months with an older missionary named William Burns, a Scottish preacher who had already seen revival in Scotland and Canada. Burns was older, more famous and far more experienced. But he watched what happened as they travelled together. Taylor later remembered it like this:

“Mr. Burns at that time was wearing English dress; but saw that while I was the younger and in every way less experienced, I had the quiet hearers, while he was followed by the rude boys, and by the curious but careless; that I was invited to the homes of the people, while he received an apology that the crowd that would follow precluded his being invited. After some weeks of observation he also adopted the native dress.”

— Hudson Taylor, A Retrospect

In plain words: the older, famous preacher noticed that the young man was being welcomed into homes while he was not. So he humbled himself and followed the younger man’s example. In a letter home Burns wrote that he had concluded “it was my duty to follow his example.”

Both men show us something about servant leadership. Taylor gave up the comfort and status of looking like a European in order to serve the Chinese people. Burns was willing to learn from someone younger and less experienced. Neither of them cared about looking important. They cared about the people they had come to reach. This is what Paul meant when he wrote, “No one has any claim on me, yet I have become everyone’s slave, so as to win over a greater number” (1 Corinthians 9:19).

Servant leadership is not always as visible as a change of clothes. Josephine Bakhita, a former slave from Sudan who became a nun in Italy, spent many years as a cook and as the doorkeeper of her convent. She greeted every visitor with kindness. When she died in 1947, crowds came to mourn her, because so many people remembered how she had made them welcome. Most servant leadership looks like that: small, faithful acts of love, repeated for years, until a whole community has been shaped by them.

Take up the towel

The world measures leaders by how many people serve them. Jesus measures leaders by how many people they serve. At the end of the story Jesus said, “Now you know these things; you are blessed if you act on them” (John 13:17). The blessing does not come from knowing about servant leadership. It comes from doing it.

Where is your towel? Where is your basin? Who are the people around you whose “feet” need washing: the tasks nobody wants, the needs nobody sees, the people nobody visits? That is where servant leadership begins.

Questions for reflection

  • Jesus washed the disciples’ feet because He “knew that the Father had put everything into his hands”. How does knowing who you are in Christ set you free to serve?
  • Peter did not want Jesus to wash his feet. Do you find it hard to let others serve you? Why?
  • Read Luke 22:24-27. Where do you see competition for position in your church or group? Where do you see it in your own heart?
  • Which of the four things that servant leadership is not (weakness, doing what people want, refusing to lead, doing everything yourself) is the biggest danger for you?
  • How do you feel when you are not given the honour or respect you expect? What does that reveal?
  • William Burns learned from a younger, less experienced man. Who could you learn from, even if they are younger or less important than you?

A step for this week

Find a humble task in your church, home or workplace that is usually left to others, or that nobody does at all. This week, do it yourself, quietly, at least twice. If you have a title or a special seat, choose one occasion to give it up without explanation. Then read John 13:1-17 again and ask the Lord to show you what He wants you to learn.

study_questions.question: What did Jesus teach by washing His disciples’ feet?
study_questions.answer: That true leaders serve. Knowing “that the Father had put everything into his hands”, Jesus took a towel and washed their feet (John 13:3-4). He said, “You call me ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord,’ and you are right” and told them to do as He had done (John 13:13-15).

study_questions.question: What is servant leadership?
study_questions.answer: It is leading the way Jesus did: “The Son of Man himself came, not so that others would serve him, but to serve them and to give his life” (Mark 10:45). It is not weakness or doing whatever people want; it is using authority for the good of others, even when that costs us.

study_questions.question: Why should leaders be careful with titles and honour?
study_questions.answer: Because titles can feed pride and set leaders above the people they serve. Jesus warned His disciples against seeking honour and status, and showed them a better way with the towel and the basin, adding, “Now you know these things; you are blessed if you act on them” (John 13:17).

fields.title: Authority Under Authority
fields.body_html:
“I myself am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. I tell one, ‘Go,’ and he goes, and another, ‘Come,’ and he comes.”

— Matthew 8:9 (OWB)

A Roman army officer once came to Jesus for help. His servant was sick and close to death. Jesus offered to come to his house, but the officer said there was no need: “Lord, I am not good enough for you to come into my house. Only give the command, and my servant will be well” (Matthew 8:8). Then he explained why he was so sure: “I myself am a man under authority, with soldiers under me” (Matthew 8:9).

Jesus was amazed. He said that He had not found faith like this anywhere in Israel. The officer, a foreigner and a soldier, had understood something that many religious people had missed. He knew that his own authority over his soldiers came from being under the authority of Rome. And he saw that Jesus also had authority, a far greater authority, which came from God.

This chapter is about authority. Every leader has some, and every leader is tempted to misuse it. The great lesson of the soldier’s faith is this: only those who are under authority can rightly hold authority.

All authority belongs to Christ

After His resurrection, Jesus met His disciples on a mountain in Galilee and said, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been placed in my hands” (Matthew 28:18). That is the starting point for everything the Bible teaches about leadership. All authority belongs to Jesus. Every other authority, in the family, in the church, in the nation, is borrowed from Him.
