Even the most powerful people on earth hold only borrowed authority. When Pilate, the Roman governor, told Jesus that he had power to free Him or to crucify Him, Jesus answered, “You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given to you from above” (John 19:11). Pilate thought his authority was his own. It was not. It had been given to him, and he would answer for how he used it.

If that was true of a Roman governor, how much more is it true of a pastor, an elder or a group leader? Whatever authority you have, you did not create it. It was given to you. It belongs to Christ, and you hold it for Him.

Jesus lived under authority

It is striking that Jesus Himself, who holds all authority, lived His earthly life under the authority of His Father. He said, “the Son cannot do anything on his own; he does only what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19). He said, “The teaching I give is not my own. It comes from the one who sent me” (John 7:16). In the garden of Gethsemane He prayed, “Yet let your will be done, not mine” (Luke 22:42).

The crowds noticed that Jesus spoke differently from their religious teachers: “He taught them like someone with authority of his own, not like their scribes” (Matthew 7:29). The scribes quoted other teachers to support their opinions. Jesus spoke as One who knew the truth from God. Yet His authority came precisely from His perfect obedience to the Father. He was the most free and the most obedient person who has ever lived.

This is the pattern for every spiritual leader. Our authority grows as our obedience grows. A leader who is not obeying God has no real spiritual authority, whatever their title says.

What spiritual authority is for

Paul was an apostle with real authority over the churches he planted. But he was careful to say what it was for. He spoke of “our authority, which the Lord gave us to build you up and not to tear you down” (2 Corinthians 10:8). He repeated it later in the same letter: he did not want to deal with them sharply, “using the authority the Lord gave me, which is for building up and not for tearing down” (2 Corinthians 13:10).

This gives us a simple test for any use of authority. Is it building people up, or tearing them down? Is it helping them grow in Christ, or making them small, afraid and dependent? Authority that tears people down for the leader’s benefit is not spiritual authority, however spiritual the leader’s words may sound.

Spiritual authority does not come from force. It is not the power to punish, threaten or control. It comes from at least four things:

  • The Word of God. A leader who faithfully teaches the Bible carries the authority of the Bible. When they speak what God has said, people should listen, not because of who the leader is, but because of who God is.
  • A godly life. People trust leaders whose lives match their words. Peter told elders to “set an example for the flock” (1 Peter 5:3). An example has more authority than a command.
  • The Holy Spirit. Spiritual authority is not something we can manufacture. It comes when the Spirit works through a leader to change people’s lives.
  • The recognition of the Church. As we saw in Chapter 4, The Call of God, God usually confirms leaders through His people. A leader whom the church has tested and appointed carries the authority of that appointment.

Four authorities over every leader

If only those under authority can rightly hold it, we need to ask: under what authority does a Christian leader stand? The Bible points to at least four.

1. Under Christ. He is the Head of the Church and the Chief Shepherd. Every decision a leader makes should be made as His servant. A leader should regularly ask, “Lord, is this what You want?”

2. Under Scripture. No leader is above the Bible. Even in the Old Testament, the king of Israel was told to write out his own copy of God’s law and to “read from it all his life ... so that he does not think himself above his fellow Israelites” (Deuteronomy 17:19-20). Paul said that if even he, or an angel from heaven, preached a different gospel, “let that one be under God’s curse” (Galatians 1:8). A leader may never add to God’s Word, take away from it or claim a private revelation that overrules it. “All Scripture is breathed out by God and is useful for teaching, for rebuking, for correcting and for training in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16). That includes rebuking and correcting the leader.

3. Under the Church and fellow leaders. No leader in the New Testament was a law to themselves. Paul, the great apostle, went to Jerusalem to lay his gospel before the other leaders, because, he said, “I did not want to find that I was running, or had run, for nothing” (Galatians 2:2). When a serious question arose about the gospel, “The apostles and the elders came together to consider this matter” (Acts 15:6). Even Peter, the leading apostle, was corrected: Paul wrote, “when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him face to face, because he was clearly in the wrong” (Galatians 2:11). Every leader needs people who can question them, correct them and, if necessary, remove them.

4. Under the authorities of the land. Paul wrote, “Everyone must submit to the authorities who govern, because no authority exists except by God’s doing” (Romans 13:1). Christian leaders should obey the law, pay their taxes and pray for those in government. But this authority has a limit. When the rulers of Jerusalem ordered the apostles to stop preaching about Jesus, “Peter and the other apostles replied, ‘It is God we must obey rather than people’” (Acts 5:29). When human authority commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, we must obey God and accept the cost. We will look at this more in Chapter 40, Persecution and the Cost.

Here is a question every leader should ask: Who can say no to me? If the honest answer is “nobody”, you are in great danger. A leader who answers to nobody will soon begin to do wrong, and nobody will stop them.

Two opposite dangers

The Bible warns against two opposite sins: rebellion against godly authority, and abuse of authority by those who hold it.

Rebellion. In the wilderness, a man named Korah gathered a group against Moses and Aaron. “You claim too much!” they said. “Every member of the congregation is holy, all of them, and the LORD is among them. What right have you to raise yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?” (Numbers 16:3). Their words sounded spiritual, but their hearts were full of envy. Earlier, Moses’ own brother and sister, Miriam and Aaron, had spoken against him in the same way. The Bible adds a striking comment: “Now Moses was exceedingly humble, more so than any other human being on earth” (Numbers 12:3). Moses did not defend himself. God defended him.

David showed a different spirit. King Saul was trying to kill him, and twice David had the chance to kill Saul first. Twice he refused: “May the LORD keep me from ever raising my hand against the LORD’s anointed!” (1 Samuel 26:11). David left it to God to deal with Saul.

The letter to the Hebrews tells believers, “Follow your leaders and yield to them. They stay awake watching over your souls, as people who will have to answer for them. Make it possible for them to do this with joy instead of sighing” (Hebrews 13:17). A church that is always complaining about its leaders, always pulling them down and always looking for someone better, makes their work a burden. Many faithful pastors have been broken by it.

Abuse of authority. But the opposite danger is just as real. The apostle John wrote about a church leader named Diotrephes, “who loves to be first among them” (3 John 9). Diotrephes refused to welcome John’s messengers, spread wicked talk about the apostle, “and that is not enough for him: he will not receive the brothers and sisters himself, he hinders those who want to receive them, and he drives them out of the church” (3 John 10). He treated the church as his own kingdom. Nobody could question him, and anyone who disagreed was thrown out.

Sadly, there are leaders like Diotrephes in every generation and every land. Respect for leaders must never become a cover for sin. David refused to kill Saul, but he did not pretend that Saul was right, and he did not stay to be killed. The Bible never asks believers to obey a leader who commands them to sin, or to keep silent about abuse. We will look at this hard subject in Chapter 35, Power, Abuse and Protecting the Vulnerable.

Going deeper: How churches are ordered

Christians have long disagreed about how authority should be arranged in the church. Some churches are led by bishops, who oversee many congregations. Some are led by groups of elders, with assemblies above them. Some are led by each local congregation together. Each of these traditions finds support in the Bible and in church history, and godly people have served in all of them.

Early leaders such as Ignatius of Antioch, writing around AD 110, placed great weight on the bishop as the centre of unity in each city. Others read the New Testament as using “elder” and “overseer” for the same office. You will find these views set out fairly in Appendix A (Chapter 53). For this chapter, the important thing is what all traditions agree on: every leader is under Christ and under His Word, and no leader should be beyond correction.

A voice from the Church: Clement and Ignatius

Around AD 96, the church in Corinth, in Greece, had a crisis. A small group of members had pushed out the elders who had led the church faithfully for years. The church in Rome heard about it and sent a long letter, which we know today as 1 Clement. It is one of the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament.

The letter is not angry. It is full of Scripture, and it calls the Corinthians to humility, again and again. It points them to Christ, to Abraham, to Moses and to David as examples of humble people. Then it speaks plainly about what had happened:

“It is disgraceful, beloved, yea, highly disgraceful, and unworthy of your Christian profession, that such a thing should be heard of as that the most stedfast and ancient Church of the Corinthians should, on account of one or two persons, engage in sedition against its presbyters.”

— 1 Clement

In plain words: it is shameful that a strong and old church should rebel against its elders because of one or two people. The letter explains that faithful elders who “have blamelessly served the flock of Christ in a humble, peaceable, and disinterested spirit” should not be thrown out. But it does not simply take the side of power. It calls the troublemakers to repent, and it urges everyone, leaders included, to love and humility. It even suggests that anyone who is causing division should be willing to leave, so that the flock of Christ can be at peace.

About fifteen years later, another leader wrote a short letter to a younger one. Ignatius, the bishop of Antioch in Syria, was being taken to Rome under guard to be killed for his faith. On the way he wrote to Polycarp, the young bishop of Smyrna, in what is now Turkey. His advice shows what kind of authority a Christian leader should hold:

“Have a care for union, than which there is nothing better. Bear all men, as the Lord also beareth thee. Suffer all men in love, as also thou doest. Give thyself to unceasing prayers. Ask for larger wisdom than thou hast. ... Stand thou firm, as an anvil when it is smitten. ... Let not widows be neglected. After the Lord be thou their protector. ... Seek out all men by name. Despise not slaves, whether men or women.”

— Ignatius of Antioch, Letter to Polycarp

In plain words: guard the unity of the church, for nothing is better. Be patient with everyone, as the Lord is patient with you. Pray without stopping. Ask God for more wisdom than you have. Stand firm, like an iron anvil that is struck again and again but does not break. Protect the widows. Know every person by name. Do not look down on slaves.

Here is spiritual authority as the early Church understood it. It is firm, like an anvil, when false teaching attacks. But it is gentle, patient and humble. It protects the weakest people in the church. It knows people by name. Polycarp took this advice to heart. He led the church in Smyrna for many years, and, as we will see later in this book, he died as a martyr, faithful to the end.

Under authority, for others

The Roman officer said, “I myself am a man under authority.” That is where every Christian leader must stand. We are under Christ, under His Word, under His Church and, as far as conscience allows, under the authorities of the land. From that place, we can use the authority given to us as Jesus did: to build up and not to tear down, to protect and not to exploit, to serve and not to be served.

This brings Part One to a close. We have seen what makes leadership spiritual, we have met the Chief Shepherd, we have thought about God’s call, we have taken up the towel, and we have learned to stand under authority. In Part Two we turn from the call to the heart. The first quality of a leader’s heart is the one that makes all the others possible: humility.

Questions for reflection

  • Read Matthew 8:5-13. What did the Roman officer understand about authority that others had missed?
  • Jesus said, “the Son cannot do anything on his own.” How does His obedience to the Father shape the way you think about your own authority?
  • Think about the last time you used your authority as a leader. Did it build people up or tear them down?
  • Of the four authorities over every leader (Christ, Scripture, the Church and the authorities of the land), which do you find hardest to submit to? Why?
  • Who can say no to you? If nobody can, what will you do about it?
  • Are you more tempted to rebel against those who lead you, or to rule over those you lead? What would repentance look like?
  • Read again Ignatius’s advice to Polycarp. Which line do you most need to hear this week?

A step for this week

Write down the names of the people who have authority over you as a leader: in your church, your family and your work. If there is nobody on your list who can correct you, ask a mature believer this week to become someone you meet with regularly and who has permission to ask you hard questions. If there is someone on your list you have been resisting or criticising, pray for them by name each day this week, and look for one way to help them do their work “with joy instead of sighing” (Hebrews 13:17).

study_questions.question: What does it mean that a leader is under authority?
study_questions.answer: Every leader serves under Christ, who said, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been placed in my hands” (Matthew 28:18). Like the centurion who said, “I myself am a man under authority” (Matthew 8:9), a leader’s right to lead comes from being under God, His Word and the wider Church.

study_questions.question: How did Jesus show what it means to live under authority?
study_questions.answer: He did only what the Father gave Him: “the Son cannot do anything on his own; he does only what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19). His teaching was “not my own” (John 7:16), and in Gethsemane He prayed, “Yet let your will be done, not mine” (Luke 22:42).

study_questions.question: What is spiritual authority for?
study_questions.answer: It is given to build people up and serve them, never to control or use them. The chapter warns against two opposite dangers: rebellion against godly leaders, and leaders who abuse the authority they hold.

fields.title: Humility
fields.body_html:
“Humble yourselves, then, under God’s powerful hand, so that he may raise you up when the time is right.”

— 1 Peter 5:6 (OWB)

A young pastor once preached his first sermon in a large church. He climbed into the pulpit with his head held high, sure that he would impress everyone. But he lost his place, forgot his points and came down red-faced and ashamed. An old woman who had been listening said to him kindly afterwards, “If you had gone up the way you came down, you would have come down the way you went up.”

We begin Part Two, The Leader’s Heart, with humility, because it is the soil in which every other good quality grows. Without it, gifts become dangerous, success becomes a trap, and authority becomes abuse. With it, even a weak and ordinary leader can be greatly used by God.

What humility is not

Many people misunderstand humility. They think it means speaking badly of yourself, refusing to accept praise, or pretending you have no gifts. But that is often pride in disguise. A person who says “I am useless” and then waits for others to disagree is still thinking about themselves.

Humility is not thinking poorly of yourself. Paul says, “do not rate yourself higher than you should. Let your thinking be sober and sensible instead” (Romans 12:3). Sober thinking means seeing yourself as you really are: not higher than the truth, and not lower than the truth either. If God has given you a gift for teaching, it is not humble to deny it. It is humble to say, “This is a gift, and it is not mine.”

Paul asked the proud Christians in Corinth three sharp questions: “Who, after all, sets you above anyone else? What do you have that was not given to you? And if it was given to you, why do you take pride in it as though it were not a gift?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). Everything we have, our life, our breath, our gifts, our salvation, has been given to us. Humility begins when we see that clearly.

What humility is

Humility is living in the truth about God and about ourselves. It has two sides.

Before God, humility is dependence. We are creatures and He is the Creator. We are sinners and He is the Saviour. We can do nothing good without Him. The humble person does not try to live as if they were independent of God. They pray because they know they need Him. They trust because they know they cannot control everything. Micah summed up what God asks of us: “to do justice, to love loyalty, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8).

Before people, humility is service. Paul wrote, “Do not act out of rivalry or out of a craving for empty glory. Instead, be humble, and regard each other as standing above yourselves. Each of you should care not just about your own concerns but about the concerns of others as well” (Philippians 2:3-4). A humble person is not always thinking about how they look, whether they are respected, or what they will gain. They are free to think about others.

Someone has put it simply: humility is not thinking less of yourself, but thinking of yourself less. The humble leader is not constantly measuring themselves against others. Their eyes are on Christ and on the people He has given them to serve.

Why humility matters so much for leaders

The Bible says the same thing again and again: “God stands against the arrogant, but he gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5:5). James quotes the same words (James 4:6), and they first appear in Proverbs (Proverbs 3:34). When something is said three times in Scripture, we should pay attention.

Think about what this means. A proud leader has God standing against them. However gifted they are, however hard they work, they are working against the grain of the universe. A humble leader has God giving them grace. However weak they are, they have the help of the Almighty. No wonder humility is the first quality of a leader’s heart.

Humility matters for leaders in at least four more ways.

  • Humble leaders can learn. A proud leader thinks they already know. A humble leader keeps asking questions, reading, listening and growing. “When pride arrives, disgrace follows close behind, but the humble have wisdom” (Proverbs 11:2).
  • Humble leaders can be corrected. When someone points out their mistake, they do not defend themselves first. They ask, “Is this true?” This protects them from many falls.
  • Humble leaders make room for others. They are not threatened when someone else has a gift. They are glad when others grow and do well.
  • Humble leaders can be trusted with success. God can bless the work of a humble leader without destroying them, because they will give Him the glory.

When leaders forget

The Bible gives us sad stories of leaders who began humbly and ended proudly. King Uzziah of Judah was a good king for many years. God helped him, and his fame spread far. “But when he had become strong, his heart grew proud, to his own ruin” (2 Chronicles 26:16). He went into the temple to burn incense, a task God had given only to the priests, and he was struck with a skin disease for the rest of his life.

King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon walked on the roof of his palace and said, “Is this not the great Babylon that I have built as a royal capital by my own mighty power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Daniel 4:30). Before he had finished speaking, God humbled him. He lost his mind and lived like an animal until he learned “that the Most High rules over human kingdoms” (Daniel 4:32). When his reason returned, he praised God and said, “he can bring down those who live in pride” (Daniel 4:37).

Notice when the danger came. Uzziah grew proud “when he had become strong”. Nebuchadnezzar grew proud when he looked at all he had built. Pride is most dangerous not when we are failing, but when we are succeeding. The leader whose church is growing, whose name is becoming known and whose plans are working needs to watch their heart most carefully. We will come back to this in Chapter 32, Pride and the Love of Praise.

The humility of Jesus

The greatest picture of humility is not a rule but a Person. Jesus said, “Put my yoke on your necks and learn from me, because I am gentle and my heart is humble. Then you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29). It is remarkable that, of all the things Jesus could have said about His heart, this is what He chose: gentle and humble.

We saw in Chapter 5, The Towel and the Basin, how Jesus “emptied himself, taking on the form of a servant” and “humbled himself, becoming obedient all the way to death, death on a cross” (Philippians 2:7-8). The Son of God, who had every right to be served, chose to serve. If humility was right for Him, it is right for us.

Jesus also offers rest. Pride is exhausting. The proud leader must always defend their reputation, compete with others and prove their worth. The humble leader has nothing to prove. They rest in what God thinks of them. That is why Jesus links a humble heart with “rest for your souls”.

The friend of the bridegroom

John the Baptist was one of the most popular preachers of his time. Crowds came from the whole country to hear him. Then Jesus began to preach, and the crowds began to leave John and follow Jesus. John’s disciples were upset. They came to him and complained that everyone was going to Jesus instead.

John answered, “No one can receive anything at all unless it has been given them from heaven” (John 3:27). Then he described himself as the friend of a bridegroom at a wedding. The friend does not want the bride for himself. He is glad when he hears the bridegroom’s voice. “This, then, is my joy, and it has been made complete. He must grow greater, but I must grow less” (John 3:29-30).

That last sentence is one of the best prayers a leader can pray: “He must grow greater, but I must grow less.” It does not mean that we become nothing. It means that our life and work point away from ourselves to Christ. A leader whose people know them better than they know Jesus has missed the point of leadership.

How to grow in humility

We cannot make ourselves humble by trying hard to feel humble. But we can put ourselves where God humbles us. Here are some practical ways.

  • Stay close to the cross. Paul said, “far be it from me to boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6:14). When we remember that Jesus had to die for our sins, it is hard to stay proud.
  • Remember where you came from. Paul never forgot that he had persecuted the Church: “Among the apostles I am the least ... It is God’s grace that has made me what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:9-10).
  • Confess your sins to others. Proud people hide their faults. Humble people bring them into the light. This was one of the great marks of the East African Revival, which we will meet later in this book.
  • Do hidden good. Jesus said, “when you give, keep it so quiet that your left hand does not know what your right hand is doing” (Matthew 6:3). Serve without being seen, and let God be your only audience.
  • Welcome correction. When someone criticises you, before you answer, ask God whether there is truth in it.
  • Take the lower place. Jesus told His followers to choose the lowest seat at a feast, not the highest (Luke 14:10). Look for chances to put others first.
  • Accept weakness. Paul begged God to take away his “thorn in the flesh”, but God answered, “My grace is enough for you, for power comes to its fullness in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Sometimes God keeps us weak so that we will stay humble and depend on Him.

A voice from the Church: Andrew Murray and William Carey

Andrew Murray was a pastor in South Africa who lived from 1828 to 1917. He was born in Graaff-Reinet, where his father was a minister, and he served churches in the Cape for most of his long life. He helped lead a revival, founded schools and wrote more than two hundred books and booklets, many of which are on Ochorus. One of the best known is a short book called Humility. In it he wrote:

“Humility, the place of entire dependence on God, is, from the very nature of things, the first duty and the highest virtue of the creature, and the root of every virtue. And so pride, or the loss of this humility, is the root of every sin and evil.”

— Andrew Murray, Humility, Chapter 1

In plain words: humility means depending on God completely. It is the first thing a creature owes to its Creator, and every other good quality grows from it, like branches from a root. Pride, which means losing this humility, is the root from which every sin grows. Murray goes on to say that the devil fell through pride, and that our first parents fell when they wanted to be like God. If pride is the root of all sin, then humility is not one good quality among many. It is the ground of all of them.

Murray’s book is not only about humility before God. He says that our humility before God is proved by how we treat other people, especially the people who annoy us, disappoint us or are less gifted than we are.

Another leader shows us what this looks like at the end of a life. William Carey was an English shoemaker who became a missionary to India in 1793. He translated the Bible, or parts of it, into more than thirty languages. He helped to found a college and worked to end the burning of widows. He is often called “the father of modern missions”. Yet when he was dying in 1834, he is remembered to have said to a young Scottish missionary, Alexander Duff, who had been praising his work: “You have been speaking about Dr Carey, Dr Carey. When I am gone, say nothing about Dr Carey. Speak about Dr Carey’s Saviour.”

Carey asked that his gravestone should carry only his name, his dates and two lines from a hymn by Isaac Watts: “A wretched, poor, and helpless worm, on Thy kind arms I fall.” The man who had done so much wanted to be remembered only as a sinner held by the arms of Christ. That is humility. It is not pretending you have done nothing. It is knowing that everything you have done was done by grace.

The way up is down

Peter wrote, “Humble yourselves, then, under God’s powerful hand, so that he may raise you up when the time is right” (1 Peter 5:6). Notice who does the lifting. We humble ourselves. God raises us up. Our task is to go low. His task is to decide when, and whether, to lift us.

This frees us from the exhausting work of self-promotion. We do not need to push ourselves forward, compare ourselves with others or fight for position. We can do the work in front of us faithfully and leave our reputation in God’s hands. As we will see in the next chapter, a leader like that can also be trusted to be the same person in secret as in public.

Questions for reflection

  • Before reading this chapter, what did you think humility was? Has your picture changed?
  • Read 1 Corinthians 4:7. List three gifts you have. How does it change your attitude to remember that each one was given to you?
  • “God stands against the arrogant, but he gives grace to the humble.” Where in your life might you be working against God because of pride?
  • Uzziah grew proud “when he had become strong”. What successes in your life or ministry could become a danger to your heart?
  • Can you pray John the Baptist’s prayer, “He must grow greater, but I must grow less”, and mean it? What makes it hard?
  • Which of the practical ways to grow in humility do you most need to begin this week?

A step for this week

Each day this week, look for one chance to take “the lower place”: let someone else speak first, give credit to someone else, accept a correction without defending yourself, or serve someone who cannot repay you. Each evening, thank God for one thing He has given you, and say aloud, “This was a gift, and it is not mine.” At the end of the week, write down what you noticed about your own heart.

study_questions.question: What is humility in a Christian leader?
study_questions.answer: Humility is not thinking badly of yourself but seeing yourself truly before God. Paul wrote, “do not rate yourself higher than you should. Let your thinking be sober and sensible instead” (Romans 12:3). Everything we have is a gift: “What do you have that was not given to you?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

study_questions.question: Why does humility matter so much for leaders?
study_questions.answer: Because “God stands against the arrogant, but he gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5:5). A proud leader falls and harms others: “When pride arrives, disgrace follows close behind, but the humble have wisdom” (Proverbs 11:2).

study_questions.question: How can a leader grow in humility?
study_questions.answer: By looking to Jesus, who humbled Himself, and by choosing to put others first: “be humble, and regard each other as standing above yourselves” (Philippians 2:3). The promise is that God lifts up the humble: “Humble yourselves, then, under God’s powerful hand, so that he may raise you up when the time is right” (1 Peter 5:6).

fields.title: Integrity: The Same in Secret
fields.body_html:
“Whoever lives honestly walks without fear, but the one who takes crooked roads will be exposed.”

— Proverbs 10:9 (OWB)

In some markets, traders sell honey that has been mixed with sugar water. From the outside the jar looks the same as pure honey. The colour is right. The label is right. But when you taste it, you know. The word “integrity” comes from a word meaning whole or undivided. A person of integrity is like pure honey: the same all the way through. What you see on the outside is what is on the inside.

This chapter is about integrity, being the same person in the pulpit, at home, in the marketplace and alone. It is one of the hardest things for a leader, because leaders are watched in public, and it is easy to give more care to how we look than to what we are.

The same in secret

Jesus kept His strongest words for religious leaders who looked good on the outside but were rotten inside. “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You wash the outside of cup and plate, but inside they are filled by robbery and self-indulgence” (Matthew 23:25). “You resemble tombs coated with whitewash. From outside they look fine, but within they are full of the bones of the dead and every kind of uncleanness” (Matthew 23:27).

The word “hypocrite” comes from the Greek word for an actor on a stage, someone who wears a mask and plays a part. A hypocrite is a leader who plays the part of a godly person in public, but lives another way in private. Jesus warned His disciples, “Watch out for the yeast of the Pharisees. I mean their hypocrisy” (Luke 12:1). Yeast is small but it spreads through the whole loaf. Hypocrisy in a leader spreads through a whole church.

Then Jesus added a warning that every leader should remember: “Everything that is covered up now will be uncovered, and every secret will come out” (Luke 12:2). Nothing stays hidden forever. Moses told the people of Israel, “you can be sure that your sin will catch up with you” (Numbers 32:23). What a leader does in secret will one day be known, either in this life or before Christ.

Samuel’s clean hands

The Bible also gives us beautiful pictures of integrity. When the prophet Samuel was old, he stood before the whole nation of Israel and asked a remarkable question: “Here I am. Bring your charges against me before the LORD and before his anointed. Whose ox did I take? Whose donkey? Whom did I cheat? Whom did I treat harshly? From whom did I take a bribe to make me look the other way? If I have, I will pay it back to you” (1 Samuel 12:3).

Imagine a leader today standing in front of their church or community and saying that. Whose money did I take? Whom did I cheat? Whom did I treat harshly? Whose bribe did I accept? The people answered Samuel: “You have not cheated us or treated us harshly, and you have not taken anything from anyone” (1 Samuel 12:4). After a whole lifetime of leading, Samuel’s hands were clean.

Could you say what Samuel said? This is a good test for any leader. If you led your church or group for thirty years, what would people say about your use of money, power and people?

Daniel, with nothing to find

Daniel lived as a captive in a foreign land, but he rose to become one of the highest officials in the empire. Other officials were jealous and tried to destroy him. “So the high officials and the satraps tried to find grounds for a charge against Daniel in his conduct of government affairs, but they could find no grounds and no corruption, because he was trustworthy; no negligence or corruption could be found in him” (Daniel 6:4).

Think about that. His enemies searched his work for mistakes, laziness and dishonesty. They found nothing. In the end they said, “We will never find any grounds for a charge against this Daniel unless it has to do with the law of his God” (Daniel 6:5). The only charge they could bring against him was that he was faithful to God.

What was the secret of Daniel’s public integrity? The same chapter tells us. When the king made a law forbidding prayer to anyone but himself, Daniel “went home to his upstairs room, where the windows opened toward Jerusalem. Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had always done” (Daniel 6:10). Notice the words “just as he had always done”. Daniel’s honesty in government grew from his faithfulness in prayer. The private life fed the public one.

The areas where integrity is tested

Integrity is tested in every part of life, but leaders are especially tested in a few areas. Here are some of them.

Money. Paul handled large gifts for the poor in Jerusalem, and he was very careful: “We are guarding against any charge that could be brought against us over this large sum we are handling. Our concern is for what is honorable, both before the Lord and before people” (2 Corinthians 8:20-21). Notice that he cared not only about being honest before God, but about being seen to be honest before people. A leader should never handle church money alone. Two people should count it, records should be kept, and the accounts should be open. We will return to this in Chapter 33, Money and Greed.

Words. Jesus said, “Let your yes be yes and your no be no” (Matthew 5:37). A leader of integrity keeps their promises. They do not exaggerate numbers to look successful. They do not tell different stories to different people. They do not flatter. Paul could say, “we never used flattery, and we never put on a show to cover up greed; God is our witness” (1 Thessalonians 2:5).

Work. A leader who is paid should give a full day’s work. A leader who works in a business should be honest in every sale and every report. Daniel’s enemies looked for “negligence” and found none. Laziness is also a failure of integrity.

The home. The truest test of a leader’s integrity is how they behave when the church door is closed. A pastor who is gentle in the pulpit but harsh with their spouse and children has a divided heart. David prayed, “Inside my own house I will live with an undivided heart” (Psalm 101:2). We will look at this in Chapter 42, The Leader’s Home.

The eyes and the mind. Job said, “I made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I look with desire at a young woman?” (Job 31:1). Today many leaders fall through what they look at in private on a phone or screen. Integrity begins in the hidden places of the mind. We will look at this in Chapter 34, Sexual Purity.

Small things. Jesus said, “Someone who is faithful in the smallest matter is faithful in large matters too, and someone who is dishonest in the smallest matter is dishonest in large matters too” (Luke 16:10). The leader who is careless with a little money, a small promise or a minor truth will be careless with large ones too.

A clear conscience

Paul spoke often about his conscience. He told the governor Felix, “That is why I, for my part, take pains to live with a blameless conscience toward God and toward people at all times” (Acts 24:16). He wrote to the Corinthians, “Here is what we take pride in, and our conscience confirms it: in the world at large, and still more with you, we have behaved with a holiness and sincerity that come from God” (2 Corinthians 1:12).

A clear conscience is one of the greatest gifts a leader can have. It gives courage, because there is nothing to hide. It gives peace, because there is no fear of being found out. It gives freedom, because you do not have to remember which story you told to whom. “Whoever lives honestly walks without fear” (Proverbs 10:9).

A guilty conscience, on the other hand, slowly destroys a leader from the inside. They become defensive, suspicious and afraid. They cannot preach about sin with power, because they know their own. They cannot correct others, because they are hiding something themselves.

When integrity has been broken

Perhaps as you read this chapter, you know that your own life is divided. There is something hidden: money taken, a lie told, a secret habit, a relationship that is wrong. What should you do?

The Bible is clear: “Whoever hides their sins will not succeed, but whoever admits them and turns away from them will receive mercy” (Proverbs 28:13). There is mercy for leaders who confess. But confession must be real. It means admitting the sin to God, and where needed to the people affected and to those who have authority over you. It means making things right where you can, as Zacchaeus paid back what he had stolen. It means accepting the consequences, which may include stepping back from leadership for a time.

That is painful. But it is far less painful than being found out, and far better than standing before Christ with a hidden sin. In Achan’s story, the hidden silver and gold buried in his tent brought disaster on the whole people (Joshua 7). Hidden sin in a leader rarely harms only the leader. We will come back to failure and restoration in Chapter 39, Failure and Restoration.

A voice from the Church: Polycarp of Smyrna

Polycarp was bishop of the church in Smyrna, a city on the coast of what is now Turkey. As a young man he had learned from the apostle John. By the middle of the second century, around AD 155, he was a very old man, loved by Christians across the region.

A wave of persecution came to Smyrna. The crowds in the stadium shouted for Polycarp to be found. His friends persuaded him to hide in a farmhouse outside the city, but he was betrayed and arrested. The soldiers who came to take him were surprised to find a gentle old man. He ordered food and drink to be given to them, and asked only for an hour to pray. He prayed for two hours, remembering by name everyone he had ever known, small and great, and the whole Church throughout the world.

He was brought into the stadium before the Roman governor. The governor wanted to save him, out of respect for his age. All Polycarp had to do was swear by the emperor and curse Christ. A letter from his church, written soon afterwards and known as The Martyrdom of Polycarp, tells us how he answered:

“Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He never did me any injury: how then can I blaspheme my King and my Saviour?”

— The Martyrdom of Polycarp

In plain words: I have served Christ for eighty-six years, and He has never once done me wrong. How could I speak against my King, who saved me? When the governor pressed him again, Polycarp said simply, “I am a Christian.” He was put to death that day.

Polycarp’s words are about courage, and we will meet him again in later chapters. But they are also about integrity. For eighty-six years he had served the same Lord. The man in the stadium was the same man who had prayed in the farmhouse, taught in the church and fed the soldiers who came to arrest him. There was no hidden life, no second self, no secret that could be used against him. When the great test came, he did not have to become someone new. He only had to go on being who he had always been.

That is the fruit of integrity. A leader who is whole in the small daily choices will be whole on the day of testing.

An honest heart

We saw in Chapter 2, What Makes Leadership Spiritual, that David led his people “with an honest heart” (Psalm 78:72). That is where integrity lives: in the heart. It cannot be put on like a robe for Sunday and taken off on Monday. It is formed slowly, by a thousand small choices to tell the truth, keep a promise, refuse a bribe and confess a sin.

Paul summed it up for the young leader Titus: “In every way set them an example by doing what is good. In your teaching show integrity and seriousness, and sound speech that cannot be criticized, so that anyone who opposes you will be ashamed, because they have nothing bad to say about us” (Titus 2:7-8). Like Daniel, may your enemies find nothing to say against you, except that you belong to God.

Questions for reflection

  • If someone followed you for a week, at home, at work and alone, would they see the same person they see at church?
  • Read 1 Samuel 12:1-5. Could you ask your people Samuel’s questions? Which one would be hardest to answer?
  • Daniel’s public honesty grew from his private prayer. How is your private life feeding, or failing to feed, your public life?
  • Of the areas where integrity is tested (money, words, work, the home, the eyes and mind, small things), which is the greatest danger for you?
  • Are there any changes you need to make in how money is handled in your church or ministry so that it is “honorable ... before people”?
  • Is there anything hidden in your life that you need to bring into the light? Who could you talk to about it?

A step for this week

Pray Psalm 139:23-24 each morning this week: “God, look deep into me and know my heart; put me to the test and know my restless thoughts. Look and see whether I am on a path that brings harm, and guide me along the road that never ends.” Ask God to show you one area where your private life and public life do not match. When He shows you, take one practical step to make it right: confess something, repay something, keep a promise you have broken, or ask someone to hold you accountable.

study_questions.question: What is integrity in Christian leadership?
study_questions.answer: Integrity means being the same person in secret as in public. “Whoever lives honestly walks without fear, but the one who takes crooked roads will be exposed” (Proverbs 10:9). Jesus warned against the hypocrisy of those who “wash the outside of cup and plate” while the inside is unclean (Matthew 23:25).

study_questions.question: How did Samuel show integrity as a leader?
study_questions.answer: At the end of his leadership he could stand before the whole people and ask, “Whose ox did I take?” (1 Samuel 12:3). No one could accuse him of cheating or taking bribes. His hands were clean.

study_questions.question: Can hidden sin stay hidden?
study_questions.answer: No. Jesus said, “Everything that is covered up now will be uncovered, and every secret will come out” (Luke 12:2), and Moses warned, “you can be sure that your sin will catch up with you” (Numbers 32:23). The chapter urges leaders whose integrity has been broken to confess and seek help now.

fields.title: Keep Watch over Yourself
fields.body_html:
“Keep a close watch on yourself and on your teaching. Persevere in them, for if you do, you will save both yourself and your hearers.”

— 1 Timothy 4:16 (OWB)

A farmer can have the best seed, the best field and the best rain, but if the blade of their hoe is broken, the work will go badly. A carpenter who never sharpens their tools will work harder and harder and produce less and less. Every worker knows that tools must be looked after.

For a spiritual leader, the most important tool is not a building, a budget or a programme. It is the leader’s own soul. This chapter is about keeping watch over yourself. It may sound selfish, but it is one of the most loving things a leader can do for the people they serve.

Watch yourself first

When Paul said goodbye to the elders of the church in Ephesus, he knew he would probably never see them again. He gave them a solemn charge: “Be on your guard, for yourselves and for the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers to shepherd the church of God” (Acts 20:28).

Notice the order: “for yourselves and for the whole flock”. Paul did not say, “Guard the flock, and if you have time left over, look after yourselves.” He put the leader’s own soul first. He wrote the same thing to Timothy, a young leader: “Keep a close watch on yourself and on your teaching” (1 Timothy 4:16). Again the order is the same: yourself, then your teaching.

Why? Because a shepherd who is spiritually sick cannot care for sick sheep. A leader whose own fire has gone out cannot light fires in others. A leader who has stopped listening to God cannot help others hear Him. The flock depends on the health of the shepherd.

“So that after preaching to others”

Paul was not afraid only for others. He was afraid for himself. He wrote: “I punish my body with blows and treat it as my servant, so that after preaching to others I will not myself be found disqualified” (1 Corinthians 9:27).

This is one of the most sobering verses in the Bible for anyone who leads. Paul, the great apostle, who had planted churches across the Roman world, knew that it was possible to preach to others and be lost yourself. It was possible to help others into the race and drop out of it yourself.

The Bible gives us examples of leaders who did exactly that. Samson was set apart by God from birth. He was given great strength. But he played with sin until one day, when his enemies came, he said, “I will go out as I did the other times and shake myself loose.” The Bible adds a terrible sentence: “But he did not know that the LORD had left him” (Judges 16:20). Samson had grown so used to God’s power that he did not notice when it had gone.

Solomon was the wisest man of his time. He built the temple and wrote proverbs. But “When Solomon was old, his wives turned his heart to follow other gods, and his heart was not wholly devoted to the LORD his God” (1 Kings 11:4). The man who had prayed one of the greatest prayers in the Bible ended his life worshipping idols.

These leaders did not fall in a day. They drifted, slowly, while they were still busy doing God’s work. That is why we must keep watch.

What we are watching for

What exactly should a leader watch in their own life? Here are some of the most important things.

Your heart. “More than anything you protect, protect your heart, because the whole course of your life flows out of it” (Proverbs 4:23). The heart is where our loves, desires and choices come from. Ask yourself regularly: What do I love most? What am I longing for? What is filling my thoughts when I am free to think about anything?

Your first love. Jesus sent a message to the church in Ephesus, the same church whose elders Paul had warned. They were working hard. They were patient. They tested false teachers. But Jesus said, “here is my complaint against you: the love you had in the beginning, you have let go” (Revelation 2:4). It is possible to do all the right things for God while no longer loving Him as you once did. Leaders are especially in danger of this, because the work itself can replace the relationship.

Your walk with God. Are you still meeting with God in prayer and in His Word for your own soul, and not only to prepare messages? We will look at this in Part Three.

Your holiness. “Be holy yourselves in all your conduct, just as the one who called you is holy” (1 Peter 1:15). What sins are you tolerating? What compromises have become normal? Paul told Timothy, “Run away from the passions of youth, and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace” (2 Timothy 2:22).

Your teaching. Paul told Timothy to watch his teaching as well as himself. Leaders can drift from the truth, slowly adding ideas that are popular, or leaving out parts of the Bible that are hard. Keep checking your teaching against Scripture.

Your gift. Paul reminded Timothy “to stir up into flame the gift God gave you” (2 Timothy 1:6). Gifts can grow cold through neglect, fear or tiredness. Fires need tending.

The danger of handling holy things

There is a special danger for those who lead God’s people. We spend our days with holy things: the Bible, prayer, worship, the Lord’s Supper, the care of souls. At first these things fill us with awe. But over time, it is easy for them to become ordinary. The preacher reads the Bible to find a sermon, not to hear God. The worship leader sings words about God without thinking about God. The pastor prays in public but rarely in private.

The Old Testament gives a frightening example. Two of Aaron’s sons, Nadab and Abihu, were priests. One day they offered “an improper fire” before the LORD, one He had not commanded. “Then fire went out from before the LORD and devoured them” (Leviticus 10:1-2). Moses explained what God had said: “Through those who come near me I will show that I am holy” (Leviticus 10:3).

We live under the new covenant of grace, and God does not deal with us in the same way. But the principle remains: those who come near to God in leadership must treat Him as holy. Familiarity with holy things is one of the greatest dangers a leader faces. The answer is not to do less, but to keep coming to God as a needy sinner, not as a busy professional.

Practical ways to keep watch

Keeping watch over yourself is not complicated, but it must be deliberate. Here are some ways that leaders across the centuries have found helpful.

  • Keep a daily time with God that is for you. Read the Bible to be fed, not only to feed others. Pray for your own soul as well as for your people.
  • Examine yourself regularly. Set aside time, perhaps once a week or once a month, to ask yourself honest questions. Appendix B (Chapter 54) offers a list of questions drawn from leaders such as Richard Baxter and John Wesley.
  • Have someone who knows you well. Every leader needs at least one person who can ask them hard questions and to whom they tell the truth. We will look at this in Chapter 46, Faithful in Little: Accountability.
  • Confess your sins quickly. Do not let sin pile up. Deal with it daily before God, and where necessary with others.
  • Notice the warning signs. Prayerlessness, irritability, secret habits, loss of joy, envy of others, hunger for praise, and the feeling that the rules do not apply to you are all signs that something is wrong.
  • Rest. A tired leader is a vulnerable leader. Jesus said, “Stay alert and pray that you will not come into testing. The spirit is eager, but human nature is weak” (Matthew 26:41). We will look at rest in Chapter 15, Rest, Retreat and Rhythm.
  • Pray David’s prayer. “God, create a pure heart for me, and make my spirit new and steady inside me” (Psalm 51:10).

A voice from the Church: Richard Baxter, Charles Spurgeon and Robert Murray M’Cheyne

Richard Baxter was a pastor in the town of Kidderminster in England in the 1600s. When he arrived, the town was known for its drunkenness and ignorance of God. By the time he left, many families held daily prayer in their homes. In 1656 he wrote a book for his fellow pastors called The Reformed Pastor. Its theme was Paul’s words in Acts 20:28, and its first great call was this:

“Take heed to yourselves, lest you be void of that saving grace of God which you offer to others, and be strangers to the effectual working of that gospel which you preach; and lest, while you proclaim to the world the necessity of a Savior, your own hearts should neglect him.”

— Richard Baxter, The Reformed Pastor

In plain words: watch yourselves. Make sure that you have received the saving grace you offer to others. Make sure that the gospel you preach has worked in your own heart. Do not tell the world that it needs a Saviour while you yourself neglect Him. Baxter goes on to warn pastors not to “famish yourselves while you prepare food for them”, that is, not to starve while cooking for others.

Two hundred years later, Charles Spurgeon, a Baptist pastor in London, gave a lecture to his students called “The Minister’s Self-Watch”. He began by comparing a preacher to a workman with tools:

“We are, in a certain sense, our own tools, and therefore must keep ourselves in order.”

— Charles Spurgeon, Lectures to My Students

Spurgeon explained that a preacher can only preach with his own voice, think with his own mind and feel with his own heart. Books, programmes and plans are useful, but they are not the leader’s nearest tools. The nearest tools are the leader’s own spirit, soul and body. If these are neglected, nothing else will make up for it.

Between Baxter and Spurgeon lived a young Scottish pastor named Robert Murray M’Cheyne. He served a church in Dundee and died in 1843 at the age of twenty-nine. In his short life many people came to faith, and his letters and sermons have encouraged leaders ever since. In a letter to another young minister in 1840, he wrote words that his friend Andrew Bonar later published:

“It is not great talents God blesses so much as great likeness to Jesus. A holy minister is an awful weapon in the hand of God.”

— Robert Murray M’Cheyne, letter of 1840, in Andrew Bonar’s Memoir and Remains

In plain words: God does not bless great gifts as much as He blesses a life that is like Jesus. A holy leader is an awesome weapon in God’s hand. (In M’Cheyne’s day, “awful” meant “full of awe”, not “very bad”.)

All three men were gifted preachers. All three said the same thing: your gifts are not your greatest asset. Your soul is. Look after it.

Saving yourself and your hearers

Paul promised Timothy that if he kept watch over himself and his teaching, “you will save both yourself and your hearers” (1 Timothy 4:16). He did not mean that Timothy could save anyone by his own power. Only Christ saves. But God uses faithful leaders as His instruments, and a leader who keeps watch over their own soul will be an instrument that God can use for a lifetime.

So keep watch, not out of fear, but out of love: love for Christ, who bought you; love for your people, who need you to be well; and love for your own soul, which matters to God as much as theirs.

Questions for reflection

  • Read Acts 20:28. Why do you think Paul put “yourselves” before “the whole flock”?
  • Samson “did not know that the LORD had left him”. What are the warning signs that a leader is drifting without noticing it?
  • Read Revelation 2:1-5. Are you still loving Jesus as you did at the beginning? How can you tell?
  • In what ways have holy things become ordinary to you? What could help you treat them as holy again?
  • Baxter warned pastors not to “famish yourselves while you prepare food for them”. When did you last read the Bible only for your own soul?
  • Who is the person who knows you well enough to warn you? If there is no one, who could you ask?

A step for this week

Set aside one hour this week, away from your usual work. Bring your Bible and a notebook. Read Acts 20:17-38 slowly. Then write honest answers to these questions: How is my love for Jesus? What sin am I tolerating? Is my teaching faithful to Scripture? Am I tired, and if so, why? What one change do I need to make? Finish by praying Psalm 51:10-12 for yourself.

study_questions.question: Why must leaders keep watch over themselves?
study_questions.answer: Because a leader’s own soul comes first. Paul told Timothy, “Keep a close watch on yourself and on your teaching” (1 Timothy 4:16), and told the Ephesian elders, “Be on your guard, for yourselves and for the whole flock” (Acts 20:28). A leader can care for others and neglect their own heart.

study_questions.question: Can a leader drift from God without knowing it?
study_questions.answer: Yes. Samson “did not know that the LORD had left him” (Judges 16:20), and Solomon’s “heart was not wholly devoted” in his old age (1 Kings 11:4). Jesus told the church in Ephesus, “the love you had in the beginning, you have let go” (Revelation 2:4).

study_questions.question: How can a leader guard their heart?
study_questions.answer: “More than anything you protect, protect your heart, because the whole course of your life flows out of it” (Proverbs 4:23). The chapter suggests time alone with God, honest friends, regular self-examination and rest, and draws on Richard Baxter, Charles Spurgeon and Robert Murray M’Cheyne.

fields.title: Love: The Motive and the Mark
fields.body_html:
“For my part, I will gladly spend everything I have, and spend myself to the last, for your sake.”

— 2 Corinthians 12:15 (OWB)

There is a kind of leader who is very good at the work but does not love the people. They plan well, preach well and organise well. But people feel used rather than cared for. They are part of the leader’s project, not part of the leader’s heart. And there is a kind of leader who makes many mistakes, but whose people would follow them anywhere, because they know they are loved.

This chapter is about love: the motive for all spiritual leadership and the mark by which the world will know we belong to Christ.

Without love, nothing

Paul wrote the most famous chapter on love in the Bible to a church that was full of gifted leaders. The Christians in Corinth had every spiritual gift. They had preachers, teachers, prophets and people who spoke in tongues. But they were proud, divided and unkind to one another. So Paul wrote:

“Suppose I speak in the tongues of human beings, and of angels too. If I do not have love, I am no more than booming bronze or a clashing cymbal. I may be able to prophesy, and know every mystery and everything there is to know; I may have all the faith there is, enough to move mountains; but if I do not have love, I am nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:1-2).

Read that slowly, and think of the gifts leaders most admire: powerful speaking, deep knowledge, great faith, sacrifice. Paul says that without love, all of them are nothing. A brilliant sermon preached without love is just noise. A great project done without love counts for nothing in heaven. “I may hand out everything I own as food for others; I may hand over my body to the flames; but if I do not have love, it does me no good at all” (1 Corinthians 13:3).

This is a hard word for leaders, because we are often measured by our gifts and our results. God measures us by our love.

What love looks like

Then Paul describes love, not as a feeling, but as a way of acting: “Love is patient; love is kind. Love does not envy, does not show off, is not puffed up. It does not behave shamefully, it does not look for its own advantage, it does not lose its temper, and it does not keep a tally of wrongs. It takes no pleasure in wrongdoing, but shares the joy of the truth. There is nothing love cannot bear, no time when it stops believing or hoping, nothing it cannot endure” (1 Corinthians 13:4-7).

Every line of this describes a loving leader.

  • Patient. A loving leader does not give up on people who grow slowly.
  • Kind. They are gentle in how they speak, even when they must say hard things.
  • Not envious. They are glad when another leader is blessed.
  • Not showing off. They do not use people as an audience for their own gifts.
  • Not looking for their own advantage. They do not lead in order to get something.
  • Not losing their temper. They do not shout at people or frighten them.
  • Not keeping a tally of wrongs. They do not keep a list of people’s failures to use against them.
  • Sharing the joy of the truth. They do not hide the truth to keep people happy.
  • Bearing, believing, hoping, enduring. They keep loving people through disappointment.

One helpful exercise is to read 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 again and put your own name in place of the word “love”: “John is patient; John is kind. John does not envy ...” Where does it ring false? That is where you need God’s grace.

Love for Christ comes first

We saw in Chapter 3, Jesus, the Chief Shepherd, that when Jesus restored Peter, He asked him three times, “Do you love me?” Each time Peter said yes, Jesus said, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17). Love for the sheep grows out of love for the Shepherd.

This matters, because people are hard to love. They disappoint us. They criticise us. They forget what we have done for them. If our love for people depends only on how they treat us, it will run out. But if it flows from our love for Christ, it has a deeper source. We serve them because we love Him, and because He loves them.

John wrote, “We love because he loved us first” (1 John 4:19). The more we know how much Christ loves us, the more we will be able to love others. A leader who is cold towards people has usually grown cold towards God first. The cure is not to try harder to love people. It is to come back to the cross and be loved by Christ again.

Jesus gave this command to His disciples on the night before He died: “love one another. In the same way that I have loved you, you too must love one another. If you have love for one another, everyone will know by this that you are my disciples” (John 13:34-35). The world will not be convinced by our buildings, our numbers or our arguments. It will be convinced by our love.

The love of a parent

Paul often described his love for the churches in the language of family. To the believers in Thessalonica he wrote, “we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother who holds her own children close. Our longing for you was such that we gladly gave you not only the gospel of God but ourselves too, for you had become dear to us” (1 Thessalonians 2:7-8).

A nursing mother does not care for her baby because it is her job. She does it because she loves the child. She gets up in the night. She is patient with crying. She gives her own strength so that the child can grow. That is how Paul felt about the churches.

He wrote to the Philippians, “God is my witness how much I long for every one of you with the deep love of Christ Jesus” (Philippians 1:8). He wrote to the Corinthians, who had hurt him badly, “I will gladly spend everything I have, and spend myself to the last, for your sake” (2 Corinthians 12:15). He even wrote of his own people, the Jews who had rejected Christ, “my sorrow is great and the pain in my heart never stops” (Romans 9:2).

Moses felt the same. When Israel sinned by worshipping a golden calf, he went back to God and prayed, “if only you would forgive their sin! But if not, then blot me out of your book that you have written” (Exodus 32:32). He would rather be lost himself than see his people lost. That is a shepherd’s heart.

Love that tells the truth

Some people think that a loving leader is one who never says anything hard. But that is not love. It is often fear. Love “takes no pleasure in wrongdoing, but shares the joy of the truth” (1 Corinthians 13:6). A loving parent corrects their child. A loving doctor tells the patient the truth about their illness. A loving leader warns, rebukes and corrects, because they care about the person’s good more than about being liked.

But love shapes how we correct. Paul says that when someone is caught in sin, “You who are spiritual must set that person right again, and do it with a gentle spirit” (Galatians 6:1). Love speaks the truth gently, privately where possible, with tears rather than anger, and always with the goal of restoring the person. We will look at this in Chapter 20, Correction and Restoration.

Love that covers

Peter wrote, “Most important of all, keep your love for one another strong and unfailing, because love covers a great many sins” (1 Peter 4:8). This does not mean hiding serious wrongdoing or protecting abusers. It means that love does not broadcast other people’s failures. It does not gossip. It gives people the benefit of the doubt. It forgives the many small offences that happen whenever people live and work together.

Leaders are often hurt by the people they serve. Someone criticises them unfairly. Someone leaves the church without a word. Someone they helped turns against them. Love does not keep “a tally of wrongs” (1 Corinthians 13:5). Paul tells us, “Be patient with one another’s faults, and when someone has a grievance against another, forgive. The Lord has forgiven you freely; you must do the same. Over all of these put on love, which binds everything together and makes it complete” (Colossians 3:13-14).

A voice from the Church: Amy Carmichael

Amy Carmichael was born in Northern Ireland in 1867. As a young woman she went to India as a missionary, and she never came home. For more than fifty years she lived at Dohnavur in the far south of India. There she and her fellow workers rescued children, many of whom were in danger of being given to temples, and raised them as their own. The Dohnavur Fellowship became a large family of hundreds of children and workers. Amy Carmichael was its leader, and the children called her “Amma”, which means “mother”.

She wrote many books. One of the shortest is called simply If. It is a list of short sentences, each beginning with “If” and ending with the same words: “then I know nothing of Calvary love.” By Calvary love she meant the love that Jesus showed on the cross at Calvary. Here are a few of her sentences:

“If I can easily discuss the shortcomings and sins of others; if I can speak casually even of a child’s wrongdoing, then I know nothing of Calvary love. ... If I do not have the patience of my Saviour with souls who grow slowly; if I know little of that painful travail until Christ is fully formed in them, then I know nothing of Calvary love. ... If I cannot happily take the second place—or the twentieth; if I cannot take the first without drawing attention to my unworthiness, then I know nothing of Calvary love. ... If praise lifts me up and blame casts me down; if I cannot rest under misunderstanding without defending myself; if I love being loved more than loving, being served more than serving, then I know nothing of Calvary love.”

— Amy Carmichael, If

Few books are as searching for a leader. Amy Carmichael did not write about love in general. She wrote about the small, daily tests of love that every leader faces: how we talk about people who fail, how patient we are with slow growth, whether we can take second place, whether we need to be praised. She knew these tests well, because she faced them every day in a large and difficult household.

Her life showed that love is not soft. She was firm, brave and demanding. She stood against powerful people to protect children. But her firmness came from love, and the children she raised knew it.

The greatest of these

Paul ends his chapter on love with these words: “As things are, then, three things last: faith, hope and love. And of these three, the greatest is love” (1 Corinthians 13:13). One day our gifts will no longer be needed. Prophecy will end. Knowledge will be complete. But love will remain forever, because God is love.

If you want to know whether you are a spiritual leader, do not first ask how gifted you are, how many people follow you or how much you have built. Ask whether you love. Ask whether the people you lead feel loved by you. That is the mark of a leader after God’s own heart.

Questions for reflection

  • Read 1 Corinthians 13:1-3. Which gift are you most tempted to rely on instead of love?
  • Put your own name in place of “love” in 1 Corinthians 13:4-7. Which line is hardest to say truthfully?
  • “We love because he loved us first.” How does remembering Christ’s love for you change the way you see difficult people?
  • Paul compared himself to a nursing mother. What would it look like for you to lead with that kind of tender care?
  • Do you find it harder to speak the truth in love, or to cover others’ faults in love? Why?
  • Which of Amy Carmichael’s “If” sentences touched you most? What does it show you about your heart?

A step for this week

Think of one person you lead whom you find difficult to love. Each day this week, pray for them by name and ask God to give you His love for them. Then do one practical act of love for them: a visit, a meal, a kind message, a word of encouragement, or a quiet act of help. Do not tell them why. At the end of the week, notice whether your feelings towards them have changed.

study_questions.question: Why is love the most important mark of a leader?
study_questions.answer: Because without love even great gifts count for nothing: “If I do not have love, I am no more than booming bronze or a clashing cymbal” (1 Corinthians 13:1). Jesus said the world would know His disciples by their love for one another (John 13:34-35).

study_questions.question: What does love look like in a leader?
study_questions.answer: “Love is patient; love is kind. Love does not envy, does not show off, is not puffed up” (1 Corinthians 13:4). It gives itself for others, as Paul wrote: “I will gladly spend everything I have, and spend myself to the last, for your sake” (2 Corinthians 12:15).

study_questions.question: Where does a leader’s love for people come from?
study_questions.answer: From God’s love for us. “We love because he loved us first” (1 John 4:19). Love for Christ comes first: before Jesus told Peter, “Feed my sheep”, He asked him, “Do you love me?” (John 21:17).

fields.title: Courage
fields.body_html:
“For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but a spirit of power and love and sound judgment.”

— 2 Timothy 1:7 (OWB)

Every leader is afraid sometimes. They are afraid of failing, of being criticised, of losing friends, of losing their position, and in some places of losing their freedom or their life. Fear is not a sin. It is a normal human feeling. The question is what we do with it. Do we let fear decide what we say and do? Or do we obey God even when we are afraid?

That is what courage is. It is not the absence of fear. It is faithfulness to God in the presence of fear. This chapter closes Part Two, on the leader’s heart, because a leader may be humble, honest, watchful and loving, and still fail if they are not brave enough to act.

“Be strong and courageous”

When Moses died, the people of Israel were standing at the edge of the promised land. Ahead of them were strong nations and walled cities. Their great leader was gone. And God gave the leadership to Joshua, who had been Moses’ assistant for forty years.

God’s first words to the new leader were about courage. Three times He said it: “Be strong and courageous, because you are the one who will lead this people to take as their inheritance the land I swore to their ancestors to give them. Only be strong and very courageous. ... Be strong and courageous. Do not tremble with fear or lose heart, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go” (Joshua 1:6-9).

Notice three things about God’s words to Joshua.

Courage is commanded. God did not say, “I hope you will feel brave.” He said, “Be strong and courageous.” Courage is a choice we make, not only a feeling we have.

Courage is tied to obedience. In the middle of His words about courage, God said, “Take care to keep the whole law that my servant Moses laid on you. Do not swerve from it to right or left” (Joshua 1:7). True courage is not recklessness. It is the courage to obey God’s Word when obedience is hard.

Courage rests on God’s presence. The reason Joshua could be brave was not his own strength. It was this: “the LORD your God is with you wherever you go” (Joshua 1:9). Moses had told him the same thing before he died: “The LORD himself goes ahead of you, and he will be with you. He will not let you go or abandon you” (Deuteronomy 31:8).

The trap of fearing people

The most common fear for leaders is not the fear of death. It is the fear of people: of what they will think, say or do. “Fear of what people may do is a trap, but whoever trusts in the LORD is kept safe” (Proverbs 29:25).

The fear of people traps leaders in many ways. It stops a pastor from preaching on a subject that will upset an important family. It stops an elder from correcting a leader who is doing wrong. It stops a believer at work from speaking up about dishonesty. It makes leaders change their message to please the crowd, or avoid difficult decisions because someone might be angry.

Paul faced this temptation and named it clearly: “Is it people I am trying to win over now, or God? Or is my aim to please people? If I were still out to please people, I would be no servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10). A leader cannot serve two masters. If you are always trying to please people, you will end up disobeying God.

Jesus gave the answer to the fear of people: “Those who kill the body have no power to kill the soul, so do not be afraid of them. Be afraid instead of him who can destroy soul and body alike in hell” (Matthew 10:28). The fear of God drives out the fear of people. When we remember how great and holy God is, the opinions of people become small.

Pictures of courage

The Bible is full of ordinary people who found extraordinary courage.

Caleb and Joshua were two of the twelve spies Moses sent into the promised land. Ten came back terrified. But Caleb said, “We must go up and take possession of it, for we are surely strong enough to conquer it” (Numbers 13:30). When the people wanted to stone them, Joshua and Caleb said, “the LORD is with us. So do not fear them!” (Numbers 14:9). Courage sometimes means standing against the majority.

Esther was a young Jewish woman who had become queen of Persia. When a law was passed to destroy her people, her cousin Mordecai asked her to go to the king, even though going without being called could mean death. He told her, “who knows? Perhaps you have become queen for a time like this” (Esther 4:14). Esther asked the people to fast for her, and then said, “Then I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish” (Esther 4:16). Courage sometimes means using a position God has given you, at great personal risk, for the sake of others.

Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refused to bow down to the gold statue of King Nebuchadnezzar. They told the king, “our God whom we serve is able to rescue us from the blazing furnace, and he will rescue us from your power, O king. But even if he does not, you must know, O king, that we will not serve your gods” (Daniel 3:17-18). Those words, “even if he does not”, are the heart of courage. They trusted God to save them, but they would obey Him even if He did not.

Peter and John were arrested for preaching about Jesus. The leaders who had crucified Jesus ordered them to stop. “The council members saw how freely Peter and John spoke, and they realized these were men without formal schooling, just ordinary people. This astonished them, and they recognized that the two had been companions of Jesus” (Acts 4:13). Their courage did not come from education or position. It came from being with Jesus.

Where courage comes from

What was the source of courage in all these people? The Bible points to several things.

  • The presence of God. “Do not be afraid, for I am with you; do not glance about in alarm, for I am your God. I give you strength; yes, I bring you help” (Isaiah 41:10). The brave leader is not alone.
  • The fear of God. When we fear God more than people, we can face anything people do.
  • A clear conscience. “The wicked run away when nobody is chasing them, but the righteous stand as bold as a lion” (Proverbs 28:1). As we saw in Chapter 8, Integrity: The Same in Secret, integrity gives courage.
  • The Holy Spirit. After Peter and John were released, the church prayed, “Let your slaves speak your word with complete boldness.” Then “every one of them was filled with the Holy Spirit, and they went on proclaiming God’s word fearlessly” (Acts 4:29, 31). They did not pray for the danger to go away. They prayed for boldness, and the Spirit gave it.
  • The prayers of others. Paul, in prison, asked the churches to pray “that I may speak of it boldly, as I must” (Ephesians 6:20). Even the bravest leaders need others to pray for their courage.
  • Hope beyond this life. A leader who knows that death is not the end can face even death with peace.

Courage in small things

Most leaders will never face a blazing furnace. But every leader faces daily tests of courage. It takes courage to:

  • tell a friend a hard truth that they need to hear;
  • admit in front of others that you were wrong;
  • refuse a bribe or a dishonest request at work;
  • preach the parts of the Bible that are unpopular;
  • stand up for someone who is being treated unjustly;
  • change something in the church that has always been done a certain way;
  • remove a leader who is causing harm, even if they are powerful;
  • keep going when the work is slow and you feel like giving up.

Paul’s instructions to the church in Corinth are a good summary: “Stay alert. Hold your ground in the faith. Be brave and be strong. Whatever you do, do it in love” (1 Corinthians 16:13-14). Notice how he ends: “do it in love.” Courage without love becomes harshness. Love without courage becomes weakness. A spiritual leader needs both.

A voice from the Church: leaders who stood

The history of the Church is full of leaders who found courage from God. Here are four of them, from four different centuries.

Athanasius of Alexandria was the bishop of the great city of Alexandria in Egypt in the 300s. In his time, a teaching spread that Jesus was not truly God but a created being. Many bishops and emperors supported it. Athanasius refused. He taught that Jesus is fully God, one with the Father. For this he was sent into exile five times, and spent many years in hiding. People later summed up his life in a Latin phrase: Athanasius contra mundum, “Athanasius against the world.” His books, such as On the Incarnation, are on Ochorus, and the Church still confesses what he defended.

Catherine of Siena was an Italian woman of the 1300s with no position in the church at all. In her time the pope had left Rome and was living in Avignon, in France, and the church was weak and divided.
