Catherine wrote to the pope, Gregory XI, again and again, urging him to return to Rome and to reform the church. She called him to be brave and to do his duty. In 1377 he returned. An ordinary woman, strong in prayer, had the courage to speak to the most powerful church leader of her age.

Martin Luther was a German monk and teacher in the 1500s. He had come to see from the Bible that we are saved by God’s grace through faith in Christ, not by our own works. In 1521 he was called before the emperor at a great meeting in the city of Worms and ordered to take back what he had written. He knew that he could be put to death. He answered that unless he was shown from Scripture and plain reason that he was wrong, he could not take anything back, because his conscience was captive to the Word of God.

Janani Luwum grew up among the Acholi people of northern Uganda, became a schoolteacher, came to a living faith through the East African Revival and was ordained. In 1974 he became Archbishop of the Church of Uganda. At that time the country was ruled by Idi Amin, and thousands of people were being killed or were disappearing. In February 1977 Luwum delivered a protest to Amin on behalf of the bishops against the killings. He knew the danger. People close to him knew what happened to those who opposed the regime. He is remembered as saying, in those last days, that he was prepared to die in the army of Jesus. He was arrested, and on 16 February 1977 he was dead. The regime said it was a car accident. Almost nobody believed it.

The book Tukutendereza on Ochorus, which tells the story of the East African Revival, makes a wise comment about Luwum. It points out that Festo Kivengere, another bishop of the revival, fled into exile soon afterwards, and that he was also right to do so. “Not everyone is called to this, and exile is not betrayal,” it says. “Do not use another man’s martyrdom to shame someone who fled.” Courage does not always mean staying in danger. Jesus Himself sometimes withdrew from those who wanted to kill Him, until His hour had come. But courage always means obeying God rather than our fear.

A spirit of power and love and sound judgment

Timothy was a young leader who seems to have been timid by nature. Paul wrote to him from prison: “For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but a spirit of power and love and sound judgment” (2 Timothy 1:7). Notice the three gifts. Power, so that we can act. Love, so that our courage serves others and not ourselves. Sound judgment, so that our courage is wise and not foolish.

If you are a timid leader, take heart. You are in good company. Moses, Jeremiah, Timothy and many others were afraid. God did not wait for them to stop being afraid before He used them. He gave them His Spirit, and He went with them. He will do the same for you.

This brings Part Two to a close. We have looked at five qualities of a leader’s heart: humility, integrity, watchfulness, love and courage. None of them can be produced by our own effort. They grow as we walk closely with God. That is the subject of Part Three, which begins with the first work of every spiritual leader: prayer.

Questions for reflection

  • What are you most afraid of as a leader? Be specific.
  • Read Joshua 1:1-9. Which of God’s words to Joshua do you most need to hear today?
  • In what ways does the fear of people trap you? Where have you changed your words or actions to please others rather than God?
  • Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego said, “even if he does not.” Is your obedience to God conditional on Him protecting you?
  • Look at the list of small acts of courage. Which one is God asking of you this week?
  • The early church prayed for boldness rather than safety. What would it look like for you to pray that prayer?

A step for this week

Think of one thing you know God wants you to do or say, but which you have been avoiding because you are afraid. Write it down. Each morning this week, read Acts 4:23-31 and pray for boldness to do it. Ask one trusted friend to pray for you too. Then, before the week ends, do it, gently and in love. Afterwards, thank God for His presence with you, whatever the result.

study_questions.question: Why do Christian leaders need courage?
study_questions.answer: Because faithful leadership often means doing or saying what is unpopular. God told Joshua again and again to be strong and courageous, and promised, “the LORD your God is with you wherever you go” (Joshua 1:9).

study_questions.question: How can a leader overcome the fear of people?
study_questions.answer: “Fear of what people may do is a trap, but whoever trusts in the LORD is kept safe” (Proverbs 29:25). Paul asked, “Is it people I am trying to win over now, or God?” (Galatians 1:10). Courage grows as we fear God more than people.

study_questions.question: Where does courage come from?
study_questions.answer: From God’s presence and Spirit. “For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but a spirit of power and love and sound judgment” (2 Timothy 1:7). Moses told Israel, “He will not let you go, and he will not abandon you” (Deuteronomy 31:6).

fields.title: Prayer First
fields.body_html:
“As for us, we will hold fast to prayer and to the service of the word.”

— Acts 6:4 (OWB)

In the early days of the Church in Jerusalem, a problem arose. The church was caring for widows by sharing food each day, but the widows from Greek-speaking families were being left out. People complained. It was a real need, and it had to be solved.

The apostles could have taken charge of the food themselves. They were the leaders, and the need was urgent. But they said, “It is not fitting for us to leave aside the word of God in order to serve at tables.” They asked the church to choose seven wise, Spirit-filled people to care for the widows. “As for us,” they said, “we will hold fast to prayer and to the service of the word” (Acts 6:2-4).

Notice which came first: prayer. The apostles did not think that serving food was unimportant. They made sure it was done well. But they knew that if they let even good work push out prayer, the whole church would suffer. This chapter begins Part Three, The Leader with God, with the first work of every spiritual leader: prayer.

Prayer is work

Many leaders think of prayer as something they do before the real work begins: a short prayer to open a meeting, a quick blessing before a sermon. But the apostles saw prayer as the real work itself. It was one of the two things they refused to give up.

Paul wrote about a man named Epaphras who “always wrestles for you in his prayers” (Colossians 4:12). The word “wrestles” is the word for a fight or a hard contest. Prayer for Epaphras was not a gentle habit. It was labour. He fought for the church in Colossae on his knees.

The prophet Samuel said something remarkable when the people of Israel asked him to pray for them: “As for me, far be it from me to sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you” (1 Samuel 12:23). Samuel saw prayerlessness not as a weakness but as a sin. A leader who stops praying for their people is failing in one of their most basic duties.

The prayer life of Jesus

The best teacher of prayer is Jesus Himself. The Gospels show us again and again that the busiest man who ever lived made time to pray.

Early in His ministry, after a long day of healing in Capernaum, “Long before daylight, he got up and went out. He went off to a lonely place and spent time there in prayer” (Mark 1:35). His disciples came looking for Him: “Everybody is out looking for you!” (Mark 1:37). The needs were endless. But Jesus had gone to be with His Father first.

As His fame grew, the pressure grew too. “Large crowds kept gathering to listen and to be healed of their illnesses. Yet he kept slipping away to places in the wilderness to pray” (Luke 5:15-16). Notice the word “yet”. The more people needed Him, the more He prayed. Most of us do the opposite. When we are busy, prayer is the first thing we drop.

Before He made the most important leadership decision of His ministry, choosing the twelve apostles, “Jesus went off to the mountain to pray, and he stayed up all night in prayer to God” (Luke 6:12). His decisions came out of prayer.

He also prayed for the people He led. On the night before He died, He told Peter, “Satan has demanded to have all of you, to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, so that your faith will not give out” (Luke 22:31-32). In His great prayer in John 17, He prayed for His disciples, and then for us: “My prayer is also for those who are going to believe in me through their message” (John 17:20). Even now, the Bible tells us, Jesus lives to pray for His people (Hebrews 7:25).

When the disciples watched Jesus pray, they asked Him, “Lord, teach us how to pray” (Luke 11:1). They never asked Him to teach them how to preach or how to do miracles. They saw that prayer was the secret of His life.

Praying for the people you lead

One of the most important things a leader does for their people is to pray for them. Paul’s letters are full of his prayers for the churches. “I have never stopped thanking God for you. I mention you whenever I pray” (Ephesians 1:16). “In every prayer I offer for all of you, I always pray with joy” (Philippians 1:4).

What did Paul pray for? Not mainly for their health or their comfort, though those things matter. He prayed that they would know God better, understand His hope and power, grow in love, and stand firm. In Ephesians 1 he asked God “to give you the Spirit who brings wisdom and revelation as you come to know him” (Ephesians 1:17). His prayers aimed at their spiritual growth.

Here are some practical ways to pray for the people you lead.

  • Pray by name. Keep a list of the people in your care, and pray through it regularly. If your church is large, divide the list across the days of the week.
  • Pray the Bible’s prayers. Use Paul’s prayers in Ephesians 1:15-23, Ephesians 3:14-21, Philippians 1:9-11 and Colossians 1:9-14. They teach us what matters most.
  • Pray before you visit or counsel. Ask God for wisdom before you meet someone, and pray with them when you can.
  • Pray for the leaders beside you. Pray for your fellow elders, deacons and workers, and ask them to pray for you.
  • Pray for those who oppose you. Jesus told us to pray for our enemies. It is hard to stay bitter towards someone you are praying for.
  • Pray for the lost. Pray for the people in your community who do not yet know Christ.

Leaders need others to pray for them

When Israel fought the Amalekites in the wilderness, Moses stood on a hill above the battle with his hands lifted up to God. “Whenever Moses held his hand high, Israel prevailed; and whenever he let it sink, Amalek prevailed” (Exodus 17:11). But Moses grew tired. So Aaron and Hur sat him on a stone and held up his hands, “one of them on each side, and so his hands stayed firm until the sun set” (Exodus 17:12).

Every leader needs an Aaron and a Hur. Paul, the great apostle, constantly asked the churches to pray for him. A wise leader gathers a small group of faithful people who will pray for them regularly, and tells them honestly what to pray for. Proud leaders find this hard, because it means admitting weakness. But it is one of the greatest protections a leader can have.

Why leaders stop praying

If prayer is so important, why do so many leaders pray so little? Here are some common reasons.

  • Busyness. There is always something urgent to do. Prayer can always wait, or so it seems. But the urgent things are rarely the most important things.
  • Self-reliance. When things are going well, we feel we can manage on our own. Prayerlessness is often a quiet form of pride. It says, “I can do this without God.”
  • Discouragement. When prayers seem unanswered, we stop asking. Jesus told a parable to teach “their need to pray at all times and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1).
  • Hidden sin. It is hard to come close to God when we are hiding something from Him.
  • Professional prayer. Leaders pray so often in public that they can forget to pray in private. Jesus said, “when you pray, go into an inner room, shut the door, and pray to your Father who is there in secret” (Matthew 6:6).

Building a life of prayer

Prayer is a relationship, not a technique. But relationships need time and habits. Here are some habits that have helped leaders through the centuries.

  • A fixed time. Daniel prayed three times a day, “just as he had always done” (Daniel 6:10). Many leaders find that the early morning, before the day’s demands begin, is best. Choose a time and protect it.
  • A place. Jesus went to “a lonely place”. Find somewhere you can be undisturbed, even if it is only a corner of a room or a quiet path.
  • The Bible open. Let God speak to you through His Word, and let your prayers grow from what you read. We will look at this in the next chapter.
  • A list. Write down the people and needs you are praying for, and note when God answers. It will build your faith.
  • Prayer through the day. Paul said, “Never stop praying” (1 Thessalonians 5:17). Short prayers while you walk, work, wait or travel keep you aware of God.
  • Special seasons. Nehemiah “mourned, and I kept fasting and praying before the God of heaven” (Nehemiah 1:4) before he began his great work. Set aside longer times of prayer, sometimes with fasting, before big decisions or in times of need.
  • Praying with others. The early Church prayed together constantly. Gather your leaders and your people to pray, not only to plan.

A voice from the Church: E. M. Bounds and John Hyde

Edward McKendree Bounds was a Methodist pastor in the United States who lived from 1835 to 1913. He served as a chaplain in the American Civil War and was taken prisoner. Later in life he gave himself to writing about prayer, rising very early each morning to pray for several hours. His best-known book, Power Through Prayer, was written for preachers. In it he wrote:

“What the Church needs to-day is not more machinery or better, not new organizations or more and novel methods, but men whom the Holy Ghost can use—men of prayer, men mighty in prayer. The Holy Ghost does not flow through methods, but through men. He does not come on machinery, but on men. He does not anoint plans, but men—men of prayer.”

— E. M. Bounds, Power Through Prayer

In plain words: the Church does not mainly need new programmes or better methods. It needs people the Holy Spirit can use, people who pray. The Spirit does not work through plans and systems, but through praying people. Bounds also warned, “Preaching which kills is prayerless preaching.” A sermon without prayer behind it may be clever, but it will not give life.

One of the people who lived out Bounds’s words was John Hyde, an American missionary who served in the Punjab, in what is now India and Pakistan, from 1892 until shortly before his death in 1912. Hyde was a quiet man, not a gifted public speaker, and he was slow of speech and a little hard of hearing, which made learning the local languages hard work. But he became known across India as “Praying Hyde”.

Around 1904 a small group of missionaries and Indian workers in the Punjab formed the Punjab Prayer Union. Hyde was one of its moving spirits. Each member signed five simple questions. The last one asked: “Will you set apart one-half hour each day as soon after noon as possible to pray for this awakening, and are you willing to pray till the awakening comes?”

The first question is just as important. It asked: “Are you praying for quickening in your own life, in the life of your fellow-workers, and in the Church?” Notice the order. Each person began by praying for their own heart before praying for anyone else. In the years that followed, a gathering for prayer and teaching held each year at Sialkot became a place where many people met God in a new way. Hyde’s friends remembered him praying through whole nights, with his Bible open, taking one promise of God and repeating it until it seemed to fill the room.

Hyde’s life asks every leader a simple question that he himself once asked: “Have we ever wept for souls? Have you? Have I?” His biography, John Hyde: A Life, is on Ochorus.

The first work

A leader who prays will make mistakes, but they will not lead alone. A leader who does not pray may be busy and successful for a while, but they are building on sand. Samuel called prayerlessness a sin. The apostles called prayer their first work. Jesus made it the pattern of His life.

If you remember nothing else from this chapter, remember this: you will never do anything more important for the people you lead than pray for them. Before you plan, pray. Before you preach, pray. Before you visit, pray. Before you decide, pray. And when you have done everything else, pray again.

Questions for reflection

  • Read Acts 6:1-7. Why did the apostles refuse to let even good work push out prayer? What good work is pushing out prayer in your life?
  • Jesus prayed more when He was busier. What happens to your prayer life when you are busy?
  • Samuel said it would be a sin to stop praying for his people. When did you last pray for each person you lead by name?
  • Who are your Aaron and Hur, the people who hold up your hands in prayer? If you have none, whom could you ask?
  • Which of the reasons leaders stop praying is most true of you?
  • Read the five questions of the Punjab Prayer Union. Which one challenges you most?

A step for this week

Make a list of everyone you lead, even if it is only a few people. Divide the list into seven parts, one for each day of the week. Each day this week, set aside at least fifteen minutes to pray for the people on that day’s list by name, using one of Paul’s prayers (Ephesians 1:15-23, Philippians 1:9-11 or Colossians 1:9-14). At the end of the week, ask two or three trusted people whether they would be willing to pray for you regularly.

study_questions.question: Why should prayer come first for a leader?
study_questions.answer: Because prayer is the leader’s first work, not an extra. When the apostles were overloaded they said, “we will hold fast to prayer and to the service of the word” (Acts 6:4). Samuel said it would be a sin to stop praying for his people (1 Samuel 12:23).

study_questions.question: How did Jesus pray while He was busy?
study_questions.answer: “Long before daylight, he got up and went out. He went off to a lonely place and spent time there in prayer” (Mark 1:35). When crowds grew, “he kept slipping away to places in the wilderness to pray” (Luke 5:16).

study_questions.question: How should a leader pray for the people they lead?
study_questions.answer: Specifically and faithfully, like Epaphras, who “always wrestles for you in his prayers” (Colossians 4:12). The chapter suggests praying for people by name, asking others to pray for you, and building a daily rhythm of prayer, drawing on E. M. Bounds and John Hyde.

fields.title: Living in the Word
fields.body_html:
“For Ezra had set his heart to study the law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and rulings in Israel.”

— Ezra 7:10 (OWB)

A woman who sells food in the market cannot give her customers what she does not have. If her pot is empty, they go away hungry. In the same way, a leader cannot feed others from an empty soul. And the food God has given for our souls is His Word.

In the last chapter we saw that the apostles gave themselves “to prayer and to the service of the word” (Acts 6:4). Prayer and the Word belong together. In prayer we speak to God. In His Word, God speaks to us. A leader who prays but does not listen to God’s Word will pray in the dark. A leader who studies the Word but does not pray will know about God without knowing Him. This chapter is about living in the Word.

Study it, do it, teach it

Ezra was a priest and teacher who led a group of Jewish exiles back from Babylon to Jerusalem. The Bible sums up the secret of his leadership in one sentence: “For Ezra had set his heart to study the law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and rulings in Israel” (Ezra 7:10).

Notice the order: study, practice, teach.

First, he studied it. Ezra did not read the Scriptures quickly or carelessly. He “set his heart” to study them. He gave them his full attention, over many years.

Second, he practised it. Ezra did not study only to know more. He studied in order to obey. What he learned, he lived.

Third, he taught it. Only after studying and obeying did he teach others. His teaching had power because it came from a life shaped by the Word.

Many leaders reverse this order. They study the Bible only to find something to teach. They teach things they have never practised. The result is teaching that may be correct but has no life in it. James warned, “Be people who carry out the word, not just people who hear it. Otherwise you are fooling yourselves” (James 1:22). A leader who teaches what they do not practise is fooling themselves, and often fooling others too.

The Word for the leader’s own soul

Before the Word is a tool for ministry, it is food for the leader. Jesus said, “No one lives on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4). Peter wrote, “Like newborn babies, crave the pure milk of God’s word, so that by it you may grow up into salvation” (1 Peter 2:2). Jeremiah said, “Your words were found, and I fed on them; your word became a joy to me and gladness to my heart” (Jeremiah 15:16).

When God gave Joshua the leadership of Israel, He did not give him a military strategy first. He gave him a book: “Keep this book of the law always on your lips, and reflect on it by day and by night, so that you take care to do all that is written in it. Then you will bring your ways to a good end, and then you will act wisely and succeed” (Joshua 1:8). Joshua’s success as a leader would depend on his daily meditation on God’s Word.

The first psalm describes people who delight in God’s instruction, who “recite it quietly to themselves day and night”. Such a person “is like a tree set out beside channels of water, which bears its fruit when its season comes, and whose leaves never dry up” (Psalm 1:2-3). Leaders face dry seasons, hot winds and long years of work. The leader whose roots go down deep into God’s Word will not wither.

What the Word does

Why is the Bible so important for leaders? Because of what it is and what it does.

It is breathed out by God. “All Scripture is breathed out by God and is useful for teaching, for rebuking, for correcting and for training in righteousness, so that the one who belongs to God may be fully capable, equipped for every good work” (2 Timothy 3:16-17). The Bible is not a collection of human ideas about God. It is God’s own Word, and it equips leaders for every good work they will ever be called to do.

It is alive. “For the word of God is alive and at work, and it has a keener edge than any two-edged sword. It reaches right in, cutting through soul and spirit, through joints and marrow, and it weighs the thoughts and purposes of the heart” (Hebrews 4:12). The Word does not only inform us. It searches us. It shows us our hidden motives. A leader who reads the Bible honestly will often be cut by it before they use it on anyone else.

It guides. “Your word is a lamp to guide my feet and a light for the road I travel” (Psalm 119:105). Leaders make many decisions. The Bible does not tell us everything, but it shows us the path of wisdom and keeps us from many wrong turns.

It protects from sin. “Deep in my heart I have kept your word safe, so that I will not sin against you” (Psalm 119:11). When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, He answered every temptation with Scripture. A leader whose heart is full of God’s Word has a weapon ready when temptation comes.

It does not fail. God says, “so it is with the word that leaves my mouth: it will not come back to me with nothing done, but it will do what I want and succeed in the errand I sent it on” (Isaiah 55:11). Our clever words may fail. God’s Word will not.

The Word points to Christ

It is possible to know the Bible well and still miss its point. Jesus said to the religious leaders of His day, “You pore over the Scriptures, since you think that eternal life is to be found in them; and they are the ones that testify about me. But you do not want to come to me so that you can have life” (John 5:39-40). They studied the Bible carefully, but they did not come to the One the Bible was about.

After His resurrection, Jesus walked with two discouraged disciples on the road to Emmaus. “Starting with Moses and going on through all the prophets, he explained to them what was written about himself in every part of the Scriptures” (Luke 24:27). Afterwards they said, “Did we not feel our hearts on fire inside us while he talked with us on the road and laid the Scriptures open to us?” (Luke 24:32).

That is what we want for ourselves and for the people we lead: hearts on fire, because we have met Jesus in the Scriptures. A leader who reads the Bible only for rules, information or sermon ideas has missed the treasure. The Bible is the place where we meet Christ.

Handling the Word correctly

Paul told Timothy, “Make every effort to stand before God tested and approved, a worker with nothing to be ashamed of, who handles the message of truth correctly” (2 Timothy 2:15). Leaders have a special responsibility, because what they teach shapes what many others believe. A wrong interpretation in the mouth of a leader can lead a whole church astray.

Here are some simple principles for handling the Word well.

  • Read the whole Bible. Do not stay only with your favourite books or verses. Read the Old Testament and the New, the hard parts and the comforting parts.
  • Read in context. Ask what the passage meant to its first readers. Read the verses before and after. A verse taken out of its setting can be made to say almost anything.
  • Let Scripture explain Scripture. When one passage is hard to understand, look at what other passages say on the same subject.
  • Read with the Church. We are not the first to read the Bible. Learn from faithful teachers of the past and present. Many of their books are on Ochorus.
  • Test new teaching. The believers in Berea “went through the Scriptures day after day to check whether what Paul said was true” (Acts 17:11). If they checked Paul, we should check every teacher, including ourselves.
  • Do not add or take away. Jesus warned the religious leaders that they made “God’s word empty for the sake of the tradition you hand down” (Mark 7:13). Leaders must be careful not to put their own ideas, or their culture’s traditions, above the Bible.

A Bible in every language

One of the great joys of the global Church today is that the Bible is now available, in whole or in part, in thousands of languages. But many leaders still do not have a full Bible in their heart language, and many cannot read well. If that is your situation, do not be discouraged. Listen to the Bible read aloud. Learn passages by heart. Ask others to read with you. The earliest Christians mostly heard the Scriptures read aloud in their gatherings. Paul told Timothy to give attention “to the public reading of Scripture” (1 Timothy 4:13). God’s Word does its work through the ear as well as the eye.

And if God has given you the ability, consider how you might help others to have His Word in their language. Some of the greatest leaders in church history were Bible translators.

A voice from the Church: George Müller and Samuel Ajayi Crowther

George Müller was a German who came to England as a young man and became a pastor in Bristol. He is best known for the orphan houses he founded, where he cared for more than ten thousand children over his lifetime without ever asking anyone for money. He prayed, and God provided. But the secret of his life was not only prayer. It was the Word.

In 1841, after many years of ministry, Müller discovered something that changed his daily life. He wrote about it in his journal, later published as The Life of Trust:

“I saw more clearly than ever that the first great and primary business to which I ought to attend every day was, to have my soul happy in the Lord. The first thing to be concerned about was not how much I might serve the Lord, how I might glorify the Lord; but how I might get my soul into a happy state, and how my inner man might be nourished.”

— George Müller, The Life of Trust

In plain words: the most important thing I must do every day is to make sure my soul is satisfied in God. Before I ask how much I can do for God, I must make sure my own heart is being fed.

Müller explained that for ten years he had begun each day by trying to pray. But his mind often wandered. Now he began instead by reading the New Testament slowly, “searching as it were into every verse, to get blessing out of it; not for the sake of the public ministry of the word, not for the sake of preaching on what I had meditated upon, but for the sake of obtaining food for my own soul.” He found that after a few minutes, his reading turned naturally into prayer: confession, thanks, requests for himself and others. By breakfast time, he said, his heart was almost always at peace.

This is a simple and practical method that any leader can use. Open the Bible. Read slowly. Turn what you read into prayer. Read for your own soul first.

Samuel Ajayi Crowther, whom we met in Chapter 4, The Call of God, shows the other side of living in the Word: giving it to others. After he was freed from slavery, he learned to read in Sierra Leone. He became one of the first people to write down his own Yoruba language. He prepared a Yoruba grammar and a dictionary, and he worked for years translating the Scriptures into Yoruba so that his people could hear God speak in their own tongue. Later he helped begin translations into other languages along the Niger River. A boy who had once been carried through his own country in chains gave that country the Word of God.

Living in the Word

A leader does not need to be a scholar to be a person of the Word. Many of the greatest leaders in the history of the Church had little formal education. What they had was a hunger for God’s Word and a daily habit of feeding on it.

The psalmist wrote, “How I love your instruction! I turn it over in my mind all day long” (Psalm 119:97). That is the goal: not just reading the Bible, but loving it, thinking about it through the day, and letting it shape every decision. A leader who lives in the Word will have something to give, because they have first received.

Questions for reflection

  • Ezra studied, practised and taught the Word, in that order. Which of the three is weakest in your life?
  • Do you read the Bible mainly for your own soul, or mainly to prepare for teaching others?
  • Read Hebrews 4:12. When did the Bible last “cut” you, by showing you something in your heart that needed to change?
  • The religious leaders studied the Scriptures but did not come to Jesus. How can you make sure you meet Christ when you read the Bible?
  • Which of the principles for handling the Word correctly do you most need to practise?
  • What could you learn from George Müller’s habit of reading slowly and turning the Word into prayer?

A step for this week

Each morning this week, before you do anything else, follow George Müller’s method. Choose a short passage, beginning with Psalm 1 on the first day and then reading one chapter of the Gospel of Mark each day after that. Read it slowly. After each verse or two, stop and turn what you have read into prayer: thanks, confession, or a request for yourself or others. Do not read to prepare a sermon. Read for your own soul. At the end of the week, write down what difference it made.

study_questions.question: How should a leader approach the Bible?
study_questions.answer: Like Ezra, who “had set his heart to study the law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach” (Ezra 7:10). Study, obey and teach, in that order. “Be people who carry out the word, not just people who hear it” (James 1:22).

study_questions.question: Why do leaders need the Word for their own souls?
study_questions.answer: Because leaders live on it too: “No one lives on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4). Jeremiah said, “Your words were found, and I fed on them; your word became a joy to me” (Jeremiah 15:16). Reading only to prepare sermons starves the soul.

study_questions.question: What does it mean to meditate on Scripture?
study_questions.answer: It means keeping God’s Word in mind and thinking it through day and night so that we live it. God told Joshua, “Keep this book of the law always on your lips, and reflect on it by day and by night” (Joshua 1:8).

fields.title: Filled with the Spirit
fields.body_html:
“Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of Armies.”

— Zechariah 4:6 (OWB)

Imagine a man pushing a car along the road. He is sweating and straining. People admire his strength. He moves the car a few metres, then stops, exhausted. Then someone points out that the car has fuel in the tank and a key in the ignition. He had been pushing it all along when he could have been driving it.

Many leaders serve God like that man. They push and strain in their own strength, and they wonder why the work is so heavy and the fruit so small. They have forgotten that God has given His Holy Spirit to do His work through them. This chapter is about the Spirit’s power in the life of a leader.

Not by might, nor by power

When the Jewish exiles returned from Babylon to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem, the task seemed impossible. They were few and poor. Their enemies opposed them. Their leader, Zerubbabel, was discouraged. Then God sent him a message through the prophet Zechariah: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of Armies” (Zechariah 4:6).

God was not saying that hard work and resources do not matter. Zerubbabel still had to build. But the work would succeed not because of human strength or numbers, but because of God’s Spirit. That is true of every work of God.

Jesus said the same thing in a different way: “I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever remains in me, with me remaining in them, is the one who bears much fruit, because you can do nothing apart from me” (John 15:5). Notice the word “nothing”. Not “a little”, but nothing. We can organise, plan, build and preach without God. But we cannot bear fruit that lasts.

The Spirit in the Old Testament leaders

Throughout the Old Testament, God gave His Spirit to the leaders He called. When Gideon faced the Midianites, “the Spirit of the LORD clothed Gideon” (Judges 6:34). When Samuel anointed David, “the Spirit of the LORD rushed on David from that day on” (1 Samuel 16:13). The prophet Micah said, “I am filled with power, with the Spirit of the LORD, with justice and strength, to tell Jacob of his rebellion and Israel of his sin” (Micah 3:8).

When Moses was overwhelmed by the burden of leading Israel, God took some of the Spirit that was on Moses and put it on seventy elders, so that they could share the work (Numbers 11:16-17). When two of them began to prophesy in the camp, a young man ran to tell Moses, expecting him to stop them. But Moses said, “Are you being jealous on my behalf? If only the LORD would put his Spirit on all his people and make every one of them a prophet!” (Numbers 11:29).

Moses’ wish came true at Pentecost. In the Old Testament, the Spirit came on certain leaders for certain tasks. In the New Testament, God pours out His Spirit on all His people.

Jesus, full of the Spirit

Even Jesus, the Son of God, did His work on earth in the power of the Holy Spirit. After His baptism, “Jesus came back from the Jordan full of the Holy Spirit, and the Spirit led him through the wilderness” (Luke 4:1). After His temptation, “Jesus went back to Galilee, and the power of the Spirit was with him” (Luke 4:14). In the synagogue at Nazareth He read from Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord rests on me, for he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor” (Luke 4:18).

If Jesus Himself depended on the Spirit, how much more do we? And Jesus promised His disciples that they would receive the same Spirit. Before He returned to heaven, He told them, “remain here in the city until power from on high clothes you” (Luke 24:49). “But when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, you will receive power, and you will bear witness to me in Jerusalem, through all Judea and Samaria, and out to the farthest end of the earth” (Acts 1:8).

Notice that Jesus told His disciples to wait. They had been with Him for three years. They had seen Him die and rise again. They knew the message. But they were not ready to lead until the Spirit came. Training and knowledge were not enough.

Leaders full of the Spirit

From Pentecost onwards, the Book of Acts is the story of leaders filled with the Spirit. On the day of Pentecost, “Every one of them was filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:4), and Peter, who had once denied Jesus, preached boldly to thousands. When Peter was arrested and questioned by the rulers, he answered, “filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 4:8).

When the church chose seven people to care for the widows, the first requirement was that they should be “full of the Spirit and of wisdom” (Acts 6:3). This is striking. They were being chosen to distribute food. Yet even for this practical task, the apostles looked first for people full of the Spirit. Stephen, one of the seven, was “a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit” (Acts 6:5). Barnabas “was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a sizable crowd was added to the Lord” (Acts 11:24).

Being full of the Spirit was not a special extra for a few super-spiritual leaders. It was the basic qualification for every leader in the early Church.

What the Spirit does for leaders

The Holy Spirit works in leaders in many ways. Here are some of them.

  • He gives power to witness. “you will receive power, and you will bear witness to me” (Acts 1:8). The Spirit makes our words about Jesus come alive.
  • He makes preaching effective. Paul said, “My message and my preaching did not depend on wisdom’s power to persuade; they were proof given by the Spirit and by power, so that your faith would be grounded not in human wisdom but in the power of God” (1 Corinthians 2:4-5).
  • He teaches and reminds. Jesus promised that the Spirit “will teach you everything and remind you of all I have said to you” (John 14:26).
  • He guides. The Spirit told the church in Antioch, “Set Barnabas and Saul apart for me” (Acts 13:2). Later He stopped Paul from going into Asia and Bithynia, and led him instead to Macedonia (Acts 16:6-10). We will look at guidance in Chapter 16, Guidance and Decisions.
  • He helps us pray. “the Spirit also lends a hand in our weakness. What we should pray for, and how, we do not know. But the Spirit himself pleads on our behalf” (Romans 8:26).
  • He gives gifts. “Each person is given a way in which the Spirit is openly at work, and it is given for the good of all” (1 Corinthians 12:7). Every gift a leader uses is a gift of the Spirit.
  • He forms character. “But the fruit the Spirit produces is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control” (Galatians 5:22-23). The qualities of the leader’s heart that we studied in Part Two are the fruit of the Spirit.
  • He glorifies Christ. Jesus said of the Spirit, “He will glorify me” (John 16:14). A leader filled with the Spirit will draw attention to Jesus, not to themselves.

“Let the Spirit fill you”

How can a leader be filled with the Spirit? Paul gives a command: “Do not get drunk on wine, for that is reckless, wasteful living. Instead, let the Spirit fill you” (Ephesians 5:18). In the Greek that Paul wrote, the command means to go on being filled. It is not a single experience, but a continuing way of life.

Paul compares being filled with the Spirit to being drunk with wine. A drunk person is controlled by what they have drunk. A person filled with the Spirit is led by the Spirit. And Paul describes what that looks like: singing to God, giving thanks “at all times and for everything”, and submitting “to one another in the reverent fear of Christ” (Ephesians 5:19-21). The signs of being filled with the Spirit are worship, thankfulness and humility.

Here are some ways to walk in the Spirit’s fullness.

  • Ask. Jesus said, “how much more will the Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” (Luke 11:13). Ask God daily to fill you.
  • Confess and turn from sin. Paul warns, “do not grieve God’s Holy Spirit” (Ephesians 4:30). Unconfessed sin blocks the Spirit’s work in us.
  • Obey His leading. “Do not smother the Spirit” (1 Thessalonians 5:19). When the Spirit prompts you to speak, give, forgive or act, obey.
  • Depend on Him. Before you preach, visit, lead or decide, pause and tell God that you cannot do it without Him.
  • Walk with Him step by step. “Since our life comes from the Spirit, let us also follow the Spirit’s lead in each step we take” (Galatians 5:25).
  • Come thirsty. Jesus said, “If anyone is thirsty, they should come to me and drink” (John 7:37). John adds, “He was speaking about the Spirit” (John 7:39). The Spirit is given to the thirsty.

Going deeper: The baptism in the Spirit

Christians agree that every believer receives the Holy Spirit when they come to faith, and that every believer is called to be filled with the Spirit. But they disagree about some questions. Is there a second experience after conversion, often called the “baptism in the Spirit”? Is it always marked by speaking in tongues? Are all the gifts described in the New Testament given today?

Some Christians, especially in Pentecostal and charismatic churches, believe that there is a distinct experience of being baptised in the Spirit, often after conversion, and that it brings power for service. Others believe that every Christian is baptised in the Spirit at conversion, and that later experiences are fresh fillings rather than a second baptism. Leaders such as D. L. Moody and R. A. Torrey, whose books are on Ochorus, spoke of a definite experience of power after conversion, though they did not all describe it in the same way.

Faithful Christians hold each of these views. What matters most for leaders is not the name we give to the experience, but whether we are actually living and serving in the Spirit’s power. A leader who argues about the Spirit but does not walk in Him has missed the point. Coram Deo, another Ochorus Original, sets out these views more fully in its chapter on the gifts of the Spirit.

A voice from the Church: D. L. Moody and Erica Sabiti

Dwight L. Moody was an American who began his working life selling shoes in Boston. He never finished school and was never ordained. Yet by the time he died in 1899, he had preached to millions of people in America and Britain.

In 1871 Moody was already a busy and successful preacher in Chicago. But two women in his church told him that they were praying for him to receive the power of the Spirit. At first he was offended. Then he began to feel a deep hunger for God. He later said that he began to cry out to God for this power. In the same year, a great fire destroyed much of Chicago, including Moody’s church and home. Soon afterwards, while he was walking down a street in New York, God met him in such an overwhelming way that, he said, he had to ask God to stop. After that, he said, he preached the same sermons as before, but now hundreds of people came to faith. In his book Secret Power, he wrote about the Spirit’s work in giving hope: “a man filled with the Spirit of God will be very hopeful.”

Half a century later and half a world away, a Ugandan clergyman named Erica Sabiti had a similar experience. He was born in 1903 in Ankole, in south-western Uganda. He studied at King’s College, Budo, and at Makerere, taught in a school and was ordained in 1933 and 1934. Then, as the book Tukutendereza puts it, “for six years, he was an ordained Anglican clergyman who had not yet met the thing this book is about.” In 1939 he travelled with his bishop to Rwanda and Burundi, and there he met the believers of the East African Revival. His ministry was transformed. He went on to become a bishop, and in 1966 he became the first African Archbishop of the Church of Uganda.

Tukutendereza draws a lesson from his story that every leader should hear: “Ordination is not the same as being filled.” Sabiti was a believer. He was trained, examined and ordained. He was doing the work. But something was still missing, until God met him in a new way.

Both men show us that it is possible to be a busy, successful and even ordained leader without the fullness of the Spirit. And both show us that God is ready to give more to leaders who are hungry for Him.

Driving, not pushing

Go back to the man pushing the car. The answer to his problem was not to push harder. It was to get in and let the engine do the work. The answer to a leader’s weakness is not more effort, but more dependence. “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.”

This does not mean that leaders do not work hard. Paul worked harder than anyone. But he said, “it was not I but God’s grace working with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10). Ask yourself honestly: What am I doing that I could do without God? If the answer is “everything”, it is time to stop pushing and ask to be filled.

Questions for reflection

  • Read Zechariah 4:6 and John 15:5. In what parts of your leadership are you relying on “might” and “power” rather than on God’s Spirit?
  • Jesus told His disciples to wait for the Spirit before they began their work. Have you ever rushed ahead without waiting on God?
  • The seven chosen to serve food had to be “full of the Spirit and of wisdom”. Does your church look for this when it chooses leaders?
  • Which of the Spirit’s works for leaders do you most need right now?
  • Is there any way in which you may be grieving or smothering the Spirit?
  • Erica Sabiti was ordained for six years before he was filled. What does his story say to you?

A step for this week

Each morning this week, read one of these passages: Acts 1:1-8, Acts 2:1-21, Acts 4:23-31, Ephesians 5:15-21, Galatians 5:16-26. Then pray, “Father, I cannot do Your work in my own strength. Fill me with Your Holy Spirit today.” Before each task of leadership during the day, pause for a moment and say, “Holy Spirit, I depend on You.” At the end of the week, notice any difference in your work and in your heart.

study_questions.question: Why do leaders need the Holy Spirit?
study_questions.answer: Because God’s work is done “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of Armies” (Zechariah 4:6). Jesus said, “I am the vine; you are the branches” (John 15:5). Without Him we can do nothing of lasting value.

study_questions.question: How did the Spirit work in leaders in the Bible?
study_questions.answer: “The Spirit of the LORD clothed Gideon” (Judges 6:34) and “rushed on David” (1 Samuel 16:13). Jesus Himself “came back from the Jordan full of the Holy Spirit” (Luke 4:1). Moses longed for the Spirit to rest on all God’s people (Numbers 11:29).

study_questions.question: What is the baptism in the Spirit?
study_questions.answer: Christians understand it differently. The chapter’s “Going deeper” section sets out the main views fairly: some see it as part of conversion, others as a later experience of power. All agree that every believer needs to be filled with the Spirit continually.

fields.title: Rest, Retreat and Rhythm
fields.body_html:
“Come away on your own, to a place without people, and get a little rest.”

— Mark 6:31 (OWB)

A farmer knows that a field cannot be planted every season without rest. If the soil is never allowed to recover, the harvest grows smaller each year until nothing grows at all. A wise farmer lets the land rest, and the next harvest is better for it.

Leaders are like that field. Many leaders, especially those who love God and love their people, work without stopping. They answer every call, attend every meeting and carry every burden. For a while it seems to work. Then the harvest grows smaller. They become tired, irritable and dry. Some become ill. Some fall into sin. Some leave the work altogether. This chapter is about rest: why God commands it, how Jesus practised it, and how leaders can build a rhythm of work and rest that lasts a lifetime.

Rest is God’s idea

Rest did not begin as a human need. It began with God. “On the seventh day God brought to an end the work he had been doing, and on the seventh day he stopped all the work he had done. God blessed the seventh day and set it apart as holy” (Genesis 2:2-3). God was not tired. He rested because His work was complete and good, and He wanted to enjoy it. And He built rest into the shape of creation.

Later, God made rest a command for His people: “Remember the Sabbath day and set it apart as holy. You have six days to labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath for the LORD your God. Do no work on it” (Exodus 20:8-10). The command included everyone: children, servants, foreigners and even animals. Nobody was to be worked without rest.

God was very clear that this applied even at the busiest times: “Rest even when the fields need plowing or the harvest is ready” (Exodus 34:21). For a farming people, that was a real test of faith. It meant trusting God to provide even when they stopped working. The Sabbath was a weekly reminder that their life depended on God, not on their own effort.

When Moses repeated the command in Deuteronomy, he gave another reason: “Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 5:15). Slaves cannot rest. Their masters work them without end. The Sabbath was a sign that God’s people were free. A leader who never rests is living like a slave, even if the master is their own ambition or their own sense of duty.

Jesus withdrew

Jesus kept the rhythm of work and rest. He worked hard. He healed until late at night. He travelled on foot from town to town. He was often hungry and tired. On one journey, “Jesus was worn out from the journey, so he sat down by the well just as he was” (John 4:6). On another, He fell asleep in a boat in the middle of a storm (Mark 4:38).

But Jesus also withdrew. We saw in Chapter 12, Prayer First, how He went out early in the morning to pray, and how “he kept slipping away to places in the wilderness to pray” (Luke 5:16). He knew that His strength came from His Father, and He made time to be with Him.

He also taught His disciples to rest. When they came back from a busy mission, full of reports of all they had done, Jesus said to them, “Come away on your own, to a place without people, and get a little rest” (Mark 6:31). The next sentence explains why: “There was a constant stream of people arriving and leaving, and they could not even find time for a meal.” The needs were real and the people were many. But Jesus did not tell His disciples to work harder. He told them to rest.

It is interesting that when they reached the quiet place, the crowds were already there waiting for them. And Jesus, moved with compassion, taught them and fed them (Mark 6:33-44). Rest is not always possible when we plan it. But Jesus still made it His intention, and He taught His disciples to do the same.

Why leaders find it hard to rest

If rest is God’s command and Jesus’ pattern, why do leaders find it so hard? Here are some reasons.

  • The needs never end. There is always another person to visit, another problem to solve, another sermon to prepare. A leader who waits until the work is finished before resting will never rest.
  • We feel indispensable. Deep down, some leaders believe that if they stop, everything will fall apart. That is a kind of pride. The work is God’s, not ours. “If the LORD does not build the house, the work of its builders comes to nothing” (Psalm 127:1).
  • We want to be needed. Some leaders find their worth in being busy and needed. Rest makes them feel useless. But our worth comes from being loved by God, not from how much we do.
  • We are afraid of what people will think. In some cultures, a leader who rests is seen as lazy. But God’s opinion matters more than people’s.
  • We do not trust God. Rest requires faith. It means believing that God will take care of the things we leave undone.
  • We have never been taught. Many leaders have only ever seen leaders who worked without rest, and they think that is what faithfulness looks like.

“He gives sleep to the one he loves”

Psalm 127 is a song for builders and leaders: “If the LORD does not build the house, the work of its builders comes to nothing. If the LORD does not guard the city, the watchman’s sleepless night is wasted. It does you no good to get up early and stay up late, eating food earned by anxious work; he gives sleep to the one he loves” (Psalm 127:1-2).

This psalm does not say that work is wrong. Builders must build, and watchmen must watch. But it says that anxious, endless work, rising early and staying up late out of worry, achieves nothing if God is not in it. And it says that sleep is a gift of God’s love. When we lie down and sleep, we are confessing that God is in control and we are not. “I will lie down in peace and fall asleep at once, because it is you, LORD, and you alone, who let me live in safety” (Psalm 4:8).

God’s care for the exhausted leader

The prophet Elijah had just won a great victory on Mount Carmel. Fire had fallen from heaven, and the people had turned back to God. But then Queen Jezebel threatened to kill him, and Elijah ran for his life. He went a day’s journey into the wilderness, “came to a broom tree and sat down under it, and he prayed that he might die. ‘It is enough,’ he said. ‘Now, LORD, take my life’” (1 Kings 19:4).

What did God do for His exhausted servant? He did not rebuke him or give him a sermon. He let him sleep. Then an angel touched him and said, “Get up and eat.” There was bread and water by his head. Elijah ate and slept again. The angel came a second time: “Get up and eat, for the journey is too much for you” (1 Kings 19:5-7). Only after Elijah had slept and eaten did God speak to him about the future.

Notice God’s tenderness: “the journey is too much for you.” God knows our limits. He does not expect us to be machines. Sometimes the most spiritual thing an exhausted leader can do is sleep and eat. We will come back to Elijah’s story in Chapter 38, Discouragement and Burnout.

A rhythm of work and rest

“There is a set time for everything, a time for every matter under the heavens” (Ecclesiastes 3:1). The goal is not to stop working, but to find a healthy rhythm. Here is a pattern many leaders have found helpful.

  • Daily: withdraw. Take time each day to be alone with God in prayer and His Word, as we saw in Chapters 12 and 13. Also get enough sleep. Leaders who sleep too little make poor decisions and are easily irritated.
  • Weekly: rest. Take one day a week to stop your usual work. For many pastors, Sunday is a working day, so another day must be set aside. Use it to rest, worship, enjoy your family and do things that renew you. Guard it carefully. Tell your people about it, and ask them to respect it except in real emergencies.
  • From time to time: retreat. Several times a year, take a longer time away, a day or more, to pray, read, think and listen to God. Jesus spent whole nights in prayer before big decisions.
  • Yearly: refresh. Where it is possible, take a longer break once a year. Many leaders cannot afford a holiday, but even a few days with family or friends away from the work can bring great refreshment.
  • Over a lifetime: seasons. Some churches give their leaders a longer time of rest and study after several years of service. Where this is possible, it can renew a leader for many more years of work.

These patterns will look different in different places. A bi-vocational pastor who works six days in the fields or the market and leads the church on Sunday faces special pressures. They may need their church’s help to find any rest at all. But the principle remains. God did not design any of His servants to work without stopping.

Martha and Mary

Jesus once visited the home of two sisters, Martha and Mary. Martha was busy preparing the meal, “being pulled in every direction by all the work of serving.” Mary “sat down at Jesus’s feet and kept listening to his words.” Martha complained that Mary was not helping. But Jesus said, “Martha, Martha, you are fretting and in a stir about so many things. Yet there is need of few things, or only of one. Mary has picked the good share, and it is not going to be taken from her” (Luke 10:39-42).

Martha was not doing anything wrong. She was serving Jesus. But she was so busy serving Him that she had no time to listen to Him. Many leaders are Marthas. They are working for Jesus all the time, but rarely sitting at His feet. Jesus invites us to choose “the good share”: time with Him that nobody can take away.

A voice from the Church: Bernard, Antony and Brother Lawrence

Bernard of Clairvaux was a French monk of the 1100s, a gifted preacher and one of the most influential church leaders of his day. One of his former monks became pope, taking the name Eugenius III. Bernard loved him and was worried for him. The pope was surrounded by legal cases, quarrels, visitors and politics from morning to night. So Bernard wrote him a long letter, which became a book called On Consideration.

In it, Bernard warned the pope that endless business could slowly harden his heart. A person who gives all their time to others and none to God, or to examining their own soul, can lose their own soul without noticing. Bernard urged him to set aside time for “consideration”: quiet reflection on God, on himself and on his duties. He reminded the pope that he too was a human being who needed God, and that he could not serve others well if he neglected his own heart. His words have helped busy leaders for nearly nine hundred years.

Long before Bernard, in the 200s and 300s, a young Egyptian named Antony heard the words of Jesus read in church, “go, sell your property, and give the money to people who are poor” (Matthew 19:21), and obeyed. He went into the desert to pray. Athanasius, the great bishop of Alexandria, later wrote his story in The Life of Antony, which is on Ochorus. Antony spent many years alone with God. But he did not stay hidden forever. People came to him for counsel, and he became a spiritual father to thousands. His solitude made him useful. He had something to give because he had spent so long receiving from God.

Brother Lawrence was a French monk of the 1600s who worked for many years in the kitchen of his monastery. He was not a leader in the usual sense. But his conversations and letters, collected in The Practice of the Presence of God, have taught many leaders how to rest in God even in the middle of work. A friend wrote of him:

“The time of business,” said he, “does not with me differ from the time of prayer; and in the noise and clatter of my kitchen, while several persons are at the same time calling for different things, I possess God in as great tranquility as if I were upon my knees at the blessed sacrament.”

— The Practice of the Presence of God

In plain words: for me, work time is no different from prayer time. Even in my noisy kitchen, with several people calling for different things at once, I enjoy God’s presence as calmly as if I were kneeling in church.

These three men teach us three kinds of rest. Bernard teaches us to stop and consider. Antony teaches us to withdraw into solitude with God. Brother Lawrence teaches us to rest in God even while we work. Every leader needs all three.

The rest that remains

The letter to the Hebrews says, “So a Sabbath rest is still waiting for God’s people. For whoever has entered God’s rest has come to rest from their own works too, just as God did from his” (Hebrews 4:9-10). Our weekly rest is a small picture of the great rest that awaits us in God’s presence forever. And it reminds us that our salvation does not depend on our works. Christ has finished the work. We can rest in Him.

Jesus’ invitation is for leaders too: “Come to me, all of you who are worn out with work and weighed down with burdens, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). If you are tired, come to Him. Lay down the burden you were never meant to carry alone. Then, rested and renewed, take up His yoke, which is “easy to wear”, and His load, which “is light” (Matthew 11:30).

Questions for reflection

  • Do you rest one day each week? If not, what is stopping you?
  • Which of the reasons leaders find it hard to rest is most true of you?
  • Read Psalm 127:1-2. Where are you working with “anxious work” rather than trust?
  • Read 1 Kings 19:1-8. What does God’s care for Elijah teach you about your own limits?
  • Are you more like Martha or Mary? What would it look like to choose “the good share” this week?
  • Which of the three kinds of rest (Bernard’s consideration, Antony’s solitude, Brother Lawrence’s presence of God at work) do you most need?

A step for this week

Choose one day this week, or part of a day, as a day of rest. Tell your family and the people you lead in advance. On that day, do not do your usual work. Spend time with God, with your family, outdoors, or doing something that renews you. Also choose one hour this week to be completely alone with God, without your phone. Use it to sit quietly, read a psalm, and tell God honestly how you are. At the end of the week, notice how you feel.

study_questions.question: Is rest important for Christian leaders?
study_questions.answer: Yes. Rest is God’s idea: “on the seventh day he stopped all the work he had done” (Genesis 2:2). Jesus told His tired disciples, “Come away on your own, to a place without people, and get a little rest” (Mark 6:31).

study_questions.question: Why do leaders find it hard to rest?
study_questions.answer: Because the needs never end, because they feel indispensable, and sometimes because their worth is tied to their work. The chapter reminds them that even Jesus “was worn out from the journey” and sat down by the well (John 4:6).

study_questions.question: What is a healthy rhythm of work and rest?
study_questions.answer: A weekly day of rest, daily time with God, and longer seasons of retreat. God commanded rest “even when the fields need plowing or the harvest is ready” (Exodus 34:21). The chapter draws on Bernard, Antony and Brother Lawrence and on the story of Martha and Mary.

fields.title: Guidance and Decisions
fields.body_html:
“Trust the LORD with your whole heart, and do not rely on your own insight. Keep him in mind in everything you do, and he will clear a straight road ahead of you.”

— Proverbs 3:5-6 (OWB)

Leaders make decisions every day. Most are small: what to say in a meeting, whom to visit, how to answer a message. Some are large: whether to plant a new church, whom to appoint as an elder, whether to move to a new place, how to respond to a crisis. Many leaders carry these decisions alone, lying awake at night and wondering whether they have chosen rightly.

God does not want His servants to lead in the dark. He has promised to guide those who seek Him: “I will give you insight and show you the road you are to take; I will advise you and keep my eye on you” (Psalm 32:8). This chapter closes Part Three by asking how leaders can seek God’s will, alone and together, and make wise decisions that honour Him.

God guides His people

The whole Bible tells the story of a God who leads. He led Abraham to a land he did not know. He led Israel through the wilderness with a cloud by day and fire by night. He spoke to the prophets. He guided David in battle. And Jesus said, “The sheep that belong to me listen to my voice; I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:27). A shepherd who did not lead would not be a shepherd at all.

Yet God’s guidance is not usually a voice from heaven telling us exactly what to do. More often, He guides us through His Word, through prayer, through the wisdom He gives, through other believers and through the way He arranges our circumstances. Learning to recognise His guidance is a lifelong lesson.

Trust, not your own insight

Proverbs 3:5-6 gives the foundation: “Trust the LORD with your whole heart, and do not rely on your own insight. Keep him in mind in everything you do, and he will clear a straight road ahead of you.”

This does not mean that we should not think. God gave us minds, and He expects us to use them. It means that we should not trust our own understanding more than we trust God. Leaders are often clever, experienced and confident. That is exactly why they are in danger of deciding without God.

The Bible gives a warning example. When Joshua was leading Israel into the promised land, a group of men came to him pretending to be from a faraway country. They wore old clothes and carried dry, mouldy bread, and they asked for a peace treaty. Joshua and the leaders looked at the evidence and it seemed convincing. “The men of Israel took some of their provisions, but they did not seek the word of the LORD” (Joshua 9:14). They made the treaty, and three days later they discovered that they had been deceived. The men lived nearby. Joshua had made a decision that seemed obvious, and he had not prayed about it.

David, by contrast, often “inquired of the LORD” before acting. When the Philistines attacked, he asked God whether to go up against them, and God said yes (1 Chronicles 14:10). When they attacked again in the same place, David did not assume the answer would be the same. He asked again, and this time God gave him a different plan (1 Chronicles 14:14). Past guidance is not a substitute for present prayer.

How God guides

F. B. Meyer, a Baptist pastor in London in the late 1800s and early 1900s, wrote a short and much-loved booklet called The Secret of Guidance, which is on Ochorus. He gave five practical directions for anyone seeking God’s will. They are a good framework for leaders.

1. Our motives must be pure. Meyer wrote that as long as we are secretly seeking our own advantage or the praise of people, “it will be simply impossible to find out God’s purpose concerning us.” Before we ask what God wants, we must ask why we want what we want. Is this decision for God’s glory and the good of His people, or for my comfort, my reputation or my ambition?

2. Our will must be surrendered. God’s will is not a menu from which we choose what we like. We must be willing to do whatever He shows us before He shows it. Jesus prayed in the garden, “let your will be done, not mine” (Luke 22:42). A leader who has already decided, and only wants God to approve, is not really seeking guidance.

3. We must seek information for our mind. God guides through understanding. Gather the facts. Study what the Bible says about the matter. Think carefully. Ask the advice of wise people. “Plans go wrong for lack of advice, but with many advisers they succeed” (Proverbs 15:22).

4. We must be much in prayer for guidance. “If any of you is short of wisdom, ask God, who gives to everyone with an open hand and without scolding, and it will be given to you” (James 1:5). Notice that God gives “without scolding”. He is not annoyed when we ask for help. He delights to give wisdom to those who ask.

5. We must wait for God’s plan to unfold. Meyer wrote that God’s inner prompting, His Word and His providence will agree: “God’s impressions within and His word without are always corroborated by His Providence around, and we should quietly wait until these three focus into one point.” In plain words: when God is guiding, the inner sense He gives us, the teaching of the Bible and the way circumstances develop will come together and point in the same direction. If they do not agree, wait.

The Word comes first

Of all the ways God guides, His Word is the most important and the most certain. “Your word is a lamp to guide my feet and a light for the road I travel” (Psalm 119:105). God will never guide us to do something His Word forbids. If someone says, “God told me to leave my wife,” or “The Spirit led me to take this money,” and the Bible clearly says otherwise, they are not hearing God.

Many decisions are already settled by Scripture. We do not need to pray about whether to forgive someone, tell the truth or care for the poor. God has already told us. Paul wrote, “do not be senseless. Come to understand what the Lord wants” (Ephesians 5:17). Much of God’s will is plainly written in the Bible. The more we know it, the more we will recognise His guidance in the matters it does not directly address.

Paul also says that guidance depends on a renewed mind: “Do not let this present age press you into its mold, but be changed through and through as your mind is made new. Then you will be able to test and recognize the will of God” (Romans 12:2). A leader whose thinking is shaped by the Bible will find it easier to discern God’s will than one whose thinking is shaped by the world.

Deciding together: the Jerusalem council

Some of the most important decisions in the Bible were made not by one leader alone, but by leaders together. The clearest example is in Acts 15.

A serious question had arisen in the early Church. Some teachers were saying that Gentile believers had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be saved. Paul and Barnabas strongly disagreed. “This led to fierce dispute and argument” (Acts 15:2). The question was so important that it could have split the Church in two.

So “The apostles and the elders came together to consider this matter” (Acts 15:6). Look at how they made their decision.

  • They met together. No single leader decided for everyone.
  • They debated openly. “After a long debate” (Acts 15:7), they did not avoid the disagreement or hurry to a conclusion.
  • They listened to experience. Peter told how God had given the Spirit to Gentiles. “The whole gathering grew quiet. Everyone listened to Barnabas and Paul as they told of the signs and wonders God had worked among the Gentiles through them” (Acts 15:12).
  • They searched the Scriptures. James quoted the prophet Amos to show that God had always planned to include the Gentiles (Acts 15:15-18).
  • A leader summed up. James said, “So my judgment is that we should not make things hard for the Gentiles who are turning to God” (Acts 15:19).
  • The whole church agreed. “Then the apostles and the elders, together with the whole church, decided” (Acts 15:22).
  • They recognised God’s guidance. In their letter they wrote, “The Holy Spirit and we ourselves have decided” (Acts 15:28).

That last phrase is beautiful: “The Holy Spirit and we ourselves.” They did not claim a private revelation. They did not simply vote. They prayed, listened, searched Scripture and discussed until they were confident that their decision was also the Spirit’s decision. This is a model for church leaders today, especially for big decisions.

Open doors and closed doors

Sometimes God guides by closing doors. On his second missionary journey, Paul and his companions went on through Phrygia and Galatia, “because the Holy Spirit had stopped them from speaking the word in Asia.” Then they tried to go to Bithynia, “but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit it.” We are not told how. Perhaps through illness, opposition or a word from a prophet. Then, at Troas, Paul saw a vision of a man saying, “Cross over to Macedonia and help us!” and they set out, “sure now that God had called us” (Acts 16:6-10).

Paul did not sit still waiting for perfect guidance. He kept moving in the direction he thought best, and God redirected him. It is often easier for God to steer a moving ship than one tied up in the harbour. But Paul was also willing to be stopped. A wise leader holds their plans loosely.

Some cautions

Seeking God’s guidance can go wrong. Here are some common dangers.

  • Signs and fleeces. Gideon asked God for a sign with a wool fleece, twice (Judges 6:36-40). God graciously answered. But Gideon was asking for confirmation of what God had already said clearly, because he was afraid. We should be careful about building decisions on signs we have invented. God may graciously use them, but they are not His usual way.
  • Feelings alone. Peace is important. Paul says, “Let the peace that Christ gives be the umpire in your hearts” (Colossians 3:15). But feelings can be affected by tiredness, fear or desire. Test your feelings by Scripture and wise counsel.
  • Claiming too much. Some leaders say “God told me” to end discussion and silence disagreement. That is a misuse of authority. Be humble about your sense of God’s leading, especially when it affects others.
  • Different words from others. When Paul was going to Jerusalem, the believers in Tyre urged him not to: “Speaking through the Spirit, they kept telling Paul not to go” (Acts 21:4). Yet Paul believed God was sending him, and he went. Sometimes faithful believers disagree about what God is saying. In the end, Paul’s friends said, “Let the Lord’s will be done” (Acts 21:14).
  • Waiting forever. Some people never decide because they are afraid of choosing wrongly. God is not trying to hide His will from us. If you have prayed, searched the Scriptures, sought counsel and your motives are pure, it is often right to take a step of faith and trust God to redirect you if necessary.

A voice from the Church: Hudson Taylor on the sands at Brighton

In 1865 Hudson Taylor was back in England after his first years in China. He was troubled by a great burden. Millions of people in China’s inland provinces had never heard the gospel, and no missionary society was sending workers there. He believed God might want him to start a new mission. But he was afraid. If he asked people to go, and they suffered or died, he would be responsible. If he started a mission without guaranteed money, how would they live?

For months he wrestled with the decision. His health began to break down. Then a friend invited him to stay in the seaside town of Brighton. On Sunday, 25 June 1865, Taylor went to church, but he could not bear to sit among a thousand comfortable Christians while millions in China were perishing. He walked out alone onto the beach. In A Retrospect he described what happened:

“There the Lord conquered my unbelief, and I surrendered myself to God for this service. I told Him that all the responsibility as to issues and consequences must rest with Him; that as His servant, it was mine to obey and to follow Him—His, to direct, to care for, and to guide me and those who might labour with me. Need I say that peace at once flowed into my burdened heart?”

— Hudson Taylor, A Retrospect

In plain words: on the beach, God overcame my unbelief, and I gave myself to Him for this work. I told Him that the results and the consequences were His responsibility. My part was to obey and follow. His part was to direct, care for and guide me and everyone who worked with me. And immediately, peace came into my heart.

Then and there, Taylor asked God for twenty-four workers, two for each of the eleven inland provinces without a missionary and two for Mongolia. He wrote the request in the margin of his Bible. Within a year, the China Inland Mission had been founded, and the first group of workers sailed for China. Over the following decades it sent hundreds of missionaries into every province.

Notice the shape of Taylor’s guidance. He had a burden that grew over time. He had studied the need. He had prayed for months. He had sought counsel. But the decisive step came when he surrendered his will completely to God and laid the responsibility for the outcome on Him. Meyer’s second direction, “our will must be surrendered”, was the key that unlocked everything else.

He will clear the road

Proverbs promises that if we trust the Lord and keep Him in mind in everything, “he will clear a straight road ahead of you” (Proverbs 3:6). Leaders do not need to know the whole road. We need to take the next step in trust. “People plot their course in their minds, but it is the LORD who guides their steps” (Proverbs 16:9).

This brings Part Three to a close. We have looked at the hidden life of a leader with God: prayer, the Word, the Spirit, rest and guidance. In Part Four we turn to the daily work of a shepherd: feeding, knowing, seeking, correcting and comforting the flock.

Questions for reflection

  • What decision are you facing right now as a leader? Have you truly sought God about it?
  • Read Joshua 9:3-15. When have you made a decision that seemed obvious without asking God?
  • Which of Meyer’s five directions (pure motives, a surrendered will, information, prayer, waiting) do you most often skip?
  • Read Acts 15:1-29. What can your church or leadership team learn from the way the Jerusalem council made its decision?
  • Have you ever said “God told me” in a way that ended discussion? How could you speak about God’s guidance more humbly?
  • Hudson Taylor found peace when he gave the responsibility for the outcome to God. What outcome do you need to give to Him?

A step for this week

Write down one decision you are facing. Then work through Meyer’s five directions on paper. First, write honestly about your motives. Second, pray a prayer of surrender: “Lord, I will do whatever You show me.” Third, write down what the Bible says that relates to this decision, and the facts you know. Fourth, pray about it every day this week. Fifth, ask at least two wise believers for their counsel. At the end of the week, see whether your inner sense, God’s Word and your circumstances are beginning to point in the same direction.

study_questions.question: How does God guide leaders?
study_questions.answer: Chiefly through His Word, and also through prayer, wise counsel, circumstances and the inner witness of the Spirit. “Trust the LORD with your whole heart, and do not rely on your own insight” (Proverbs 3:5). He promises, “I will give you insight and show you the road you are to take” (Psalm 32:8).

study_questions.question: Why should leaders make decisions with others?
study_questions.answer: Because “Plans go wrong for lack of advice, but with many advisers they succeed” (Proverbs 15:22). The early Church settled a great question together at the Jerusalem council, and Joshua erred when “they did not seek the word of the LORD” (Joshua 9:14).

study_questions.question: What should I do when I do not know what to decide?
study_questions.answer: Ask God. “If any of you is short of wisdom, ask God, who gives to everyone with an open hand and without scolding” (James 1:5). Test the decision by Scripture, seek counsel, and be ready to say with Jesus, “let your will be done, not mine” (Luke 22:42).

fields.title: Feed My Sheep
fields.body_html:
“Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.”

— John 21:17 (OWB)

On a beach in Galilee, early in the morning, the risen Jesus cooked breakfast for His disciples. Only a few days earlier, Peter had denied Him three times. Now Jesus asked Peter three times, “Do you love me?” Each time Peter said yes. And each time Jesus gave him the same kind of work: “Feed my lambs.” “Shepherd my sheep.” “Feed my sheep” (John 21:15-17).

Notice what Jesus did not say.
