He did not say, “If you love me, build a large church,” or “If you love me, become famous.” He said, “If you love me, feed my sheep.” The test of Peter’s love for Christ would be his care for Christ’s people. And the first way he would care for them was by feeding them.

This chapter begins Part Four, Shepherding the Flock. In Part Three we saw that a leader must first be fed by God in prayer and in His Word. Now we turn to the people. A shepherd who does not feed the sheep is not a shepherd, however busy he or she may be.

Whose sheep are they?

Jesus said “my lambs” and “my sheep”. The flock does not belong to Peter. It belongs to Christ. Paul told the elders of Ephesus to “shepherd the church of God, which he won for himself through his own blood” (Acts 20:28). Peter later wrote to other leaders, “Tend God’s flock among you as shepherds do” (1 Peter 5:2).

This changes everything about how we feed people. We are not feeding our own followers so that they will admire us. We are feeding the people Jesus bought with His blood, so that they will grow strong in Him. They are not ours to use. They are His to serve. A cook in a great house does not choose what pleases the cook. The cook prepares what the master has asked for, for the master’s guests.

It also brings comfort. When the flock is weak or scattered, we do not carry the weight alone. The sheep are Christ’s, and He cares for them more than we ever could.

The hunger of the crowd

One day, when Jesus came ashore, “he saw a great crowd. He felt deep pity for them, for they were like sheep with no shepherd, and he began to teach them at length” (Mark 6:34). Notice what His pity led Him to do. He did heal people and feed them with bread. But here, the first thing His compassion did was teach.

We sometimes think that teaching is cold and that caring is warm. Jesus did not think so. He saw that people without the truth of God are like sheep lost on a hillside. They do not know where to find food or water or safety. The kindest thing He could do for them was to tell them the truth about God.

In many places today the Church is growing quickly, but teaching has not kept up. There are many new believers and few trained teachers. Some churches have plenty of noise and excitement, but people go home hungry. Others have long services, but the sermons are about the preacher’s opinions, the latest news, or how to become rich. The Bible warns about this: “a time will come when people will not put up with sound teaching. Instead, wanting to hear what their ears itch for, they will gather around them a great number of teachers to suit their own desires” (2 Timothy 4:3). A leader who loves the sheep will give them real food, even when they would prefer sweets.

Feeding them well

What does it mean to feed God’s people well? The Bible gives us several marks.

Feed them with the Word. Paul’s last charge to Timothy was plain: “Preach the word. Be ready whether the time seems right or not. Correct, rebuke and encourage, with great patience and careful teaching” (2 Timothy 4:2). Our own stories, ideas and experiences may help to explain the Word, but they cannot replace it.

Feed them with the whole Word. Paul told the Ephesian elders, “I never drew back from making known to you God’s whole plan” (Acts 20:27). He did not choose only the popular parts. Over time, a faithful leader teaches the whole story of the Bible: creation, the fall, the promises to Israel, Christ’s life, death and resurrection, the Church, and the new creation. People who only ever hear a few favourite subjects will be weak and unbalanced.

Help them understand. When Ezra read the law to the people after the exile, the Levites “read from the book, from the law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood what was read” (Nehemiah 8:8). Reading is not enough. We must explain. When the Ethiopian official was reading Isaiah in his chariot, Philip asked him, “Do you know what it is you are reading?” He answered, “How could I ... if no one guides me?” (Acts 8:30-31). Many people in our churches are asking the same question. Use simple words. Use pictures from daily life, as Jesus did with seeds, sheep, coins and bread. In places where many languages are spoken, teach in the language people think and pray in.

Feed them what they can take. Paul told the Corinthians, “Milk was what I gave you to drink, not solid food, since you could not yet take it” (1 Corinthians 3:2). New believers need the simple truths first. But Hebrews warns that people should not stay on milk for ever: “you ought to be teachers by now; yet once more you need someone to teach you the most basic elements” (Hebrews 5:12). A good shepherd gives milk to the young and solid food to the growing, and leads them on to maturity.

Aim at maturity in Christ. Paul summed up his whole ministry like this: “Christ is the one we proclaim. We warn every person and teach every person with all wisdom, so that we may bring every person before God mature in Christ” (Colossians 1:28). The goal is not to fill people’s heads, nor to make them depend on us. The goal is grown-up Christians who know Christ, obey Him and can feed others.

In public and from house to house

Feeding the flock does not happen only from the pulpit. Paul reminded the Ephesian elders, “You know how I held back nothing that was for your good, but made it known to you and taught you, in public and from house to house” (Acts 20:20).

Some of the most important teaching happens in small places: a Bible study in a home, a conversation over a meal, a leader reading Scripture with a new believer under a tree, a mother teaching her children at bedtime. The first Christians “gave themselves fully to the apostles’ teaching and to the shared life, to the breaking of bread and to the prayers” (Acts 2:42). Teaching and shared life went together.

Jesus told His followers to make disciples and to “teach them to keep everything I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:20). Notice the words “to keep”. The aim of teaching is not only that people know what Jesus commanded, but that they do it. That kind of teaching needs more than a sermon. It needs example, conversation, questions and practice. In the next chapter we will see why a shepherd must know each sheep in order to feed them well.

The teacher’s own life

Paul told Timothy, “Keep a close watch on yourself and on your teaching. Persevere in them, for if you do, you will save both yourself and your hearers” (1 Timothy 4:16). Notice the order again: first yourself, then your teaching. We saw in Chapter 9, Keep Watch over Yourself, that a leader’s own soul comes first. The same is true when we teach.

People do not only listen to our words. They watch our lives. If a leader teaches about patience and is known for shouting at his wife, the people will believe what they see, not what they hear. If a leader teaches generosity and is known to be greedy, the sermon will be empty. But when a leader’s life matches the Word, even simple teaching has great power.

A voice from the Church: Augustine and Charles Spurgeon

Augustine was a bishop in Hippo, in North Africa, in the late fourth and early fifth centuries. Before he became a Christian, he had been a teacher of public speaking. He knew all the tricks of a clever speaker. After he came to Christ, he wrote a book called On Christian Doctrine to help preachers and teachers. In it he quoted a famous Roman speaker who said a good speaker must teach, delight and persuade. Augustine agreed, but he said that teaching comes first. Delight and persuasion matter, but if people do not understand the truth, nothing else helps. He also wrote that there is no point in a golden key that cannot open the door, and no shame in a wooden key that can. What matters is not fine words but that the truth reaches the hearer.

Then Augustine said something every teacher needs to hear:

“But whatever may be the majesty of the style, the life of the speaker will count for more in securing the hearer’s compliance.”

— Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, Book IV

In plain words: however well you speak, your life will do more than your words to help people obey God.

Fourteen centuries later, Charles Spurgeon trained hundreds of young pastors in London. His talks to them are collected in Lectures to My Students, which is on Ochorus. Spurgeon had no patience with sermons that sounded nice but gave no food:

“Sermons should have real teaching in them, and their doctrine should be solid, substantial, and abundant. We do not enter the pulpit to talk for talk’s sake; we have instructions to convey important to the last degree, and we cannot afford to utter pretty nothings.”

— Charles Spurgeon, Lectures to My Students

In plain words: a sermon must teach something real. We do not preach just to fill the time. God has given us a message of the greatest importance, so we cannot waste people’s time with nice words that say nothing.

Spurgeon also begged his students to keep Christ at the centre. He wrote, “O that Christ crucified were the universal burden of men of God.” He warned them not to be pulled away into guessing about the end of the world, or arguing about politics, while people around them were dying without Christ. Whatever we teach, every road must lead back to Jesus and His cross.

Do you love Him?

Come back to the beach in Galilee. Peter had failed badly. But Jesus did not give up on him. He restored him with a question and a command: “Do you love me? Feed my sheep.” Peter spent the rest of his life doing exactly that. Years later he wrote to other leaders, “Tend God’s flock among you as shepherds do” (1 Peter 5:2). The man who had been fed by Jesus on the beach became a feeder of others.

Jesus asks every leader the same question. Do you love Him? Then feed His sheep. Prepare carefully. Teach clearly. Give the whole Word. Explain it simply. Live what you teach. And do it for love of Him, because they are His sheep and He bought them with His blood.

Questions for reflection

  • Read John 21:15-17. Why do you think Jesus connected Peter’s love for Him with feeding His sheep?
  • Jesus’ pity for the crowd led Him to teach them (Mark 6:34). Do you see teaching as an act of love? Why or why not?
  • Are the people you lead hearing the whole story of the Bible, or only a few favourite subjects?
  • Read Nehemiah 8:8. What could you do to help people understand the Bible better, not only hear it read?
  • Are the people you teach growing towards maturity, or are they still on milk? What would help them grow?
  • Augustine said the life of the speaker counts for more than the style. Where does your life support your teaching, and where does it undermine it?

A step for this week

Choose one person you lead who is young in faith. Arrange to meet them this week, in their home or yours, and read a short passage of Scripture together, such as Mark 6:30-44. Read it aloud, explain it simply, and ask them two questions: “What does this show us about Jesus?” and “What should we do because of it?” Then pray together. Notice how much they understand, and what they still need. Let that shape what you teach next.

study_questions.question: What did Jesus mean when He told Peter to feed His sheep?
study_questions.answer: He gave Peter the work of caring for His people, especially by teaching them His Word. The sheep belong to Christ, who “won for himself through his own blood” the Church (Acts 20:28). Peter later told elders, “Tend God’s flock among you as shepherds do” (1 Peter 5:2).

study_questions.question: Why did Jesus teach the crowds?
study_questions.answer: Because of compassion: “He felt deep pity for them, for they were like sheep with no shepherd, and he began to teach them” (Mark 6:34). Teaching God’s Word is one of the main ways a shepherd feeds people.

study_questions.question: How can a leader feed the flock well?
study_questions.answer: By preaching the Word faithfully and patiently, “whether the time seems right or not” (2 Timothy 4:2), even when people want only what their ears itch to hear. Feeding happens in public teaching and from house to house, and the teacher’s own life must match the message.

fields.title: Knowing the Sheep
fields.body_html:
“Know how your flocks are doing, and keep your mind on your herds.”

— Proverbs 27:23 (OWB)

A herder in the hills knows his animals. He knows which goat is old and slow, which one is about to give birth, which one always wanders off towards the road, and which one is limping because of a thorn in its foot. He does not treat them all the same. He cannot, because they are not all the same. And if he does not know them, he cannot care for them.

In the last chapter we saw that a shepherd must feed the flock. But you cannot feed people well if you do not know them. A sermon can be preached to a crowd. But shepherding happens one person at a time. This chapter is about knowing the sheep.

The Shepherd who knows His sheep

Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd. I know those who are mine, and those who are mine know me” (John 10:14). He also said that the shepherd “calls each of his own sheep by name and leads them out” (John 10:3).

Think about how Jesus dealt with people in the Gospels. He did not have one method for everyone. To Nicodemus, a teacher of the law, He spoke about being born again (John 3). To the Samaritan woman at the well, He spoke about living water and gently uncovered her painful past (John 4). To the rich young man, He said, “Go and sell everything you own, and give the money to the poor” (Mark 10:21), because money was the thing that held his heart. To Zacchaeus, the hated tax collector, He simply said He was coming to his house (Luke 19:5). To Thomas, who doubted, He showed His wounds (John 20:27). To Peter, after his failure, He asked three times, “Do you love me?” (John 21:15-17).

Each person received what they needed, because Jesus knew each one. He is our model. We cannot know people the way He does, for He sees the heart. But we can learn their names, their stories, their burdens and their dangers.

Shepherds who did not know

In Chapter 3, Jesus, the Chief Shepherd, we read God’s judgement on the shepherds of Israel in Ezekiel 34. Look at what they failed to do: “You have not strengthened the weak or healed the sick or bandaged the injured. You have not brought back the strays or gone looking for the lost” (Ezekiel 34:4).

Notice that God names different kinds of sheep: the weak, the sick, the injured, the strays and the lost. Each one needed something different. The weak needed strength. The sick needed healing. The injured needed bandaging. The strays needed bringing back. The lost needed searching for. The bad shepherds did none of this, because they were caring only for themselves. They did not even notice who was weak and who was lost.

Then God promised to be the shepherd Himself: “I will search for the lost and bring back the strays. I will bandage the injured and strengthen the sick” (Ezekiel 34:16). A shepherd after God’s heart will do the same. But first we must notice which sheep is which.

Different people, different care

Paul gave the church in Thessalonica a short but very wise instruction: “We urge you, brothers and sisters: correct those who are out of line, encourage the fainthearted, stand by the weak, and be patient with everyone” (1 Thessalonians 5:14).

Look closely at this verse. Paul names three kinds of people, and gives each a different kind of care.

  • Those who are out of line need to be corrected. They are drifting, careless or disobedient. Gentle words alone will not help them. They need a clear warning.
  • The fainthearted need to be encouraged. They are timid, anxious or discouraged. A sharp warning would crush them. They need to hear hope.
  • The weak need someone to stand by them. They are struggling, perhaps with sickness, poverty or a sin they cannot yet overcome. They need practical help and someone close.

And then Paul adds: “be patient with everyone.” Every kind of person tests a leader’s patience in a different way.

The danger is to give the wrong medicine. If we warn the fainthearted, we break them. If we only comfort the careless, we let them go on to destruction. A doctor who gave every patient the same medicine would kill some of them. A leader who treats everyone the same will harm some of them too. That is why we must know the sheep.

How to know the flock

The proverb says, “Know how your flocks are doing” (Proverbs 27:23). How can a leader do this?

Learn names. It sounds small, but it matters. A person who is known by name feels that they belong. Jesus calls His sheep by name.

Visit people where they live. You learn more about a family in one hour in their home than in a year of greeting them at the church door. You see their work, their children, their struggles. Paul taught “from house to house” (Acts 20:20).

Listen more than you speak. Ask good questions. “How is your walk with God?” “What is hard for you right now?” “How can I pray for you?” Then listen to the answer, and remember it.

Watch for changes. Notice who has stopped coming, who looks tired or troubled, who has gone quiet. Often the first sign of a sheep in danger is that it drifts to the edge of the flock.

Care for the sick. James wrote, “Is anyone among you ill? That person should call for the elders of the church, and they should pray over the sick person” (James 5:14). Times of sickness, birth, death and trouble are when people most need their shepherds, and when they remember most who came.

Share the work. No one can know a thousand people well. Jesus had twelve close disciples, and three who were closest. A wise leader of a large church makes sure that every person is known by someone: an elder, a deacon, a small group leader. We will look at this more in Part Five, Leading Together.

The danger of the crowd

Some leaders love crowds. They feel alive in front of hundreds of people. But they feel uncomfortable sitting with one grieving widow or one confused young man. They would rather preach than visit.

Crowds can hide a lot. A leader can preach to a full room every week and not know that a young couple’s marriage is falling apart, or that an old man has not eaten properly for a week, or that a teenager is thinking of leaving the faith. The crowd looks healthy, but individual sheep are dying.

Paul did not only preach to crowds. He told the Ephesian elders that for three years he had not stopped, “night or day, admonishing each one of you with tears” (Acts 20:31). Each one. That is shepherding.

A voice from the Church: Gregory the Great and Richard Baxter

Gregory the Great, whom we met in Chapter 2, What Makes Leadership Spiritual, was bishop of Rome at the end of the sixth century. His Book of Pastoral Rule was read by church leaders for a thousand years. The whole third part of the book is about one simple idea: people are different, so they must be taught differently.

Gregory said that a teacher is like a musician playing a harp. The musician plays one song, but does not strike every string in the same way. So a leader “ought to touch the hearts of his hearers out of one doctrine, but not with one and the same exhortation.” In plain words: we teach the same truth to everyone, but we apply it differently to each person. Gregory gave a long list of the kinds of people who need different counsel. It begins like this:

“Men and women. The poor and the rich. The joyful and the sad. Prelates and subordinates. Servants and masters. The wise of this world and the dull. The impudent and the bashful. The forward and the fainthearted. The impatient and the patient.”

— Gregory the Great, The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part III

The list goes on for many lines. Gregory explained that “the medicine which abates one disease aggravates another”, which means that a medicine that cures one illness can make another illness worse. A rich man and a poor man, a proud woman and a timid one, need different words.

A thousand years later, Richard Baxter, whom we met in Chapter 9, Keep Watch over Yourself, put this into practice in the English town of Kidderminster. His book The Reformed Pastor, which is on Ochorus, is built on Acts 20:28, “Be on your guard, for yourselves and for the whole flock.” Baxter took the words “the whole flock” seriously:

“It is necessary, that we should know every person that belongeth to our charge; for how can we take heed to them, if we do not know them? We must labor to be acquainted, not only with the persons, but with the state of all our people.”

— Richard Baxter, The Reformed Pastor

In plain words: we must know every person in our care, because we cannot look after people we do not know. We must learn not only their names but the state of their souls.

Baxter did not only write this. He did it. His parish had more than eight hundred families. So he and his assistant set aside every Monday and Tuesday, “from morning almost to night”, and met with fifteen or sixteen families each week, one family at a time, to talk with them about their faith. In this way they met every family in the parish each year. Baxter wrote that he saw more fruit from these personal meetings “than from all my public preaching to them.” Over the years, the town was changed. It is said that when Baxter arrived, there was hardly a family on some streets that worshipped God at home. By the time he left, there were streets where hardly a family did not.

Most of us will not lead eight hundred families. But all of us can ask Baxter’s question: do I know the people God has put in my care?

Known and loved

Many people in our world feel unknown. In big cities, people live close together but no one knows their name. In villages, people may be known, but their deepest struggles are hidden. In the Church of Jesus Christ, it should be different. Every person should be known, and loved, by someone who cares for their soul.

The Good Shepherd knows His sheep, and they know Him. As His under-shepherds, we are called to be like Him. Not to manage crowds, but to know people. Not to handle numbers, but to care for souls, one by one, by name.

Questions for reflection

  • Read John 4 and John 3 side by side. How did Jesus deal differently with Nicodemus and the Samaritan woman?
  • Read 1 Thessalonians 5:14. Think of the people you lead. Who needs correction? Who needs encouragement? Who needs someone to stand by them?
  • Have you ever given the wrong medicine, by warning someone who needed comfort, or comforting someone who needed warning? What happened?
  • How many of the people you lead could you name? How many homes have you visited this year?
  • Is there anyone in your church who is not known well by any leader? How could that change?
  • What could you learn from Baxter’s practice of meeting families one by one?

A step for this week

Write down the names of the people you lead. Next to each name, write one thing you know about the state of their soul right now. Where you cannot write anything, mark the name. This week, visit or call at least three of the people you marked. Ask them, “How is your walk with God?” and “How can I pray for you?” Listen carefully, pray with them, and write down what you learn.

study_questions.question: Why should a leader know the people personally?
study_questions.answer: Because that is how Jesus shepherds: “I am the good shepherd. I know those who are mine, and those who are mine know me” (John 10:14). He “calls each of his own sheep by name” (John 10:3). “Know how your flocks are doing” (Proverbs 27:23).

study_questions.question: Do different people need different care?
study_questions.answer: Yes. The weak need strengthening, the sick healing, the injured bandaging, and the lost seeking (Ezekiel 34:4, 16). Gregory the Great taught that a pastor must speak differently to different people, and Richard Baxter visited every family in his parish.

study_questions.question: How can a leader get to know a large congregation?
study_questions.answer: By visiting homes, keeping a list of names and praying through it, sharing leadership with others who each know a few people well, and watching for those who are slipping away unnoticed in the crowd.

fields.title: Seeking the Lost
fields.body_html:
“The Son of Man came to look for what was lost and to save it.”

— Luke 19:10 (OWB)

When a child goes missing in a village, everything stops. The market closes. The fields are left. Neighbours run in every direction calling the child’s name. Nobody says, “We still have the other children, so it does not matter.” Nobody goes home to sleep until the child is found.

That is how God feels about lost people. And a leader after His heart will feel the same.

In the last two chapters we thought about feeding the flock and knowing the sheep. But a shepherd’s work is not only inside the fold. Jesus said, “I have other sheep as well, which are not of this fold. I must bring them too” (John 10:16). This chapter is about seeking the lost.

The heart of the seeking God

Luke 15 contains three stories that Jesus told when the religious leaders complained that He welcomed sinners and ate with them. A shepherd loses one sheep out of a hundred. A woman loses one coin out of ten. A father loses one son out of two.

In each story, something precious is lost. In each story, there is a search, or a long wait. And in each story, there is a party when the lost is found. Jesus said of the shepherd, “when he finds it, he hoists it onto his shoulders, delighted” (Luke 15:5). And then He explained: “one sinner who repents will bring more joy in heaven than ninety-nine righteous people who have no need to repent” (Luke 15:7).

Notice who was listening. The stories were told to religious leaders who did not care about the lost. The older brother in the third story is a picture of them. He was angry that his father welcomed the younger son home. He had stayed close to the house, but his heart was far from his father’s heart.

This is a warning for every leader. It is possible to work hard in the church for years, to be faithful in meetings and services, and yet not share the Father’s joy over one sinner who comes home. If the salvation of the lost does not move us, we have not understood the heart of God.

Jesus came to seek

Jesus summed up His whole mission when He spoke to Zacchaeus: “The Son of Man came to look for what was lost and to save it” (Luke 19:10). He did not wait for the lost to come to Him. He went to them. He went to the house of a tax collector. He talked with a Samaritan woman at a well. He touched lepers. He crossed the lake to a man possessed by demons. His enemies called Him “a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Luke 7:34), and meant it as an insult. Jesus wore it as a badge of love.

When He called His first disciples, He said, “Come, follow me ... and I will make you fishers of people” (Matthew 4:19). Following Jesus and fishing for people go together. You cannot really follow Him without going where He goes, and He goes after the lost.

Do the work of an evangelist

Paul wrote to Timothy, who was a pastor and teacher in Ephesus, “do the work of an evangelist, and carry out your ministry fully” (2 Timothy 4:5). Some people have a special gift for evangelism. But every leader is called to do the work, whether they have the gift or not.

Many pastors spend all their time with believers. Their week is full of meetings, sermons, visits and problems inside the church. Years pass and they have not had one real conversation with someone who does not know Christ. When that happens, the church usually follows. A church becomes like its leaders. If the leaders do not seek the lost, the people will not either.

Paul asked a series of questions: “How, then, are they to call on him if they have not believed in him? And how are they to believe in him if they have never heard him? And how are they to hear without someone proclaiming?” (Romans 10:14). Somebody must tell them. God’s plan is to reach people through people.

How leaders seek the lost

Pray for the lost by name. Keep a list of people you know who do not follow Christ: neighbours, relatives, colleagues, people you meet in the market. Pray for them often. In Chapter 12, Prayer First, we saw that prayer is the first work. That is as true in evangelism as anywhere.

Build real friendships. Jesus ate with sinners. He did not keep them at arm’s length. Many people come to faith through a friend they trust. Be a real friend, not someone who is kind only in order to win a convert.

Speak about Christ clearly. Friendship is not enough on its own. At some point the lost must hear the good news: that God made us, that we have sinned and turned from Him, that Jesus died for our sins and rose again, and that all who turn from sin and trust in Him are forgiven and made new. Learn to explain this simply, in a few minutes, in the language of the people you are speaking to.

Be ready to answer. Peter wrote, “Be ready at all times to make your defense to anyone who asks you for the reason behind the hope you hold” (1 Peter 3:15). People have real questions. Listen to them with respect, and answer honestly. If you do not know the answer, say so, and find out.

Become all things to all people. Paul wrote, “To all people I have become all things, so that one way or another I may save some” (1 Corinthians 9:22). He did not change the message, but he changed his manner so that the message could be heard. A leader who seeks the lost will learn the customs, the questions and the fears of the people around them.

Take others with you. Jesus sent His disciples out two by two. When you go to share the gospel, take a younger believer with you. They will learn more from watching you than from any class.

Open the doors of the church. Make sure that when a stranger comes, they are welcomed, not stared at. Make sure that the gospel is explained clearly in your gatherings, so that a visitor could understand how to be saved.

The fear that keeps us silent

Why do so many leaders find this hard? Often it is fear: fear of rejection, fear of looking foolish, fear of not knowing what to say, and in some places, fear of real danger. We will think about danger and persecution in Chapter 40, Persecution and the Cost.

Paul himself knew this fear. He asked the Ephesians to pray that he would “be given the words to make known with boldness the mystery of the gospel” (Ephesians 6:19). If the great apostle needed prayer for courage, so do we. Remember Chapter 11, Courage. Courage is not the absence of fear. It is obeying God while you are afraid.

Remember too that the result is not in our hands. We plant and water, but God gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6). Our part is to be faithful in telling. His part is to open hearts.

A voice from the Church: David Brainerd, Samson Occom and Charles Spurgeon

David Brainerd was a young American missionary in the 1740s who worked among the Native peoples of New York, Pennsylvania and New Jersey. He was often sick with tuberculosis, often lonely, and for a long time saw almost no fruit. But he never stopped praying for the people he longed to reach. His diary, which is on Ochorus, shows a heart on fire for the lost. He wrote:

“I cared not where or how I lived, or what hardships I went through, so that I could but gain souls to Christ.”

— David Brainerd, Life and Diary of David Brainerd

On another night he wrote that he had wrestled in prayer and that “I wanted to wear out my life in his service, and for his glory.” In the summer of 1745 he came to a small settlement of the Delaware people at a place called Crossweeksung, in New Jersey. Within weeks, God began to move. Many people came to faith, wept over their sin and found peace in Christ. Brainerd died two years later, aged only twenty-nine. But his diary has sent many people into mission ever since.

Brainerd was an outsider to the people he served. Samson Occom was one of them. Occom was born in 1723 among the Mohegan people of Connecticut. As a teenager he came to faith during the great revival that swept through New England. He learned to read, studied, and became a minister. For the rest of his life he preached to Native peoples across New England and New York, often in great poverty, often treated with disrespect by white church leaders. In his old age he helped Christian families from several Native peoples form a new town called Brothertown, where they could worship God together. Occom shows us that the best person to reach a people is often someone from among them. A leader who seeks the lost will also raise up seekers from among those who are found.

In London a century later, Charles Spurgeon called the work of winning souls “the chief business of the Christian minister” and “that most royal employment”. His talks on the subject are collected in The Soul Winner, which is on Ochorus. He also warned his students that it would cost them:

“An ordinary person may rest in his bed all night, but a surgeon will be called up at all hours; a farming man may take his ease at his fireside, but if he becomes a shepherd he must be out among the lambs, and bear all weathers for them.”

— Charles Spurgeon, The Soul Winner

In plain words: other people can rest, but a doctor is called out at any hour of the night, and a shepherd must go out in every kind of weather to look after the lambs. Those who seek the lost will be called on at times and in ways that cost them.

Rejoicing with heaven

Proverbs says, “whoever wins people over is wise” (Proverbs 11:30). There is no greater joy in a leader’s life than seeing someone come to Christ. Paul called the believers he had led to faith “my joy and my crown” (Philippians 4:1).

Heaven throws a party when one sinner repents. Do not let your leadership become so busy with the ninety-nine that you never go after the one. Pray for the lost. Go to them. Tell them about Jesus. And when one comes home, join the party.

Questions for reflection

  • Read Luke 15. Which character in these stories are you most like: the seeking shepherd, the searching woman, the waiting father, or the older brother?
  • When did you last have a real conversation about Jesus with someone who does not know Him?
  • Do the people you lead see you seeking the lost? What are you teaching them by your example?
  • Could you explain the good news of Jesus clearly in three minutes, in the language of the people around you? Try it.
  • What fear most often keeps you silent? What would courage look like for you this week?
  • Samson Occom reached his own people. Whom could you encourage and train to reach their own community?

A step for this week

Write down the names of five people you know who do not follow Christ. Pray for each of them by name every day this week. Then choose one of them and spend time with them: share a meal, visit their home or help them with something. Look for a natural moment to tell them what Jesus means to you. If you can, take a younger believer with you, and afterwards talk together about what you learned.

study_questions.question: Why should church leaders seek the lost?
study_questions.answer: Because that is why Jesus came: “The Son of Man came to look for what was lost and to save it” (Luke 19:10). He said, “I have other sheep as well, which are not of this fold. I must bring them too” (John 10:16).

study_questions.question: What does heaven think when one person repents?
study_questions.answer: Jesus said that “one sinner who repents will bring more joy in heaven than ninety-nine righteous people who have no need to repent” (Luke 15:7). The shepherd who finds his lost sheep carries it home on his shoulders, delighted.

study_questions.question: Are pastors called to evangelism too?
study_questions.answer: Yes. Paul told the pastor Timothy, “do the work of an evangelist, and carry out your ministry fully” (2 Timothy 4:5). The chapter tells of David Brainerd, Samson Occom and Charles Spurgeon, and how leaders can overcome the fear that keeps them silent.

fields.title: Correction and Restoration
fields.body_html:
“Brothers and sisters, suppose someone is caught out in some wrongdoing. You who are spiritual must set that person right again, and do it with a gentle spirit. Keep an eye on yourself as you do, in case you are tempted too.”

— Galatians 6:1 (OWB)

When a bone is broken, a good doctor does not ignore it, hoping it will heal by itself. If it is left alone, it may heal crooked, and the person may limp for life. But neither does the doctor hit the broken leg with a stick. The doctor sets the bone carefully, binds it firmly, and then gives it time to heal. Setting a bone hurts. But it is done for the sake of healing.

The word Paul uses in Galatians 6:1 for “set that person right again” was used for mending fishing nets and for setting broken bones. That is the picture of correction in the Church. It is not punishment for its own sake. It is the careful, painful, loving work of putting something broken back into its right place.

This is one of the hardest parts of leadership. Many leaders avoid it completely. Others do it harshly. This chapter is about doing it the way Jesus would.

Correction is love

Some people think that love means never saying anything hard. But the Bible says the opposite. “At the time it is given, no discipline seems a matter for joy; it seems a matter for sorrow. But afterward it pays back those who have been trained by it with a harvest of peace” (Hebrews 12:11). God disciplines His children because He loves them. A father who never corrects his children does not love them more. He loves them less.

Proverbs says, “A friend’s wounds can be trusted, but an enemy’s kisses come in plenty” (Proverbs 27:6). An enemy will flatter you while you walk towards a cliff. A true friend will tell you the truth, even when it hurts.

Jesus said, “When your brother or sister does wrong, warn them. Then if they repent, forgive them” (Luke 17:3). Both halves matter. Warning without forgiveness is cruel. Forgiveness without warning is careless. In Chapter 10, Love: The Motive and the Mark, we saw that real love seeks the good of the other person. Sometimes that good is a hard word.

A leader who never corrects anyone is not being kind. Usually they are afraid: afraid of conflict, afraid of losing people, afraid of being disliked. But sin left alone does not stay small. It spreads, like rot in a basket of fruit. And the person who is sinning is left to go further into danger, while their leaders say nothing.

The first step: privately

Jesus gave clear steps for dealing with sin among believers: “If a brother or sister sins against you, go and confront them about it, with only the two of you present. If they will listen to you, you have won your brother or sister back” (Matthew 18:15).

Notice three things. First, go. Do not wait for them to come to you. Second, go privately, with only the two of you present. Do not begin by telling others, and do not announce it in public. Third, notice the goal: “you have won your brother or sister back.” The aim is not to win the argument but to win the person.

In many cultures it is very hard to speak to someone directly about a problem. People prefer to send a message through someone else, or to speak about the problem to everyone except the person concerned. But that is not the way of Jesus. Gossip destroys. Speaking quietly and honestly to the person is the first step of love. In some cultures a respected go-between may be wise, especially when there is a great difference of age or rank. But even then, the aim is honest, gentle speech with the person, not talk behind their back.

Only if the private conversation fails do we take the next steps: “go back with one or two others,” and then, if necessary, “bring the matter before the church” (Matthew 18:16-17). Each step is slower and more serious. Each step gives the person another chance to listen.

How to correct

Paul tells us not only that we should correct, but how.

With a gentle spirit. “You who are spiritual must set that person right again, and do it with a gentle spirit” (Galatians 6:1). Anger, sarcasm and shaming rarely help. Gentleness does not mean weakness. It means strength under control.

Watching yourself. “Keep an eye on yourself as you do, in case you are tempted too” (Galatians 6:1). Before you correct someone else, examine your own heart. Jesus warned against trying to take a speck out of someone’s eye while there is a plank in your own (Matthew 7:3-5). Remember that you too are capable of the same sin.

Patiently. “The Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach and patient with difficult people, gently correcting those who oppose him. Perhaps God will grant them repentance” (2 Timothy 2:24-25). Notice who brings repentance: God. Our job is to speak truthfully and kindly. His job is to change the heart.

With respect. “Never speak harshly to an older man, but appeal to him as you would to a father. Treat younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters, with complete purity” (1 Timothy 5:1-2). Correction should fit the person: their age, their relationship to you, and their dignity.

Carrying their load. Paul goes on, “Take up one another’s heavy loads, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). We do not correct someone and then walk away. We stay beside them and help them carry the weight of change.

Courage to speak

When King David committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged for her husband to be killed, God sent the prophet Nathan to him. Nathan told David a story about a rich man who stole a poor man’s only lamb. David was furious at the rich man. Then Nathan said, “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7).

Nathan was speaking to a king who had just killed a man to hide his sin. He could have lost his life. But he spoke, wisely and bravely. And David repented. Psalm 51, one of the greatest prayers of repentance ever written, came out of that conversation.

Notice that Nathan was wise as well as brave. He did not shout at David in front of the court. He told a story that helped David see his own sin before he was named. Good correction often helps people see the truth for themselves.

Leaders also need courage to correct other leaders, including those above them. Paul once corrected Peter publicly, because Peter’s behaviour was leading others astray (Galatians 2:11-14). For dealing with accusations against leaders, Paul gave careful rules: “Do not listen to an accusation against an elder unless it is supported by two or three witnesses” (1 Timothy 5:19). Leaders must be protected from false accusations. But leaders who keep on sinning must not be protected from the truth. In Chapter 35, Power, Abuse and Protecting the Vulnerable, we will see that where there is abuse, especially of children, the Church must never cover it up.

The goal: restoration

In the church at Corinth, a man had sinned seriously, and the church had disciplined him. He repented. But some in the church still wanted to keep him at a distance. Paul wrote, “The penalty that most of you imposed on this man is enough for him. So now you should turn the other way: forgive him and comfort him, or he may be swallowed up by grief that is more than he can bear. So I urge you to confirm your love for him openly” (2 Corinthians 2:6-8).

This is a word many churches need. Some churches are slow to correct, but once they do, they never forgive. The person who repents is treated as a second-class Christian for the rest of their life. That is not the gospel. When someone truly repents, the church must forgive them, comfort them and show them love openly.

James wrote, “if one of you wanders away from the truth and someone brings that person back, let the one who does so know this: whoever brings a sinner back from the wrong path will save that sinner’s soul from death” (James 5:19-20). Restoration is not a small thing. It is saving a life.

Restoration to fellowship is not always the same as restoration to leadership. A leader who has fallen seriously may be fully forgiven and welcomed, and still need a long time before they lead again, if ever. We will look at this more in Chapter 39, Failure and Restoration.

Receiving correction

Leaders must also learn to be corrected. The psalmist prayed, “Let a righteous person strike me: that is loyal love. Let them reprove me: that is oil for my head, and may my head never refuse it” (Psalm 141:5).

Many leaders find this very hard. They are used to correcting others, not being corrected. They may become defensive or angry, or find a way to remove the person who dared to speak. But a leader who cannot be corrected is in great danger. “Whoever hides their sins will not succeed, but whoever admits them and turns away from them will receive mercy” (Proverbs 28:13). Thank God for anyone who loves you enough to tell you the truth.

A voice from the Church: Gregory the Great and the East African Revival

Gregory the Great, whom we met in Chapter 2, What Makes Leadership Spiritual, wrote in his Book of Pastoral Rule about the balance between kindness and firmness. He used the story of the Good Samaritan, who poured both wine and oil on the wounds of the injured man (Luke 10:34). In Gregory’s day, wine was used to clean a wound and oil to soothe it.

“For whosoever superintends the healing of wounds must needs administer in wine the smart of pain, and in oil the softness of loving-kindness, to the end that through wine what is festering may be purged, and through oil what is curable may be soothed. Gentleness, then, is to be mingled with severity.”

— Gregory the Great, The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part II

In plain words: anyone who treats wounds must use both wine, which stings, and oil, which soothes. The wine cleans out what is infected. The oil helps what can be healed. So a leader must mix gentleness with firmness. Gregory went on to say that people should be neither wounded by too much harshness nor made careless by too much softness.

In the twentieth century, the East African Revival, which began in Rwanda and Uganda in the 1930s, became known for a practice it called “walking in the light”. The phrase comes from 1 John 1:7: “if we walk in the light, just as he is in the light, we share fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus, his Son, goes on cleansing us from every sin.” The book Tukutendereza on Ochorus explains that the believers of the Revival “meant it as a practice, not a mood: open honesty before God and before one another, continuously, in company.”

The believers met regularly in small fellowships. There they confessed their sins openly to one another, and they lovingly pointed out sin they saw in each other. They also went to people they had wronged and put things right. Correction was not something leaders did to other people. Everyone, leaders included, lived in the open. As Tukutendereza says, “You did not confess that you were a sinner; you confessed what you had done.” And their great song of the Revival, “Tukutendereza Yesu”, praised the blood of Jesus that cleanses. Correction always led back to the cross.

The Revival had its own struggles, and at times its fellowships could become harsh. But at its best it showed that correction is safest where everyone, including the leader, walks in the light.

Setting the bone

Come back to the picture of the broken bone. A doctor who loves the patient will set it, even though it hurts. A doctor who does not care will ignore it, or handle it roughly. Jesus is the Great Physician. He never ignored sin, and He never crushed a sinner. He told the woman caught in adultery, “I do not condemn you either. Go, and from now on do not sin any more” (John 8:11).

Ask God for His heart: truthful enough to speak, gentle enough to heal, and patient enough to stay with the person until they are whole again.

Questions for reflection

  • Do you tend to avoid hard conversations, or to hold them harshly? Why?
  • Read Matthew 18:15-17. In your culture, what makes it hard to go to someone privately? How can you follow Jesus’ steps wisely?
  • Read Galatians 6:1-2. What does “with a gentle spirit” look like in practice?
  • Is there anyone in your church who repented of a sin but has never been fully welcomed back? What would 2 Corinthians 2:6-8 ask of you?
  • How do you respond when someone corrects you? Who has permission to tell you the truth?
  • What could you learn from the East African Revival’s practice of walking in the light?

A step for this week

Think of one person you have been avoiding a hard conversation with. Spend time in prayer, first examining your own heart (Galatians 6:1). Then go to them privately, this week if you can. Speak gently and honestly, listen carefully, and aim to win them back, not to win the argument. Then ask one trusted friend to be someone who will tell you the truth about yourself, and thank them when they do.

study_questions.question: How should a leader correct someone who has sinned?
study_questions.answer: Gently, with the aim of restoring them. “You who are spiritual must set that person right again, and do it with a gentle spirit” (Galatians 6:1). Jesus said to go first in private: “go and confront them about it, with only the two of you present” (Matthew 18:15).

study_questions.question: Is correcting someone loving?
study_questions.answer: Yes, when it is done in love. “A friend’s wounds can be trusted” (Proverbs 27:6). Discipline feels hard at the time, but afterward it brings a harvest of peace (Hebrews 12:11). Silence when someone is going astray is not kindness.

study_questions.question: What is the goal of church discipline?
study_questions.answer: Restoration, not punishment. The Lord’s servant must be “kind to everyone, able to teach and patient with difficult people” (2 Timothy 2:24). The chapter compares it to setting a broken bone, and draws on Gregory the Great and the East African Revival.

fields.title: Comfort in Suffering and Grief
fields.body_html:
“He comforts us in every hardship we face, so that we in turn can comfort people facing any hardship, passing on to them the same comfort God gives us.”

— 2 Corinthians 1:4 (OWB)

In many parts of the world, when someone dies, the whole community comes to the house. Neighbours sit with the family for days. Some bring food. Some sing. Many say very little. They simply come, and stay. Their presence says what words cannot: “You are not alone.”

The people we lead will face sickness, loss and death. Children die. Marriages break. Jobs are lost. Wars and floods destroy homes. Bodies grow old and weak. A leader cannot prevent these sorrows. But a leader can be there in them, and can point people to the God who is there too. This chapter, the last in Part Four, is about comfort in suffering and grief.

The God of all comfort

Paul opens his second letter to the Corinthians with praise: “Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the merciful Father and the God from whom all comfort comes” (2 Corinthians 1:3). Paul wrote this after terrible suffering. A few verses later he says he had been weighed down so heavily that he had “given up hope even of staying alive” (2 Corinthians 1:8). Yet he begins with praise, because in that darkness he had found God to be a comforter.

The Bible is full of this picture of God. Through Isaiah He said, “Bring comfort, bring comfort to my people” (Isaiah 40:1). And He described Himself as a gentle shepherd: “He will gather the lambs into his arm and carry them close against his chest, and he will lead the nursing ewes with care” (Isaiah 40:11). The psalmist wrote, “The LORD stays close to those whose hearts are broken, and rescues those whose spirits are crushed” (Psalm 34:18).

Before we can comfort others, we must know this God for ourselves. A leader who has never brought their own grief to God will have little to offer others in theirs.

Comforted in order to comfort

Paul goes on: “He comforts us in every hardship we face, so that we in turn can comfort people facing any hardship, passing on to them the same comfort God gives us” (2 Corinthians 1:4).

This is one of the hidden gifts of suffering. When God comforts us in our pain, He is also preparing us to comfort others. A pastor who has lost a child can sit with grieving parents in a way no one else can. A leader who has walked through depression can understand others in darkness. A widow can comfort a widow. Nothing in our lives is wasted in God’s hands.

This means that leaders should not hide all their own sorrows from their people. There is a time to share, wisely, how God has met us in our pain. People are often more helped by our honest weakness than by our strength.

Jesus wept

When Jesus’ friend Lazarus died, Jesus came to the village of Bethany. Lazarus’ sister Mary fell at His feet, weeping. “When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her weeping too, he was deeply indignant in spirit and greatly troubled. ‘Where have you laid him?’ he asked. They said to him, ‘Lord, come and see.’ Jesus wept” (John 11:33-35).

This is astonishing. Jesus knew that in a few minutes He would raise Lazarus from the dead. He had the answer to Mary’s grief in His hands. And yet He wept. He did not rush past her pain to the solution. He entered her sorrow first. And He was angry, “deeply indignant”, at death itself, the enemy that tears families apart.

Leaders are often tempted to rush. We want to fix the problem, quote a verse, explain why it happened, and move on. But Jesus shows us a better way. Before we speak, we weep. Before we explain, we stay. The Bible tells us to “Share the joy of those who are glad, and the tears of those who weep” (Romans 12:15). Sometimes the most Christlike thing a leader can do is cry with someone.

And remember who our Saviour is. Isaiah called Him “a man of pains, no stranger to sickness” (Isaiah 53:3). Hebrews says, “the high priest we have is not one who cannot share the feeling of our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15). When we sit with the suffering, we are not bringing them a distant God. We are bringing them to One who has suffered too.

Miserable comforters

The book of Job shows us both good and bad comfort. When Job lost his children, his wealth and his health, three friends came to see him. At first they did very well: “they sat with him on the ground for seven days and seven nights. No one said a word to him, because they saw how great his suffering was” (Job 2:13).

Then they started talking. For many chapters they explained to Job that he must have sinned, that God was punishing him, and that if he repented everything would be well again. They were wrong. At the end of the book, God was angry with them. Job had called them “miserable comforters” (Job 16:2).

Here are some things that make us miserable comforters:

  • Explaining too quickly. “This happened because…” Often we do not know why. It is better to say, “I do not know why,” than to say something false about God.
  • Blaming the sufferer. Some teachers say that all sickness and poverty are caused by a lack of faith or by hidden sin. Sometimes sin does bring suffering. But often it does not. Jesus’ disciples once asked whether a blind man or his parents had sinned. Jesus said neither (John 9:1-3).
  • Hurrying their grief. “It is time to move on.” Grief takes time, often years. Be patient.
  • Using verses as bandages. “For people who love God, all things work together and lead to good” (Romans 8:28) is true. But spoken too soon, without love, it can feel like a slap. Let the truth be spoken at the right time and in the right way.
  • Disappearing. Many people are surrounded at the funeral and alone a month later. Good comforters come back.

Practical comfort

What can a leader do?

Go. Visit the sick, the dying and the grieving. Go to hospitals, homes and funerals. Your presence matters more than your words.

Listen. Let people tell their story, again and again if they need to. Let them be angry or confused. The psalms are full of honest complaints to God: “How long, LORD? Will you go on forgetting me for good?” (Psalm 13:1). God is not offended by honest grief. Teach people that they can bring it to Him.

Pray. Pray with them and for them. When they cannot pray, pray for them. James tells the sick to call the elders to pray (James 5:14).

Help practically. Bring food. Help with children, fields, bills or the funeral. Organise the church to care, so that the burden does not fall on one person.

Speak hope at the right time. Christians do grieve, but Paul says we do not “grieve as others do who have no hope. We believe that Jesus died and rose again” (1 Thessalonians 4:13-14). At the right moment, speak of the resurrection, of Christ’s presence, and of the day when “Every tear he will wipe from their eyes. Death will be no more” (Revelation 21:4).

Remember. Write down the date of a death and visit or call the family on that day the next year. It may mean more to them than anything else you do.

A voice from the Church: Samuel Rutherford and Corrie ten Boom

Samuel Rutherford was a pastor in the small village of Anwoth in south-west Scotland in the seventeenth century. He knew grief himself. His wife died after a long and painful illness, and he lost children too. In 1636 he was banished from his parish because of his writings and sent to live in the city of Aberdeen, far from his people. From there, and throughout his life, he wrote letters of comfort and encouragement to the people he loved. They have been read by suffering Christians ever since, and they are on Ochorus as Letters of Samuel Rutherford.

One of his letters was written to a woman whose daughter had died:

“I was indeed sorrowful at my departure from you, especially since ye were in such heaviness after your daughter’s death. Yet I do persuade myself, ye know that the weightiest end of the cross of Christ that is laid upon you lieth upon your strong Saviour.”

— Samuel Rutherford, Letter II

In plain words: I was sad to leave you, especially because you were so heavy with grief after your daughter died. But I believe you know that the heaviest part of the cross you are carrying is resting on Jesus, your strong Saviour. Rutherford imagined the cross as a heavy beam carried by two people. The mother carried one end. Christ carried the heavier end. Then Rutherford quoted Isaiah, that in all their troubles the Lord Himself was troubled (Isaiah 63:9), and he added, “When ye do tire, He will bear both you and your burden.”

Rutherford did not pretend that grief was small. He wept with the grieving. But he pointed them to Christ, who carries both the sufferer and the suffering.

Three centuries later, Corrie ten Boom was a watchmaker in the Dutch city of Haarlem. During the Second World War her family hid Jewish people from the Nazis in a secret room in their home. In 1944 they were arrested. Corrie and her sister Betsie were sent to Ravensbrück, a terrible concentration camp in Germany. There, among lice, hunger and cruelty, the two sisters held Bible readings and prayed with the other women. Betsie grew weak and died in the camp in December 1944. Corrie was released shortly afterwards.

After the war, Corrie spent the rest of her long life travelling the world, comforting people with the comfort God had given her. In her later book The Hiding Place, she remembered Betsie saying near the end that they must tell people there is no pit so deep that God’s love is not deeper still. The biography Corrie ten Boom: A Life on Ochorus notes that these exact words come from the later book, not from Corrie’s first account written in 1945. But the truth behind them was tested in one of the darkest places on earth. Corrie became, in Paul’s words, someone who could comfort “people facing any hardship” because she had been comforted in hers.

The end of Part Four

We have now seen five pictures of the shepherd’s work: feeding the sheep, knowing the sheep, seeking the lost, correcting and restoring, and comforting the suffering. None of these can be done from a distance. Each one requires a leader to come close to people, as Jesus came close to us.

The Good Shepherd carries the lambs close against His chest. As His under-shepherds, we are called to carry people too: in prayer, in presence and in love. And when we are tired, He carries both us and our burden.

Questions for reflection

  • Think of a time when someone comforted you well in a time of grief. What did they do? What did they not do?
  • Read John 11:32-36. Why do you think Jesus wept, even though He was about to raise Lazarus?
  • Which of the habits of “miserable comforters” are you most tempted towards?
  • Read 2 Corinthians 1:3-7. How has God comforted you in a way that has helped you comfort others?
  • Who in your church is grieving now, or was grieving a few months ago and may now feel forgotten?
  • What does Rutherford’s picture of Christ carrying “the weightiest end” of the cross mean to you?

A step for this week

Make a list of people in your church or community who are sick, grieving or going through great hardship, including any whose loss was some months ago. This week, visit at least two of them. Do not go with a sermon. Go to listen and to be present. Ask them, “How are you, really?” and let them talk. Before you leave, pray with them briefly. If there is a practical need, ask the church to help meet it.

study_questions.question: How can I comfort someone who is grieving?
study_questions.answer: By being present, listening, praying and helping practically, rather than giving quick answers. God “comforts us in every hardship we face, so that we in turn can comfort people facing any hardship” (2 Corinthians 1:4). Job’s friends show what not to do.

study_questions.question: Did Jesus grieve?
study_questions.answer: Yes. At the tomb of Lazarus, when He saw Mary weeping, He was deeply moved and wept (John 11:33-35). Grief is not a lack of faith. “The LORD stays close to those whose hearts are broken” (Psalm 34:18).

study_questions.question: Where can a leader find comfort when they are suffering?
study_questions.answer: In “the God from whom all comfort comes” (2 Corinthians 1:3). Paul himself had “given up hope even of staying alive” (2 Corinthians 1:8), yet found God faithful. The chapter draws on Samuel Rutherford and Corrie ten Boom.

fields.title: No Lone Leaders
fields.body_html:
“This way of doing things is not good. You are sure to wear out, both you and the people who are with you. The load is too heavy for you; you cannot carry it by yourself.”

— Exodus 18:17-18 (OWB)

In many villages, when a house needs a new roof, the whole community comes to help. One person alone could never lift the heavy beams. But with twenty people, the work is done in a day, and there is singing and food at the end. Everyone has a part. Some carry. Some tie. Some cook. The roof goes up because no one tried to do it alone.

This chapter begins Part Five, Leading Together. In Part Four we looked at the work of shepherding: feeding, knowing, seeking, correcting and comforting. If you read those chapters and thought, “I cannot possibly do all of that,” you were right. You cannot. God never meant you to.

Moses and the heavy load

After Israel left Egypt, Moses led them through the wilderness. Every day, from morning until evening, people came to him with their disputes and questions, and he alone judged them all. When his father-in-law Jethro saw this, he said, “This way of doing things is not good. You are sure to wear out, both you and the people who are with you. The load is too heavy for you; you cannot carry it by yourself” (Exodus 18:17-18).

Jethro gave Moses wise advice. Moses should keep doing the things only he could do: praying for the people, teaching them God’s laws and dealing with the hardest cases. But he should choose other leaders to share the work. “Pick out able men, men who fear God, who can be relied on and who hate gain got by cheating. Put them in charge of the people as officers over thousands, over hundreds, over fifties and over tens.” Then, Jethro said, “make your load lighter, and they will carry it with you” (Exodus 18:21-22).

Notice that Jethro was not a great prophet. He was a priest of Midian, an outsider. But Moses was humble enough to listen to good advice, and he did what Jethro said. Sometimes God sends wisdom through unexpected people.

Later in the wilderness, Moses was crushed again by the complaints of the people. He cried out to God, “I cannot carry this whole people on my own. The load is too heavy for me” (Numbers 11:14). God answered by telling him to gather seventy elders. “I will take some of the Spirit that rests on you and place it on them. Then they will share the burden of the people with you, so that you will not have to carry it alone” (Numbers 11:17).

God’s answer to the overworked leader was not “try harder”. It was “share the load”.

The New Testament pattern

When we look at the churches in the New Testament, we find something striking. They were almost never led by one person alone.

Jesus Himself chose twelve apostles and sent them out “in pairs” (Mark 6:7). When the church in Jerusalem faced the problem of the widows, the apostles asked the church to choose seven people “of good reputation, full of the Spirit and of wisdom” to share the work (Acts 6:3). When Paul and Barnabas started new churches, “In each church they appointed elders” (Acts 14:23). The word is plural: elders, not one elder. Paul told Titus to “appoint elders in every town” (Titus 1:5). Paul wrote to the church at Philippi “together with the overseers and deacons” (Philippians 1:1).

Look at the leaders of the church in Antioch, the first great missionary church: “Barnabas, Simeon known as Niger, Lucius the Cyrenian, Manaen, a childhood companion of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul” (Acts 13:1). Barnabas came from Cyprus. Simeon was called “Niger”, which means “black”, and he was probably from Africa. Lucius came from Cyrene, in North Africa. Manaen had grown up in the palace of a king. Saul was a Jewish scholar from Tarsus. It was a team of very different people, from different nations and backgrounds, leading together. And it was from that team that the Holy Spirit sent out the first missionaries.

Different churches have organised their leadership in different ways through history. We set out the main forms fairly in Appendix A, Chapter 53, How Churches Are Led. But across all these forms, the New Testament pattern is clear: leadership is shared.

The body needs every part

Why does God work this way? Because of what the Church is. Paul says the Church is a body: “We have many parts in a single body, and the parts do not all have the same task. In the same way, many as we are, we are one body in Christ” (Romans 12:4-5). “So the eye cannot tell the hand, ‘I can do without you,’ and the head cannot tell the feet, ‘I can do without you’” (1 Corinthians 12:21).

No single leader has all the gifts. One is a good teacher but poor with money. One is a wonderful comforter but cannot organise. One sees the future clearly but forgets the people alongside. God has spread His gifts across the whole body, so that we need each other.

Paul also explains the purpose of leaders: Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers “to equip God’s holy people for the work of serving, so that the body of Christ would be built up” (Ephesians 4:11-12). Notice that. The leaders’ job is not to do all the work. It is to equip God’s people to do the work. A pastor who does everything alone is not being faithful. He is stopping others from doing what God has called them to do.

The Preacher in Ecclesiastes puts it simply: “Two are better than one ... If one of them falls, the other can help that one up. But woe to anyone who falls alone” (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10). Leaders who work alone are in danger. When they are tired, no one notices. When they are wrong, no one corrects them. When they fall, no one is there to lift them up.

Why leaders try to do it alone

If shared leadership is God’s way, why do so many leaders do everything themselves?

  • Pride. “No one else can do it as well as I can.” Sometimes that is true at first. But others will never learn if they are never given the chance.
  • Fear of losing control. If others share the work, they will also share the decisions. Some leaders are afraid of that. We will think about the danger of power in Chapter 35, Power, Abuse and Protecting the Vulnerable.
  • Insecurity. Some leaders fear that if others do well, they will be less needed or less admired. But a secure leader rejoices when others shine.
  • Culture. In some cultures, the leader is expected to be like a chief who decides everything. People even expect it. But the Church must follow Christ, not only its culture.
  • Impatience. It is quicker to do it yourself than to teach someone else. That is true today. But in five years, the leader who trained others will have many workers, and the leader who did not will still be alone.

Here is a simple test. Ask yourself: “If I were sick for three months, what would happen to the work?” If everything would stop, something is wrong.

How to share the load

Pray for co-workers. Jesus told His disciples, “pray to the Lord of the harvest, and ask him to send out workers into his harvest” (Matthew 9:38). Before you look for helpers, pray for them.

Look for character first. Jethro said to look for people who “fear God, who can be relied on and who hate gain got by cheating”. The apostles looked for people “full of the Spirit and of wisdom”. Skill can be taught. Character is harder to build.

Give real responsibility. Do not just give people small tasks while you keep every decision. Give them real work and let them make real decisions, including some mistakes.

Keep what only you can do. The apostles held fast to prayer and to the service of the word (Acts 6:4). Moses kept teaching and the hardest cases. Know what God has called you specially to do, and give the rest away.

Meet together. A team needs time together, to pray, plan, encourage one another and solve problems. Leaders who share work but never meet will drift apart.

Listen to your team. “Plans go wrong for lack of advice, but with many advisers they succeed” (Proverbs 15:22). Ask your fellow leaders what they think, and let them change your mind.

A voice from the Church: John Wesley and his helpers

John Wesley was an Anglican minister in England in the eighteenth century. Through his preaching, and that of his brother Charles and George Whitefield, tens of thousands of people came to faith. Wesley rode many thousands of miles on horseback, preaching in fields, market places and mines. But he could never have cared for all those new believers by himself.

The answer came in an unexpected way. In February 1742, the Methodist society in the city of Bristol had a debt to pay. Wesley’s Journal, which is on Ochorus, records what they agreed: “that the whole society should be divided into little companies or classes—about twelve in each class; and ... that one person in each class should receive the contribution of the rest.” Each week, a class leader visited the members to collect a penny. Soon they realised that the class leader could also ask how each person’s soul was doing. The class meeting was born. Ordinary men and women, shopkeepers, miners and servants, became shepherds of a dozen people each. Through these classes, hundreds of thousands of believers were known, cared for and helped to grow.

Wesley also had to learn to share the preaching. He was an ordained priest and believed that only ordained men should preach. When he was away, he left a young man called Thomas Maxfield in charge of the society in London, to meet the classes and explain the Scriptures. Maxfield began to preach. Wesley was upset and hurried back to London to stop him. But his mother, Susanna Wesley, warned him:

“Take care what you do with respect to that young man; for he is as surely called of God to preach as you are. Examine what have been the fruits of his preaching, and hear him yourself.”

— Susanna Wesley, as told in Susanna Wesley by Eliza Clarke

Wesley listened to Maxfield preach, and he saw God’s hand. He said, “It is the Lord ... let Him do what seemeth Him good. What am I that I should withstand God?” In plain words: this is God’s work, so let God do what He thinks best. Who am I to stand in God’s way? From then on, Wesley appointed many lay preachers. They carried the gospel across Britain, to America and beyond.

Wesley’s story shows two things. First, God often provides co-workers in surprising ways, through a small practical need or an unexpected person. Second, even great leaders must be humble enough to see God working through others, and to let them work.

Not alone

Perhaps you are a pastor in a small church, and you feel that you carry everything alone. Perhaps you are tired, as Moses was. Hear Jethro’s words: “you cannot carry it by yourself.” Hear God’s promise: “they will share the burden of the people with you, so that you will not have to carry it alone.”

Look around you. There are people in your church with gifts you have not yet noticed. Pray for them. Call them. Train them. Trust them. And let the roof be lifted by many hands. In the next chapter we will look at how to raise up new leaders.

Questions for reflection

  • Read Exodus 18:13-26. In what ways are you like Moses before Jethro spoke to him?
  • If you were sick for three months, what would happen to the work you lead?
  • Which of the reasons leaders work alone is most true of you?
  • Look at the leaders of the church in Antioch (Acts 13:1). What does their variety teach us about leadership teams today?
  • Who in your church has gifts that are not being used? What could you give them to do?
  • What can you learn from Susanna Wesley’s advice to her son?

A step for this week

Make a list of everything you do in your leadership in a normal week. Mark each item: “Only I can do this,” “Someone else could do this with training,” or “Someone else could do this now.” Choose one item from the last group and, after prayer, ask someone to take it on this week. Choose one from the middle group and begin training someone to do it. Then arrange a time to meet and pray with the other leaders you work with.

study_questions.question: Why should leaders not work alone?
study_questions.answer: Because the load is too heavy for one person. Jethro told Moses, “You are sure to wear out, both you and the people who are with you” (Exodus 18:18). Moses later said, “I cannot carry this whole people on my own” (Numbers 11:14).

study_questions.question: What is the New Testament pattern of leadership?
study_questions.answer: Shared leadership. Jesus sent His disciples out “in pairs” (Mark 6:7). Paul and Barnabas appointed elders, plural, “In each church” (Acts 14:23), and Paul told Titus to “appoint elders in every town” (Titus 1:5).

study_questions.question: How can a leader share the work?
study_questions.answer: By recognising the gifts of others, training them, giving them real responsibility and trusting them, as Moses did when God placed His Spirit on seventy elders to “share the burden” (Numbers 11:17). John Wesley’s many lay helpers show how much can be done together.

fields.title: Making Leaders
fields.body_html:
“And what you heard from me before many witnesses, pass on to trustworthy people who will be able to teach others as well.”

— 2 Timothy 2:2 (OWB)

A farmer who eats all his grain will have a good meal this year. But next year he will have nothing to plant. A wise farmer always keeps back the best seed. He plants it, and from one handful he may harvest a whole field. His work does not end with this year’s harvest. It goes on into the years to come.

Leaders are like that farmer. We can use all our energy on this year’s work: this Sunday’s sermon, this month’s problems. Or we can also plant seed for the future, by raising up new leaders. In the last chapter we saw that no leader should work alone. In this chapter we ask where the other leaders come from. The answer is that, under God, we make them.

Four generations in one verse

Read the verse at the top of this chapter again. Paul wrote it to Timothy near the end of his life: “And what you heard from me before many witnesses, pass on to trustworthy people who will be able to teach others as well” (2 Timothy 2:2).

Count the people in that verse. First there is Paul. Then there is Timothy, who heard from Paul. Then there are the “trustworthy people” to whom Timothy will pass it on. And then there are the “others” whom they will teach. Four generations of leaders in one sentence.

Paul was not only thinking about the church in his day. He was thinking about the church after he was gone, and after Timothy was gone. The test of a leader is not only what happens while they are there. It is what continues after they leave.

Notice too what kind of people Timothy was to choose: “trustworthy people”. Not the most popular, the richest or the most talented, but the faithful. And they had to be people who would “teach others as well”. Timothy was not looking for people who would simply admire him. He was looking for people who would pass it on.

Jesus made leaders

Jesus preached to crowds, but He gave most of His time to a small group. “He appointed twelve to be with him, and to be sent out to proclaim the message” (Mark 3:14). Notice the order. First, “to be with him”. Then, “to be sent out”.

Jesus’ method of training leaders was mainly His own company. For three years the disciples ate with Him, walked with Him, watched Him pray, heard Him teach, saw Him heal and listened to His answers to His enemies. They learned not mainly from lectures but from life.

Then He sent them out to practise. He sent the Twelve “to announce the kingdom of God and to heal those who were ill” (Luke 9:2). Later He sent seventy-two others “in pairs ahead of him” (Luke 10:1). When they came back, “full of joy”, He talked with them about what had happened (Luke 10:17-20). He corrected them when they were wrong. He was patient when they were slow. And at the end, He handed the whole mission into their hands.

Many of our training methods are the opposite. We put people in a classroom, give them information and a certificate, and then send them out alone. Classes have their place. But Jesus shows us that leaders are made mainly by being with a leader, doing the work alongside them, and talking about it afterwards.

Moses and Joshua, Elijah and Elisha

The Old Testament gives us two great examples of leaders who prepared those who came after them.

Joshua was Moses’ assistant for forty years. He went with Moses up the mountain. He stayed at the tent of meeting. He led the army while Moses prayed. At the end of his life, Moses publicly handed over leadership: “with all Israel looking on, said to him, ‘Be strong and courageous’” (Deuteronomy 31:7). And after Moses died, “Joshua son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom, since Moses had laid his hands on him” (Deuteronomy 34:9). The people followed Joshua because Moses had prepared him, and had shown the people that he was the one God had chosen.

Elisha followed the prophet Elijah for years. When Elijah was about to be taken up to heaven, Elisha would not leave his side. He asked, “Please let me receive a double portion of your spirit” (2 Kings 2:9). After Elijah was gone, the other prophets said, “The spirit of Elijah has come to rest on Elisha” (2 Kings 2:15).
