Elisha went on to do even more miracles than his teacher.

Both stories show the same thing. God’s work did not die with the great leader, because the great leader had made room for the next one.

Barnabas, the encourager

One of the greatest leader-makers in the New Testament was not Paul but Barnabas. His name means “son of encouragement”.

When Saul (later called Paul) first came to Jerusalem after his conversion, “every one of them feared him” (Acts 9:26). He had been killing Christians. Who would trust him? “Barnabas, however, took him in hand and brought him to the apostles” (Acts 9:27). Barnabas risked his own reputation for Saul.

Later, when the church in Antioch was growing, Barnabas went to Tarsus “to search for Saul, and when he had found him he brought him to Antioch. For an entire year the two of them ... taught a sizable crowd” (Acts 11:25-26). At first, the Bible speaks of “Barnabas and Saul”. Soon it speaks of “Paul and Barnabas”. Barnabas did not mind that the younger man became more famous than he was.

Barnabas did the same for a young man called John Mark. Mark had left Paul and Barnabas in the middle of their first journey. Paul refused to take him again, and the quarrel was so sharp that Paul and Barnabas parted ways (Acts 15:37-39). Barnabas gave Mark a second chance. Years later, Paul himself wrote, “Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is helpful to me in my work” (2 Timothy 4:11). Mark became the writer of one of the four Gospels. Without Barnabas, we might have lost both Paul and Mark.

Every church needs people like Barnabas: leaders who notice others, believe in them, take risks for them and give them a second chance.

How to make leaders

Pray and look. Jesus spent a whole night in prayer before He chose the Twelve (Luke 6:12). Ask God to show you whom to invest in. Look for faithfulness, hunger for God and a teachable spirit, not only talent.

Let them be with you. Take them with you when you visit, preach, pray or solve problems. Let them see your life up close. Paul could say, “Take me as your model, just as I take Christ as mine” (1 Corinthians 11:1), and “Put into practice what you learned and received from me, what you heard and saw in me” (Philippians 4:9).

Give them real work. Begin with small things and add more as they prove faithful. Paul said that those who would serve “should first be tested” (1 Timothy 3:10). He also warned, “Do not be in a hurry to lay hands on anyone” (1 Timothy 5:22).

Talk about it afterwards. After they lead a study, preach or visit someone, sit with them. Ask, “What went well? What was hard? What did you learn?” This is where much of the real training happens.

Encourage the young. Paul told Timothy, “Do not let anyone look down on you because you are young” (1 Timothy 4:12). In many cultures, the young are expected to wait many years before leading. Respect for age is good. But do not waste the gifts God has given to the young.

Train women and men. Priscilla and Aquila together “took him in and taught him the way of God more precisely” when they met the gifted preacher Apollos (Acts 18:26). We will think about this further in Chapter 26, Men and Women in the Work of God.

Give them your heart. Paul wrote to the Thessalonians, “we gladly gave you not only the gospel of God but ourselves too, for you had become dear to us” (1 Thessalonians 2:8). Leaders are not made by programmes alone. They are made by love.

Let them go further than you. The goal is not to make copies of yourself, or followers who depend on you for ever. It is to make leaders who will be stronger than you, go further than you and train others in turn.

A voice from the Church: Polycarp, Irenaeus and the East African Revival

In Chapter 8, Integrity: The Same in Secret, we met Polycarp, the bishop of Smyrna who was put to death for Christ in the second century. Polycarp had learned from the apostle John. And Polycarp in turn taught younger men. One of them was Irenaeus, who later became a bishop in Lyon, in Gaul (now France), and one of the great teachers of the early Church.

Many years later, Irenaeus wrote to an old friend who had left the true faith. He reminded him of the days when they had both, as young men, listened to Polycarp. The letter is preserved by the historian Eusebius in his Church History, which is on Ochorus:

“I remember the events of that time more clearly than those of recent years. For what boys learn, growing with their mind, becomes joined with it; so that I am able to describe the very place in which the blessed Polycarp sat as he discoursed, and his goings out and his comings in, and the manner of his life.”

— Irenaeus, quoted in Eusebius, Church History, Book V

In plain words: I remember those days better than recent years. What we learn when we are young grows with us and becomes part of us. I can still picture the place where Polycarp sat and taught, how he came and went, and the way he lived.

Irenaeus went on to say that Polycarp used to tell them about his conversations with John “and with the others who had seen the Lord”. Notice what Irenaeus remembered: not only Polycarp’s words, but his life, his habits, even the place where he sat. John taught Polycarp. Polycarp taught Irenaeus. Irenaeus taught others. This is 2 Timothy 2:2 in real history.

Eighteen centuries later, in East Africa, the same pattern appeared. Simeon Nsibambi was a public health officer in Kampala, Uganda, in the 1920s. He was not ordained and had no theological training. In 1929 he met a tired English missionary doctor called Joe Church, and asked him what was missing in his life. The two men knelt and prayed together, and both were changed. The book Tukutendereza on Ochorus describes what happened next. Nsibambi did not build an organisation. He “had children in the faith, and they had children, and that is the whole of his method.” He led his own brother to a living faith. Others he touched carried the message to Rwanda, Kenya and beyond. From 1941 he was too ill to leave his house, and he watched most of it from a distance. But the revival he helped begin shaped churches across East Africa for generations.

Joe Church shows another side of leader-making. He was the trained European missionary, with a mission board behind him. Yet he let an African layman teach him. And when the revival grew, he did not make himself its head. As Tukutendereza puts it, “The revival’s leadership went African early and stayed there.” He was willing to be “one man among them rather than over them”.

That was what Henry Venn, whom we met in Chapter 4, The Call of God, had hoped for. Venn led the Church Missionary Society in London in the nineteenth century. He taught that the aim of mission was churches that were self-governing, self-supporting and self-spreading, led by their own people. A missionary’s work, he said, should lead to the day when the missionary was no longer needed.

Keep back the seed

Your greatest work may not be the sermons you preach or the buildings you build. It may be the people you train. Moses had Joshua. Elijah had Elisha. Jesus had the Twelve. Barnabas had Paul and Mark. Paul had Timothy. Polycarp had Irenaeus. Whom do you have?

Questions for reflection

  • Read 2 Timothy 2:2. Can you trace four generations of faith in your own life? Who taught the person who taught you?
  • Jesus chose the Twelve first “to be with him”. How much time do the people you are training spend with you, outside formal meetings?
  • Who has been a Barnabas to you? Whom could you be a Barnabas to?
  • Is there a “John Mark” in your church, someone who failed once and has never been given a second chance?
  • What did Irenaeus remember about Polycarp? What will the people you train remember about you?
  • If you left your church tomorrow, who would be ready to lead?

A step for this week

Pray this week for God to show you one or two faithful people to invest in. Then invite one of them to come with you when you next lead, visit, preach or pray with someone. Afterwards, sit with them and ask, “What did you see? What did you learn? What would you do differently?” Plan to give them a real task to do within the next month, and to talk with them about it afterwards.

study_questions.question: How does a leader make new leaders?
study_questions.answer: By passing on what they have received to others who can teach still others: “pass on to trustworthy people who will be able to teach others as well” (2 Timothy 2:2). This verse holds four generations of leaders.

study_questions.question: How did Jesus train His disciples?
study_questions.answer: “He appointed twelve to be with him, and to be sent out to proclaim the message” (Mark 3:14). They lived with Him first, then He sent them out to serve, and later sent out seventy-two “in pairs ahead of him” (Luke 10:1).

study_questions.question: What can we learn from Moses and Joshua about training leaders?
study_questions.answer: Moses kept Joshua close for years, encouraged him publicly with “Be strong and courageous” (Deuteronomy 31:7), and laid hands on him, so that Joshua “was full of the spirit of wisdom” (Deuteronomy 34:9). Leaders are made over time, by example and trust.

fields.title: Unity and Peacemaking
fields.body_html:
“Father, I ask that all of them may be one. Just as you are in me and I am in you, so may they too be in us, so that the world may come to believe that you sent me.”

— John 17:21 (OWB)

A broom made of a single straw cannot sweep a floor. It bends and breaks. But when many straws are tied together, the broom is strong and does its work. Many cultures have a saying like this. A single stick breaks easily. A bundle of sticks does not.

On the night before He died, Jesus prayed for His Church. Of all the things He could have asked for us, He asked this: “that all of them may be one” (John 17:21). And He gave the reason: “so that the world may come to believe that you sent me.” The unity of His people is part of the message. When Christians are divided, the world finds it harder to believe. When they are one, the world sees something it cannot explain.

In the last two chapters we saw that leaders must work in teams and raise up other leaders. But teams can quarrel. Churches can split. Christians can despise one another because of tribe, language, class or denomination. This chapter is about the leader’s duty to guard unity and to make peace.

Unity is a gift to be kept

Paul wrote, “Spare no effort to keep the unity the Spirit gives, with peace as the bond that holds you together” (Ephesians 4:3). Notice two things.

First, unity is something “the Spirit gives”. We do not create it. When people come to Christ, they are joined to Him and to one another by the Holy Spirit. Paul goes on, “There is one body and one Spirit ... one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Ephesians 4:4-6). Our unity is already real, because it rests on what God has done.

Second, we must “keep” it, and “spare no effort” to do so. Unity is like a fire. God lights it, but we must guard it, or it will go out. Paul tells us how: “Be humble and gentle in every way, and be patient, putting up with one another in love” (Ephesians 4:2). Humility, gentleness, patience and love. These are the tools of unity. Pride, harshness and impatience destroy it.

One new people

The early Church was made of people who had hated one another. Jews and Gentiles. Slaves and masters. Men and women who had never been treated as equals. Paul wrote, “There is no Jew or Greek, there is no slave or free person, there is no male and female, for all of you are one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28).

Paul did not mean that these differences disappeared. A Jew was still a Jew, and a slave was still a slave in Roman law. He meant that in Christ, these differences no longer divide us or rank us. “Christ himself is our peace. He has made the two groups into one, and has broken down the wall that divided them, the hostility between them” (Ephesians 2:14).

And the Bible’s final picture of the Church is the same. John saw “a crowd so vast that no one could number it. They came from every nation and from all tribes and peoples and languages, and they stood before the throne and before the Lamb” (Revelation 7:9). Every tribe. Every language. Together, worshipping one Lord.

This is a great challenge for leaders in our world. In many places, churches are divided along the lines of tribe or ethnic group, rich and poor, old and young, or one language and another. Sometimes leaders even encourage this, because it is easier to lead people who are like us. But a church that welcomes only one kind of person is preaching a smaller gospel than the Bible’s. We will look at the sin of tribalism and favouritism more closely in Chapter 36, Envy, Rivalry and Favouritism.

“I am for Paul”

The church in Corinth was full of gifted people. But it was also full of quarrels. Paul wrote, “every one of you takes a side: ‘I am for Paul,’ ‘I am for Apollos,’ ‘I am for Cephas,’ ‘I am for Christ.’ Has Christ been parceled out? Was it Paul who was crucified for you?” (1 Corinthians 1:12-13).

The Corinthians were dividing around leaders. Each group had its favourite preacher. Paul refused to be the head of a party. He said, “What, then, is Apollos? And what is Paul? Servants through whom you came to believe” (1 Corinthians 3:5).

Leaders today face the same temptation. It is pleasant to have a group who are loyal to you, who prefer you to other leaders. Some leaders even encourage it. They speak quietly against other pastors. They build their own little kingdom inside the church, or pull people away from one church to start their own. This is a serious sin. It treats Christ’s body as if it were ours to divide.

Here is a test for every leader: am I building my own group, or Christ’s Church? Do I rejoice when another church grows, or do I feel threatened? Do I speak well of other faithful leaders, or do I find ways to make myself look better than them?

Agreeing in the Lord

Not all disunity is about big doctrines. Often it is about two people who cannot get along. In the church at Philippi, there were two women, Euodia and Syntyche, who had been faithful workers with Paul. But now they had fallen out. Paul wrote, “I appeal to Euodia and I appeal to Syntyche to agree with each other in the Lord. Yes, and I ask you, my true partner, to help these women” (Philippians 4:2-3).

Notice three things. Paul named the problem openly, but gently. He did not take sides. And he asked another leader to help them make peace. A wise leader does not ignore quarrels between believers. Left alone, they grow and spread. But neither does a wise leader rush in to judge. They help both sides to come together “in the Lord”.

Jesus said that making peace is more urgent than worship: “if you are bringing your offering to the altar and there you remember that a brother or sister has something against you, leave your offering there in front of the altar. Go and make peace with them first, and then come back and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:23-24).

The work of a peacemaker

Jesus said, “Blessed are those who make peace: they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). Notice that He did not say “those who keep quiet” or “those who avoid trouble”. He said those who make peace. Peacemaking is active work. Here are some ways leaders do it.

  • Make peace first in your own relationships. “If it can be done, and so far as it lies with you, keep peace with everyone” (Romans 12:18). A leader who is at war with others cannot make peace between them.
  • Listen to both sides. Before you speak, understand. Most quarrels have hurt on both sides.
  • Name the problem honestly. Peace is not pretending nothing is wrong. Real peace often comes only after the truth has been spoken.
  • Call people to forgive. “Be patient with one another’s faults, and when someone has a grievance against another, forgive. The Lord has forgiven you freely; you must do the same” (Colossians 3:13).
  • Hold fast to the essentials, and be generous on other matters. “Welcome anyone whose faith is weak, but not in order to quarrel over their opinions” (Romans 14:1). Not every difference is worth a fight.
  • Refuse gossip. Do not repeat stories that damage others. Do not listen to them either.
  • Bring people to the cross. At the foot of the cross we are all sinners saved by grace. No one there is higher than anyone else.

Unity and truth

Unity does not mean that truth does not matter. Jesus prayed for unity in the same prayer where He said, “Your word is truth” (John 17:17). Paul, who worked so hard for unity, also warned strongly against false teaching (Galatians 1:6-9). There are times when faithful leaders must separate from teaching that denies the gospel.

But many divisions in church history have not been about the gospel at all. They have been about leaders’ pride, about money, about tribe, or about small matters of practice. A saying from the seventeenth century puts it well: “In essentials unity, in non-essentials liberty, in all things charity.” In plain words: agree on what is essential, give freedom on what is not, and love one another in everything. The saying was first written by a German Lutheran teacher called Rupertus Meldenius during the terrible religious wars of his day. It was later loved and repeated by Richard Baxter, the English pastor we met in Chapter 9, Keep Watch over Yourself, who longed to see Christians of different churches live in peace.

A voice from the Church: Clement, Cyprian and Gahini

Around the end of the first century, the church in Corinth was again divided. Some younger members had pushed out their faithful elders. The church in Rome sent them a letter, which we know as the First Epistle of Clement. It is one of the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament, and it is on Ochorus. Clement wrote:

“Why are there strifes, and tumults, and divisions, and schisms, and wars among you? Have we not [all] one God and one Christ? Is there not one Spirit of grace poured out upon us? And have we not one calling in Christ? Why do we divide and tear to pieces the members of Christ?”

— Clement of Rome, First Epistle of Clement

In plain words: why are you fighting and dividing? Do we not all have one God, one Christ, one Holy Spirit and one calling? Why are we tearing apart the body of Christ? Clement also told them, “Take up the epistle of the blessed Apostle Paul”, reminding them that Paul had already written to them about this very problem.

A century and a half later, Cyprian was bishop of Carthage in North Africa. After a time of cruel persecution, the church there was torn apart by quarrels over how to treat believers who had denied Christ under pressure. Rival groups set up rival bishops. Cyprian wrote a book called On the Unity of the Church, now in Treatises of Cyprian on Ochorus. He used pictures from nature:

“As there are many rays of the sun, but one light; and many branches of a tree, but one strength based in its tenacious root; and since from one spring flow many streams ... yet the unity is still preserved in the source.”

— Cyprian of Carthage, On the Unity of the Church

In plain words: the sun has many rays but one light. A tree has many branches but one strong root. Many streams flow from one spring. In the same way, the Church is spread far and wide, but it is one, because it comes from one source. Cyprian added that a branch broken from the tree cannot grow buds.

In the twentieth century, at the mission hospital at Gahini in Rwanda, there was real tension between the African staff and the European missionaries, over authority, money and respect. One of the African staff, Yosiya Kinuka, was at the centre of it. When the East African Revival came, it did not cover over the conflict. As the book Tukutendereza puts it, what the revival did was “to force it into the open and require both sides to confess.” Africans and Europeans repented to one another. The book draws a lesson every leader should hear: “Unity that costs nothing is not unity.” Much of what we call unity, it says, “is an agreement not to mention things.” True unity was made at Gahini “between people who had been genuinely at odds.”

So that the world may believe

The psalmist sang, “See how good it is, how lovely, when brothers and sisters live together in harmony!” (Psalm 133:1). Jesus said, “If you have love for one another, everyone will know by this that you are my disciples” (John 13:35).

A divided church preaches a weak gospel, however good its sermons are. A united church, where people of different tribes, classes and languages love one another, preaches a strong gospel before it says a word. Leaders after God’s heart will spare no effort to keep that unity, and will be called children of God.

Questions for reflection

  • Read John 17:20-23. Why do you think Jesus connected the unity of His people with the world believing in Him?
  • Is your church divided along lines of tribe, class, language or age? What would it take to change that?
  • Are you building your own group, or Christ’s Church? How do you feel when another church or leader does well?
  • Is there anyone you need to make peace with before you next lead worship (Matthew 5:23-24)?
  • Which matters in your church are essentials, and which are non-essentials where people should have freedom?
  • What does Gahini teach about the difference between peace-keeping and peacemaking?

A step for this week

Think of a broken relationship in your church, or between you and another leader or church. Pray about it every day this week. Then take one step towards peace: a visit, a phone call, an apology, or an offer to help two others meet. If you are the one who has caused hurt, say so plainly. Also, this week, speak well in public of one faithful leader from another church or group, and pray for their work.

study_questions.question: Why does unity matter in the church?
study_questions.answer: Jesus prayed that all His followers “may be one” so that the world may believe (John 17:21). Unity is a gift of the Spirit that we must keep: “Spare no effort to keep the unity the Spirit gives, with peace as the bond” (Ephesians 4:3).

study_questions.question: How can a leader be a peacemaker?
study_questions.answer: By being humble, gentle and patient, “putting up with one another in love” (Ephesians 4:2), by refusing to take sides in factions, and by helping people agree in the Lord. Christ “has broken down the wall that divided” people (Ephesians 2:14).

study_questions.question: Should unity be kept at the cost of truth?
study_questions.answer: No. Unity and truth belong together. The chapter explains how to hold firm on the essentials of the faith while extending grace on secondary matters, drawing on Clement, Cyprian and the East African Revival at Gahini in Rwanda.

fields.title: Criticism, Opposition and Conflict
fields.body_html:
“A gentle reply calms anger, but a hurtful word makes tempers flare.”

— Proverbs 15:1 (OWB)

A tree that grows tall catches more wind. The small bushes on the ground hardly feel the storm, but the tall tree bends and shakes. It is the same with leaders. The moment you stand up to lead, you will be criticised. Some criticism will be fair. Some will be unfair. Some people will oppose you openly. And sooner or later, you will find yourself in conflict with another leader, perhaps even a good friend.

No leader escapes this. Moses did not. Nehemiah did not. Paul did not. Jesus Himself did not. The question is not whether you will face criticism, opposition and conflict, but how you will respond. This chapter looks at all three.

Receiving criticism

When someone criticises us, our first reaction is usually to defend ourselves. We explain, we argue, or we attack back. Sometimes we go quiet and nurse our hurt for weeks.

The Bible calls us to a different response. “To love discipline is to love knowledge; to hate correction is plain stupidity” (Proverbs 12:1). “Fools think their own way is right, but the wise listen to advice” (Proverbs 12:15). James adds, “Every person should be eager to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19).

When you are criticised, try these steps.

  • Stop and pray before you answer. Do not reply in the heat of the moment. A message written in anger is usually regretted.
  • Ask, “Is there any truth in this?” Even unfair criticism often contains a grain of truth. If God is using it to show you something, receive it.
  • Consider the source, but do not dismiss it. A hostile person may still be right. A friend may still be wrong.
  • Thank the person if you can. It takes courage for most people to criticise a leader. If they came to you directly, that is better than talking behind your back.
  • Change what needs changing. If the criticism is true, admit it plainly, and do something about it.
  • Let go of what is false. If it is not true, commit it to God and move on.

When King David was fleeing from his son Absalom, a man named Shimei walked beside the road, cursing him and throwing stones. One of David’s soldiers wanted to kill him. But David said, “Leave him alone and let him curse, because the LORD has told him to. Perhaps the LORD will look on my distress and repay me with good in place of his cursing today” (2 Samuel 16:11-12). David did not assume that he was always in the right. He was willing to believe that God might be speaking to him, even through an enemy.

Not taking everything to heart

At the same time, a leader cannot carry every word that is said about them. The Preacher in Ecclesiastes gives wise advice: “do not take to heart everything people say, or you may hear your servant cursing you. For you know in your heart that you yourself have often cursed others” (Ecclesiastes 7:21-22).

In other words, people will say unkind things about you. Do not go looking for them. And remember that you have said unkind things about others too. That should make you humble, and it should make you patient.

Some leaders are so hungry for approval that every criticism wounds them deeply. They cannot rest until everyone is happy with them. This is a kind of slavery. Paul wrote, “If I were still out to please people, I would be no servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10). We serve one Master. His opinion is the one that matters most.

Facing opposition: Nehemiah

Nehemiah was a Jewish official in the Persian court who returned to Jerusalem to rebuild its broken walls. From the first day, he faced opposition. His enemies, Sanballat and Tobiah, used almost every weapon that opponents still use today.

Mockery. “What are these feeble Jews doing? Will they restore the wall by themselves?” Tobiah added, “if a fox climbed up on it, it would break down their stone wall!” (Nehemiah 4:2-3). Nehemiah did not answer them. He prayed and kept working.

Threats. The enemies planned to attack. Nehemiah’s response was simple and balanced: “we prayed to our God and posted a guard day and night” (Nehemiah 4:9). He trusted God and took sensible action. He told the frightened people, “Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome” (Nehemiah 4:14).

Distraction. His enemies invited him to a meeting, planning to harm him. Nehemiah replied, “I am doing a great work and cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it to come down to you?” (Nehemiah 6:3). Not every invitation to argue deserves an answer. Some opposition is designed only to stop the work.

Lies and fear. They spread false reports about him and tried to frighten him into hiding in the temple (Nehemiah 6:5-13). Nehemiah refused to act out of fear.

And the wall was finished in fifty-two days (Nehemiah 6:15). The enemies lost all their confidence, “for they knew that this work had been done with the help of our God” (Nehemiah 6:16).

Facing opposition: Moses

Some opposition comes from inside the people of God. In the wilderness, a man named Korah, with two hundred and fifty leaders, rose up against Moses and Aaron. “You claim too much!” they said. “What right have you to raise yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?” (Numbers 16:3).

Look at what Moses did: “When Moses heard this, he fell facedown” (Numbers 16:4). His first response was not to argue or to fight back. It was to fall before God. Then he left the judgement to God. The Bible says that “Moses was exceedingly humble, more so than any other human being on earth” (Numbers 12:3). A humble leader does not need to defend their position. They leave it in God’s hands.

This is the way of Jesus. “People heaped abuse on him, yet he did not answer abuse with abuse. As he suffered, he made no threats, but went on handing himself over to the God who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). Paul wrote, “Do not pay anyone back with evil for the evil done to you ... Do not let evil defeat you; defeat evil with good” (Romans 12:17, 21).

Conflict between leaders

Perhaps the hardest kind of conflict is between good leaders who love God. The Bible is honest about this. Paul and Barnabas had worked together for years. Barnabas had brought Paul into the ministry. But when they planned their second journey, they disagreed about John Mark, who had left them on their first journey. “The quarrel grew so heated that the two of them parted ways. Barnabas took Mark and sailed off to Cyprus, while Paul picked Silas” (Acts 15:39-40).

It is a sad verse. But God used even this. Instead of one missionary team, there were now two. Paul went on “making the churches strong” (Acts 15:41). Barnabas gave Mark a second chance, and Mark later became useful even to Paul (2 Timothy 4:11). The story does not end with the quarrel.

There is another kind of conflict in Acts 15: a disagreement about doctrine. Some teachers said that Gentile believers had to be circumcised to be saved. “This led to fierce dispute and argument” (Acts 15:2). The church did not ignore it, and it did not split over it. “The apostles and the elders came together to consider this matter” (Acts 15:6). They listened to each other, looked at what God was doing, searched the Scriptures, and reached a common decision: “The Holy Spirit and we ourselves have decided” (Acts 15:28).

Here is wisdom for conflict between leaders:

  • Meet face to face. Do not fight by letters, messages or rumours.
  • Listen first. Make sure you understand the other person’s view before you answer it.
  • Separate the person from the issue. You can disagree strongly and still love and respect each other.
  • Look to Scripture together. Let God’s Word, not personal pride, be the judge.
  • Know what matters most. Some differences are about the gospel. Most are not.
  • If you must part, part well. Do not speak against each other afterwards. Pray for each other. Leave the door open for reconciliation.

A voice from the Church: John Wesley and George Whitefield

John Wesley and George Whitefield were the two greatest preachers of the eighteenth-century revival in Britain and America. They had been friends at Oxford. It was Whitefield who first persuaded Wesley to preach in the open air, to crowds of thousands. They worked side by side in the early years.

But they came to disagree deeply about a question of doctrine: how God’s choosing of people for salvation relates to human free will. Whitefield held one view and Wesley the other. Both published their views, and the quarrel became public. Wesley’s Journal, which is on Ochorus, records a painful meeting in March 1741. Whitefield told him “that he and I preached two different gospels; and therefore he not only would not join with or give me the right hand of fellowship, but was resolved publicly to preach against me and my brother.” Their followers took sides. The movement split.

Yet even at the height of the quarrel, Wesley acted with some grace. When a private letter from Whitefield attacking him was printed without permission and handed out to Wesley’s own people, Wesley told the congregation, “I will do just what I believe Mr. Whitefield would, were he here himself.” Then he tore it up in front of them, and everyone else did the same.

Over time, the two men were reconciled. They never fully agreed on the doctrine. But they came to see each other again as brothers in Christ, preached in each other’s chapels, and spoke warmly of each other. When Whitefield died in America in 1770, he had asked that Wesley preach his funeral sermon in London. Wesley wrote in his Journal:

“An immense multitude was gathered together from all corners of the town ... It was an awful season: all were still as night; most appeared to be deeply affected.”

— John Wesley, Journal, November 1770

In plain words: a huge crowd came from every part of the city. It was a solemn time. Everyone was completely silent, and most were deeply moved. Wesley prayed that God would use the occasion to call “all His children to love one another”. He also hoped that God had struck “a blow to that bigotry which had prevailed for many years”, the narrow spirit that had divided the two groups.

The story of Wesley and Whitefield shows that even great and godly leaders can quarrel bitterly. But it also shows that a quarrel does not have to be the end of the story.

One blind eye and one deaf ear

Charles Spurgeon often told his students that “a minister ought to have one blind eye and one deaf ear.” He explained what he meant in a lecture now in Lectures to My Students, Second Series, on Ochorus. He did not mean that a leader should ignore real problems. He meant that a leader should not go looking for every unkind word, every bit of gossip and every small offence. Many things are best not seen and not heard. He warned his students not to be drawn into parties and cliques: “Know nothing of parties and cliques, but be the pastor of all the flock, and care for all alike.” And he added, “Blessed are the peacemakers, and one sure way of peacemaking is to let the fire of contention alone. Neither fan it, nor stir it, nor add fuel to it, but let it go out of itself.”

In plain words: some quarrels are best left alone. If you keep talking about them, you feed them. If you stop, they often die out on their own.

A gentle answer

“A gentle reply calms anger, but a hurtful word makes tempers flare” (Proverbs 15:1). Most of us know this verse. Few of us live it when we are criticised or opposed. But every leader who has finished well has had to learn it.

Jesus said, “love your enemies, and pray for the people who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). That is the final answer to opposition. Pray for your critics. Bless your opponents. Seek peace with those you disagree with. And keep building the wall.

Questions for reflection

  • Think of the last time you were criticised. How did you respond? What would you do differently now?
  • Read 2 Samuel 16:5-12. What do you learn from David’s response to Shimei?
  • Read Nehemiah 4 and 6. Which of the weapons used against Nehemiah have you faced? How did he respond to each?
  • Is there a conflict with another leader that you have left unresolved? What step could you take?
  • What do you learn from the story of Wesley and Whitefield?
  • What would it mean for you to have “one blind eye and one deaf ear”? Where would that be wise, and where would it be wrong?

A step for this week

Think of a recent criticism you received, fair or unfair. Write it down. Then pray over it and ask, “Lord, is there any truth in this for me?” Write down what you hear. If there is truth in it, take one step to change, and if possible thank the person who said it. Then pray by name for anyone who has opposed you, asking God to bless them.

study_questions.question: How should a leader respond to criticism?
study_questions.answer: By listening first and asking whether it is true. “Every person should be eager to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19). “The wise listen to advice” (Proverbs 12:15). And “A gentle reply calms anger” (Proverbs 15:1).

study_questions.question: Should a leader take every criticism to heart?
study_questions.answer: No. Ecclesiastes says, “do not take to heart everything people say” (Ecclesiastes 7:21). When Shimei cursed him, David said, “Leave him alone and let him curse” and trusted God with it (2 Samuel 16:11).

study_questions.question: How can two Christian leaders handle disagreement?
study_questions.answer: With honesty, humility and love, without breaking fellowship. The chapter tells how John Wesley and George Whitefield disagreed deeply about doctrine and quarrelled in public, yet were reconciled, and Whitefield asked Wesley to preach at his funeral.

fields.title: Men and Women in the Work of God
fields.body_html:
“In those days I will pour out my Spirit even on my servants, men and women alike, and they will prophesy.”

— Acts 2:18 (OWB)

Walk into almost any church in the world on a Sunday morning, and count the people. In most places, more than half of them will be women. Then ask who prays for the sick in the week, who teaches the children, who visits the lonely, who cooks for the funerals, who leads the prayer meetings and who keeps the church going when times are hard. Very often, the answer is the same: women.

The Church of Jesus Christ has always depended on the faith and work of women. And yet in many places, women’s gifts are ignored, wasted or even despised. This chapter, the last in Part Five, Leading Together, is about men and women working together in the work of God. It will look first at what the Bible shows us, which almost all Christians agree on. Then, in a “Going deeper” section, it will set out fairly the main views on a question where faithful Christians disagree: whether some offices in the church are for men only.

Made together in God’s image

The story begins at creation. “So God created human beings in his image. In the image of God he created them; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). Men and women alike bear God’s image. Both were given the task of caring for God’s world. Neither is a lesser copy of the other.

When sin entered the world, it broke this partnership. Men began to rule over women in harsh and selfish ways (Genesis 3:16). Much of human history, in every culture, shows the sad results. In many places today, girls are given less food and less education than boys, wives are beaten, and widows are thrown out of their homes. The gospel speaks against all of this. Peter tells husbands to honour their wives as those who “will inherit the grace of life together with you” (1 Peter 3:7). Men and women are fellow heirs of God’s grace.

Women who led and served in the Bible

The Bible is full of women whom God used in remarkable ways.

  • Miriam, Moses’ sister, was called “the prophetess” and led the women of Israel in praise after the crossing of the sea (Exodus 15:20).
  • Deborah was “a prophet” who “was judging Israel at that time ... and the Israelites came up to her to have their disputes decided” (Judges 4:4-5). She called Barak to lead the army, and went with him into battle.
  • Huldah was a prophet in Jerusalem. When the lost book of the law was found in the temple, King Josiah sent the high priest and his officials to her to ask what God was saying (2 Kings 22:14).
  • The women who followed Jesus, Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna “and many others”, travelled with Jesus and the Twelve and “were using their own resources to provide for them” (Luke 8:1-3).
  • Mary Magdalene was the first person to see the risen Lord. Jesus sent her to tell the disciples, and she went and said, “I have seen the Lord!” (John 20:18).
  • Priscilla, with her husband Aquila, taught the gifted preacher Apollos “the way of God more precisely” (Acts 18:26). Paul called them “my fellow workers in Christ Jesus” (Romans 16:3).
  • Philip’s four daughters “prophesied” (Acts 21:9).
  • Phoebe carried Paul’s letter to the Romans. Paul called her a servant or deacon of the church in Cenchreae, and “a patron to many, and to me as well” (Romans 16:1-2). Bible translations differ on the best word here.
  • Euodia and Syntyche, Paul said, “have fought side by side with me for the gospel” (Philippians 4:3).
  • Lois and Eunice, Timothy’s grandmother and mother, passed on the faith that shaped one of the great leaders of the early Church (2 Timothy 1:5).

In Romans 16 alone, Paul names eight women, among them Tryphaena, Tryphosa and Persis, “women who work hard in the Lord” (Romans 16:12). He did not see women as spectators in the work of the gospel. He saw them as fellow workers.

The Spirit on sons and daughters

On the day of Pentecost, Peter explained what was happening by quoting the prophet Joel: “I will pour out my Spirit on all humanity. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy ... In those days I will pour out my Spirit even on my servants, men and women alike, and they will prophesy” (Acts 2:17-18).

The Holy Spirit gives His gifts to all believers. Peter wrote, “Each of you has received a gift; use it to serve one another” (1 Peter 4:10). Each of you, man or woman. The question for every leader is not whether women have gifts, for the Bible is clear that they do. The question is whether we are helping them to use those gifts, or wasting them.

Wasted gifts

Imagine a farmer who has ten good oxen but lets only five of them pull the plough. The other five stand in the field, strong and ready, but never used. The farmer works twice as hard as he needs to, and the harvest is smaller than it should be. That is what happens when churches ignore the gifts of half their members.

Whatever view a church holds about the offices of pastor and elder, there is a great deal of work in God’s kingdom that almost all Christians agree women may do. They may pray, prophesy (1 Corinthians 11:5), evangelise, teach children and other women (Titus 2:3-4), care for the sick and poor, serve as missionaries, translate Scripture, lead ministries, counsel, give wise advice to the church’s leaders, and much more. Yet in many churches, even these things are not encouraged.

Here are some questions for every leader, whatever their view:

  • Do the women in my church know that God has given them gifts, and that the church needs them?
  • Are women trained and encouraged, or only given the cooking and the cleaning?
  • When decisions are made that affect the whole church, are the wisdom and experience of women heard?
  • Is my church a safe place for women and girls? We will return to this in Chapter 35, Power, Abuse and Protecting the Vulnerable.
  • Do I honour the work of women in public, as Paul did in Romans 16?

Going deeper: the debate about church offices

Christians who love the Bible and want to obey it have come to different conclusions about whether women may serve as pastors, elders or bishops. This is not a debate between those who believe the Bible and those who do not. It is a debate about how to understand certain passages. Here are the two main views, stated as their own supporters would state them. Readers can skip this section and come back to it later.

The first view is often called complementarian. It holds that men and women are equal in worth and dignity, but that God has given them different roles that complement each other. In the church, it holds, the office of elder or pastor, which carries the responsibility of overseeing the church and its teaching, is for qualified men. Its supporters point to 1 Timothy 2:12, where Paul writes, “I do not allow a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man”, and note that Paul grounds this in creation (“For Adam was formed first, and then Eve”, 1 Timothy 2:13), not only in the customs of his day. They also point out that Jesus chose twelve men as apostles, and that the qualifications for elders in 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1 are written with men in view. Supporters of this view encourage women to use their gifts widely, including in teaching and leading in many settings, while keeping the office of elder for men.

The second view is often called egalitarian. It holds that all ministries and offices in the church are open to both men and women, according to their gifts and calling. Its supporters point to the women who led in the Bible, such as Deborah, Huldah, Priscilla and Phoebe, and to Junia, whom Paul describes in Romans 16:7 in words that many translations render “prominent among the apostles” (others translate it “well known to the apostles”). They point to the Spirit being poured out on sons and daughters, and to Galatians 3:28, “there is no male and female, for all of you are one in Christ Jesus.” They believe that passages such as 1 Timothy 2:11-15 and 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 addressed particular problems in particular churches, and were not meant to forbid women from all teaching and leadership for all time.

There are also many positions in between, and churches in the same family often differ. Some allow women to preach but not to be senior pastor. Some ordain women as deacons but not as elders. Some, such as many in the Pentecostal tradition, have long recognised women as evangelists and church planters.

Whatever view you hold, here is some counsel.

  • Study the passages yourself, carefully and in context, with prayer. Do not simply follow your culture, whether traditional or modern.
  • Hold your view with humility. Faithful, godly, learned Christians hold the other view. Treat them as brothers and sisters, not as enemies.
  • Follow the teaching of your church unless your conscience truly forbids it, and if you disagree, raise it with your leaders respectfully, as we saw in Chapter 6, Authority Under Authority.
  • Do not let the debate become an excuse to waste the gifts of women in all the many ministries where no one disputes they may serve.

A voice from the Church: daughters of the King

Church history is full of women whose faith and work changed the world. Here are four from four continents.

Susanna Wesley was the wife of a pastor in the village of Epworth in England, and the mother of John and Charles Wesley. In the winter of 1711 to 1712, while her husband was away in London, she began to hold readings and prayers in her kitchen on Sunday evenings for her children and servants. Neighbours asked to come. Soon there were far more people than the house could hold. When her husband wrote to object, partly because she was a woman, she answered him in a letter that is quoted in Eliza Clarke’s life of her, on Ochorus:

“As I am a woman, so I am also a mistress of a large family. And though the superior charge of the souls contained in it lies upon you, as head of the family, and as their minister, yet in your absence I cannot but look upon every soul you leave under my care as a talent committed to me, under a trust, by the great Lord of all the families of heaven and earth.”

— Susanna Wesley, letter to her husband, 6 February 1712

In plain words: yes, I am a woman, but I am also in charge of a large household. You are the head of the family and its minister. But while you are away, I must treat every soul you leave in my care as a treasure that God has trusted me with. Notice that Susanna did not reject her husband’s authority. She honoured it. But she also refused to bury the talent God had given her. Her son John never forgot those kitchen meetings.

Amanda Berry Smith was born into slavery in Maryland, in the United States, in 1837. After her family gained their freedom, she worked for years as a washerwoman. She became a powerful evangelist, and travelled to preach in England, in India, and for eight years in Liberia in West Africa. Her Autobiography is on Ochorus.

Mary Slessor was a mill worker from Dundee in Scotland who went as a missionary to Calabar in what is now south-eastern Nigeria in 1876. She lived among the people of Okoyong, learned their language and customs, rescued twin babies who would otherwise have been left to die, and was eventually trusted by both the people and the British government to act as a local judge. Her life, Mary Slessor: A Life, is on Ochorus.

Pandita Ramabai was born in India in 1858. She became a great scholar of Sanskrit, came to faith in Christ, and gave her life to the widows and orphans of India. At her community at Mukti, near Pune, she cared for some two thousand women and children at a time. In the last years of her life she translated the whole Bible from Hebrew and Greek into the everyday Marathi of village women. Pandita Ramabai: A Life, on Ochorus, records that she called herself a sweeper: “I sweep into this compound as many as I can get ... child-widows, deserted wives, and orphans of every kind.”

We could add many more: Dora Yu, the Chinese evangelist through whose preaching the young Watchman Nee came to Christ in 1920; Catherine Booth, who helped found the Salvation Army; and the many unnamed women of the East African Revival. The Church has been carried on the shoulders of its daughters as much as its sons.

Fellow workers

Paul ended his letter to the Romans with a long list of greetings to men and women who had worked with him. He called them “fellow workers”, “dear”, “hard-working” and “in Christ”. A leader after God’s heart will see the Church the same way: not as a few leaders and many spectators, but as a body of sons and daughters, each with gifts from the same Spirit, working together for the same Lord.

Questions for reflection

  • Read Romans 16:1-16. What strikes you about the women Paul greets, and how he speaks of them?
  • Which women have most shaped your own faith? How did God use them?
  • In your church, are the gifts of women used, or wasted? What could change?
  • Read the two views in “Going deeper”. Which do you hold? Can you state the other view fairly, in a way its supporters would accept?
  • How can you hold your view on this question with both conviction and humility?
  • What do you learn from Susanna Wesley’s letter to her husband?

A step for this week

Make a list of the women in your church or ministry, and next to each name write one gift you see in her. This week, speak to at least two of them. Tell them what gift you see, thank them for how they serve, and ask how the church could help them use that gift more. If you lead a leadership team, ask the team together: “Whose gifts are we not using, and why?”

study_questions.question: Can women serve in the work of God?
study_questions.answer: Yes. Men and women are made together in God’s image (Genesis 1:27), and at Pentecost the Spirit was poured out “on my servants, men and women alike” (Acts 2:18). Women such as Deborah, Mary Magdalene, Priscilla and Phoebe served God in many ways.

study_questions.question: What does the Bible say about women in church leadership?
study_questions.answer: Faithful Christians disagree about whether women may hold certain church offices. The chapter’s “Going deeper” section sets out the main views fairly. All agree that the gifts God gives women must not be wasted.

study_questions.question: Which women in the Bible served in God’s work?
study_questions.answer: Deborah, who “was judging Israel at that time” (Judges 4:4); the women who provided for Jesus “using their own resources” (Luke 8:3); Mary Magdalene, who announced, “I have seen the Lord!” (John 20:18); and Priscilla, who explained “the way of God more precisely” to Apollos (Acts 18:26).

fields.title: Vision: Seeing What God Sees
fields.body_html:
“Write down the vision; make it plain on tablets, so that whoever reads it can run. For the vision still waits for its appointed time.”

— Habakkuk 2:2-3 (OWB)

A man who builds a house first sees it in his mind. Before he digs the foundations, he knows where the door will be, how many rooms there will be and which way the windows will face. Without that picture, he would pile up stones and hope for the best. With it, every day’s work has a purpose.

Leaders need to see where they are going. In the business world this is often called “vision”. But the word is used in many ways, and some of them are not Christian at all. This chapter begins Part Six, Vision and Mission. It asks: what is a true vision for God’s people, where does it come from, and how should a leader hold it?

A verse to read carefully

Many leaders have quoted an old English translation of Proverbs 29:18: “Where there is no vision, the people perish.” They have used it to say that a church needs a leader with a big plan, or it will die. But this is not what the verse means.

In the Hebrew, the word translated “vision” means a revelation from God, the kind of message a prophet receives. The Open Word Bible, like most modern translations, makes this plain: “Where there is no prophetic revelation, a people throws off all restraint; but how blessed are those who keep God’s instruction!” (Proverbs 29:18).

The verse is about God’s Word, not a leader’s plans. When God’s people do not hear from Him, they lose their way and do whatever they like. When they keep His instruction, they are blessed. So the first and greatest vision any church needs is not a leader’s dream. It is God’s Word, clearly heard and faithfully obeyed. In whatever language you read this book, look at how your own Bible translates this verse, and teach it carefully.

What true vision is

If vision is not a leader’s dream, what is it? A true vision is seeing what God has said He will do, and believing it enough to act.

God has already told us a great deal about the future. He has promised that “all the families of the earth will be blessed through” Abraham (Genesis 12:3). He has promised a vast crowd “from every nation and from all tribes and peoples and languages” standing before the throne (Revelation 7:9). He has promised, “See, I am making everything new!” (Revelation 21:5). Jesus taught us to pray, “May your kingdom come. May your will be done on earth, as it is done in heaven” (Matthew 6:10).

These promises are the big picture. Within that big picture, God often gives particular leaders and churches a particular part to play. He showed Abraham a land. He showed Nehemiah a ruined wall. He showed Paul a man from Macedonia pleading, “Cross over to Macedonia and help us!” (Acts 16:9). Each of these was a glimpse of how God’s great purpose would be worked out in one place, through one person or people.

So a true vision has three marks. It comes from God. It fits with what He has already said in Scripture. And it serves His glory and His kingdom, not our name.

False vision

The Bible warns about leaders who claim to see things that God has not shown them. Through Jeremiah, God said, “Do not listen to what the prophets are prophesying to you; they are filling you with empty hopes. They speak visions that come from their own minds, and not from the mouth of the LORD” (Jeremiah 23:16).

This is a real danger today. Some leaders announce great visions: a church of ten thousand, a building larger than any in the city, a ministry on television across the nation. Sometimes God does lead people to do great things. But sometimes these “visions” are only personal ambition dressed up in Bible verses. The leader wants to be important, and calls it God’s plan.

Here are some questions to test a vision:

  • Does it come out of prayer, or only out of my own thinking?
  • Does it fit with Scripture, and with the character of Jesus?
  • Who will get the glory if it succeeds: God, or me?
  • Have mature, godly people confirmed it, or am I the only one who sees it?
  • Am I willing to give it up if God says no?
  • Does it serve people, or use them?

In Chapter 16, Guidance and Decisions, we looked at how God guides. The same wisdom applies here. A true vision can be tested, and should be.

Nehemiah: vision born in prayer

The best example of godly vision in the Bible may be Nehemiah. He was a servant of the king of Persia, far from Jerusalem. One day, visitors told him that “The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates have been burned.” Look at his response: “When I heard these words, I sat down and wept. For some days I mourned, and I kept fasting and praying before the God of heaven” (Nehemiah 1:3-4).

Notice that Nehemiah’s vision began with a burden. He did not start with a plan. He started with tears. He saw a need that broke his heart, and he took it to God. His prayer in Nehemiah 1 is full of confession and of God’s promises. Only after months of prayer did he act.

When the king asked what was wrong, Nehemiah “prayed to the God of heaven” in the moment, and then answered, “send me to Judah ... so that I can rebuild it” (Nehemiah 2:4-5). When he arrived in Jerusalem, he did not announce his plan at once. He went out at night, quietly, to inspect the walls. “I had not told anyone what my God was putting into my heart to do for Jerusalem” (Nehemiah 2:12).

Then, at the right time, he gathered the people: “You see the trouble we are in: Jerusalem lies in ruins ... Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem.” He told them how God had helped him. And the people answered, “Let us start building!” (Nehemiah 2:17-18).

Notice the order: a burden, then prayer, then careful looking, then sharing the vision with others, then working together. Nehemiah’s vision did not belong to him alone. He helped the people see what he saw, until it became their vision too.

Holding a vision in faith

God told Habakkuk, “Write down the vision; make it plain on tablets, so that whoever reads it can run. For the vision still waits for its appointed time ... Though it lingers, wait for it; it will certainly come and will not be late” (Habakkuk 2:2-3).

Here is wisdom for leaders. First, make the vision plain. If people cannot understand where you are going, they cannot go with you. Say it simply, and say it often.

Second, be patient. God’s visions often take longer than we expect. Abraham waited twenty-five years for the son God had promised. Joseph waited many years in slavery and prison before his dreams came true. Some visions are not fulfilled in the lifetime of the person who first sees them. Hebrews says of Abraham and the patriarchs, “All these died still holding to faith. They did not receive what was promised, but they saw it from far off and welcomed it” (Hebrews 11:13).

Third, obey. Paul told King Agrippa, “I did not resist the heavenly vision” (Acts 26:19). A vision is not something to admire. It is something to obey, step by step, even when the road is hard.

And fourth, expect God to do more than you imagine. Paul prayed to the God “who is able to do all things, far beyond anything we ask or think, by the power that is at work in us” (Ephesians 3:20). Many leaders do not dream too big. They dream too small, because they forget how great God is.

A voice from the Church: William Carey

William Carey was a shoemaker and village pastor in England in the eighteenth century. He had little formal schooling. But as he mended shoes, he kept a map of the world on the wall of his workshop, and he read every book about distant lands he could find. He was troubled that millions of people had never heard of Christ, and that most churches of his day did nothing about it. Many believed that if God wanted the far nations to be saved, He would do it without human help.

In 1792, Carey preached to a meeting of ministers in the English town of Nottingham. His text was Isaiah 54:2-3: “Make room in your tent; let the curtains of your dwellings be spread wide, and hold nothing back ... For you will burst out to the right and to the left.” The sermon was never printed. But as the book The Fire on the Altar on Ochorus explains, our earliest account comes from John Ryland, who heard it. He wrote that Carey was:

“chiefly endeavouring to enforce our obligations to expect great things from God, and to attempt great things for God.”

— John Ryland, describing Carey’s sermon of 1792

In plain words: Carey urged them that it was their duty to expect great things from God, and to try to do great things for God. These words became the motto of his life. Notice the order. First expect, then attempt. Carey’s vision did not begin with his own strength. It began with confidence in what God had promised.

Even after the sermon, the ministers were ready to go home with nothing decided. But Carey would not let the matter drop. A few months later, a small group of them formed a society to send missionaries. The next year Carey sailed for India. He stayed there for the rest of his life, about forty years, and never returned home. For seven years he saw almost no fruit. His wife suffered terribly from mental illness. Fire destroyed years of his translation work. Yet he kept going. With his co-workers, he translated the Bible, in whole or in part, into many languages of India and Asia. He also started schools, fought against cruel customs and inspired a whole movement of missions.

Carey is remembered as describing himself very simply: “I can plod.” His vision was large, but the way he fulfilled it was patient, ordinary, daily work. That is how most God-given visions are fulfilled.

Seeing what God sees

Jesus “saw the crowds” and “felt deep pity for them” (Matthew 9:36). Nehemiah heard of a broken wall and wept. Carey looked at a map and saw people who had never heard of Christ. True vision begins when we see the world as God sees it: its needs, its brokenness and its people, and also His promises for it.

Ask God to give you eyes to see. Then pray until the burden becomes a plan, share it until others see it too, and work until God fulfils it, in His time.

Questions for reflection

  • How have you heard Proverbs 29:18 used? Having read what it actually says, how should it be taught?
  • Is there a need in your community that breaks your heart, as the broken wall broke Nehemiah’s? What have you done with that burden?
  • Use the questions in “False vision” to test something you hope to do. What do they show you?
  • Read Nehemiah 2:11-18. What steps did Nehemiah take before he told others his plan?
  • Is your vision plain enough for others to understand it and “run” with it?
  • Carey said, “Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God.” Which do you find harder: expecting or attempting?

A step for this week

Set aside an hour this week to pray about your community, as Nehemiah prayed about Jerusalem. Ask God to show you what He sees: its needs, its people and His promises for it. Write down what comes to mind. Then read Nehemiah 1 and 2 slowly. At the end of the week, share what you have written with one or two trusted leaders, and ask them whether they see it too.

study_questions.question: What is vision in Christian leadership?
study_questions.answer: It is seeing what God sees and wants to do, and holding it in faith. God told Habakkuk, “Write down the vision; make it plain on tablets, so that whoever reads it can run” (Habakkuk 2:2). True vision serves God’s kingdom: “May your kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10).

study_questions.question: Does Proverbs 29:18 mean that people perish without a leader’s vision?
study_questions.answer: Not exactly. In the OWB it reads, “Where there is no prophetic revelation, a people throws off all restraint” (Proverbs 29:18). It is about God’s word revealed, not a leader’s plans. The chapter reads the verse carefully before building on it.

study_questions.question: How is vision born?
study_questions.answer: Often in prayer and sorrow over what is broken. When Nehemiah heard about Jerusalem, “I sat down and wept. For some days I mourned, and I kept fasting and praying” (Nehemiah 1:4). The chapter warns against false visions that come from a leader’s own heart (Jeremiah 23:16).

fields.title: Wisdom and Planning
fields.body_html:
“Hand over what you do to the LORD, and your plans will stand firm.”

— Proverbs 16:3 (OWB)

A farmer does not wait until the rains come to think about planting. Long before, he mends his tools, chooses his seed, prepares the ground and decides which crop goes in which field. He watches the sky and listens to the old people who know the seasons. Then, when the rain falls, he is ready. But the farmer also knows that he cannot make it rain. He plans carefully, and then he trusts God for the harvest.

In the last chapter we saw that a true vision comes from God. But a vision without a plan is only a wish. This chapter is about the wisdom of planning: how godly leaders turn what God has shown them into wise, practical steps, while still depending on Him.

Is planning unspiritual?

Some Christians think that planning shows a lack of faith. “If God is leading us,” they say, “why do we need to plan? Let us just pray and follow the Spirit.” Others plan so much that they leave no room for God at all. Both are mistakes.

The Bible honours careful planning. “The plans of the diligent bring nothing but gain, but all who rush in haste come to nothing but need” (Proverbs 21:5). “A house is built through wisdom and made secure through understanding” (Proverbs 24:3). Proverbs even points us to the ant, which “gets its food ready in summer and gathers its supplies at harvest time” (Proverbs 6:8).

Jesus Himself used planning as a picture of discipleship. “If any of you planned to build a tower, would you not sit down first and add up the expense, to find out whether you could afford to finish it? If you lay the foundation and cannot finish the job, everyone who sees it will start to make fun of you” (Luke 14:28-29). In many towns you can see half-finished church buildings, started with great excitement and then left for years, because no one counted the cost. Jesus’ words are a warning to leaders.

Joseph, in Egypt, made one of the greatest plans in the Bible. God showed Pharaoh, through dreams, that seven years of plenty would be followed by seven years of famine. Joseph advised Pharaoh to store up grain during the good years, “as a food supply ... for the land to draw on during the seven years of famine” (Genesis 41:35-36). God gave the revelation. Joseph made the plan. Millions of lives were saved.

So planning is not the opposite of faith. Done rightly, it is an act of faith. It takes God’s promises seriously enough to prepare for them.

Plans held in God’s hand

At the same time, the Bible reminds us that our plans are not the final word. “People plot their course in their minds, but it is the LORD who guides their steps” (Proverbs 16:9). “People have many plans in their minds, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will prevail” (Proverbs 19:21).

James warns those who make plans as if they controlled the future: “Listen now, you who say, ‘Today or tomorrow we will travel to a certain city, stay there a year, run a business, and make a profit.’ Yet you do not know what your life will be like tomorrow. You are a puff of vapor ... What you ought to say instead is this: ‘If the Lord wills, we will live, and we will do this or that’” (James 4:13-15).

James is not saying, “Do not plan.” He is saying, “Plan humbly.” Hold your plans in an open hand. Be ready for God to change them. Paul planned to go to Spain (Romans 15:24). As far as we know from the Bible, he never got there. Instead, God sent him to Rome in chains. Paul’s plans changed, but God’s purpose did not fail.

Here is a simple test: do I pray and then plan, or plan and then pray? Many leaders make all their decisions and then ask God to bless them. A wiser way is to begin with prayer, plan in prayer, and keep praying as the plan unfolds. “Hand over what you do to the LORD, and your plans will stand firm” (Proverbs 16:3).

Nehemiah the planner

In the last chapter, we saw that Nehemiah’s vision began with prayer and tears. Now look at how carefully he planned.

He prepared before he asked. When the king asked Nehemiah what he wanted, he already knew. He asked for letters of safe passage to the governors on the way and a letter to the keeper of the king’s forest for timber, naming the gates and the wall he needed it for (Nehemiah 2:7-8). He had thought it through.

He inspected before he spoke. When he arrived in Jerusalem, he went out by night and “inspected the walls of Jerusalem, which had been broken down, and its gates, which had been destroyed by fire” (Nehemiah 2:13). He saw the problem with his own eyes before he made his plans public.

He divided the work. Nehemiah 3 is a long list of names. Each family or group built the section of wall nearest their home. The high priest and his fellow priests “set to work and rebuilt the Sheep Gate” (Nehemiah 3:1). Goldsmiths, perfume-makers, merchants and rulers all had their part. A big task became many small ones.

He adjusted the plan when trouble came. When enemies threatened, Nehemiah changed the plan: “half of my men did the work while the other half held the spears, shields, bows and armor” (Nehemiah 4:16). He did not abandon the work. He adapted it.

The wall was finished in fifty-two days. Nehemiah’s faith and his planning worked together.

Practical wisdom for planning

Here are some principles that will help any leader, in a village church or a city ministry.

  • Begin with prayer and Scripture. Ask what God has said, and what He is already doing.
  • Know your situation. Like Nehemiah, look carefully. Who are the people? What are the needs? What resources do you have?
  • Set priorities. You cannot do everything. Choose a few important things and do them well. “Get your work outside in order and your fields ready first; after that, build your house” (Proverbs 24:27). Some things must come first.
  • Count the cost. Before you start a building, a school or a new ministry, ask how much money, time and people it will need, not only to begin but to finish and to keep going.
  • Seek advice. “Plans go wrong for lack of advice, but with many advisers they succeed” (Proverbs 15:22). Ask your fellow leaders, and people who have done similar work.
  • Share the work. As we saw in Chapter 22, No Lone Leaders, give each person a part they can carry.
  • Keep honest records. Write down what is given and what is spent. Paul took great care with money “for what is honorable, both before the Lord and before people” (2 Corinthians 8:21). We will look at this more in Chapter 33, Money and Greed.
  • Review and adjust. After a season, look back. What worked? What did not? Be willing to stop things that are no longer fruitful.
  • Use time wisely. “Make good use of every opportunity” (Ephesians 5:16). “Teach us, then, to reckon our days rightly, so that our hearts may grow wise” (Psalm 90:12).

Remember also that planning looks different in different places. In some cultures, leaders write detailed plans. In others, decisions are made by long conversation under a tree until everyone agrees. Both can be wise. What matters is that the work is done thoughtfully, prayerfully and together, “properly and in good order” (1 Corinthians 14:40).

A voice from the Church: Hudson Taylor and George Müller

Hudson Taylor was an English missionary to China in the nineteenth century. In 1865 he was back in England, sick and burdened. Vast areas of inland China had no missionary at all. He believed God wanted him to start a new mission to reach them, but he was afraid of the responsibility. What if he led others to China and they ran out of money or died?

In his book A Retrospect, which is on Ochorus, he describes what happened one Sunday in June 1865, on the beach at Brighton:

“There the Lord conquered my unbelief, and I surrendered myself to God for this service. I told Him that all the responsibility as to issues and consequences must rest with Him; that as His servant, it was mine to obey and to follow Him—His, to direct, to care for, and to guide me and those who might labour with me.”

— Hudson Taylor, A Retrospect

In plain words: God overcame my lack of faith, and I gave myself to Him for this work. I told Him that the results were His responsibility. My part was to obey and follow. His part was to lead, care for and guide me and everyone who worked with me.

Notice what came next. Taylor did not stop at a general prayer. He wrote down a specific request in the margin of his Bible: twenty-four workers, two for each of eleven inland provinces that had no missionary, and two for Mongolia. That was faith turned into a plan. The China Inland Mission was formed, and the next year Taylor sailed with a party of missionaries. In time, thousands served with the mission.

George Müller, whom we met in Chapter 13, Living in the Word, showed the same balance. He cared for thousands of orphans in Bristol, England, without ever asking anyone for money. He told only God about his needs. But he was not careless. The introduction to his book The Life of Trust, on Ochorus, notes that he was never in debt and that “His accounts have been annually audited by a competent committee.” Every gift was recorded and every expense written down. Müller’s life shows that trusting God completely and keeping careful records belong together.

The farmer and the rain

Come back to the farmer. He prepares his fields with great care. He chooses the best seed. He works hard from morning until night. And then he looks up to the sky and waits for God to send the rain. He would be foolish not to plan. He would be foolish to think his planning makes the crops grow.

That is the way of a wise leader. Plan carefully. Count the cost. Divide the work. Keep good records. And then hand everything over to the Lord, who alone gives the growth. “If the LORD does not build the house, the work of its builders comes to nothing” (Psalm 127:1).

Questions for reflection

  • Do you tend to plan too little, trusting God to sort it out, or too much, leaving no room for Him? Why?
  • Do you pray and then plan, or plan and then pray?
  • Read Luke 14:28-30. Is there a project in your church that was started without counting the cost? What can be learned from it?
  • Read Nehemiah 3. What does it teach you about dividing a big task among many people?
  • Hudson Taylor said the results were God’s responsibility and obedience was his. How would that change the way you carry your work?
  • Are the records of money and decisions in your ministry clear and honest? Who checks them?

A step for this week

Choose one area of your ministry that needs a plan. Spend time in prayer about it first. Then write down, on one page: what you believe God wants to happen, what you have now, three priorities for the next six months, what each will cost in time, money and people, and who will do each part. Share the page with your fellow leaders, ask for their advice, and pray over it together. Write “If the Lord wills” at the top.

study_questions.question: Is planning unspiritual for a Christian leader?
study_questions.answer: No. Scripture commends wise planning: “The plans of the diligent bring nothing but gain” (Proverbs 21:5). Jesus spoke of counting the cost before building a tower (Luke 14:28). Planning and prayer belong together.

study_questions.question: How do our plans relate to God’s will?
study_questions.answer: We plan, but God guides. “People plot their course in their minds, but it is the LORD who guides their steps” (Proverbs 16:9). So we hold plans loosely and commit them to Him: “Hand over what you do to the LORD, and your plans will stand firm” (Proverbs 16:3).

study_questions.question: What does Nehemiah teach about planning?
study_questions.answer: Nehemiah prayed, then planned carefully, gathered resources, organised the people, and guarded against opposition. He shows that faith and practical wisdom work together, as do Hudson Taylor and George Müller in the chapter’s story.

fields.title: To the Nations
fields.body_html:
“It is not enough that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and bring home the survivors of Israel. I will make you a light for the nations as well, so that you may be my salvation to the farthest edge of the earth.”

— Isaiah 49:6 (OWB)

A river that has no outlet becomes a swamp. The water flows in, but it does not flow out, and soon it grows still, stale and full of mosquitoes. A river that flows on, through many lands, gives life wherever it goes.

Churches can be like this too. A church that only receives, and never sends, grows inward and stale. A church that sends people, prayer and gifts out to the nations stays fresh and alive. In Chapter 19, Seeking the Lost, we thought about reaching the people around us. In this chapter we lift our eyes further, to the ends of the earth.

God’s heart for the nations

God’s plan to bless the nations is not an extra added at the end of the Bible. It runs from beginning to end. When God called Abraham, He promised, “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3). The psalmists sang, “Tell the nations of his glory, and all the peoples of the wonders he has done” (Psalm 96:3), and prayed, “May the peoples give you thanks, God; may every people give you thanks!” (Psalm 67:3).

Through Isaiah, God spoke to His Servant, whom the New Testament shows to be Jesus: “It is not enough that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob ... I will make you a light for the nations as well, so that you may be my salvation to the farthest edge of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). Even saving Israel was “not enough” for God’s great heart. He wanted the whole world.

And the Bible ends with that hope fulfilled: a crowd from “every nation and from all tribes and peoples and languages”, crying out with a loud voice, “To our God, seated on the throne, and to the Lamb, salvation belongs!” (Revelation 7:9-10). One day every language you have ever heard, and thousands you have never heard, will be used to praise Jesus.

The Great Commission

After His resurrection, Jesus gave His followers their task: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been placed in my hands. Go, then, and make disciples of all the nations: baptize them into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teach them to keep everything I have commanded you. And remember this: I myself am with you every day, until the close of the age” (Matthew 28:18-20).

Notice the four “alls”. All authority belongs to Jesus. All the nations are the target. Everything He commanded must be taught. And He is with us every day, all the days. The command is great, but the authority behind it and the presence with it are greater.

Before He ascended, Jesus said, “when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, you will receive power, and you will bear witness to me in Jerusalem, through all Judea and Samaria, and out to the farthest end of the earth” (Acts 1:8). The book of Acts tells how this began: from Jerusalem, to Samaria, to Antioch, to Asia, to Greece and finally to Rome.

Every church leader is a mission leader

Some leaders think that mission is a special interest for a few enthusiasts. But the Great Commission was given to the whole Church. Every pastor, elder and leader is responsible for helping their church take part in it.

Look at how the gospel first reached the nations. After the death of Stephen, persecution scattered the believers from Jerusalem. “Those who had been scattered went from place to place, announcing the good news of the message” (Acts 8:4). At first they spoke only to Jews. “Some of them, though, were from Cyprus and Cyrene. When they came to Antioch, they spoke to Greek-speaking Gentiles too” (Acts 11:20). These unnamed believers, some of them from North Africa, were the first to take the gospel across the great divide between Jews and Gentiles. They were not apostles. They were ordinary believers.
