Then the church at Antioch, led by its team of prophets and teachers, became the first church to send missionaries deliberately. “While they were serving the Lord in worship and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Set Barnabas and Saul apart for me, for the work I have called them to do.’ Then, after more fasting and prayer, they laid their hands on the two men and let them go” (Acts 13:2-3). Notice that the church sent its best leaders. It did not send the people it could spare. It gave away its most gifted teachers.

From everywhere to everywhere

For several centuries, most missionaries came from Europe and North America. Many of them served faithfully and sacrificially, and we owe them much. Some also mixed the gospel with their own culture, or with the power of empire, and did harm.

Today the picture has changed. Most Christians now live in Africa, Asia and Latin America. Missionaries are sent from Korea, Brazil, Nigeria, India, the Philippines, China and many other countries. Africans plant churches in Europe. Latin Americans serve in the Middle East. Asians serve in Africa. The gospel now flows from everywhere to everywhere.

This means that no church is too poor or too small to take part. The church at Philippi was not rich, yet Paul wrote, “yours was the only church that went into partnership with me in an account of giving and receiving” (Philippians 4:15). It also means that no church should only receive. If your church was planted by missionaries, it is now your turn to send.

How a church takes part

Not everyone is called to go to another country. But everyone can take part.

  • Pray. Pray for the nations, for peoples who have not yet heard, and for missionaries by name. Many churches pray for one country or people group each week.
  • Give. Support those who go. John wrote that we should supply missionaries “for the next stage of their journey in a manner worthy of God ... It is our duty, then, to take in and support such people, and so become fellow workers with the truth” (3 John 6-8).
  • Send. Watch for people whom God is calling, and prepare and release them, as Antioch did.
  • Go. Some will go far. Others will cross a smaller border: to another tribe, another language group or another part of the city.
  • Welcome. Many people from unreached nations now live as migrants, refugees or students in other countries. The nations may be living in your own town.
  • Teach mission. Help your people see that the whole Bible is a missionary book, and that the Great Commission belongs to them.

Paul’s own ambition was “to preach the gospel where Christ was not yet known” (Romans 15:20). There are still many peoples in the world with no church among them and no Bible in their language. A leader after God’s heart will not be content until they hear.

Gospel and culture

When the gospel crosses from one culture to another, wise leaders must learn to tell the difference between the gospel itself and the culture it came wrapped in. Paul became “all things” to all people so that he might save some (1 Corinthians 9:22). The gospel does not require an African to become European, or an Indian to become American. It calls every culture to bow to Christ, and it keeps what is good in every culture while rejecting what is sinful.

This is why it matters so much that people hear the gospel in their own language, through their own people where possible, and are led by leaders from among themselves. Henry Venn’s vision, which we met in Chapter 23, Making Leaders, was of churches that were self-governing, self-supporting and self-spreading. That is still the goal.

A voice from the Church: John R. Mott and Samuel Ajayi Crowther

John R. Mott was an American Methodist layman who, at the end of the nineteenth century, helped lead a great movement of students who gave their lives to world mission. In 1900 he wrote a book whose title became the watchword of thousands: The Evangelization of the World in This Generation. It is on Ochorus. Mott did not mean that everyone in the world would be converted within thirty years. He explained what he meant:

“It means to give all men an adequate opportunity to know Jesus Christ as their Saviour and to become His real disciples.”

— John R. Mott, The Evangelization of the World in This Generation

In plain words: it means giving every person a real chance to know Jesus Christ as their Saviour and to become His true followers. And Mott pointed out why it had to be “this generation”: “The evangelization of the world in this generation, therefore, means the preaching of the Gospel to those who are now living.” The only people we can reach are the people alive today. Every generation must reach its own.

Samuel Ajayi Crowther, whom we met in Chapter 4, The Call of God, was one of the great missionaries of Africa. As a boy he had been captured and sold into slavery, and carried down the coast of West Africa in a slave ship. In 1854, as an ordained minister, he travelled back up the Niger River on a missionary journey, and kept a diary. It is on Ochorus as Journal of an Expedition up the Niger. In one town he spoke with a chief about the sacrifice of Christ. He used a simple picture the chief could understand:

“What would you think of any persons, who, in broad daylight like this, should light their lamps to assist the brilliant rays of the sun to enable them to see better?” He said, “It would be useless; they would be fools to do so.”

— Samuel Ajayi Crowther, Journal of an Expedition up the Niger

Then Crowther explained that just as one sun is enough to light the whole world, so the sacrifice of Jesus Christ is enough to take away our sins, and no other sacrifices are needed. He used the world of his hearers to explain the gospel, and he spoke through an interpreter in a language the chief understood.

Crowther was one of thousands of African, Asian and Latin American believers who have carried the gospel to their neighbours. Tiyo Soga, the first Black South African to be ordained as a minister, in 1856, translated The Pilgrim’s Progress into the Xhosa language and wrote hymns that are still sung. In northern China, a scholar named Xi Shengmo, known to missionaries as Pastor Hsi, was set free from opium addiction through Christ in 1879. He went on to open refuges where hundreds of others were set free. Many of the greatest missionaries in history never left their own continent.

Lift up your eyes

Jesus said to His disciples, “In the way that the Father has sent me, I am sending you” (John 20:21). The Father sent the Son across the greatest distance there is, from heaven to earth. The Son sends us across every distance on earth: across the street, across the tribe, across the ocean.

The prophet Habakkuk looked forward to the day when “the earth will be as full of knowing the glory of the LORD as the sea is full of water” (Habakkuk 2:14). That day is coming. Leaders after God’s heart will lead their churches to play their part in it.

Questions for reflection

  • Read Genesis 12:1-3 and Revelation 7:9-10. How does the whole Bible show God’s heart for the nations?
  • Is your church sending, or only receiving? What would change if it began to send?
  • Read Acts 13:1-3. What do you learn from the way the church at Antioch sent missionaries?
  • Which peoples near you, or far away, have no church among them? How could your church pray for them?
  • What is the difference between the gospel and the culture it comes wrapped in? Can you think of an example?
  • Mott said every generation must reach its own. What does that mean for your church today?

A step for this week

Choose one people group or country where few people know Christ. Find out what you can about it: its language, its religion and whether there is any church among them. This week, lead your church, small group or family in praying for that people by name. Then ask your leaders: “How could our church pray, give, send or go, so that we are a sending church and not only a receiving one?”

study_questions.question: Why should every church leader care about mission to the nations?
study_questions.answer: Because God’s heart has always been for all peoples. He promised Abraham that “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3), and Jesus commanded, “Go, then, and make disciples of all the nations” (Matthew 28:19).

study_questions.question: What does “from everywhere to everywhere” mean?
study_questions.answer: It means mission is no longer mainly from the West to the rest. Churches in Africa, Asia and Latin America now send missionaries across the world, and every church, wherever it is, can be a sending church.

study_questions.question: How can a local church take part in world mission?
study_questions.answer: By praying for the nations, giving, sending and caring for missionaries, welcoming people from other lands, and helping members see the vision of every nation and tribe before the throne (Revelation 7:9). The chapter draws on John R. Mott and Samuel Ajayi Crowther.

fields.title: Justice, Mercy and the Poor
fields.body_html:
“He has told you, mortal, what is good. And what does the LORD ask of you except to do justice, to love loyalty, and to walk humbly with your God?”

— Micah 6:8 (OWB)

A man lies by the side of the road. He has been robbed and beaten, and he is dying. A priest comes along the road, sees him, and crosses to the other side. Then a temple worker does the same. They were both religious leaders. Perhaps they were on their way to lead worship. Then a Samaritan, a man the others despised, stops. He bandages the man’s wounds, puts him on his own donkey, takes him to an inn and pays for his care.

Jesus told this story to a teacher of the law who asked, “Who is my neighbour?” At the end, Jesus asked him which of the three had been a neighbour to the wounded man. He answered, “The one who was merciful to him.” Jesus said, “You go, then, and do the same” (Luke 10:36-37).

Notice who failed in the story: the religious leaders. It is possible to be very busy with religious work and to walk past people who are suffering. This chapter is about the leader’s call to justice and mercy, and to care for the poor.

The God who sees the poor

The God of the Bible has a special care for those who are weak, poor and without power. “He sees that orphans and widows get justice, and he loves the outsider living among you and gives them food and clothing” (Deuteronomy 10:18). “Whoever oppresses the poor insults the One who made them, but kindness to the needy honors him” (Proverbs 14:31).

Because God cares for the poor, His people must too. God told Israel, “You too must love the outsider, since you were outsiders yourselves in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 10:19). They had known slavery. They must never make others slaves.

Through the prophet Jeremiah, God spoke of a good king, Josiah: “He defended the cause of the poor and the needy, and then all was well. Is that not what it means to know me? declares the LORD” (Jeremiah 22:16). That is a remarkable statement. Defending the poor is part of what it means to know God.

Worship that God rejects

The prophets often spoke against people who were very religious but did not care about justice. Through Isaiah, God told the people that their fasting meant nothing to Him while they oppressed their workers and quarrelled. Then He said what kind of fast He wanted: “loose the bonds that wickedness has tied, untie the ropes of the yoke, send the crushed away free ... Is it not to break your bread with someone who is hungry, to take the wandering poor into your home, to clothe the naked person you meet” (Isaiah 58:6-7).

And God made a promise to those who do this: “Then like the dawn your light will break forth ... Then when you call, the LORD will answer; when you cry out for help, he will say, ‘I am here’” (Isaiah 58:8-9).

Amos said the same thing more sharply. God did not want their songs and festivals while the poor were crushed. “Instead, let justice roll on like water, and righteousness like a stream that never runs dry” (Amos 5:24).

Leaders must take this seriously. A church can have beautiful worship, long prayers and powerful preaching, and still displease God if it ignores the suffering around it, or if its leaders treat the poor unjustly.

Jesus and the poor

When Jesus began His ministry, He read from Isaiah in the synagogue at Nazareth: “The Spirit of the Lord rests on me, for he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor. He has sent me to announce freedom to the captives and sight to the blind, to set the downtrodden free” (Luke 4:18).

Throughout His life, Jesus welcomed the people others pushed aside: lepers, beggars, widows, children, foreigners and sinners. He fed the hungry crowds. He healed the sick without asking for payment.

And He taught that at the final judgement, He will say to His people, “when I was hungry, you gave me food; when I was thirsty, you gave me a drink; when I was a stranger, you took me into your home; when I had no clothes, you dressed me; when I was sick, you looked after me; when I was in prison, you came to see me.” When they ask when they did this, He will answer, “each time you did it for one of these my brothers and sisters, even the least of them, you did it for me” (Matthew 25:35-40).

Jesus is found among the poor. When we serve them, we serve Him.

Faith that works

The early Church took this seriously. In Jerusalem, “No one among them lacked anything”, because believers shared what they had (Acts 4:34). When Paul’s ministry to the Gentiles was approved by the leaders in Jerusalem, “They asked only that we keep remembering the poor, and that is the very thing I was eager to do” (Galatians 2:10).

James was blunt: “Suppose a brother or sister has no proper clothes and not enough food for the day, and one of you tells them, ‘Go in peace; keep warm and eat well,’ but you do not give them what the body needs. What use is that? It is the same with faith: if it has no works, it is dead in itself” (James 2:15-17). He also wrote, “religion that is pure and untainted looks like this: going to the help of orphans and widows in their trouble” (James 1:27).

John asked a hard question: “Suppose someone has enough of this world’s goods and notices a brother or sister in need, yet shuts their heart against them. How can the love of God remain in such a person?” (1 John 3:17).

Caring for the poor is not a distraction from the gospel. It is part of the life the gospel creates. We are not saved by good works. But we are saved “for good works, which God made ready in advance so that we would live our lives doing them” (Ephesians 2:10).

Mercy and justice

The Bible calls us both to mercy and to justice. They are related, but they are not the same.

Mercy meets the immediate need. It feeds the hungry man today. It bandages the wounded traveller, as the Samaritan did. Every church can do this: share food, visit the sick, care for widows and orphans, welcome refugees.

Justice asks why the man is hungry, and works to change what is wrong. It asks why the road to Jericho is full of robbers. It speaks up for those who are treated unfairly. “Open your mouth for those who have no voice, for the cause of all who are left to perish. Speak out and judge rightly; take up the case of the poor and the needy” (Proverbs 31:8-9). “Go after justice. Set the oppressor straight. Give the fatherless child a fair hearing; stand up for the widow in court” (Isaiah 1:17).

Leaders need wisdom here. Not every leader is called to be involved in politics, and the Church must never become simply a political party. But leaders cannot stay silent when people in their own communities are being cheated, enslaved, trafficked or abused. In many places, the pastor is one of the few people the poor trust. That is a sacred responsibility. We will think about leaders in public life in Chapter 45, Leaders at Work and in Society.

Leaders must also look at their own churches. Are the poor welcome, or are the best seats kept for the rich? James warned against exactly this (James 2:1-4). Are workers employed by the church paid fairly and on time? Do church leaders use their position to gain land or money from those who cannot refuse? Justice begins at home.

Small mercies

Many leaders feel overwhelmed by the needs around them. There is so much poverty, so much injustice. What difference can one small church make?

Jesus said, “whoever gives one of these little ones no more than a cup of cold water because that one is a disciple ... such a person will never lose their reward” (Matthew 10:42). God sees small mercies. A meal for a widow. School fees for an orphan. A visit to a prisoner. A word spoken for someone who has been cheated. None of these is wasted. Paul wrote, “whenever we have the chance, we should do good to everyone, and above all to those who belong to the family of faith” (Galatians 6:10).

A voice from the Church: Basil, Allen and Jones, and Wilberforce

In the fourth century, Basil was bishop of Caesarea, in what is now central Turkey. During a terrible famine he sold his own inherited property to feed the hungry, and he gathered food and served it to the poor with his own hands. Later he built a great complex outside the city to care for the sick, the poor, travellers and people with leprosy, whom others would not touch. It had a hospital, houses for the poor and workshops. His friends called it a “new city”. It became a model for Christian hospitals in the centuries that followed.

In 1793, a terrible yellow fever swept through the American city of Philadelphia. Thousands died, and everyone who could afford to leave fled. Two Black pastors, Absalom Jones and Richard Allen, who had been born into slavery and had bought their own freedom, were asked to help. As the book The Fire on the Altar on Ochorus tells, they met, prayed and agreed to go. In a pamphlet written the following year, they said:

“The Lord was pleased to strengthen us, and remove all fear from us, and disposed our hearts to be as useful as possible.”

— Absalom Jones and Richard Allen, 1794

In plain words: God made us strong, took away our fear and made us willing to help in every way we could. For weeks they and other Black helpers nursed the sick, buried the dead and cared for orphaned children. Many of them caught the fever. And when a printer named Mathew Carey accused Black nurses of cheating the sick, Jones and Allen answered him firmly, with the facts.

William Wilberforce was a member of the British Parliament in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. After he came to a living faith in Christ as a young man, he thought about leaving politics to become a minister. But a wise friend, the former slave-ship captain John Newton, encouraged him to stay, and to serve God in Parliament. In 1787 Wilberforce wrote in his diary that God had set before him two great tasks: ending the slave trade and changing the moral life of the nation. For twenty years he and his friends worked, prayed, wrote and spoke against the slave trade. They were mocked, threatened and defeated again and again. In 1807 the British slave trade was finally ended by law. Just days before his death in 1833, Parliament voted to end slavery itself across most of the British Empire. His book A Practical View of Christianity, which called comfortable Christians to real faith, is on Ochorus.

Each of these leaders saw suffering, refused to cross to the other side of the road, and acted, at great cost, in the name of Christ.

Do justice, love mercy, walk humbly

Micah summed it up in one sentence: “what does the LORD ask of you except to do justice, to love loyalty, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8). Justice, loyal love and humble walking with God belong together. A leader after God’s heart will not separate them.

Go, then, and do the same.

Questions for reflection

  • Read Luke 10:25-37. Why do you think Jesus made the religious leaders the ones who walked past?
  • Read Isaiah 58:6-10. What kind of “fast” does God want from your church?
  • Who in your community has no one to speak for them? What could your church do for them?
  • What is the difference between mercy and justice? Which does your church practise more?
  • Is your church a place where the poor feel welcome and are treated fairly? How do you know?
  • What do you learn from Absalom Jones and Richard Allen during the 1793 fever?

A step for this week

Walk through your community this week with your eyes open, and ask God to show you who is suffering: widows, orphans, the sick, refugees, prisoners, workers who are cheated. Choose one person or family, and do one practical act of mercy for them this week. Then gather your leaders and ask: “Is there any injustice in our community that we should speak about or act against? Is there any injustice in our own church that we must put right?”

study_questions.question: Why should church leaders care for the poor?
study_questions.answer: Because God does. “He sees that orphans and widows get justice, and he loves the outsider” (Deuteronomy 10:18). “Whoever oppresses the poor insults the One who made them, but kindness to the needy honors him” (Proverbs 14:31).

study_questions.question: What is the difference between mercy and justice?
study_questions.answer: Mercy meets immediate needs, like the Samaritan who cared for the wounded man. Justice addresses the causes, defending “the cause of the poor and the needy” (Jeremiah 22:16). God asks for both: “to do justice, to love loyalty, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8).

study_questions.question: What kind of worship does God reject?
study_questions.answer: Worship that ignores injustice. Through Isaiah God said the fast He wants is to “loose the bonds that wickedness has tied” and share bread with the hungry (Isaiah 58:6-7). The chapter tells of Basil, Richard Allen and Absalom Jones, and William Wilberforce.

fields.title: Leading in Revival and Change
fields.body_html:
“LORD, I have heard of your fame, and I stand in awe. LORD, renew your work in our own time; in our own time make it known; in wrath, remember mercy.”

— Habakkuk 3:2 (OWB)

After a long dry season, the first rains are an extraordinary thing. The dust turns to mud. Seeds that have lain hidden in the ground for months suddenly push up green shoots. Rivers that were only stones begin to run. Within weeks, the whole land looks different. No farmer can make this happen. But every farmer knows what to do when it comes: plough, plant, and work hard while the rain lasts.

Again and again in history, God has sent seasons like this to His Church. People call them revivals or awakenings. Believers who were cold become warm. Hidden sins are confessed. Many people come to faith in a short time. Whole communities are changed.

This chapter, the last in Part Six, Vision and Mission, is about leading in such seasons. It is also about the other kind of change most leaders face far more often: the slow, patient work of helping a church to change when there is no great revival at all.

“Bring us back to life once more”

The Bible is full of prayers for revival. The psalmist cried, “Will you not bring us back to life once more, and let your people be glad in you?” (Psalm 85:6). Habakkuk prayed, “LORD, renew your work in our own time” (Habakkuk 3:2). He had heard what God had done in the past, and he longed to see it again in his own day.

God gave a promise to Solomon when the temple was dedicated: “if my people who bear my name humble themselves and pray, seek my face and turn back from their evil ways, then I myself will hear from heaven. I will forgive their sin and heal their land” (2 Chronicles 7:14). This promise was first given to Israel. But it shows us the pattern of every true revival: humility, prayer, seeking God and turning from sin, followed by God’s forgiveness and healing.

Notice that revival begins with God’s own people. The verse does not say, “if the unbelievers repent”. It says, “if my people”. Revival is first of all the Church being brought back to life.

What revival looks like

In the days of Nehemiah, after the wall was built, the people gathered to hear Ezra read the law. “All the people were weeping as they heard the words of the law” (Nehemiah 8:9). A few weeks later, they gathered again, “fasting, dressed in sackcloth ... They stood and confessed their sins” and “read from the book of the law of the LORD their God for a quarter of the day, and for another quarter they confessed their sins and worshiped the LORD their God” (Nehemiah 9:1-3).

On the day of Pentecost, after Peter preached, “about 3,000 people joined them.” Then look at what followed. “They gave themselves fully to the apostles’ teaching and to the shared life, to the breaking of bread and to the prayers ... at home they broke bread, eating their food with joyful and simple hearts, praising God ... And each day the Lord brought into their company more people who were being saved” (Acts 2:41-47).

Across history, true revivals have shared many of the same marks:

  • A deep sense of God’s holiness and of personal sin.
  • Open confession and real repentance, including putting wrongs right.
  • A new love for Jesus and joy in His salvation.
  • A new hunger for the Bible and for prayer.
  • Love and unity among believers, often across old divisions.
  • Many people coming to faith.
  • Changed lives that last, seen in homes, workplaces and communities.

Testing what is happening

When God moves powerfully, strange things can happen too. Some people weep, shake or cry out. Some claim visions or prophecies. Some leaders become proud of “their” revival. And sometimes things that look like revival are really only excitement, manipulation or even the work of evil spirits.

The Bible tells us to be neither too quick to reject nor too quick to accept. “Do not smother the Spirit; do not look down on prophecy. Test everything; keep hold of what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:19-21). “Dear friends, do not believe just any spirit; test the spirits to find out whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1).

How do we test? Jesus said, “You will know them by what their lives produce” (Matthew 7:16). The real question is not how loud or emotional the meetings are. It is whether people are becoming more like Jesus. Do they love Christ more? Do they love the Bible more? Are they more humble, more honest, more loving to others? Are they confessing sin and putting things right? Is Christ being exalted, or a person?

Leaders in times of revival need two kinds of courage. They need courage to welcome what God is doing, even when it is unfamiliar. And they need courage to correct what is wrong, gently and firmly, so that the work is not spoiled. Paul reminded the excited church in Corinth, “God is the God of peace, not of disorder” (1 Corinthians 14:33).

Going deeper: can we bring revival?

Christians have long disagreed about the leader’s part in revival. Some, following the American pastor Jonathan Edwards in the eighteenth century, have stressed that revival is “a surprising work of God”. We can pray and prepare, but we cannot cause it. God sends it when He chooses, as He sends the rain.

Others, following the American evangelist Charles Finney in the nineteenth century, have stressed the human part. In his Revival Lectures, which are on Ochorus, Finney wrote boldly, “A revival of religion is not a miracle.” He meant that God works through the ordinary means He has given, such as preaching, prayer and repentance, and that when His people use these means faithfully, revival will usually follow. He took his text from Hosea: “plow up your unplowed ground. It is time to seek the LORD, until he comes and rains righteousness” (Hosea 10:12).

Both views hold part of the truth. Revival is God’s work, and no leader can command it. Yet God calls His people to pray, to repent and to break up the hard ground of their hearts. Some have put it this way: we cannot make the rain fall, but we can plough the field and be ready when it comes.

Leading slow change

Most leaders will not see a great revival in their lifetime. But every leader will need to lead change. A church may need to become more welcoming to the poor, to start teaching the Bible more clearly, to train new leaders, to begin praying together, to change an unhelpful custom or to face a hidden sin. These changes usually come slowly.

Jesus wrote to the church in Ephesus, “the love you had in the beginning, you have let go. So call to mind the height you have fallen from. Repent, and act as you did at the start” (Revelation 2:4-5). Every church drifts over time. Part of a leader’s work is to call it back.

Here is wisdom for leading change:

  • Begin with prayer and with your own heart. Change in a church usually begins with change in its leaders. Ezra was “praying and confessing, weeping and throwing himself down before the house of God” before the people followed (Ezra 10:1).
  • Explain why. People will accept change more easily when they understand the reason for it, especially when it is clearly rooted in Scripture.
  • Honour the past. Do not despise what those before you built. Thank God for it, even as you change it.
  • Listen first. Find out what people fear and why. Often their concerns contain wisdom.
  • Bring other leaders with you. A change pushed by one person rarely lasts. Build agreement among your fellow leaders first.
  • Change what matters most. Not every custom is worth a fight. Choose the changes that really serve the gospel.
  • Go at a pace people can follow. A shepherd leading a flock with lambs cannot walk at a soldier’s speed (Genesis 33:13-14).
  • Be patient and keep going. Some changes take years. Do not give up.

And remember this: the surest way to see lasting change is to pray for the Holy Spirit to do what only He can do. Programmes can rearrange a church. Only God can revive it.

A voice from the Church: Jonathan Edwards and Pandita Ramabai

Jonathan Edwards was a pastor in the small town of Northampton, in New England, in the eighteenth century. He saw two great seasons of revival in his own church and town, in the 1730s and 1740s. He also saw the problems: false conversions, wild excitement, pride and division. So he spent years studying how to tell true spiritual life from false. His book Religious Affections, which is on Ochorus, begins with this conviction:

“True religion, in great part, consists in holy affections.”

— Jonathan Edwards, Religious Affections

In plain words: real faith is not only a matter of the mind. It is a heart that truly loves, fears, delights in and longs for God. Edwards defended the deep feelings of revival against those who wanted only a cold, dry religion. But he also warned that strong feelings alone prove nothing. At the end of the book he gave what he called “the chief of all the signs” of true grace: a changed life. “Christian practice, or a holy life, is a great and distinguishing sign of true and saving grace,” he wrote. The best test of a revival is not what happens in the meetings, but how people live afterwards.

In 1905, revival came to Mukti, the community for widows and orphans led by Pandita Ramabai in western India, whom we met in Chapter 26, Men and Women in the Work of God. For months beforehand, Ramabai and her co-workers had prayed for it. By June, more than five hundred women and girls were meeting twice a day to pray. Then, late in June, the Holy Spirit came upon them. Girls were found on their knees, weeping, praying and confessing their sins. The revival spread to many other parts of India.

How did Ramabai lead it? Pandita Ramabai: A Life, on Ochorus, tells us. At first she did not want the story told, in case people praised Mukti instead of God. Then she came to believe she had been wrong to hide God’s glory. She took a group of her girls to the city of Poona and confessed in public that she had “neglected her opportunities of preaching Christ boldly.” Then she sent out praying bands of young women to other schools, orphanages and mission stations, to pray for the Christians there. She told them:

“Our work will bear lasting fruit ... if we pray more and work less.”

— Pandita Ramabai, as recorded in Pandita Ramabai: A Life

Ramabai was one of the hardest-working leaders in India. She ran schools, farms and homes for two thousand people. Yet she knew where lasting fruit comes from.

“In our own time”

Habakkuk prayed, “renew your work in our own time.” He had heard the stories of what God had done for earlier generations. He was not content only to remember. He wanted to see it.

Leaders after God’s heart will pray the same prayer. They will lead the patient work of change week by week. They will test what is happening, keep hold of what is good, and point all the glory to God. And they will plough the hard ground, and pray for rain.

Questions for reflection

  • Read 2 Chronicles 7:14. Which of its four conditions (humble themselves, pray, seek my face, turn from evil) most needs attention in your church?
  • Have you ever seen or heard of a true revival? What were its marks?
  • Read 1 Thessalonians 5:19-21. Are you more likely to “smother the Spirit” or to accept things without testing them?
  • Edwards said that a changed life is “the chief of all the signs”. How would that test change the way you judge spiritual experiences?
  • What change does your church need most? Which of the principles for leading change will you need most?
  • Ramabai said, “pray more and work less.” What would that look like in your leadership?

A step for this week

Gather two or three other leaders or believers this week and pray together for revival, beginning with yourselves. Read Psalm 85 and Habakkuk 3:1-2 aloud, and turn them into prayer. Confess sins honestly to God. Then ask one another: “What one change does our church most need? What is the first small step towards it?” Agree to meet and pray together again next week.

study_questions.question: What is revival?
study_questions.answer: Revival is a season when God brings His people back to life, often with deep repentance, love for the Word and many coming to Christ. The psalmist prayed, “Will you not bring us back to life once more, and let your people be glad in you?” (Psalm 85:6).

study_questions.question: Can church leaders bring revival?
study_questions.answer: Christians answer differently. The chapter’s “Going deeper” section explains the views. All agree that leaders can pray, repent and prepare: “if my people who bear my name humble themselves and pray” (2 Chronicles 7:14).

study_questions.question: How should leaders test what happens in revival?
study_questions.answer: With openness and discernment: “Do not smother the Spirit; do not look down on prophecy. Test everything; keep hold of what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:19-21). Jonathan Edwards and Pandita Ramabai both led in revival and both tested it carefully.

fields.title: Pride and the Love of Praise
fields.body_html:
“The crucible tests silver and the furnace gold, and praise tests a person.”

— Proverbs 27:21 (OWB)

A goldsmith tests gold by putting it in the fire. If it is pure, it comes out shining. If it is mixed with cheaper metals, the fire shows it. The Bible says that praise is like that fire. When people praise us, what is really in our hearts comes out.

Many leaders are tested by hardship and pass the test. They stay faithful through poverty, opposition and persecution. But when success comes, when crowds gather and people speak well of them, something changes. They begin to enjoy the praise. Then they begin to need it. And slowly, without noticing, they begin to take for themselves the glory that belongs to God.

This chapter begins Part Seven, Dangers on the Road. Here we look plainly at the sins that most often ruin leaders. We begin with the oldest of them all: pride.

The oldest sin

When Paul listed the qualities needed in an overseer, he gave this warning: “He must not be a recent convert, or he may become proud and fall under the same judgment as the devil” (1 Timothy 3:6). Many Christians have understood this to mean that pride was the devil’s own sin, the sin that turned an angel into an enemy of God. Whatever the full story, Paul is clear: pride is especially dangerous for those who are given leadership too soon.

God says, “My glory I will not hand over to anyone else” (Isaiah 42:8). Pride is trying to take what God will not share. That is why the Bible says, “God sets himself against the proud, but to the humble he gives grace” (James 4:6). Notice the words “sets himself against”. A proud leader is not only making a mistake. They have God as their opponent.

“Pride comes first, then the crash; a haughty spirit, then the fall” (Proverbs 16:18). History is full of leaders who proved this proverb true.

Two kings who took the glory

King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon was the most powerful man in the world. One evening, “as he was strolling on the roof of the royal palace of Babylon, the king said, ‘Is this not the great Babylon that I have built as a royal capital by my own mighty power and for the glory of my majesty?’” (Daniel 4:29-30). Count the words about himself: I have built, my own power, my majesty. “The words were still on the king’s lips when a voice came down from heaven” (Daniel 4:31). He lost his mind and lived like an animal for a season, until he learned “that the Most High rules over human kingdoms” (Daniel 4:32).

God was merciful to Nebuchadnezzar. When his sanity returned, he praised God and said, “he can bring down those who live in pride” (Daniel 4:37). God humbled him in order to rescue him.

King Herod Agrippa was not so fortunate. When he gave a speech in his royal robes, the crowd shouted, “A god is speaking, not a human being!” He did nothing to stop them. “At once an angel of the Lord struck him, since he had not given the glory to God” (Acts 12:22-23).

The difference between these two stories is not that one king was proud and the other was not. Both were proud. The difference is that one repented and gave glory to God, and the other did not.

King Uzziah of Judah is a warning too. He was a good king for many years. God helped him greatly. “His fame spread far and wide, for he was wonderfully helped until he became strong. But when he had become strong, his heart grew proud, to his own ruin” (2 Chronicles 26:15-16). Notice the danger: success. It was not in his weakness that Uzziah fell, but in his strength.

The many faces of pride

Pride does not always look like boasting. It wears many disguises, and leaders need to recognise them.

  • The love of praise. John wrote of some leaders who believed in Jesus but would not say so, “they loved the glory that people give more than the glory that God gives” (John 12:43). Do I feel hurt when no one thanks me? Do I fish for compliments after I preach?
  • The love of position. John wrote about a church leader called Diotrephes, “who loves to be first among them” (3 John 9). He refused to welcome other leaders, spread lies about them and put out of the church those who wanted to welcome them. Pride often shows itself in a leader who cannot share power.
  • The love of titles and honour. Jesus warned about leaders who were “fond of the seat of honor at banquets and the front seats in the synagogues, of respectful greetings in the marketplaces” (Matthew 23:6-7). Some leaders today insist on long titles, special chairs and special treatment.
  • Religious show. “Take care not to put your righteousness on show for others to see” (Matthew 6:1). A leader can pray, fast and give in order to be seen.
  • Taking credit. Talking about “my church”, “my ministry”, “my converts”. Allowing people to think that we did what God did.
  • Comparing. Measuring ourselves against other leaders, and feeling either superior or bitterly envious. We will look at envy in Chapter 36, Envy, Rivalry and Favouritism.
  • Being unteachable. Unable to receive correction, as we saw in Chapter 25, Criticism, Opposition and Conflict.
  • Spiritual pride. Feeling that we are more holy, more gifted or more spiritual than others. This is perhaps the most dangerous form, because it hides behind holy things.

Why praise is so dangerous

Jesus asked a searching question: “How could you believe? You accept glory from one another, while the glory that comes from the only God is something you do not seek” (John 5:44). The love of human praise does not only spoil our leadership. It can make faith itself impossible. When people’s opinion matters more to us than God’s, we will say and do what pleases people, and not what pleases God.

Leaders are especially exposed to this danger. People thank us, praise our preaching and look up to us. In many cultures, leaders are given great honour simply because of their position. That honour is not wrong in itself. But it is like strong wine. A little may do no harm. Too much, too often, and we become drunk on it.

The way of escape

How can a leader be protected from pride?

Remember that everything is a gift. “What do you have that was not given to you? And if it was given to you, why do you take pride in it as though it were not a gift?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). Your gifts, your opportunities, your fruit: all of it came from God.

Give the glory back at once. When you are praised, do not store it up in your heart. Turn it into thanksgiving immediately. “Do not give us the glory, LORD, do not give it to us. Give it to your name” (Psalm 115:1). This was Herod’s great failure. He let the praise stay with him.

Serve in secret. Jesus told us to give, pray and fast in secret, where only the Father sees (Matthew 6:1-18). Do some good things that no one will ever know about.

Let others praise you, if they must. “Let someone else praise you, not your own mouth” (Proverbs 27:2). Do not talk about your own achievements.

Remember what you are. Jesus said that when we have done everything we were told, we should say, “We are unworthy servants. We have done no more than we were bound to do” (Luke 17:10). Paul said, “do not rate yourself higher than you should. Let your thinking be sober and sensible instead” (Romans 12:3).

Welcome humbling. When God allows failure, criticism or weakness, it may be His mercy, protecting us from pride. Paul said his “thorn in the flesh” was given to keep him from becoming proud (2 Corinthians 12:7).

Boast in the cross. Paul wrote, “far be it from me to boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6:14). At the cross we see what our sin cost, and how much we owe. It is very hard to be proud while standing there.

In Chapter 7, Humility, we looked at the beauty of the humble heart. Here we see the other side: what happens when humility is lost. The cure for pride is not to think badly of ourselves. It is to think rightly of God, and to look at Him so much that we forget to look at ourselves.

A voice from the Church: Augustine and Thomas à Kempis

Augustine, the North African bishop whom we met in Chapter 17, Feed My Sheep, wrote his Confessions around the year 400. The book is a long prayer to God, telling the story of his life and his sins. It is on Ochorus. In Book 10, he examines his heart as a bishop. He confesses that the temptations of the body troubled him less than a quieter temptation: the love of praise. He asked God whether this temptation could ever leave him in this life:

“To wish, namely, to be feared and loved of men, for no other end, but that we may have a joy therein which is no joy? A miserable life this and a foul boastfulness!”

— Augustine, Confessions, Book X

In plain words: can I ever be free of wanting people to respect me and love me, just so that I can enjoy their admiration, which is not real joy at all? That is a miserable way to live, and an ugly kind of pride.

Augustine noticed something even more subtle. A leader may notice their love of praise and fight against it, and then become proud of fighting it. He wrote that it “often glories more vainly of the very contempt of vain-glory”. In plain words: we can even become proud of how humble we are. Pride is so clever that it can feed on our efforts to defeat it. Augustine’s answer was not to try harder, but to keep throwing himself on God’s mercy.

A thousand years later, Thomas à Kempis was a monk in the Netherlands in the fifteenth century. He wrote The Imitation of Christ, one of the most widely read Christian books in history, which is on Ochorus. He gave this counsel:

“If you wish to learn and appreciate something worth while, then love to be unknown and considered as nothing.”

— Thomas à Kempis, The Imitation of Christ

In plain words: if you want to learn something truly valuable, learn to be happy when no one knows your name. Thomas also wrote, “All men are frail, but you must admit that none is more frail than yourself.” A leader who believes that will not be easily puffed up.

Whose applause?

One day every leader will stand before Christ. On that day, the praise of crowds will mean nothing. Only one voice will matter. Jesus asked, “How could you believe? You accept glory from one another, while the glory that comes from the only God is something you do not seek.”

Seek His glory, not your own. Work for His “well done”, not the applause of people. “Humble yourselves, then, under God’s powerful hand, so that he may raise you up when the time is right” (1 Peter 5:6).

Questions for reflection

  • Read Proverbs 27:21. When you are praised, what does it reveal about your heart?
  • Read Daniel 4:28-37 and Acts 12:21-23. What made the difference between Nebuchadnezzar and Herod?
  • Which of the “faces of pride” do you recognise most in yourself?
  • Read 3 John 9-10. Have you seen leaders like Diotrephes? Do you see anything of him in yourself?
  • Augustine said we can become proud even of fighting pride. Have you seen this in your own heart?
  • What would it mean for you to “love to be unknown”?

A step for this week

This week, every time someone praises or thanks you, quietly pray in your heart, “Not to us, LORD, but to Your name be the glory,” before you answer them. Do at least one act of service in secret that no one will know about. At the end of the week, ask a trusted friend, “Where do you see pride in me?” and listen without defending yourself.

study_questions.question: Why is pride so dangerous for leaders?
study_questions.answer: Because “Pride comes first, then the crash; a haughty spirit, then the fall” (Proverbs 16:18), and “God sets himself against the proud” (James 4:6). Paul warned that a new believer should not lead, “or he may become proud” (1 Timothy 3:6).

study_questions.question: How does praise test a leader?
study_questions.answer: “The crucible tests silver and the furnace gold, and praise tests a person” (Proverbs 27:21). Praise reveals whether we live for God’s glory or our own. God says, “My glory I will not hand over to anyone else” (Isaiah 42:8).

study_questions.question: What happened to Nebuchadnezzar when he became proud?
study_questions.answer: He boasted of “the great Babylon” he had built, and “The words were still on the king’s lips when a voice came down from heaven” (Daniel 4:30-31). He was humbled until he acknowledged that God rules. The chapter draws on Augustine and Thomas à Kempis.

fields.title: Money and Greed
fields.body_html:
“For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some people, eager for money, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs.”

— 1 Timothy 6:10 (OWB)

In the story of the prophet Elisha, a powerful army commander named Naaman came to be healed of a serious skin disease. God healed him, and Naaman offered Elisha a great gift of silver and clothing. Elisha refused it. He wanted Naaman to know that God’s grace cannot be bought.

But Elisha’s servant, Gehazi, watched the silver leave. He said to himself, “My master has let this Aramean Naaman off without taking any of the things he brought ... I will chase after him and take something from him” (2 Kings 5:20). He ran after Naaman, told a lie, took the silver and hid it in his house. When he came back, Elisha asked, “Where have you been, Gehazi?” He lied again. Elisha said, “Was not my heart there with you ...? Is this a time for taking money?” (2 Kings 5:25-26). Gehazi left with Naaman’s disease on his own skin.

Gehazi had spent years beside one of the greatest prophets who ever lived. He had seen miracles. And he threw it all away for a bag of silver. Money has ruined many leaders since. This chapter looks honestly at leaders and money.

Money is not evil, but its love is deadly

Notice what Paul says: “the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil” (1 Timothy 6:10). Money itself is not evil. It can feed the hungry, build schools, support missionaries and care for widows. But the love of money is like a root under the ground. You cannot see it, but from it grows “all kinds of evil”: lies, theft, injustice, broken families, and leaders who wander from the faith.

Jesus said, “No one can serve two masters ... You cannot serve both God and money” (Matthew 6:24). Money is not a neutral tool for the human heart. It wants to be served. It promises security, power and respect. Jesus warned, “Take care! Keep yourselves from every kind of greed. Even when someone has more than enough, life does not come from the things a person owns” (Luke 12:15).

That is why the Bible names this so clearly in the qualifications for leaders. An overseer must be “not someone who loves money” (1 Timothy 3:3), “not greedy for money” (Titus 1:7). Peter told elders to shepherd the flock “not to make money for yourselves, but gladly and readily” (1 Peter 5:2).

Selling the gifts of God

When the apostles laid hands on believers in Samaria and they received the Holy Spirit, a man named Simon, who had practised magic, offered them money. “Let me have this power too,” he said. Peter answered sharply, “To ruin with you and your silver! You thought you could get the gift of God with money” (Acts 8:19-20).

This sin, trying to buy or sell spiritual things, became known in church history as “simony”, after Simon. It has taken many forms. In the Middle Ages, church offices were bought and sold. Today, the same sin appears when leaders charge money for prayer, sell “anointed” oil, water or cloths, promise healing or blessing in exchange for a gift, or give church positions to those who pay most.

The prophet Micah described the leaders of his day: “Her leaders give judgment for a bribe, her priests teach for pay, and her prophets tell fortunes for money. Yet they lean on the LORD and say, ‘Is not the LORD among us?’” (Micah 3:11). They used God’s name to make money, and still believed God was pleased with them. That is a terrible blindness.

The prosperity gospel

In many parts of the world today, a false teaching has spread widely. It is often called the “prosperity gospel”. It teaches that God always wants believers to be rich and healthy, that poverty and sickness are signs of weak faith or sin, and that if you give money to the preacher or the church, God will repay you many times over.

This teaching uses Bible verses. It quotes promises such as Malachi 3:10, where God says He will “open the windows of heaven”, and Luke 6:38, “Give, and gifts will come to you.” God does bless generous giving. But the prosperity gospel twists these promises in several ways.

  • It makes money the reward of faith. But Jesus said, “Do not pile up treasures for yourselves on earth” (Matthew 6:19). The great reward of the gospel is Christ Himself, and treasure in heaven.
  • It makes poverty a curse. But Jesus was born in a stable, had “nowhere to lay down his head” (Luke 9:58), and said the poor are blessed. Many of the most faithful believers in history have been poor.
  • It treats giving as an investment. We give because God has given to us, not to get more back.
  • It enriches the preacher. Very often, the people grow poorer while the leader buys cars, houses and aeroplanes.

Paul warned about people who “think godliness is a way to make money” (1 Timothy 6:5). Instead, he said, “Godliness is indeed great gain, when it comes with contentment. For we brought nothing into the world, and we can take nothing out of it” (1 Timothy 6:6-7). A leader after God’s heart will refuse this false gospel, and protect the flock from it.

Paul’s example

Paul had the right to be supported by the churches. He wrote, “the Lord directed that those who announce the gospel should live from the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:14). It is right for churches to support their pastors and missionaries fairly. Many faithful pastors are underpaid, and their families suffer.

But Paul often chose not to use this right. He worked as a tentmaker so that no one could accuse him of preaching for money. He told the Ephesian elders, “I never set my heart on anyone’s silver or gold or clothing. You know yourselves that I provided for my own needs, and for those who were with me, with these hands” (Acts 20:33-34). He wrote, “we are not like the many who trade in the word of God for gain” (2 Corinthians 2:17), and, “we never used flattery, and we never put on a show to cover up greed; God is our witness” (1 Thessalonians 2:5).

Many leaders in the world today are “tentmakers” too. They farm, teach, trade or work in offices, and lead churches as well. This is an honourable calling, not a second-class ministry.

Practical wisdom for leaders

Keep honest accounts. Never handle church money alone. Have at least two people count every offering and sign for it. Keep written records. Have the accounts checked by someone independent. Paul took great care when he carried a large gift for the poor in Jerusalem: “Our concern is for what is honorable, both before the Lord and before people” (2 Corinthians 8:21).

Keep church money and personal money separate. Never borrow from church funds, even meaning to repay it.

Be open about your pay. Let your church leaders know what you receive. Hidden payments and secret gifts breed suspicion.

Live simply. “If we have food and clothing, we will be content with that” (1 Timothy 6:8). Paul said, “I have learned to be content. I know how to get by on little, and I know how to handle having plenty” (Philippians 4:11-12). A leader’s lifestyle preaches as loudly as their sermons.

Give generously. Leaders should be among the most generous people in the church. Paul reminded the elders of Jesus’ words, “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35).

Avoid debt where you can. Debt makes a leader a servant of the lender, and can push a leader into compromise.

Refuse gifts that come with strings. If a wealthy member gives in order to control the church, or to escape correction, the gift is a trap.

Pray the prayer of Agur: “give me neither poverty nor wealth, but feed me with the bread I need each day, so that I do not have too much and disown you ... or have too little and steal” (Proverbs 30:8-9).

The Ochorus book Faithful with Little takes all of this further, for every believer and not only for leaders. It would be a good book to read together with your church.

A voice from the Church: the Didache and John Wesley

One of the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament is a short book called the Didache, which means “teaching”. It was probably written in Syria or Palestine around the end of the first century, and it gave simple instructions to young churches. Already, so early, the Church had to deal with travelling preachers who used the gospel to make money. The Didache gave a clear test. A travelling apostle should stay a day or two and then move on, taking only bread for the journey:

“But if he ask money, he is a false prophet.”

— The Didache, chapter 11 (translated by J. B. Lightfoot)

In plain words: a preacher who asks you for money for himself is a false prophet. It also said that if anyone claimed to speak by the Spirit and said, “Give me silver,” the church should not listen to him. The first Christians knew that the love of money was a sure sign of a false teacher.

John Wesley, the eighteenth-century English preacher whom we met in Chapter 22, No Lone Leaders, preached a famous sermon called “The Use of Money”. It is in his Sermons on Several Occasions, on Ochorus. He summed up the Christian’s duty in three rules: “Gain all you can”, honestly and without harming yourself or others; “save all you can”, by not wasting money on luxury and show; and “give all you can”. He explained why the third rule matters most:

“When the Possessor of heaven and earth brought you into being, and placed you in this world, he placed you here not as a proprietor, but a steward.”

— John Wesley, “The Use of Money”

In plain words: God, who owns heaven and earth, did not put you in the world as an owner, but as a manager of what is His. Wesley lived this. As his books sold, he earned a great deal of money, but he kept his own living costs almost the same for most of his life and gave the rest away. When he died, he left very little money behind.

Would you still serve?

Here is a searching question for every leader: if there were no salary, no gifts and no honour, would I still serve here? Peter told the elders to shepherd “gladly and readily”, not for gain. The Chief Shepherd has promised a reward that money cannot buy: “a crown of glory that will never wither” (1 Peter 5:4).

Gehazi ran after silver and lost everything. Elisha refused the silver and kept his soul. Choose Elisha’s way.

Questions for reflection

  • Read 2 Kings 5:15-27. What was Gehazi’s real sin? Where do you see the same temptation today?
  • Have you seen the prosperity gospel in your area? How would you explain to someone, gently and from Scripture, what is wrong with it?
  • How is money handled in your church? Would your accounts stand up to an honest, independent check?
  • Read Acts 20:33-35. In what ways could you follow Paul’s example?
  • Wesley said we are stewards, not owners. How would that change the way you use what you have?
  • Would you still serve where you are if there were no pay or gifts?

A step for this week

Look honestly at how money is handled in your ministry. This week, make sure that at least two people count and record every offering, and that the records can be checked. If you handle money alone, change that now. Then look at your own household budget. Write down how much you give, and pray about whether God is calling you to give more. If you have taken anything that was not yours, make it right this week.

study_questions.question: Is money evil?
study_questions.answer: No, but loving it is deadly. “For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some people, eager for money, have wandered from the faith” (1 Timothy 6:10). A church leader must be “not someone who loves money” (1 Timothy 3:3).

study_questions.question: What does the Bible say about the prosperity gospel?
study_questions.answer: The chapter warns that teaching which promises wealth in return for giving twists the gospel. Jesus said, “You cannot serve both God and money” (Matthew 6:24) and, “life does not come from the things a person owns” (Luke 12:15).

study_questions.question: How can a leader handle money with integrity?
study_questions.answer: By keeping church money open and accountable, never handling it alone, living simply and contentedly, and refusing to profit from ministry, as Gehazi did when he chased after Naaman (2 Kings 5:20). The chapter draws on the Didache and John Wesley.

fields.title: Sexual Purity
fields.body_html:
“This is God’s will for you: that you be holy. Keep away from sexual immorality. Each of you should know how to keep your own body under control, with holiness and respect.”

— 1 Thessalonians 4:3-4 (OWB)

A great tree can stand for a hundred years. It survives storms, droughts and fires. Then one day it falls, and people are amazed. But when they look at the stump, they see that it had been rotting inside for years. Small insects had been eating it from within, quietly, where no one could see.

Many leaders fall in exactly this way. Their fall is sudden and public. But it began long before, in small, hidden compromises. Of all the ways leaders fall, sexual sin is among the most common and the most destructive. It breaks marriages, wounds children, destroys churches and brings shame on the name of Christ. This chapter speaks plainly about it, because silence has helped many leaders to fall.

Joseph: the young man who ran

Joseph was a young slave in Egypt, far from his family. “The LORD was with Joseph, and he became a successful man” (Genesis 39:2). His master trusted him with everything. Then his master’s wife began to tempt him. “Sleep with me,” she said, day after day.

Look at how Joseph answered: “He has put everything he owns under my care ... The only thing he has denied me is you, since you are his wife. How could I commit so great a wrong, and sin against God?” (Genesis 39:8-9). Joseph saw clearly that this would be a betrayal of his master and, above all, a sin against God.

Then look at what he did. “She urged Joseph day after day, but he would not listen to her or agree to lie beside her or be in her company” (Genesis 39:10). He kept his distance. And when one day she grabbed his clothes when no one else was in the house, “he ran from her and got outside, leaving the garment in her grip” (Genesis 39:12).

Joseph lost his coat. He was falsely accused and thrown into prison. But he kept his integrity, and God was with him even there. It is better to lose your coat, your job and your reputation than your purity.

Paul gives the same advice: “Get away from sexual immorality!” (1 Corinthians 6:18). “Run away from the passions of youth, and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace” (2 Timothy 2:22). Some temptations should be fought. Sexual temptation should be fled.

David: the king who stayed home

David is the opposite story. He was a man after God’s own heart, the great king, the writer of psalms. But one spring, “at the season when kings set out on campaign ... David himself stayed behind in Jerusalem. As evening came on, David got up from where he had been lying and walked back and forth on the roof of the royal palace. From the roof he saw a woman bathing” (2 Samuel 11:1-2).

Notice the steps of his fall. He was not where he should have been. He was idle. He looked, and kept looking. He asked who she was. He sent for her. He slept with her. When she became pregnant, he tried to hide it. When that failed, he arranged for her husband Uriah to be killed in battle. One sin led to another, each worse than the last. James describes this process exactly: “each person is tempted by their own desire, which draws them out and lures them like bait. Desire conceives and bears sin, and sin, once it is full grown, gives birth to death” (James 1:14-15).

Notice too that David was the king. Bathsheba was not in a position to refuse him. Today we would see this not only as adultery but as a powerful man abusing his power over a woman who could not say no. When a leader uses his position to draw someone into sexual sin, it is not simply an “affair”. It is an abuse of power. We will look at this in Chapter 35, Power, Abuse and Protecting the Vulnerable.

David’s sin had terrible consequences for his family and his kingdom for the rest of his life. But when the prophet Nathan confronted him, he repented. Psalm 51 is his prayer: “God, create a pure heart for me, and make my spirit new and steady inside me” (Psalm 51:10).

It starts in the heart

Jesus taught that purity is not only about what we do. “I tell you, a man who looks at a woman with the aim of wanting her for himself has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). The same is true for women who look at men.

Job said, “I made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I look with desire at a young woman?” (Job 31:1). He made a decision in advance about what he would and would not look at. “More than anything you protect, protect your heart, because the whole course of your life flows out of it” (Proverbs 4:23).

In our day, this has become harder than ever. Pornography is available on almost every phone, in every language, in private. Many leaders, including pastors, are secretly trapped by it. It may seem harmless because no one else is involved. But it poisons the mind, damages marriages, treats people made in God’s image as objects, often feeds on the exploitation of the poor and the trafficked, and prepares the way for greater sin. If you are caught in this, do not hide. Confess it to God and to a trusted, mature believer, and get help. There is a way out.

Walls of protection

“So anyone who feels sure of standing should watch out, or they may fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12). No leader is too strong, too old or too spiritual to fall. The wise leader builds walls of protection before the attack comes. Proverbs says of the immoral woman, “Keep well away from her, and do not even come near her front door” (Proverbs 5:8). Do not go near the door.

Here are some walls that have helped many leaders. They must be applied wisely in different cultures, but the principles hold everywhere.

  • Guard your eyes. Decide in advance what you will not watch or look at. Put protection on your phone and computer. Do not take your phone to bed.
  • Be careful about being alone. Avoid situations where you are alone, in private, with someone of the opposite sex who is not your spouse or close family, especially in counselling, travel or late at night. Meet where others can see. Leave doors open. Take someone with you on visits.
  • Watch your emotions. Many affairs begin not with physical attraction but with emotional closeness. If you find yourself sharing your heart more with someone else than with your spouse, or looking forward to seeing them too much, that is a warning sign.
  • Speak well of your spouse in public. And never complain about your marriage to someone of the opposite sex.
  • Tend your marriage. “Find your joy in the woman you married when you were young” (Proverbs 5:18). A healthy, loving marriage is one of the strongest walls. We will look at this in Chapter 42, The Leader’s Home.
  • Be accountable. Have at least one or two trusted people who have permission to ask you hard questions about your purity, and answer them honestly. We will return to this in Chapter 46, Faithful in Little: Accountability.
  • Know your weak times. Tiredness, loneliness, discouragement, success and travel are times of special danger. David fell when he was idle and at the height of his power.
  • Remember the cost. Picture the faces of your spouse, your children, your church and the people who came to faith through you. “Can a man carry fire against his chest and not set his clothes alight?” (Proverbs 6:27).

Some people worry that these boundaries mean treating women, or men, with suspicion, or keeping women out of ministry. That is not the aim. Paul told Timothy to treat “older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters, with complete purity” (1 Timothy 5:2). The aim is to protect everyone, including the people we work with, so that men and women can serve together with honour and trust.

God’s grace is strong enough

This chapter may feel heavy. But hear the good news. “The testing that has gripped you is only what all people face. But God is faithful, and he will not allow the testing to go past your strength. Along with the testing he will also make the way out” (1 Corinthians 10:13). Paul also reminds us, “your body is a temple where the Holy Spirit lives ... You do not belong to yourselves. You were bought, and a price was paid for you” (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). The Holy Spirit lives in you. He is stronger than any temptation.

And if you have already fallen, there is forgiveness. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous: he will forgive our sins and cleanse us from every kind of wrongdoing” (1 John 1:9). Repentance for a leader will mean confessing honestly, not only to God but to those you have wronged and to those who have authority over you. It will usually mean stepping back from leadership for a time, perhaps for good. It will mean accepting the consequences without blaming others. And it will mean a long road of rebuilding trust. We will look at that road in Chapter 39, Failure and Restoration. But God’s grace is greater than our sin.

A voice from the Church: Augustine

Augustine, the North African bishop whom we have met in earlier chapters, knew the power of sexual sin from the inside. As a young man he lived with a woman for many years without marrying her, and had a son by her. He longed to follow Christ, but he could not bring himself to give up his sinful pleasures. In his Confessions, on Ochorus, he remembered how he had prayed as a young man:

“Give me chastity and continency, only not yet.”

— Augustine, Confessions, Book VIII

In plain words: Lord, make me pure, but not yet. He explained that he was afraid God would answer him too quickly. He wanted his desires satisfied, not taken away. Many people pray like that. They want to be free one day, but not today.

At last, in a garden in Milan, in great distress, he wept and cried, “How long, how long, ‘to-morrow, and tomorrow?’ Why not now?” Then he heard a child’s voice from a nearby house, singing, “Take up and read; take up and read.” He opened the letters of Paul and read the first words his eyes fell on. They were from Romans 13: “not in sexual immorality and shameless excess ... put on the Lord Jesus Christ like clothing, and do not make plans to satisfy the desires of the flesh” (Romans 13:13-14). Augustine wrote that at once, “all the darkness of doubt vanished away.” He was converted, and he became one of the greatest leaders the Church has ever known.

Augustine’s story shows two things. Sexual sin is a powerful chain. But Christ is more powerful, and He can set anyone free.

Many centuries later, in 1948, a young American evangelist called Billy Graham met with his small team in a hotel in the town of Modesto, California. They had seen other evangelists fall through money, sexual sin and pride. So they made a set of simple commitments together. One was that none of them would travel, meet or eat alone with a woman other than his wife. Graham kept these commitments for the rest of his long ministry. Whatever we think of the details, the principle is wise: decide on your walls before the battle, and keep them, together with others.

Holy in body and heart

Paul says, “This is God’s will for you: that you be holy” (1 Thessalonians 4:3). Purity is not only about avoiding scandal. It is about belonging to God, body and soul. “So bring glory to God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:20).

The tree that stands for a hundred years is not the one that never faces storms. It is the one whose heart is sound. Guard your heart. Build your walls. Run when you must. And trust the One who is able to keep you from falling.

Questions for reflection

  • Read Genesis 39:6-12. What did Joseph do to protect himself? What can you learn from him?
  • Read 2 Samuel 11:1-5. What were the steps that led to David’s fall? Where do you see similar steps in your own life?
  • Which of the “walls of protection” do you already have? Which have you quietly let fall?
  • Do you have someone who has permission to ask you hard questions about your purity? If not, who could you ask?
  • Have you ever prayed, as Augustine did, “make me pure, but not yet”? What would it mean to say “now”?
  • How can boundaries protect both leaders and the people they serve, without excluding anyone from ministry?

A step for this week

This week, write down the boundaries you will keep to protect your purity, using the list in this chapter as a guide. Share them with your spouse, if you are married, and with one trusted, mature believer of the same sex. Ask that person to check on you regularly. If there is any secret sin in your life, including pornography, confess it this week to God and to that person, and ask for help to find a way out.

study_questions.question: How can a leader stay sexually pure?
study_questions.answer: By guarding the heart and building walls of protection, and by running from temptation: “Get away from sexual immorality!” (1 Corinthians 6:18). “Run away from the passions of youth, and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace” (2 Timothy 2:22).

study_questions.question: What can we learn from Joseph and Potiphar’s wife?
study_questions.answer: Joseph refused her day after day and, when she grabbed him, “he ran from her and got outside, leaving the garment in her grip” (Genesis 39:12). He saw that sin would be against God. David, by contrast, stayed home when he should have been at war, and fell.

study_questions.question: Is there hope for a leader who has fallen into sexual sin?
study_questions.answer: Yes. God’s grace is strong enough to forgive and heal. The chapter urges full confession, accountability and restoration, and tells how Augustine was set free from sexual sin by God’s grace.

fields.title: Power, Abuse and Protecting the Vulnerable
fields.body_html:
“Do not rule harshly over the people given into your charge; set an example for the flock instead.”

— 1 Peter 5:3 (OWB)

A shepherd carries a staff. With it he can guide the sheep, pull a lamb out of a thorn bush, or drive away a wolf. But the same staff could be used to beat the sheep. The staff itself is not good or evil. What matters is the shepherd’s heart.

Every leader carries power. It may be the power of a title, of knowledge, of money, of being trusted, or of speaking for God. Power is not evil in itself. God gives it so that leaders can protect and serve. But power can also be used to control, to frighten, to take and to harm. This chapter is about the abuse of power in the Church, and about the leader’s sacred duty to protect the vulnerable, especially children. It is one of the most important chapters in this book.

Shepherds who fed on the flock

God’s word through Ezekiel is one of the strongest warnings in the Bible: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel who have been taking care of themselves! Should not shepherds take care of the flock? You eat the fat, you dress in the wool, and you slaughter the best animals, but you do not take care of the flock ... You have ruled them with force and cruelty instead” (Ezekiel 34:2-4).

These leaders used the flock for themselves. They took the best food and clothing. They ruled with harshness. God’s judgement was clear: “I am against the shepherds” (Ezekiel 34:10).

The sons of Eli, the high priest, were the same. They were priests at the house of God, but “they did not know the LORD.” They took the best meat from the sacrifices by force (1 Samuel 2:12-16). Worse still, “they slept with the women serving at the entrance to the tent of meeting” (1 Samuel 2:22). They used their position at God’s house to exploit the people who came to worship.

And notice Eli. He knew. “He kept hearing of all that his sons were doing.” He spoke to them, but he did nothing to stop them. God said He would judge Eli’s family “because of the guilt he knew about: his sons were bringing a curse on themselves, and he did not restrain them” (1 Samuel 3:13). Eli’s sin was not that he abused people. It was that he knew about the abuse and did not act. That is a warning to every leader who hears of abuse and stays silent.

Not so among you

Jesus taught His disciples a completely different way of using power: “You know that those who are thought of as rulers of the nations lord it over their people, and their important men use their power over them. That is not how it is among you. Instead, whoever among you wants to become great must be your servant” (Mark 10:42-43).

Peter, who heard these words, later wrote to elders: “Do not rule harshly over the people given into your charge; set an example for the flock instead” (1 Peter 5:3). Paul wrote to the Corinthians, “We do not mean that we are masters of your faith. Rather, we work alongside you to bring you joy” (2 Corinthians 1:24).

In Chapter 5, The Towel and the Basin, we saw that Christian leadership is servant leadership. In Chapter 6, Authority Under Authority, we saw that every leader is under Christ. The abuse of power is the opposite of both. It turns the servant into a master and forgets the Master above.

What spiritual abuse looks like

Abuse of power in the Church does not always involve violence. Often it is hidden behind spiritual language. Paul warned the Corinthians that they were too ready to put up with false leaders: “you put up with it if someone holds you in bondage, if someone eats you up, if someone takes you in, if someone lords it over you, if someone hits you in the face” (2 Corinthians 11:20). Here are some signs of spiritual abuse.

  • Fear. People are afraid of the leader. They do not dare to ask questions or disagree.
  • Control. The leader decides who people may marry, where they may work, whom they may speak to, or controls their money.
  • Using God’s name as a weapon. “If you leave this church, God will curse you.” “Touch not the Lord’s anointed.” Words like these are used to silence anyone who raises a concern.
  • No accountability. The leader answers to no one. No one checks the money or the decisions.
  • Secrecy. Problems are always hidden “to protect the ministry”. Those who speak up are punished, shamed or pushed out.
  • Taking. The leader takes money, labour, gifts or sexual favours from people, especially from those who are poor or dependent.
  • Heavy burdens. Jesus said of the Pharisees, “They bundle up heavy loads and pile them on the shoulders of others, but they refuse to move those loads even with a finger” (Matthew 23:4).

Here is a searching question for every leader: do people feel safe to tell me the truth? Do they feel free to say no to me? If not, something may be wrong.

Jesus and the little ones

Jesus had a special love for children. When His disciples tried to send them away, He said, “Let the children be. Do not prevent them from coming to me, because the kingdom of heaven is for those who are like them” (Matthew 19:14). He also gave one of His most terrifying warnings: “if anyone leads into sin one of these little ones who believe in me, that person would be better off sunk far out at sea with a great millstone fastened around their neck” (Matthew 18:6). And He said, “Take care never to look down on a single one of these little ones. I tell you, their angels in heaven stand always in the presence of my Father in heaven” (Matthew 18:10).

Sadly, children have been abused in churches all over the world, in every tradition, by pastors, priests, teachers, youth leaders and others whom they trusted. Again and again, church leaders have known and covered it up, to protect the abuser, the church’s name or themselves. Often the abused child was not believed, or was blamed, or was told to forgive and stay silent. This has caused deep and lasting harm to many people, and has driven many away from Christ. It is a great evil.

Never cover it up

Leaders must be absolutely clear about this. When abuse of a child, or of any vulnerable person, is suspected or reported, these things must be done.

  • Take it seriously and listen. Listen calmly to the person who tells you. Believe that they may be telling the truth. Do not blame them. Do not promise to keep it secret.
  • Protect the vulnerable first. Make sure the child or vulnerable person is safe from the accused person at once.
