  • Report it to the proper authorities. Abuse of a child is a crime, not only a sin. Paul says the governing authority is “God’s servant ... one who avenges and brings wrath on anyone who does wrong” (Romans 13:4). Report it to the police and child-protection authorities. Do not try to deal with it only inside the church.
  • Do not confront the accused person privately first. In Chapter 20, Correction and Restoration, we saw the steps of Matthew 18:15. Those steps are for ordinary sins between believers. They are not for crimes against children. Going privately to an abuser can put the child in greater danger and allow evidence to be hidden.
  • Remove the accused from ministry while the matter is investigated, especially from any contact with children.
  • Never protect the abuser because he is gifted, powerful, popular or a relative. No reputation, no church and no ministry is worth more than a child.
  • Care for the person who was harmed, for as long as it takes. Get them help.

“Do not share in the deeds of darkness, which produce nothing good. Show them up for what they are instead” (Ephesians 5:11). Jesus said, “Whatever is hidden will be shown plainly” (Luke 8:17). What a church hides, God will one day reveal. It is far better that the Church brings it into the light itself.

In some places, the authorities themselves may not be trustworthy. Even there, leaders must do everything they can to protect the vulnerable, get them to safety and seek justice. “Rescue those being dragged off to death ... If you say, ‘But we knew nothing about this,’ does not the one who weighs hearts see the truth?” (Proverbs 24:11-12).

Building a safe church

Every church, however small, should take simple steps to protect children and vulnerable adults.

  • Check carefully anyone who will work with children before they begin.
  • Never let one adult be alone and out of sight with a child. Use two adults, open doors and open rooms.
  • Teach children that their bodies belong to them, that no one may touch them in a wrong way, and that they can always tell a trusted adult.
  • Have a clear written plan for what to do if abuse is reported, and make sure every leader knows it.
  • Name a trusted person, ideally a man and a woman, whom anyone can go to with a concern, including concerns about the senior leader.
  • Make sure that no leader, including the senior pastor, is above accountability.

A voice from the Church: Gregory the Great and Amy Carmichael

Gregory the Great, whom we met in Chapter 2, What Makes Leadership Spiritual, wrote in his Book of Pastoral Rule about how leaders should think of their power. He reminded them that all human beings are equal by nature, and that leadership is given for the good of others:

“Hence all who are over others ought to consider in themselves not the authority of their rank, but the equality of their condition and rejoice not to be over men, but to do them good. For indeed our ancient fathers are said to have been not kings of men, but shepherds of flocks.”

— Gregory the Great, The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part II

In plain words: leaders should not think about how high their position is. They should remember that they are just as human as the people they lead. Their joy should not be in being above people, but in doing them good. Abraham and the patriarchs were not kings over people, but shepherds of flocks.

Amy Carmichael was an Irish missionary who went to South India in 1895 and never came home. In those days, some little girls were given to Hindu temples, where they were later “married to the god” and used for sexual purposes by men. On 7 March 1901, a little girl of about seven, called Preena, ran away from a temple house and came to the bungalow where Amy was staying. She climbed onto Amy’s knee and told her story. She had been unhappy and unloved. The woman who kept her had burned her fingers as a punishment. She had once escaped to her mother, but she had been taken back. “I have come to stay,” she told Amy.

Amy kept her. From that day, Amy and her co-workers gave their lives to protecting children in danger. As the biography Amy Carmichael: A Life on Ochorus notes, not all the children she took in came from temples. Many were babies or small children who had nowhere else to go. Over the years, the work grew into the Dohnavur Fellowship, a large family of hundreds of rescued children, cared for in safety and love. Amy faced fierce opposition, threats and even court cases. But she would not hand a child back into danger. Her first book about India, Things as They Are, which is on Ochorus, told the Church plainly about evils many did not want to hear about.

Gregory teaches leaders how to hold power. Amy shows what it looks like to use it for the little ones.

God the defender

The psalmist wrote, “LORD, you have heard what the humble long for; you steady their hearts and bend down to listen, to give justice to the orphan and the oppressed, so that mere mortals made of earth will strike terror no more” (Psalm 10:17-18).

God is the defender of the vulnerable. He sees every hidden abuse. He hears every child who cries. He will judge every shepherd who fed on the flock. And He calls His leaders to be like Him: to use their staff to protect, never to strike, and to make His house a safe place for the little ones.

Questions for reflection

  • Read Ezekiel 34:1-10. How did the shepherds of Israel use their power? Where do you see the same today?
  • Read 1 Samuel 2:22-25 and 3:13. What was Eli’s sin? Why is it so serious?
  • Do people feel safe to tell you the truth, or to say no to you? How could you find out?
  • Does your church have a clear plan for protecting children and responding to abuse? If not, what is the first step?
  • Why is it wrong to deal with child abuse only privately, using Matthew 18:15?
  • What do you learn from Amy Carmichael’s refusal to hand Preena back?

A step for this week

Meet with your fellow leaders this week to talk about safety in your church. Ask: “Who works with our children? Are they never alone with a child? Do our children know whom to tell? What would we do if someone reported abuse, even by a leader?” Write down a simple plan, and decide when you will share it with your church. Then ask two or three people you lead, “Do you ever feel afraid to disagree with me?” and listen carefully to the answer.

study_questions.question: What is spiritual abuse?
study_questions.answer: It is using spiritual authority to control, frighten, shame or exploit people. Peter told elders, “Do not rule harshly over the people given into your charge; set an example for the flock instead” (1 Peter 5:3). Paul wrote, “We do not mean that we are masters of your faith” (2 Corinthians 1:24).

study_questions.question: What should a church do when abuse happens?
study_questions.answer: Never cover it up. Protect the victim, report crimes to the proper authorities, and hold the abuser accountable. Eli was judged because his sons sinned and “he did not restrain them” (1 Samuel 3:13).

study_questions.question: How can a church protect the vulnerable?
study_questions.answer: By building safeguards: clear policies, checks on workers with children, never one adult alone with a child, and accountability for every leader, including the most senior. God is against shepherds who feed on the flock (Ezekiel 34:10).

fields.title: Envy, Rivalry and Favouritism
fields.body_html:
“Are you being jealous on my behalf? If only the LORD would put his Spirit on all his people and make every one of them a prophet!”

— Numbers 11:29 (OWB)

Two farmers have fields side by side. One year the rain falls more on one field than the other, and one farmer’s harvest is twice as large. The other farmer can rejoice with his neighbour and thank God for the food in the village. Or he can let bitterness grow in his heart, until he cannot greet his neighbour in the road. The rain was the same gift from the same God. The difference is in the heart of the man who received less.

Leaders face this test constantly. Another church grows faster than ours. Another preacher is invited to speak at the big conference. A younger leader is praised more than we are. And something dark stirs in the heart. This chapter, the last in Part Seven, Dangers on the Road, looks at envy and rivalry between leaders. It also looks at a close relative of envy: favouritism, the sin of treating some people as more important than others because of their tribe, class, wealth or family.

Saul and David

The saddest example of envy in the Bible is King Saul. After David killed Goliath, the women came out of the towns singing, “Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.” Saul could not bear it. “They have credited David with tens of thousands,” he said, “and me with mere thousands. What more is left for him but the kingdom?” And then come these terrible words: “From that day on, Saul watched David with suspicion” (1 Samuel 18:7-9).

David had done nothing wrong. He was loyal to Saul. He had saved Israel. But Saul’s envy turned him against the very person God had sent to help him. For years he hunted David, tried to kill him and wasted his kingdom’s strength on a rivalry that existed only in his own heart. “A calm heart gives life to the body, but envy is decay in the bones” (Proverbs 14:30). Envy rotted Saul from the inside.

Moses and Joshua

Compare Moses. In Chapter 22, No Lone Leaders, we saw how God put His Spirit on seventy elders to share Moses’ load. Two of them, Eldad and Medad, had stayed in the camp, but the Spirit came on them too, and they began to prophesy. A young man ran to tell Moses. Joshua, Moses’ loyal assistant, said, “My lord Moses, stop them!”

Moses answered, “Are you being jealous on my behalf? If only the LORD would put his Spirit on all his people and make every one of them a prophet!” (Numbers 11:28-29).

What a heart! Moses did not feel threatened when God used others. He wished that God would use everyone. Joshua was jealous for Moses’ sake, which can seem like loyalty. But Moses saw that it was really a narrow spirit.

Jesus’ disciples had the same narrow spirit. John said, “Teacher, we saw a man throwing out demons in your name. We tried to stop him, since he did not go around with us.” Jesus replied, “Do not stop him ... Anyone not against us is for us” (Mark 9:38-40). Notice the words “he did not go around with us.” The man was not doing anything wrong. He simply was not part of their group.

“He must grow greater”

In Chapter 7, Humility, we met John the Baptist. When his disciples complained that everyone was now going to Jesus instead of to him, John answered, “No one can receive anything at all unless it has been given them from heaven ... He must grow greater, but I must grow less” (John 3:27-30).

John’s first sentence is the cure for envy: “No one can receive anything at all unless it has been given them from heaven.” If another leader has a larger church, a greater gift or more fruit, it has been given from heaven. To envy them is to complain against God’s choices. Jesus told a parable about workers in a vineyard who grumbled because others were paid the same for less work. The owner said, “Do I not have the right to do as I please with what belongs to me? Or do you look on my generosity with an evil eye?” (Matthew 20:15).

Paul went even further. While he was in prison, some other preachers were preaching Christ “from jealousy and a spirit of rivalry”, hoping to make Paul’s suffering worse. His answer? “What does it matter? All that matters is that in every way, whether as a pretext or in truth, Christ is being proclaimed, and in that I rejoice” (Philippians 1:15-18). Paul cared more about Christ being known than about who got the credit.

The fruit of rivalry

James describes what happens when envy rules: “if bitter jealousy and selfish ambition fill your hearts, do not boast, and do not lie against the truth. This is not the kind of wisdom that comes down from above ... Wherever jealousy and selfish ambition are found, disorder follows, and every kind of evil deed” (James 3:14-16).

Rivalry between leaders shows itself in many ways: speaking quietly against another pastor; refusing to work with churches of another group; “stealing” members from a neighbouring church; competing over the size of buildings or crowds; refusing to share a platform; or splitting a church to start one’s own. Paul told the Corinthians, “as long as there is jealousy and quarreling among you, are you not living by the flesh?” (1 Corinthians 3:3).

The cure is to “take the lead in honoring one another” (Romans 12:10). Paul says the body of Christ is one: “if one part is honored, all the parts share its joy” (1 Corinthians 12:26). When another church grows, our church has grown, because we belong to the same body. Can you rejoice when another leader is blessed? That is one of the clearest tests of a heart after God.

Favouritism

Envy looks at those above us with resentment. Favouritism looks at people and ranks them. Both deny that every person stands equal before God.

Jacob loved Joseph more than his other sons and gave him a special robe. “His brothers saw that their father loved him more than any of them, and they hated him so much that they could not say a friendly word to him” (Genesis 37:4). A father’s favouritism nearly led to murder and split the family for twenty years.

James warned the churches: “My brothers and sisters, you do not hold the faith of our glorious Lord Jesus Christ while you show favoritism, do you?” He described a rich man given the best seat while a poor man is told to stand. “If you show favoritism, you commit sin” (James 2:1, 9). Paul charged Timothy “to do nothing out of favoritism” (1 Timothy 5:21).

In the Church today, favouritism takes many forms.

  • Tribalism and ethnic favouritism. Giving positions, help or honour to people of my own tribe, ethnic group or language, and overlooking others. In many parts of the world, this is one of the deepest sins in the Church, and it has even contributed to violence and war.
  • Caste and class. Treating people as higher or lower because of the family they were born into, or their education or work. In some places, believers of different castes still will not eat together or marry.
  • Wealth. Giving the rich the best seats, the leadership positions and the final word, because they give the most money.
  • Family. Handing church leadership to sons, daughters and relatives because they are family, not because God has called and equipped them.
  • Race. Treating believers of one colour or nation as more important than another.

Peter had to learn this lesson the hard way. God showed him in a vision that he must not call any person unclean. When he went to the house of Cornelius, a Gentile, he said, “In truth I now see that God does not favor one person over another. Instead, in every nation he accepts those who fear him” (Acts 10:34-35). Yet years later, in Antioch, Peter drew back from eating with Gentile believers, out of fear of what others would think. Paul “opposed him face to face, because he was clearly in the wrong” (Galatians 2:11). Even great leaders can slip back into favouritism. It must be resisted again and again.

A voice from the Church: Allen, Crowther and Sabiti

Richard Allen, whom we met in Chapter 30, Justice, Mercy and the Poor, was a former slave and a Methodist preacher in Philadelphia. Black and white Methodists worshipped together at St George’s Church, and Black members had given money for the building. But one Sunday, probably around 1792, they were told to sit in the upstairs gallery. As they knelt in prayer, a church trustee began pulling Absalom Jones up off his knees. Allen later wrote, as The Fire on the Altar on Ochorus records: “By this time prayer was over, and we all went out of the church in a body, and they were no more plagued with us in the church.” Allen went on to found Bethel Church, which became the mother church of the African Methodist Episcopal Church. A church that would not let Black believers kneel beside white ones had sinned against the body of Christ.

Samuel Ajayi Crowther, whom we met in Chapter 4, The Call of God, became the first African bishop of the Anglican Church in 1864. He led the mission on the Niger for many years. But near the end of his life, in 1890, a group of young English missionaries, who had been in Africa only a few months, began to criticise the African clergy. At a meeting at Onitsha, they suspended several African ministers, some of whom Crowther had ordained himself, including his own son, while he sat there. Samuel Ajayi Crowther: A Life, on Ochorus, describes how the old bishop “rose trembling to his feet to dissociate himself from what had been done.” He remained bishop until he died the next year. But his authority had been badly broken by his own side. Some of the criticisms may have had truth in them. But the way the young men acted showed a spirit of racial superiority that grieved many, and its effects on the Church in Nigeria lasted for years. The biography quotes the psalm: “For it was not an enemy that reproached me; Then I could have borne it.”

Erica Sabiti shows the way of healing. When he was chosen in 1966 to be the first Ugandan archbishop of the Anglican Church in Uganda, there was bitter opposition. He came from the Banyankore people of the south-west, and some insisted that the archbishop must come from the Baganda. As the book Tukutendereza on Ochorus says, “The dispute was not theological. It was ethnic, and it was ugly, and it ran for years.” In the end, the bishops met, and “the nine diocesan bishops confessed the sins that had contributed to the division, and then together recognised Erica as their archbishop.” The book draws the lesson: “The church’s ugliest divisions are not theological.” And: “Confession works on institutions too.” Through it all, Sabiti did not campaign against his opponents or split the church. He waited, and let the confession come.

Room for every servant

There is room in God’s kingdom for every servant He calls. There is no shortage of grace, no shortage of work and no shortage of reward. “Then each one will have from God whatever praise is due” (1 Corinthians 4:5). Another leader’s success does not take anything away from you. Another tribe’s blessing does not reduce yours.

Pray for the leaders you envy. Honour the people you are tempted to overlook. Welcome to your table those whom others push to the gallery. And say with Moses, “If only the LORD would put his Spirit on all his people!”

Questions for reflection

  • Read 1 Samuel 18:6-9. Have you ever felt what Saul felt when someone else was praised more than you? What did you do with it?
  • Read Numbers 11:24-29 and Mark 9:38-40. Why is it so easy to be suspicious of those who do not “go around with us”?
  • Can you rejoice when another church or leader is blessed? Name one leader you could pray for and honour this week.
  • Which form of favouritism is the greatest danger in your church or community: tribe, caste, class, wealth, family or race?
  • What do you learn from Crowther’s experience in 1890?
  • Sabiti’s bishops healed an ethnic division by confessing their own part in it. Is there a division in your church that needs the same?

A step for this week

Think of one leader or church you feel envious of or in competition with. Pray for them by name every day this week, asking God to bless them even more. If you can, contact them and encourage them. Then look honestly at your own church: who sits in the best places, who holds the positions and who is overlooked? Ask your fellow leaders whether there is any favouritism you need to confess and put right together.

study_questions.question: How does envy harm leaders?
study_questions.answer: “A calm heart gives life to the body, but envy is decay in the bones” (Proverbs 14:30). Saul’s envy of David began when women sang David’s praises: “From that day on, Saul watched David with suspicion” (1 Samuel 18:9).

study_questions.question: How did Moses respond to rivalry?
study_questions.answer: When Joshua wanted to stop others prophesying, Moses said, “Are you being jealous on my behalf? If only the LORD would put his Spirit on all his people” (Numbers 11:29). Jesus likewise said, “Do not stop him” (Mark 9:39).

study_questions.question: What did John the Baptist teach about rivalry?
study_questions.answer: When his followers left for Jesus, John said, “No one can receive anything at all unless it has been given them from heaven ... He must grow greater, but I must grow less” (John 3:27-30). The chapter also warns against favouritism by tribe, class or wealth.

fields.title: Loneliness and Hidden Burdens
fields.body_html:
“At my first defense no one came to support me; everyone deserted me. May it not be held against them. But the Lord stood by me and gave me strength.”

— 2 Timothy 4:16-17 (OWB)

A man carrying a heavy load on his head walks through the market. People greet him, buy from him and talk with him. But none of them can feel the weight on his neck. Only he knows how heavy it is, how far he has carried it, and how much longer he must go.

Leaders often carry loads like this. They are surrounded by people, but they feel alone. They know things they cannot share: a family in crisis, a secret sin in the church, a hard decision, a threat, a quarrel among the elders. They are expected to be strong, wise and cheerful. Many people need them, but few people ask how they are. This chapter begins Part Eight, Leading Through Hardship. We begin with the loneliness of leadership and the hidden burdens nobody else sees.

“My anxious care for all the churches”

Paul listed many of the sufferings he had faced for Christ: beatings, shipwrecks, prison, hunger, danger from robbers and from false believers (2 Corinthians 11:23-27). Then he added something that was perhaps harder than all of them: “And apart from all these other things, there is what presses on me day after day: my anxious care for all the churches. Is anyone weak without my feeling weak as well? Is anyone made to fall without my burning inside?” (2 Corinthians 11:28-29).

This is the hidden burden of every true shepherd. It presses “day after day”. When people we love fall into sin, we burn inside. When they are weak, we feel it. Others may go home after the meeting and forget. The leader carries it into the night.

Paul at the end

Near the end of his life, Paul wrote his last letter from a prison in Rome. Listen to how lonely he was: “Do your best to come to me soon. Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. Crescens has gone to Galatia and Titus to Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me” (2 Timothy 4:9-11). He asked Timothy to bring his cloak, because winter was coming, and his books (2 Timothy 4:13). And then: “At my first defense no one came to support me; everyone deserted me” (2 Timothy 4:16).

Paul had planted churches across the Roman world. Thousands had come to faith through him. And at his trial, no one stood with him. But notice two things. First, he forgave: “May it not be held against them.” Second, he found God faithful: “But the Lord stood by me and gave me strength” (2 Timothy 4:17).

The loneliness of Jesus

No one was ever as lonely as Jesus. His family thought He was out of His mind (Mark 3:21). His own town rejected Him. His disciples often misunderstood Him. On the night before He died, He took Peter, James and John into the garden of Gethsemane. “Horror and anguish came over him. He said to them, ‘My soul is filled with grief, grief enough to die. Wait here and stay awake’” (Mark 14:33-34). He asked His closest friends to be with Him. Three times He came back and found them asleep. “Simon, are you asleep? Did you not have the strength to stay awake a single hour?” (Mark 14:37). And when the soldiers came, “they all left him and ran” (Mark 14:50).

Jesus had foretold this: “you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me” (John 16:32). Then, on the cross, He experienced even the loneliness of being forsaken by God, as He bore our sin.

This means that no leader’s loneliness is beyond Jesus’ understanding. He knows what it is to be surrounded by crowds and understood by no one. He knows what it is to be let down by friends. And because He was forsaken, He can promise us, “I will not ever let you go, and I will never, never abandon you” (Hebrews 13:5).

Why leaders are lonely

Leaders are lonely for many reasons. Knowing them can help.

  • Confidential burdens. Leaders hear secrets they must keep. They cannot share them, even with their closest friends.
  • Decisions. In the end, someone must decide. When the decision is hard, the one who makes it often stands alone.
  • Criticism. When people are unhappy, the leader is often the one they blame.
  • Distance. Some people treat leaders differently. They are careful what they say. They put the leader on a pedestal, and it is lonely up there.
  • Expectations. Many leaders believe that they must always look strong, so they hide their own struggles.
  • Moving. Missionaries and pastors who move to new places leave their friends and families behind.
  • Self-made walls. Some leaders are lonely because they will not let anyone in. Pride, fear or past hurts make them keep everyone at a distance.

Elijah, after his great victory on Mount Carmel, ran into the wilderness and said, “I alone am left” (1 Kings 19:10). It felt true, but it was not. God told him, “I will leave 7,000 in Israel, everyone whose knees have not bent to Baal” (1 Kings 19:18). Loneliness often tells us we are more alone than we really are. We will look more at Elijah in the next chapter, Chapter 38, Discouragement and Burnout.

Bringing loneliness to God

The Bible gives us words for our loneliness. David prayed in a cave while hiding from Saul: “Look to my right and see: there is no one who knows me. Every way of escape is gone; nobody looks out for me. I cry out to you, LORD. I say, ‘You are my shelter, all I have in the land of the living’” (Psalm 142:4-5). Another psalmist prayed, “Turn toward me and show me grace, for I am lonely and in misery” (Psalm 25:16).

Psalm 88 is one of the darkest prayers in the Bible. It ends with no comfort at all: “You have taken far from me those I love and my friends; my one companion is the dark” (Psalm 88:18). It is a great gift that this psalm is in the Bible. It tells us that God is not offended by our honest darkness. We can bring it to Him just as it is.

And God answers. “Do not be afraid, for I am with you; do not glance about in alarm, for I am your God. I give you strength; yes, I bring you help” (Isaiah 41:10). “If my father and my mother were to leave me, the LORD would still gather me in” (Psalm 27:10).

Letting others in

God is our first companion. But He also gives us people. “God gives the lonely a home to live in” (Psalm 68:6). Even Jesus wanted His friends near Him in Gethsemane. Paul begged Timothy to come. A leader is not more spiritual for having no friends.

When David was hunted by Saul and hiding in the wilderness, “Saul’s son Jonathan set out and went to David at Horesh, and he gave him fresh strength in God” (1 Samuel 23:16). Every leader needs a Jonathan: a friend who comes, and who helps them find strength in God.

Here are some ways to fight loneliness.

  • Be honest with God about how you feel, using the psalms.
  • Find one or two true friends with whom you can be fully honest. “Some friends stay closer than a brother” (Proverbs 18:24). Often these will be people outside your own church, such as other pastors or leaders in a nearby town.
  • Meet with other leaders regularly, to pray and share burdens. Many pastors’ groups have saved leaders from despair.
  • Let your spouse in, if you are married, as far as is wise. Do not carry everything alone at home.
  • Accept help. “Take up one another’s heavy loads” (Galatians 6:2). That includes letting others carry yours.
  • Remember the 7,000. You are part of a great family of believers across the world and across history.
  • Seek help when loneliness becomes darkness. If you feel hopeless for a long time, speak to someone you trust, and if possible to a trained counsellor or doctor.

A voice from the Church: David Brainerd and David Livingstone

David Brainerd, whom we met in Chapter 19, Seeking the Lost, spent his first year as a missionary in 1743 at a place called Kaunaumeek, in the forests of New York, living alone in a rough hut among the Native people he served. His diary, which is on Ochorus, records his loneliness honestly:

“My circumstances are such that I have no comfort of any kind, but what I have in God. I live in the most lonesome wilderness; have but one single person to converse with that can speak English ... I have no fellow-christian to whom I may unbosom myself, or lay open my spiritual sorrows; with whom I may take sweet counsel in conversation about heavenly things, and join in social prayer.”

— David Brainerd, diary, 18 May 1743

In plain words: I have no comfort here except God. I live in a very lonely wilderness. Only one person here speaks my language. I have no Christian friend to open my heart to, to share my spiritual struggles with, to talk with about God, or to pray with. Notice what Brainerd missed most: not comfortable food or a good bed, though he had neither, but a Christian friend to pray with. Yet notice also the first sentence. He did have comfort in God, and it carried him through.

David Livingstone was a Scottish doctor and missionary who travelled across much of southern and central Africa in the nineteenth century. He spent long years apart from his wife Mary and their children, often in danger and sickness. In 1862, at last, Mary joined him on the Zambezi River. For a few weeks they were together again. Then she caught fever and died, at a place called Shupanga, on 27 April 1862. David Livingstone: A Life, on Ochorus, tells how he wrote in his journal that he was left alone in the world by one whom he had felt to be a part of himself, and that for the first time in his life he felt willing to die. He did not lose his faith. His journal was full of prayer and hope of heaven. But it was also full of grief that did not hurry to be comforted.

Livingstone’s story is also a warning. His biography shows a man who had sacrificed much for the gospel, but who had also often left his family to carry great loneliness of their own. We will think about the leader’s home in Chapter 42, The Leader’s Home.

Not alone

Paul, abandoned at his trial, wrote, “But the Lord stood by me and gave me strength.” Jesus, abandoned by His friends, said, “Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me.” Brainerd, alone in the forest, wrote that he had no comfort “but what I have in God.”

If you are a lonely leader, you are in good company. Bring your loneliness to God. Let one or two people in. Carry your hidden burdens to the One who carries you. And remember that the Good Shepherd, who was left alone for you, has promised never to leave you alone.

Questions for reflection

  • Read 2 Corinthians 11:28-29. What burdens do you carry “day after day” that others do not see?
  • Read 2 Timothy 4:9-18. How did Paul respond to being deserted?
  • Which of the reasons leaders are lonely are true for you?
  • Who knows the real you? Have you let anyone in?
  • Who is your Jonathan? Whose Jonathan could you be?
  • Read Psalm 142 aloud as your own prayer. What do you want to say to God about your loneliness?

A step for this week

This week, write down the burdens you are carrying that no one else knows about, and pray through the list using Psalm 142. Then contact one leader in another church or town whom you trust and respect. Ask them to meet you for a meal or a long walk. Tell them honestly how you are, and ask how they are. Pray together, and agree to meet again.

study_questions.question: Why are Christian leaders often lonely?
study_questions.answer: Because they carry burdens they cannot share with everyone, they may be set apart by their role, and some face opposition alone. Paul wrote of “my anxious care for all the churches” (2 Corinthians 11:28) and said, “everyone deserted me” (2 Timothy 4:16).

study_questions.question: Was Jesus lonely?
study_questions.answer: Yes. In Gethsemane He said, “My soul is filled with grief, grief enough to die” (Mark 14:34), and His friends fell asleep. He knows the loneliness of leadership from the inside.

study_questions.question: What can a lonely leader do?
study_questions.answer: Bring it to God, who stays near, as Paul found: “But the Lord stood by me and gave me strength” (2 Timothy 4:17). Then let trusted friends in. The chapter draws on David Brainerd and David Livingstone.

fields.title: Discouragement and Burnout
fields.body_html:
“He gives strength to the exhausted and builds up the power of those who have none.”

— Isaiah 40:29 (OWB)

An oil lamp can burn through the whole night. But if no one fills it, the flame grows smaller and smaller. It may flicker for a long time, giving less and less light, until at last it goes out. Nobody blew it out. It simply ran dry.

Many leaders run dry like this. They do not fall into great sin. They do not stop believing. They simply grow tired, then weary, then empty. They keep going through the motions, but the joy has gone. Some lie awake at night. Some cannot pray. Some quietly decide that they will leave the ministry. Some fall into a darkness that feels like it will never lift. This chapter looks at discouragement and burnout, and at how God meets His servants when the lamp is nearly out.

Elijah under the broom tree

Elijah had just seen the greatest victory of his life. On Mount Carmel, fire had fallen from heaven, and the people had cried out, “The LORD, he is God!” (1 Kings 18:39). Then a message came from Queen Jezebel: by this time tomorrow you will be dead. And the bold prophet broke.

“When Elijah saw how things stood, he got up and fled for his life ... He came to a broom tree and sat down under it, and he prayed that he might die. ‘It is enough,’ he said. ‘Now, LORD, take my life, for I am no better than my ancestors’” (1 Kings 19:3-4).

Look at the signs of burnout in Elijah. He was exhausted after a long struggle. He was afraid. He ran away from everyone, even leaving his servant behind. He felt like a failure: “I am no better than my ancestors.” He wanted to die. And he believed he was completely alone: “I alone am left” (1 Kings 19:10). As we saw in Chapter 37, Loneliness and Hidden Burdens, this was not true. But it felt true.

Notice when it happened. It did not come after a defeat, but after a great victory. Many leaders find that the hardest days come after the big event: after the crusade, the building opening, the conference. The body and the soul have been running on high energy, and when it is over, they crash.

How God cared for Elijah

In Chapter 15, Rest, Retreat and Rhythm, we saw the first part of God’s answer. He did not rebuke Elijah. He let him sleep. He sent an angel with bread and water, and said, “Get up and eat, for the journey is too much for you” (1 Kings 19:7). God knew His servant was a body as well as a soul. “For he knows what we are made of; he does not forget that we are only dust” (Psalm 103:14).

But God did not stop there. After Elijah had rested, God led him to Mount Horeb, the mountain where He had spoken to Moses. There God asked him a question: “What are you doing here, Elijah?” (1 Kings 19:9). He let Elijah pour out his complaint. Then God showed Himself. “A mighty, fierce wind was splitting the mountains ... but the LORD was not in the wind. After the wind came an earthquake; the LORD was not in the earthquake. Then came fire after the earthquake, but the LORD was not in the fire. And when the fire had passed, a faint sound, thin as silence” (1 Kings 19:11-12). Other English Bibles call it “a still small voice” or “a gentle whisper”.

Elijah had seen God in the fire on Carmel. Now he needed to learn that God is also present in the quiet. The tired leader does not always need another great event. Often he or she needs to hear God’s gentle voice again.

Finally, God gave Elijah work to do, and a companion. “Go back the way you came,” He said, and told him to anoint new kings, “and anoint Elisha son of Shaphat from Abel-meholah to be prophet in your place” (1 Kings 19:15-16). He also told him the truth: there were 7,000 others who had stayed faithful (1 Kings 19:18).

So God restored Elijah in four ways:

  • Rest and food for his body.
  • His presence, in a gentle voice, for his soul.
  • The truth, to correct the lie that he was alone.
  • A new purpose and a companion, so that he would not carry the work alone again.

You are not the first

Elijah was not the only servant of God who reached the end of his strength. Moses cried out to God, “I cannot carry this whole people on my own. The load is too heavy for me. If you are going to deal with me like this, then put me to death at once” (Numbers 11:14-15). Jeremiah, mocked and beaten for preaching God’s word, cursed the day he was born (Jeremiah 20:14). Jonah, angry and tired under the sun, asked to die (Jonah 4:8).

Even Paul wrote, “We were weighed down so heavily, so far past our strength, that we had given up hope even of staying alive” (2 Corinthians 1:8). And yet he added, “That was so that our confidence would rest, not on ourselves, but on God, who raises the dead” (2 Corinthians 1:9).

The Bible does not hide these moments. It is honest about the weakness of God’s greatest servants. This is a comfort. If you feel discouraged or empty, you are not a failure as a Christian. You are standing where Moses, Elijah, Jeremiah and Paul once stood.

Talking to your own soul

The writer of Psalms 42 and 43 was in deep discouragement. He remembered the days when he had led the crowds to worship, and now he felt far from God. “Day and night I have fed on my tears,” he wrote (Psalm 42:3). But he did something wise. He began to speak to his own soul: “Why are you bent so low, my soul? Why this unrest inside me? Wait for God in hope; I will give him thanks again, for the rescue that comes from his presence” (Psalm 42:5).

He says these words three times (Psalm 42:5, 42:11 and 43:5). He does not pretend he is happy. He admits that his soul is “bent so low”. But he refuses to let his feelings have the last word. He tells his soul to hope in God.

Discouraged leaders often listen to their feelings: “You are a failure. Nothing has changed. God has forgotten you. Give up.” The psalmist teaches us to answer back with the truth of God. Paul did the same: “So we do not give up. Our outer self may be decaying, but our inner self is being made new day after day. Our troubles are light and last only a moment, and they are bringing about for us an eternal glory” (2 Corinthians 4:16-17).

Clay pots

Paul gives a picture that every tired leader needs: “But we hold this treasure in pots made of clay, so that the power, great beyond measure, may be God’s and may not come from us. In every way we are under pressure, but not cornered; we are at a loss, but not utterly at a loss; we are hunted, but not deserted; we are thrown down, but not destroyed” (2 Corinthians 4:7-9).

A clay pot is ordinary, fragile and easily cracked. God has chosen to put the treasure of the gospel in pots like that, in weak and ordinary people like us. Why? So that everyone can see that the power comes from God and not from us. Our weakness is not a mistake in God’s plan. It is part of His plan.

And God is gentle with cracked pots. Isaiah said of the coming Servant, Jesus: “He will not snap off a split reed or smother a wick that is barely burning” (Isaiah 42:3). If your lamp is barely burning, Jesus will not put it out. He will tend it. He still says, “Come to me, all of you who are worn out with work and weighed down with burdens, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

Why leaders burn out

Discouragement can come from many directions. It helps to know where it is coming from.

  • Overwork. Jethro told Moses, “You are sure to wear out, both you and the people who are with you. The load is too heavy for you” (Exodus 18:18). Many leaders try to do everything themselves.
  • No rest. Leaders who never take a day off, never sleep enough and never have a holiday will one day break. “It does you no good to get up early and stay up late, eating food earned by anxious work; he gives sleep to the one he loves” (Psalm 127:2).
  • No visible fruit. Years of work with little to show can wear down the strongest heart.
  • Conflict and criticism. Constant opposition drains the soul. We looked at this in Chapter 25, Criticism, Opposition and Conflict.
  • Grief and loss. Leaders carry their own sorrows as well as other people’s.
  • Poverty. Many pastors in the world struggle to feed their families. Worry about money exhausts body and mind.
  • Hidden sin or unbelief. Sometimes the dryness comes from a hidden sin, or from trying to serve in our own strength rather than God’s.
  • Illness. Some darkness has a physical cause. Depression is a real illness, not simply a lack of faith.

Steps back to strength

“We must not tire of doing good. When the right time comes we will bring in the harvest, as long as we do not slacken” (Galatians 6:9). How can a discouraged leader keep going, or begin again?

  • Look after your body. Sleep, eat, walk and rest, as Elijah did. This is not unspiritual. It is obedience.
  • Tell God the truth. Pray the psalms of lament. God can handle your honesty.
  • Tell someone else. Do not hide it. Speak to a trusted friend, your spouse, or a mature leader. Burnout grows in secret.
  • Share the load. Let others do some of the work. You are not the Messiah. We saw this in Chapter 22, No Lone Leaders.
  • Take a proper break. If you can, step away for a time. Sometimes a leader needs weeks or months, not one day.
  • Remember why you began. Read again the story of your call. Remember the people who have come to Christ.
  • Get medical help. If you feel hopeless for weeks, cannot sleep, cannot function, or have thoughts of ending your life, please speak to a doctor or counsellor as soon as you can. Seeking help is not a lack of faith. If you are in danger, tell someone today.
  • Wait for God. “Those who wait for the LORD will take on fresh strength. They will climb high on outspread wings like eagles. They will run and not wear out; they will walk and not tire” (Isaiah 40:31).

And if you lead other leaders, watch over them. Ask them how they really are. Make sure they rest. Help them when they are struggling. Do not treat a tired leader as a weak one.

A voice from the Church: Charles Spurgeon and Hudson Taylor

Charles Spurgeon, the great London preacher whom we met in Chapter 9, Keep Watch over Yourself, suffered from deep depression for much of his life. He also suffered from painful illness, and in 1856, when he was only twenty-two, a false alarm of fire during one of his services caused a panic in which seven people died. For a time afterwards he was almost crushed.

Spurgeon did not hide his struggles from his students. He gave them a lecture called “The Minister’s Fainting Fits”, which is in his Lectures to My Students on Ochorus. He began honestly:

“Fits of depression come over the most of us. Usually cheerful as we may be, we must at intervals be cast down. The strong are not always vigorous, the wise not always ready, the brave not always courageous, and the joyous not always happy.”

— C. H. Spurgeon, “The Minister’s Fainting Fits”

In plain words: most of us go through times of depression. Even cheerful people are sometimes low. Strong, wise, brave and joyful people are not always strong, wise, brave and joyful.

He told them that it had happened to him at the very start of his work in London, when great crowds began to come. “My success appalled me,” he said, and it “cast me into the lowest depth.” He even thought of running away to a small village. He also warned them, as Jesus did, that they needed rest: “The bow cannot be always bent without fear of breaking. Repose is as needful to the mind as sleep to the body.”

He ended the lecture with words of hope for those in the dark:

“Should the power of depression be more than ordinary, think not that all is over with your usefulness ... Live by the day—ay, by the hour. Put no trust in frames and feelings. Care more for a grain of faith than a ton of excitement.”

— C. H. Spurgeon, “The Minister’s Fainting Fits”

In plain words: if your depression is very deep, do not think God can no longer use you. Live one day at a time, even one hour at a time. Do not trust your moods and feelings. A small amount of real faith is worth more than a great deal of excitement. Spurgeon, the most famous preacher of his age, was a clay pot, and God used him for nearly forty years.

James Hudson Taylor, the founder of the China Inland Mission whom we met in Chapter 5, The Towel and the Basin, reached his own breaking point in 1869. The mission had faced riots, criticism and quarrels. He was worn out, and deeply discouraged by his own spiritual failures. He even wondered whether he should give up. Then a letter came from a younger colleague, John McCarthy. As the Ochorus book Key Teachings of Hudson Taylor explains, Taylor’s biographers record its message: the way forward was not striving harder after faith, but resting on the Faithful One. Taylor came to see that he did not have to carry the mission on his own strength. Christ would carry it, and carry him. It changed the rest of his life. Hard sorrows still lay ahead, including the death of his wife Maria the next year. But he faced them from a place of rest.

The lamp refilled

Elijah lay down under the broom tree and asked to die. But his story did not end there. God fed him, met him, told him the truth and gave him Elisha. Later, Elijah was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind, and his work went on in the one he had trained.

If you are discouraged, your story has not ended either. The God who “gives strength to the exhausted” has not forgotten you. Rest. Tell Him the truth. Let others help you. And wait for Him, because those who wait for the LORD will take on fresh strength. “In the Lord your hard work is never wasted” (1 Corinthians 15:58).

Questions for reflection

  • Read 1 Kings 19:1-18. Which of Elijah’s signs of burnout do you recognise in yourself?
  • God restored Elijah through rest, His presence, the truth and a companion. Which of these do you most need now?
  • Read Psalm 42. What does it look like to “talk to your own soul”?
  • Read 2 Corinthians 4:7-18. How does the picture of clay pots change the way you see your weakness?
  • Which of the causes of burnout are most present in your life?
  • Spurgeon said, “Care more for a grain of faith than a ton of excitement.” What does that mean for you?
  • Is there a leader you know who is running dry? How could you help them?

A step for this week

Be honest this week about how full or empty your lamp is. On a scale from one to ten, how tired are you in body, in mind and in spirit? Write it down. Then choose one practical step: an early night, a day off, a walk, a meal with a friend, or a visit to a doctor. Tell one trusted person how you really are. Pray Psalm 42 aloud, and speak to your own soul: “Wait for God in hope.”

study_questions.question: How did God care for Elijah when he was burnt out?
study_questions.answer: Elijah sat under a broom tree and asked to die (1 Kings 19:4). God let him sleep, fed him and said, “Get up and eat, for the journey is too much for you” (1 Kings 19:7). Then He spoke to him gently and gave him fresh work and companions.

study_questions.question: Is it a sin for a leader to be discouraged?
study_questions.answer: No. Many faithful servants have been. God “knows what we are made of; he does not forget that we are only dust” (Psalm 103:14). Charles Spurgeon wrote of his “fainting fits”, and Hudson Taylor passed through deep darkness in 1869.

study_questions.question: What are the steps back from burnout?
study_questions.answer: Rest and care for the body, honest talk with God and with others, help from a doctor or counsellor where needed, lightening the load, and renewed dependence on God, who “gives strength to the exhausted” (Isaiah 40:29).

fields.title: Failure and Restoration
fields.body_html:
“Do not gloat over me, my enemy! I have fallen, but I will rise. Though I sit in darkness, the LORD is my light.”

— Micah 7:8 (OWB)

When a bone breaks, a good doctor does two things. First, he or she sets the bone straight, even though it hurts. Then the doctor holds it firmly in place, sometimes for many weeks, while it heals. If the bone is not set, it may heal crooked, and the person will limp for life. If it is never allowed to rest, it will not heal at all.

Every leader fails. Some failures are small mistakes. Some are serious sins that wound many people. When a leader fails, there are two great dangers. One is to hide the break and carry on as if nothing has happened. The other is to believe the break can never heal. This chapter looks at failure and restoration: what honest repentance looks like, what consequences may follow, and how Christ restores those who fall.

Peter: the leader who denied his Lord

Peter was the leader of the twelve. On the night before Jesus died, Jesus warned him: “Simon, Simon, Satan has demanded to have all of you, to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, so that your faith will not give out. And you, once you have turned back, must strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:31-32).

Peter was sure of himself. “Lord, I am ready to go to prison with you, and even to die with you.” Jesus answered, “I tell you, Peter, before a rooster crows today, you will have said three times that you do not know me” (Luke 22:33-34).

A few hours later, in the courtyard of the high priest, a servant girl said that Peter had been with Jesus. Peter denied it. Then again. Then a third time. “At that very moment, while he was still speaking, a rooster crowed. And the Lord turned and looked at Peter ... He went outside and wept bitterly” (Luke 22:60-62).

Notice three things about Jesus’ words before the fall. First, He knew Peter would fail, and He still chose him. Second, He prayed for Peter before he fell. Third, He spoke of the future: “once you have turned back, must strengthen your brothers.” Jesus already saw Peter on the other side of his failure, restored and strengthening others.

“And Peter too”

On the morning of the resurrection, the angel at the empty tomb gave the women a message: “go and tell his disciples, and Peter too, that he is going on ahead of you to Galilee” (Mark 16:7). “And Peter too.” Peter may have thought that he was no longer one of the disciples. The risen Lord made sure he knew he was not forgotten.

Then, beside the Sea of Galilee, Jesus cooked breakfast for His disciples over a charcoal fire. Peter had denied Him beside a fire. Now, beside another fire, Jesus asked him three times, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” Three denials, three questions. “Peter was hurt because Jesus asked him a third time, ‘Do you love me?’ Peter replied, ‘Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.’ Jesus said to him, ‘Feed my sheep’” (John 21:17).

Jesus did not pretend the failure had not happened. The three questions brought it gently back into the light, and they hurt. But Jesus did not leave Peter in his shame. He gave him back his work: “Feed my lambs ... Shepherd my sheep ... Feed my sheep.” And He ended with the same words He had spoken when He first called Peter: “Follow me” (John 21:19).

A few weeks later, at Pentecost, Peter stood up in Jerusalem, in the same city where he had denied Jesus, and preached. About three thousand people believed. The man who had failed most publicly became the first great preacher of the Church.

John Mark: the young man who quit

John Mark went with Paul and Barnabas on their first missionary journey. But partway through, he left them and went home (Acts 13:13). We are not told why. When the time came for the second journey, Barnabas wanted to take Mark again. “But Paul did not think it right to take with them a man who had left them in Pamphylia and had not gone on with them to the work. The quarrel grew so heated that the two of them parted ways. Barnabas took Mark and sailed off to Cyprus” (Acts 15:38-39).

Who was right? Perhaps both. Paul was right that the work needed people who would not quit. Barnabas, whose name means “son of encouragement”, was right that a young man who had failed needed another chance.

Years later, the story has a beautiful ending. Paul wrote from prison, “Mark, the cousin of Barnabas ... if he comes to you, make him welcome” (Colossians 4:10). He called Mark one of his “fellow workers” (Philemon 24). And in his very last letter, Paul wrote to Timothy, “Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is helpful to me in my work” (2 Timothy 4:11). The young man who quit became the one Paul wanted beside him at the end. Many believe he also wrote the Gospel of Mark.

Some of the people who fail under your leadership will one day be your most helpful fellow workers. Be a Barnabas to them.

David: the cost of hidden sin

We looked at David’s fall in Chapter 34, Sexual Purity. Notice now what happened after it. For many months David hid his sin. He later described that time: “While I kept quiet, my bones wore away with my groaning the whole day long. Day and night your hand pressed hard on me” (Psalm 32:3-4). Hidden sin does not stay quiet. It eats at the soul and the body.

When Nathan the prophet confronted him, David did not argue, blame Bathsheba or defend himself. He said simply, “I have sinned against the LORD.” And Nathan answered, “The LORD has taken away your sin. You will not die” (2 Samuel 12:13). God forgave David at once. But Nathan went on to tell him of the painful consequences that would follow (2 Samuel 12:14). Forgiveness is complete. But forgiveness does not always remove the consequences of what we have done.

David’s prayer of repentance, Psalm 51, has been prayed by fallen leaders for three thousand years. “God, be gracious to me in keeping with your loyal love; in the fullness of your compassion, wipe away my rebellious acts ... I myself know my rebellious acts, and my sin is never out of my sight” (Psalm 51:1, 3). “The sacrifices that God accepts are a broken spirit. A heart that is broken and crushed, God, you will never reject” (Psalm 51:17).

Not every failure is sin

It is important to tell the difference between different kinds of failure.

  • Mistakes. A plan that did not work, a wrong decision made in good faith, a sermon that fell flat. These are part of being human. Learn from them, apologise where needed, and move on.
  • Weakness. Losing your temper when exhausted, failing to visit someone who needed you, fear that kept you silent. These need confession and growth.
  • Serious sin. Adultery, theft, abuse, deliberate lies, cruelty. These need deep repentance, and usually have serious consequences for the leader’s ministry.

Some leaders treat every mistake as a terrible sin, and live under constant guilt. Others treat serious sin as a small mistake, and refuse to face its weight. Both are wrong. Ask God, and wise friends, to help you see your failure as it really is.

What true repentance looks like

“Whoever hides their sins will not succeed, but whoever admits them and turns away from them will receive mercy” (Proverbs 28:13). When a leader has sinned seriously, true repentance will usually include these things.

  • Confession without excuses. Saying “I have sinned”, as David did, not “mistakes were made” or “I was under pressure”.
  • Confession to the right people. To God first. Then to those who were harmed, if that is safe and wise for them. Then to those who have authority over you.
  • Turning away. Stopping the sin completely, and cutting off whatever made it possible.
  • Making it right. Where possible, repaying what was taken and repairing what was damaged. Zacchaeus said, “if I have taken anything from anyone by cheating, I am paying it back four times over” (Luke 19:8).
  • Accepting consequences. Not demanding to be trusted again at once. Not blaming those who hold you to account.
  • Submitting to others. Allowing wise, mature believers to walk with you and to decide with you what happens next.

A leader who says “I am sorry” but then demands to keep his or her position, attacks those who raised the problem, or hides part of the truth, has not yet fully repented.

Restored to Christ, and restored to leadership

Paul wrote, “suppose someone is caught out in some wrongdoing. You who are spiritual must set that person right again, and do it with a gentle spirit. Keep an eye on yourself as you do, in case you are tempted too” (Galatians 6:1). The church must always offer forgiveness and welcome to a repentant leader. We saw how to correct gently in Chapter 20, Correction and Restoration.

But there is an important difference between being restored to Christ and to the fellowship of the church, and being restored to leadership. The first is a gift of grace, and is offered freely to everyone who repents. “Those who are in Christ Jesus now face no sentence of condemnation” (Romans 8:1). The second is a question of trust and character. Scripture says a leader must be “someone no one can fairly criticize” (1 Timothy 3:2), and “well thought of by outsiders” (1 Timothy 3:7).

So when a leader has fallen into serious sin, wise churches usually do these things:

  • They ask the leader to step down from leadership, at least for a time.
  • They provide care, counselling and accountability for the leader and for his or her family.
  • They care first and most for anyone who was harmed.
  • They allow a long time, often years, for trust to be rebuilt and for real change to be seen.
  • They decide together, not alone, whether the leader can ever lead again, and in what kind of role.

Some leaders, after a long time of proven change, are restored to fruitful ministry. Others are not, and serve Christ faithfully in other ways. Both are signs of grace. Where a leader has abused a child or a vulnerable person, the safety of the vulnerable must always come first, and such a person should not be given a position of trust over them again. We saw this in Chapter 35, Power, Abuse and Protecting the Vulnerable.

A voice from the Church: John Bunyan and John Newton

John Bunyan was a poor tinker, a mender of pots and pans, in seventeenth-century England. He became a preacher, spent twelve years in prison for preaching, and wrote The Pilgrim’s Progress. He also wrote the story of his own soul in a book called Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, which is on Ochorus. For years he was tormented by his sins and by the fear that God had rejected him. Then one day, walking in a field, a sentence came into his mind: “Thy righteousness is in heaven.” He wrote:

“I also saw, moreover, that it was not my good frame of heart that made my righteousness better, nor yet my bad frame that made my righteousness worse; for my righteousness was Jesus Christ Himself, the same yesterday, and to-day, and for ever.”

— John Bunyan, Grace Abounding, 229

In plain words: I saw that my good feelings did not make me more right with God, and my bad feelings did not make me less right with God. My righteousness was Jesus Christ Himself, who never changes. Bunyan wrote, “Now did my chains fall off my legs indeed.” This is the ground of every restoration. We do not stand before God on our own record, good or bad, but on Christ’s.

John Newton was born in London in 1725. As a young man he was a sailor, and later the captain of ships carrying enslaved Africans across the Atlantic. Even after he began to follow Christ, he continued in the slave trade for some years. His repentance grew slowly, and it is part of his story that it took so long. In time he became a much-loved pastor at Olney and then in London, and he wrote the hymn “Amazing Grace”. Late in his life, in 1788, he publicly confessed his part in the slave trade and joined the campaign to end it, encouraging the young William Wilberforce, whom we met in Chapter 30, Justice, Mercy and the Poor.

Newton never forgot what he had been. He wrote the words for his own gravestone, which are recorded in the Ochorus book Men Who Tended the Flock:

“John Newton, Clerk, once an infidel and libertine, a servant of slaves in Africa, was, by the rich mercy of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, preserved, restored, pardoned, and appointed to preach the faith he had long laboured to destroy.”

— John Newton, his epitaph

In plain words: John Newton, minister, was once an unbeliever and a man who lived in sin, and served the slave trade in Africa. But by the great mercy of Jesus Christ, he was kept alive, brought back, forgiven, and given the work of preaching the faith he had once tried to destroy.

Notice the four words: preserved, restored, pardoned, appointed. That is the story of every failed servant whom God restores. Newton’s story also teaches us that repentance can take time to reach every part of our lives, and that true repentance will one day work to undo the harm we have done.

Fallen, but rising

“For the righteous may fall seven times and still get up again” (Proverbs 24:16). The difference between the righteous and the wicked is not that the righteous never fall. It is that they get up again, by God’s grace.

Paul, who once persecuted the Church, wrote, “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and I am the worst of them. But I was shown mercy for this very reason: so that in me, the worst of all, Christ Jesus could show how completely patient he is” (1 Timothy 1:15-16). If you have failed, bring your failure into the light. Do not hide the break. Let it be set, even if it hurts. Accept the time it takes to heal. And listen for the voice of the One who asked Peter, “Do you love me?”, and then said, “Follow me.”

Questions for reflection

  • Read Luke 22:31-34 and John 21:15-19. What do you learn about how Jesus treats those who fail?
  • Read Acts 15:36-40 and 2 Timothy 4:11. Who is the John Mark in your ministry? How could you be a Barnabas to them?
  • Read Psalm 32:3-5. Have you ever experienced what David felt while he kept quiet about his sin?
  • Why is it important to tell the difference between mistakes, weakness and serious sin?
  • What is the difference between restoration to fellowship and restoration to leadership? Why does it matter?
  • Newton’s epitaph says “preserved, restored, pardoned, and appointed”. Which of these words means most to you?
  • Is there a failure in your life that you are still hiding?

A step for this week

Read Psalm 51 slowly and prayerfully this week. If there is a sin you have been hiding, confess it to God, and then to one mature, trusted believer, and ask them to help you take the next right step. If you have hurt someone, ask God how to make it right. Then think of someone in your church who has failed and feels ashamed. Go to them this week, as Jesus went to Peter, and tell them they are not forgotten.

study_questions.question: Can a leader who fails be restored?
study_questions.answer: Yes. Peter denied Jesus three times, yet the risen Lord sent word to “his disciples, and Peter too” (Mark 16:7), restored him by asking three times, “Do you love me?”, and said, “Follow me” (John 21:17-19).

study_questions.question: What does true repentance look like?
study_questions.answer: It owns the sin without excuse, grieves over it before God, confesses it to those harmed, makes things right where possible, and accepts the consequences. David’s confession after his sin with Bathsheba is a model.

study_questions.question: Is every failure a sin?
study_questions.answer: No. Some failures come from weakness, inexperience or circumstances. John Mark quit on a mission journey but Paul later wrote that he was “helpful to me in my work”. “I have fallen, but I will rise. Though I sit in darkness, the LORD is my light” (Micah 7:8).

fields.title: Persecution and the Cost
fields.body_html:
“Have no fear of anything you are going to suffer ... Stay faithful even to death, and I will give you the crown of life.”

— Revelation 2:10 (OWB)

A farmer takes a handful of seed and throws it into the ground. To someone who does not understand farming, it looks like waste. The seed disappears into the dark soil. It is buried and seems lost. But in time, green shoots rise, and the field is covered with grain.

For two thousand years, the enemies of the Church have tried to bury it. They have imprisoned its leaders, burned its books, closed its buildings and killed its people. And again and again, the Church has grown where it was most fiercely attacked. Today, in many countries, believers face prison, violence and loss for following Christ. Leaders are often the first targets. This chapter is about leading through persecution, and about the cost of following Jesus.

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution”

Jesus did not hide the cost of following Him. In the Sermon on the Mount, He said, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of righteousness: the kingdom of heaven is theirs. You are blessed when people abuse you and persecute you and spread all sorts of evil lies about you for my sake. Rejoice and celebrate, because a great reward is waiting for you in heaven. That is how they persecuted the prophets who came before you” (Matthew 5:10-12).

He told His disciples, “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before it hated you ... ‘A servant is not greater than his master.’ If they have persecuted me, they will persecute you too” (John 15:18, 20). Paul wrote plainly to Timothy, “everyone who wants to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted” (2 Timothy 3:12). And Peter wrote to churches facing trouble, “Dear friends, the fire that is burning among you has come to test you; do not be taken aback by it, as though something alien to you were happening” (1 Peter 4:12).

Persecution is not strange. It is normal for the people of God. Many believers in safe places are surprised by this. Many believers in dangerous places already know it well.

The apostles who rejoiced

After Pentecost, the leaders in Jerusalem arrested the apostles and ordered them to stop preaching. In Chapter 6, Authority Under Authority, we saw Peter’s answer: “It is God we must obey rather than people” (Acts 5:29). Then the council “summoned the apostles, had them beaten, and commanded them to stop speaking in the name of Jesus. Then they released them. As they went out from the council, the apostles were glad: they had been found worthy to bear shame for the sake of the Name. Every day, both in the temple and in people’s homes, they went on teaching without a break” (Acts 5:40-42).

Notice three things. They were glad, not because pain is good, but because they shared in the sufferings of Christ. They counted it an honour. And they did not stop. They went on teaching every day.

Earlier, when they were first threatened, the church did not pray for safety. They prayed, “Now, Lord, take notice of their threats. Let your slaves speak your word with complete boldness” (Acts 4:29). When Paul and Silas were beaten and locked in the inner prison at Philippi, “At midnight, as Paul and Silas prayed, they sang praises to God, and the prisoners listened” (Acts 16:25).

What persecution looks like

Persecution takes many forms. In some places, it is violent: believers are beaten, imprisoned, driven from their homes or killed. Churches are burned. Pastors disappear. In other places, it is quieter but still painful.

  • Rejection by family. A young person who turns to Christ may be thrown out of the family home, disowned or forced into marriage.
  • Loss of work and income. Believers may be refused jobs, lose their businesses or be denied help that others receive.
  • Laws and officials. Governments may forbid meetings, require registration and control, or punish those who share their faith.
  • Violence from neighbours. In some places, the danger comes not from the government but from mobs, armed groups or the local community.
  • Mockery and lies. Even in free countries, believers may be laughed at, misrepresented or pushed out of public life.

We must be careful not to call every difficulty persecution. Peter wrote, “If you are insulted because you bear the name of Christ, you are blessed” (1 Peter 4:14). But he also warned that we should not suffer for doing wrong (1 Peter 4:15). If people dislike us because we are rude, proud or foolish, that is not persecution. Believers in comfortable places should also remember that brothers and sisters elsewhere are paying a far higher price. “Keep in mind those in prison, as if you were in chains alongside them, and those who are being ill-treated, since you also live in a body” (Hebrews 13:3).

Leading a church under pressure

How should a leader lead when the church is under threat? Here is some wisdom from Scripture and from churches that have lived through persecution.

  • Prepare the flock before it comes. Teach your people that suffering is part of following Christ. Ground them in the Word. Help them memorise Scripture, since Bibles may be taken away.
  • Raise up many leaders. If the church depends on one leader, it can be destroyed by one arrest. Train others, so the church can continue without you. We saw this in Chapter 23, Making Leaders.
  • Meet in small groups. The early church met “in people’s homes” (Acts 5:42). Small groups can keep going when large meetings cannot.
  • Be wise, not reckless. Jesus said, “I am the one sending you out, like sheep with wolves all around. So be shrewd like snakes, yet harmless like doves” (Matthew 10:16). Courage does not mean seeking danger.
  • Know when to move. Jesus also said, “If they hunt you down in one town, escape to the next” (Matthew 10:23). Paul escaped from Damascus in a basket (Acts 9:25). In Chapter 11, Courage, we saw that exile is not betrayal. Each leader must seek God about whether to stay or go.
  • Care for the families of prisoners. When a leader is arrested, his or her family often suffers most. The church must care for them.
  • Love your enemies. Jesus said, “love your enemies, and pray for the people who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). Stephen, as he was stoned, prayed, “Lord, do not charge them with this sin” (Acts 7:60).
  • Answer with gentleness. “Be ready at all times to make your defense to anyone who asks you for the reason behind the hope you hold. Yet answer with gentleness and with reverence for God” (1 Peter 3:15-16).
  • Never deny Christ. Leaders may be pressured to sign statements, betray other believers or give up their faith. Settle in your heart now that you will not.

The blood of the martyrs

When Stephen was killed, “a fierce persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem, and everyone except the apostles was driven out into the country districts of Judea and Samaria” (Acts 8:1). It looked like a disaster. But Luke tells us what happened next: “Those who had been scattered went from place to place, announcing the good news of the message” (Acts 8:4). The persecution spread the gospel further.

Paul saw the same in prison: “what has happened to me has moved the gospel forward rather than holding it back ... my chains have given most of the brothers and sisters confidence in the Lord, so that they dare to speak the word far more boldly and without fear” (Philippians 1:12, 14).

Around the year 200, a Christian writer in North Africa named Tertullian wrote to the Roman rulers who were killing believers. His words are often remembered in a short form: “The blood of Christians is seed.” The more they were cut down, the more they grew. This has been true again and again. In the twentieth century, the church in China was cut off from the world, its leaders imprisoned and its missionaries sent away. When the doors opened again, the Church had grown, by most estimates, many times over.

The book of Revelation describes believers who overcame the devil: “They have overcome him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony; they did not hold their lives dear, even in the face of death” (Revelation 12:11).

A voice from the Church: Ignatius and Perpetua

In Chapter 8, Integrity: The Same in Secret, we heard Polycarp tell the Roman governor that he had served Christ for eighty-six years. Some forty years before Polycarp died, his friend Ignatius, the bishop of Antioch whom we met in Chapter 6, Authority Under Authority, was taken under guard to Rome to be killed by wild animals. On the way he wrote letters to the churches. To the Christians in Rome, who might have tried to save him, he wrote:

“Let me be given to the wild beasts, for through them I can attain unto God. I am God's wheat, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts that I may be found pure bread [of Christ].”

— Ignatius of Antioch, Letter to the Romans

In plain words: let me be thrown to the wild animals, because through them I will come to God. I am like wheat that belongs to God, and the teeth of the animals will grind me like a mill, so that I may become pure bread for Christ. Ignatius did not see his death as the end of his service, but as its completion. He wrote that only then would he be truly a disciple of Jesus Christ.

In the year 203, in Carthage in North Africa, a young woman named Perpetua was arrested with several other new believers. She was about twenty-two and had a baby son. Her slave, Felicity, was also arrested, and gave birth in prison shortly before they died. Perpetua kept a diary in prison, which has come down to us. In it she tells how her father, who was not a believer, begged her again and again to give up her faith. She pointed to a water jar and asked him whether it could be called by any other name than what it was. He said no. She told him that in the same way, she could not call herself anything other than what she was: a Christian. Perpetua and Felicity died together in the arena. Their names have been honoured by the Church ever since.

A voice from the global Church: Watchman Nee and Yona Kanamuzeyi

Watchman Nee was a Chinese preacher and writer whose books have been read all over the world. After the Communist government came to power, he was arrested in April 1952, at the age of forty-eight. The biography Watchman Nee: A Life, on Ochorus, tells how he was sentenced to fifteen years in prison, and how the fifteen years became twenty. He was never freed. He died in 1972. The biography tells that a note was reportedly found beneath his pillow, a simple confession that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, that He died for sinners and rose again, and that Nee died believing in Him.

Yona Kanamuzeyi was a deacon in Rwanda and a man of the East African Revival. On 24 January 1964, during the violence that followed Rwanda’s independence, soldiers took him away and drove him to a river. As the book Tukutendereza on Ochorus records, witnesses remembered that he sang a hymn as he was led to the river, “There Is a Happy Land”. Before he was shot, he asked permission to write in his journal. He wrote: “We are going to heaven,” and asked that the journal be given to his wife. The book draws a lesson every leader should hear: “You will meet your crisis with the habits you already have.” Kanamuzeyi’s courage at the river grew out of many years of ordinary, daily faithfulness.

Faithful to death

Jesus said to the church in Smyrna, Polycarp’s city, “Have no fear of anything you are going to suffer ... Stay faithful even to death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Revelation 2:10). Not every leader will face prison or death. But every leader is called to be ready.

Paul asked, “Who can tear us away from the love of Christ? Trouble, or anguish, or persecution? Hunger, or lack of clothing, or danger, or the sword?” And he answered, “in all of this we are winning, and winning by far, through the one who loved us” (Romans 8:35, 37). The seed that falls into the ground is not lost. It is planted.

Questions for reflection

  • Read Matthew 5:10-12 and Acts 5:40-42. Why could the apostles rejoice after being beaten?
  • What forms of persecution do believers face in your country or community?
  • If you were arrested tomorrow, would your church be able to continue? What would need to change?
  • How do you decide whether to stay in danger or to move to safety?
  • How can your church “keep in mind those in prison” (Hebrews 13:3)?
  • Kanamuzeyi met his crisis with the habits he already had. What habits are you building now?
  • Is there anything you would deny Christ to keep? What would it take to settle that today?

A step for this week

This week, learn about believers who are being persecuted in another part of the world, and pray for them by name with your church. If your church faces pressure, sit down with your fellow leaders and ask: “If our main leader were taken away tomorrow, who would lead? Where would we meet? What would we need?” Write down a simple plan. Then memorise Romans 8:35-39 and pray it as your own.

study_questions.question: How should Christians respond to persecution?
study_questions.answer: With faithfulness and even joy. Jesus said, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of righteousness” (Matthew 5:10). The apostles, after being beaten, left rejoicing and kept preaching (Acts 5:40-42).

study_questions.question: Should Christians expect persecution?
study_questions.answer: Yes. “Everyone who wants to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted” (2 Timothy 3:12). Peter wrote, “do not be taken aback by it” (1 Peter 4:12). Jesus said that if the world hated Him, it would hate His followers too (John 15:18).

study_questions.question: How can a leader lead a church under pressure?
study_questions.answer: By preparing the people with God’s Word, obeying God first, “It is God we must obey rather than people” (Acts 5:29), and staying faithful to the end: “Stay faithful even to death” (Revelation 2:10). The chapter tells of Ignatius, Perpetua, Watchman Nee and Yona Kanamuzeyi.

fields.title: The Hidden Years
fields.body_html:
“He shaped me into a keen, polished arrow and tucked me away in his quiver.”

— Isaiah 49:2 (OWB)

A great tree in the forest may stand a hundred feet tall. But before it grew upward, it grew downward. For years, while almost nothing could be seen above the ground, its roots were going deep into the earth, searching for water and holding on to rock. When the storms came later, those hidden roots kept it standing.

God often works the same way with leaders. Before He uses them in public, He prepares them in private. There are years of waiting, years of small and ordinary work, years when nobody seems to notice them. These hidden years can feel wasted. They are not. This chapter, the last in Part Eight, Leading Through Hardship, is about the hidden years: waiting, obscurity and small beginnings, and how God prepares His servants out of sight.

Moses: forty years with the sheep

Moses grew up in the palace of Pharaoh. “Moses was schooled in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he had power in what he said and in what he did” (Acts 7:22).
