At forty, he decided to help his people. He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew slave, “and when he saw no one there, he struck the Egyptian dead and buried him in the sand” (Exodus 2:12). He tried to lead in his own strength and his own time, and it ended in murder and failure. He ran for his life to the land of Midian.

Then came the hidden years. “When forty more years had gone by, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire within a bush” (Acts 7:30). For forty years the prince of Egypt looked after another man’s sheep in the desert. “Moses was looking after the flock of his father-in-law Jethro” (Exodus 3:1).

What happened in those years? Moses learned the desert, the same desert through which he would one day lead Israel for forty years. He learned to care for sheep, which is what God would call him to do with His people. And he lost his confidence in himself. At forty he had been ready to lead without God. At eighty, when God called him, he said, “Who am I to go to Pharaoh?” (Exodus 3:11). God could now use him, because Moses no longer trusted in Moses. As we saw in Chapter 7, Humility, he became “exceedingly humble, more so than any other human being on earth” (Numbers 12:3).

Joseph: refined in prison

Joseph had dreams from God when he was seventeen. Then his brothers sold him as a slave. In Egypt he was falsely accused and thrown into prison, as we saw in Chapter 34, Sexual Purity. He was forgotten there. The psalmist describes those years: “Joseph, who was sold to be a slave. Shackles bruised his feet, and his neck was locked in iron, until the day his own words came true; the word of the LORD refined him” (Psalm 105:17-19).

“The word of the LORD refined him.” Like gold in a fire, Joseph was being purified. He was thirty when he stood before Pharaoh (Genesis 41:46). About thirteen years had passed since his dreams. But even in prison, “the LORD was with Joseph” (Genesis 39:21). He served faithfully where he was. He cared for the other prisoners. He interpreted their dreams. And when the moment came, he was ready to lead a nation through famine.

Years later, Joseph could look back and say to his brothers, “Evil was what you planned against me; good was what God planned by it, so as to bring about what you see today: the lives of a great many people saved” (Genesis 50:20).

Jesus: thirty years in Nazareth

The most remarkable hidden years of all belong to Jesus. The eternal Son of God lived for about thirty years in a small town that people looked down on. We know almost nothing about those years. Luke tells us only this: “So he went back down with them to Nazareth, and he lived under their authority ... And Jesus advanced in wisdom and in stature, and in favor with God and with people” (Luke 2:51-52). When He began to preach, the people of Nazareth said, “Is he not the carpenter, the son of Mary?” (Mark 6:3).

For thirty years, the Saviour of the world made doors, tables and ploughs. He obeyed His parents. He worked with His hands. “Jesus was about thirty years old when he began his work” (Luke 3:23). His public ministry lasted only about three years. His hidden years lasted ten times as long.

And at the end of those hidden years, before He had preached a single sermon or done a single miracle, the Father spoke from heaven at His baptism: “You are my dearly loved Son. I take delight in you” (Mark 1:11). The Father was pleased with the hidden years. If Jesus was content to spend thirty years in obscurity, we should not be impatient with ours.

Paul and David: prepared out of sight

After Paul met Christ on the road to Damascus, he did not rush into fame. “I did not at once turn to any human being for advice ... Instead I went away to Arabia, and afterward I came back to Damascus. Three years later I did go up to Jerusalem” (Galatians 1:16-18). After a short visit, he went home to Tarsus, and for years we hear little of him. At last, Luke tells us, “Barnabas then set out for Tarsus to search for Saul, and when he had found him he brought him to Antioch” (Acts 11:25-26). Paul’s great missionary journeys began more than ten years after his conversion.

David was anointed as king while still a boy. When the prophet Samuel came, his father did not even think to call him: “There is still the youngest. He is out looking after the sheep” (1 Samuel 16:11). David went back to the sheep. Then for years he served Saul and ran from him. But the hidden years shaped him. “He singled out David, his servant, and called him away from the sheepfolds ... He cared for them as a shepherd with an honest heart and led them with skillful hands” (Psalm 78:70, 72). The skills of the shepherd became the skills of the king.

What God does in the hidden years

Why does God so often make His leaders wait? The Bible suggests many reasons.

  • He builds character before giving a platform. Gifts can grow quickly. Character grows slowly. A leader whose gift is greater than his or her character will one day fall.
  • He removes self-confidence. Moses had to lose his trust in himself before he could trust God fully.
  • He tests faithfulness. “Someone who is faithful in the smallest matter is faithful in large matters too” (Luke 16:10). God watches what we do with small things.
  • He teaches skills. David learned to fight lions and bears with the sheep. Moses learned the desert. Jesus learned to work.
  • He deepens our roots. A leader who has learned to walk with God when nobody is watching will stand when the storms come.
  • He prepares the moment. “For the vision still waits for its appointed time ... Though it lingers, wait for it; it will certainly come and will not be late” (Habakkuk 2:3).

Isaiah describes the Servant of the Lord saying, “He shaped me into a keen, polished arrow and tucked me away in his quiver” (Isaiah 49:2). An arrow in the quiver is hidden. But it is not forgotten. It is being kept ready for the moment the archer chooses.

Do not despise small beginnings

When the exiles returned to Jerusalem and began to rebuild the temple, some of the older people wept. The new building was so small compared to the great temple of Solomon. But God spoke through the prophet Zechariah: “Who has despised the day of small beginnings?” (Zechariah 4:10).

Many leaders today serve in small places: a village church of twenty people, a Bible study in a home, a children’s class, a ministry nobody has heard of. They may feel that their work is unimportant. But God does not measure as we do. Jesus compared the kingdom of God to a mustard seed: “Of all the seeds it is the smallest”, but it grows into a great plant (Matthew 13:31-32).

Here are some ways to be faithful in the hidden years:

  • Do the work in front of you well. “Whatever you are doing, put your whole self into the work, as for the Lord and not for people” (Colossians 3:23).
  • Walk with God in secret. “Your Father, who sees what is hidden, will repay you” (Matthew 6:4).
  • Learn. Read, study, ask questions, and learn from older leaders.
  • Serve under others. Like Joshua under Moses and Elisha under Elijah, learn by serving someone else’s vision.
  • Do not push yourself forward. Let God open the doors. Pushing open doors He has not opened leads to the kind of failure Moses had at forty.
  • Wait with hope. “Keep waiting for the LORD. Stand firm and be brave in heart. Yes, wait for the LORD” (Psalm 27:14).

A voice from the Church: Brother Lawrence and Josephine Bakhita

In Chapter 15, Rest, Retreat and Rhythm, we met Brother Lawrence, the French monk of the 1600s who spent many years working in the kitchen of his monastery in Paris. He never held high office. He cooked meals and, later, mended sandals. Yet people came from far away to learn from him how to live in the presence of God. The Practice of the Presence of God, on Ochorus, records that he was pleased when he could pick up a straw from the ground “for the love of God, seeking Him only, and nothing else, not even His gifts.” Nothing was too small to be done for God. The hidden kitchen became a place of worship.

Josephine Bakhita was born in Darfur, in what is now Sudan, around 1869. When she was a small child, she was kidnapped by slave traders. The shock was so great that she forgot her own name. Her captors called her Bakhita, which means “fortunate”. She was sold several times and was cruelly treated, and her body carried the scars of it for the rest of her life. In 1883 she was bought by an Italian official and later taken to Italy, where she worked as a nanny.

In Venice, she was placed for a time with a community of Christian sisters, the Canossian Sisters. There she learned about Jesus, and she came to love Him. When her mistress wanted to take her back to Africa, Bakhita refused to leave, and in 1889 an Italian court ruled that she was free, because slavery was not allowed in Italy. A few weeks later, in January 1890, she was baptised and took the name Josephine. She chose to stay with the sisters, and later became one of them.

For more than forty years she lived in a convent in the small Italian town of Schio. She cooked, sewed and embroidered, and for years she was the doorkeeper. She was the one who opened the door to visitors and to the poor. The children of the town loved her. She was gentle, cheerful and full of prayer. She is remembered for saying that if she were to meet the men who had kidnapped and tortured her, she would kneel and kiss their hands, because without them she would not have come to know Jesus. She died in 1947. In 2000 she was honoured by the Catholic Church as a saint, and she has become a symbol of hope for many people who have been trafficked or enslaved.

Bakhita never preached to great crowds or led a large organisation. Her life was spent in hidden service at a convent door. Yet her quiet faithfulness, her forgiveness and her joy have touched people all over the world.

No season is wasted

Moses had his forty years with the sheep. Joseph had his prison. Jesus had Nazareth. Paul had Arabia and Tarsus. David had the sheepfolds. None of these seasons was wasted.

If you are in a hidden season now, take heart. You are not forgotten. You are an arrow in God’s quiver. Do the work in front of you, walk with God where nobody sees, and wait for His time. And if God never brings you into public view, that is not failure either. Many of His greatest servants lived and died in hidden places, and the Father who sees in secret will reward them openly.

Questions for reflection

  • Read Exodus 2:11-15 and 3:1-11. How was Moses different at eighty from what he had been at forty?
  • Read Psalm 105:17-19. What does it mean that “the word of the LORD refined” Joseph?
  • Jesus spent about thirty years in Nazareth before His public ministry. What does this teach you about God’s timing?
  • Are you in a hidden season now? What might God be doing in you through it?
  • Which of the “small beginnings” in your ministry are you tempted to despise?
  • What do you learn from Brother Lawrence’s kitchen and Bakhita’s convent door?
  • Are you faithful where nobody is watching?

A step for this week

This week, choose one small, hidden task in your church or community that nobody will thank you for: cleaning, visiting, cooking, mending or praying. Do it carefully, for the Lord. Do not tell anyone. Then spend time with God thanking Him for the hidden seasons of your life so far, and ask Him what He wants to teach you in this one.

study_questions.question: Why does God give leaders hidden years?
study_questions.answer: To prepare them. Moses spent forty years with sheep before leading Israel (Acts 7:30), Joseph was refined in prison, and Jesus lived thirty years in Nazareth. The Servant of the Lord says, “He shaped me into a keen, polished arrow and tucked me away in his quiver” (Isaiah 49:2).

study_questions.question: What does God do in the hidden years?
study_questions.answer: He humbles us, deepens our character, teaches us to depend on Him and trains us in faithfulness in small things. Moses, once confident, became the man who asked, “Who am I to go to Pharaoh?” (Exodus 3:11).

study_questions.question: How can I serve faithfully when no one notices?
study_questions.answer: By doing small tasks for God and not for praise. Brother Lawrence found God among the pots and pans, and Josephine Bakhita served for years as a doorkeeper. No season with God is wasted.

fields.title: The Leader’s Home
fields.body_html:
“My household and I will serve the LORD.”

— Joshua 24:15 (OWB)

In many villages there is a saying about the shoemaker’s children: they are the ones who go barefoot. The shoemaker makes shoes for the whole village, but he is so busy that he never has time to make shoes for his own family.

Many leaders’ families know this feeling. The pastor visits every sick person in the church but never sits at his own child’s bedside. The leader counsels every troubled marriage but has no time for her own husband. The missionary reaches a whole people group but loses his own children. This chapter begins Part Nine, The Leader’s Life. We begin at home, because a leader’s first flock is their own household.

The home in Scripture

From the beginning, God gave the family a central place in passing on faith. Moses told Israel, “Keep these words that I am commanding you today close to your heart. Teach them carefully to your children, and speak of them as you sit in your house and as you go on your way, as you lie down and as you rise” (Deuteronomy 6:6-7). Faith was to be taught not only in the tent of meeting, but at the table, on the road and at bedtime.

Joshua, at the end of his life, stood before all Israel and made a choice for his whole family: “Whom will you serve? ... My household and I will serve the LORD” (Joshua 24:15). Before he led the nation, he led his home.

Paul made this a qualification for church leaders: “He must manage his own household well and see that his children obey him and are respectful in every way. (If someone does not know how to manage his own household, how can he take care of God’s church?)” (1 Timothy 3:4-5). The home is a training ground and a testing ground. The way we lead at home shows the way we will lead in the church. As we saw in Chapter 8, Integrity: The Same in Secret, the leader must be the same person at home as in the pulpit. David prayed, “Inside my own house I will live with an undivided heart” (Psalm 101:2).

Eli and Samuel: a warning

In Chapter 35, Power, Abuse and Protecting the Vulnerable, we saw the sin of Eli’s sons, and how Eli knew what they were doing but “did not restrain them” (1 Samuel 3:13). Eli was a priest and a judge. He served at the house of God for many years. He even trained the boy Samuel. But he failed his own sons.

The sad thing is that Samuel later made the same mistake. “In his old age Samuel appointed his sons as judges over Israel ... But his sons did not follow his ways. They turned aside after dishonest gain; they took bribes and bent justice” (1 Samuel 8:1, 3). Samuel was one of the greatest leaders in Israel’s history. But his own sons were so corrupt that the people used them as a reason to ask for a king.

Even good leaders can neglect their homes. Busy, faithful, successful ministry is no protection. The leader must choose, again and again, to give the family time, attention and love.

Marriage: loving as Christ loved

For leaders who are married, the marriage is the centre of the home. Paul wrote to all believers, “you will submit to one another in the reverent fear of Christ” (Ephesians 5:21). Then he gave husbands a command that no husband has ever fully kept: “Husbands, love your wives the way Christ loved the church and handed himself over for her” (Ephesians 5:25). Christ’s love is the model: patient, sacrificial, faithful and serving. Paul also warned, “Husbands, love your wives and never turn harsh or bitter against them” (Colossians 3:19). Peter told husbands to live with their wives “with understanding” and to honour them as those who “will inherit the grace of life together with you, so that nothing stands in the way of your prayers” (1 Peter 3:7).

Notice that last phrase. The way a leader treats his or her spouse affects their prayer life. A leader cannot be harsh at home and expect to be powerful in prayer.

Here are some marks of a healthy leader’s marriage.

  • Time together. Protected time to talk, rest and enjoy one another, not only to discuss church problems.
  • Partnership. Many great leaders were married to people who were partners in the work. Paul greeted “Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus” (Romans 16:3). They taught Apollos together, in their home (Acts 18:26).
  • Honour in public. Speak well of your spouse to others. Never make them the subject of jokes in a sermon.
  • Faithfulness. We saw the walls of protection in Chapter 34, Sexual Purity.
  • Freedom. The spouse of a pastor is not an unpaid staff member. They have their own gifts and calling, and should not be forced into a role the church expects.
  • Honesty. Share your struggles with each other, as far as is wise.

Children: bringing them up in the Lord

“Fathers, do not drive your children to anger. Instead, bring them up with the Lord’s training and correction” (Ephesians 6:4). “Fathers, do not keep provoking your children, or they will lose heart” (Colossians 3:21). These words apply to mothers too.

Children of leaders face special pressures. Everyone watches them. They are expected to be perfect. They see the church’s problems up close. They may feel that their parent loves the church more than them. Some grow bitter against God because of the way the church treated their parent.

How can leaders help their children?

  • Be present. Children need your time, not only your money or your advice. Eat together. Play together. Go to their events. Put down the phone.
  • Let faith be real at home. Pray together, read the Bible together, and talk about God naturally, “as you sit in your house and as you go on your way”. Let them see you pray, repent and trust God.
  • Do not use them as examples. Do not make your children’s lives sermon illustrations without their permission.
  • Protect them from the church’s expectations. Let them be children. They are not small pastors.
  • Protect them from church conflict. Do not pour out your anger about church members at the dinner table.
  • Say sorry. When you fail your children, apologise to them. This teaches them more about the gospel than many sermons.

When the home is not perfect

No leader’s home is perfect. Some leaders have children who walk away from God, even after being raised with love. Some have unbelieving spouses. Some are widowed or divorced. Some long for children and have none. Some are single parents. Some carry deep wounds from their own childhood.

Grace reaches into these homes too. Timothy, a great young leader, came from a home where his father was apparently not a believer. Paul reminded him of the “sincere faith, which first lived in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice” (2 Timothy 1:5). God worked through a mother and grandmother in a mixed home.

If you have a child who has wandered, remember the father in Jesus’ parable, who watched the road every day. “His father caught sight of him while he was still far away, and his heart went out to him. He ran to meet him” (Luke 15:20). Keep praying. Keep loving. Keep the door open. A child’s choice is not always the parent’s failure.

Churches must also be careful. The qualification in 1 Timothy 3 is about the way a leader leads the home, not about whether every child turns out perfectly. A church should not punish a faithful leader for the free choices of an adult child. But where a leader’s home is in serious trouble, it is often wise for that leader to step back for a time and put their family first.

Practical wisdom for the leader’s home

  • Put your family in your diary. If your family time is not planned, the church will fill it.
  • Take a weekly day off, and spend part of it with your family.
  • Take holidays together, even simple ones.
  • Learn to say no. Not every request is God’s call. As we saw in Chapter 22, No Lone Leaders, share the work so that you are not always away.
  • Ask your family how they are. Ask your spouse and older children, “Do you feel that you get my best, or only what is left?” Listen to the answer.
  • Make your home a place of welcome. Hospitality can be a joy shared by the whole family, not a burden on one person.
  • Churches, care for your leaders’ families. Pay your leaders enough to provide for their families (1 Timothy 5:8). Protect their days off. Do not expect the spouse and children to be perfect.

A voice from the Church: Jonathan and Sarah Edwards, and William and Catherine Booth

Jonathan Edwards, the New England pastor and thinker whom we met in Chapter 31, Leading in Revival and Change, married Sarah Pierpont in 1727. They had eleven children. Edwards was a scholar who spent many hours a day in his study. But each evening he read to his family and prayed with them. Sarah ran a busy household of thirteen, with a constant stream of guests, and she was a woman of deep prayer. By every account, their marriage was unusually happy. We must also say honestly, as the Ochorus book Key Teachings of Jonathan Edwards does, that the household owned enslaved people, whose labour made the study hours possible. Even a godly home can be blind to a great wrong, as we saw in Chapter 30, Justice, Mercy and the Poor.

In 1758 Edwards became president of the college at Princeton. He was there only a few weeks when he died after a smallpox inoculation went wrong. Sarah was not with him. The same book tells how, near the end, he left a message for her about “the uncommon union” between them and his hope that it would continue for ever. When Sarah heard the news, she wrote that God had made her adore His goodness in giving them her husband for so long, and that she and her children were left to God. She died six months later. Their marriage was a partnership in faith that their children never forgot.

William and Catherine Booth founded the Salvation Army in nineteenth-century London. They married in 1855 and had eight children, several of whom went on to lead the Army on three continents. As Key Teachings of Catherine Booth, on Ochorus, describes, from the beginning “she was his counsellor as much as his companion.” They argued, prayed and planned together. She was a great preacher in her own right, and they carried the work as true partners. Their home was not quiet or easy. But they raised their children in the work, not apart from it, and their children shared their parents’ passion for the poor.

Neither home was perfect. But both show that great ministry and a loving home are not enemies. They can strengthen each other.

Unless the LORD builds the house

“If the LORD does not build the house, the work of its builders comes to nothing” (Psalm 127:1). Leaders build many things: churches, ministries, programmes and buildings. But no ministry success can make up for a neglected home.

Your family is not a distraction from your ministry. It is part of your ministry, and the first part. Give them your best, not only what is left. And trust the Lord to build your house.

Questions for reflection

  • Read Deuteronomy 6:4-9. How is faith taught in your home, at the table, on the road and at bedtime?
  • Read 1 Samuel 3:13 and 8:1-5. Why do you think Eli and Samuel failed with their sons?
  • If you are married, how would your spouse describe the way you love them? Ask them.
  • Do your children feel that the church comes before them?
  • What pressures do the children of leaders face in your church or culture? How could your church help?
  • If your home is not what you hoped it would be, how does God’s grace meet you there?
  • What do you learn from the Edwardses and the Booths?

A step for this week

This week, sit down with your diary and mark out time for your family: a day off, a meal together, an outing or an evening at home. Keep it as carefully as a meeting with an important guest. If you are married, ask your spouse, “Do you feel that you get my best, or only what is left?” and listen without defending yourself. If you have children, ask them what they most enjoy doing with you, and do it this week.

study_questions.question: Why does a leader’s home matter?
study_questions.answer: Because a leader “must manage his own household well” (1 Timothy 3:4), and because the home is the first place where faith is lived and taught: “Teach them carefully to your children” (Deuteronomy 6:7). “My household and I will serve the LORD” (Joshua 24:15).

study_questions.question: What warning does Eli’s family give to leaders?
study_questions.answer: Eli served God publicly but failed to deal with his sons’ sin; “he did not restrain them” (1 Samuel 3:13). Even Samuel’s sons “did not follow his ways” (1 Samuel 8:3). Leaders must not give the church their best and the family what is left.

study_questions.question: What if a leader’s home is not perfect?
study_questions.answer: No home is. The chapter speaks with grace to leaders whose children have strayed or whose marriages are struggling, urges them to seek help, and points to Jonathan and Sarah Edwards and William and Catherine Booth, honestly, with their flaws.

fields.title: Single and Serving
fields.body_html:
“I want you to live as is fitting and to stay close beside the Lord with nothing to draw you away.”

— 1 Corinthians 7:35 (OWB)

In many cultures, a person who is not married is treated as if they are not yet a full adult. At family gatherings, they are asked again and again, “When will you marry?” In church, they may be given the children’s work but not a place among the leaders. People pity them, or worry about them, or try to find them a husband or wife. Some single people begin to feel that their life has not really started.

But the Bible tells a different story. The Lord Jesus Himself never married. The apostle Paul was single for at least most of his ministry. Many of the Church’s greatest leaders, missionaries and servants have served God single. In the last chapter, Chapter 42, The Leader’s Home, we looked at leaders with families. This chapter looks at single leaders. Singleness is not a waiting room. It is a full and honoured calling.

Jesus, the single man

We sometimes forget that the most complete human being who ever lived was single. Jesus did not marry. He had no children of His own. Yet His life was not incomplete or less than fully human. He had deep friendships: with Peter, James and John, with Mary, Martha and Lazarus, with the women who travelled with Him and supported Him. He loved children. He knew what it was to be lonely, but He was never without His Father.

If singleness made a person less than whole, then Jesus would have been less than whole. He was not. That alone should change the way the Church thinks about single people.

Paul’s teaching: a gift and a freedom

Paul wrote the longest teaching in the Bible on singleness and marriage, in 1 Corinthians 7. He said, “I would like everyone to be as I am. Yet God gives each person a gift of their own, to one this way and to another that” (1 Corinthians 7:7). Marriage is a gift. Singleness is also a gift. Neither is better in God’s sight. Both are callings.

Paul then explained one advantage of singleness for ministry: “I want you to be free from cares that divide you. The unmarried man gives his care to the things of the Lord, how he may please him. But the married man gives his care to the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and he is pulled two ways. And the unmarried woman ... gives her care to the things of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:32-34). He added at once, “I tell you this to help you, not to throw a noose over you” (1 Corinthians 7:35). He was not forcing anyone to stay single, or saying that married people are less devoted. He was saying that single people have a special freedom to give themselves to the Lord’s work.

Jesus also spoke of some who do not marry “for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let anyone who is able to accept this accept it” (Matthew 19:12).

Single servants in Scripture

The Bible is full of single people whom God used.

  • Jeremiah was told by God, “Do not marry, and do not have sons or daughters in this place” (Jeremiah 16:2). His singleness was itself a message to the nation about the coming judgement.
  • Philip’s daughters. Luke tells us that Philip the evangelist “had four daughters who were not married, and they prophesied” (Acts 21:9). They were known for their ministry.
  • Anna was widowed after seven years of marriage and lived for decades as a widow, serving God in the temple with fasting and prayer (Luke 2:36-38). She was one of the first to recognise the baby Jesus.
  • Phoebe, whom Paul commended to the church in Rome as “a deacon of the church in Cenchreae” and “a patron to many” (Romans 16:1-2), is not said to have had a husband. As we saw in Chapter 26, Men and Women in the Work of God, English Bibles differ on whether to call her a “deacon” or a “servant”.
  • Paul himself.

And God gives a special promise to those who have no children: “within my house and inside my walls I will set up for them a monument and a name worth more than sons and daughters. I will give each of them a name that lasts forever” (Isaiah 56:5).

Singleness takes many forms

Single leaders are not all the same.

  • Some have chosen not to marry, in order to give themselves to a particular work.
  • Some long to marry but have not found the right person.
  • Some are widowed, and carry grief as well as aloneness.
  • Some are divorced, and may carry pain, shame or the care of children alone.
  • Some are single because of illness, disability, family duties or the shortage of believing partners. In many churches around the world, there are far more believing women than believing men.

Each of these deserves understanding, not assumptions. The church should not treat every single person as if they are simply waiting for marriage. Nor should it tell those who long for marriage that their longing is wrong.

The joys and challenges of single leaders

Single leaders often have great freedom. They can travel, move, take risks and give time in ways that would be much harder with a family. Many of the pioneers of world mission were single, and a great many of them were women. They were free to go to the hardest places.

But single leaders also face real challenges.

  • Loneliness. Coming home to an empty house after a hard day of ministry can be very painful. We looked at this in Chapter 37, Loneliness and Hidden Burdens.
  • Sexual temptation. Single people are called to purity, as married people are, and the struggle can be hard. The walls of protection in Chapter 34, Sexual Purity, apply to single leaders too.
  • Overwork. Because they have no family waiting at home, single leaders are often expected to do more. Some never rest. The church may treat them as if they have no needs.
  • Being overlooked. In some churches, single people are not trusted with leadership, simply because they are not married.
  • Suspicion and gossip. Single leaders may be the subject of rumours, especially about their friendships.
  • Pressure. Constant questions about marriage can wound deeply.

How the Church can honour single leaders

Jesus promised, “anyone who has left a home, brothers or sisters, mother or father, children or land because of me and because of the gospel will receive a hundred times as much now, in this present time: homes, brothers, sisters, mothers, children and land, together with persecutions” (Mark 10:29-30). How does Jesus give these “homes, brothers, sisters, mothers, children”? Through His Church. “God gives the lonely a home to live in” (Psalm 68:6). The church is meant to be the family of the single person.

  • Include them. Invite single people into your home and your family life. Let your children know them as aunts and uncles in Christ.
  • Honour their calling. Do not treat singleness as a problem to be solved. Stop asking “When will you marry?” Ask instead, “How is your work? How can we pray for you?”
  • Give them leadership. Recognise and appoint single people with the gifts and character to lead, as Jesus and Paul did.
  • Protect their rest. Do not overload them because they have “more time”.
  • Provide friendship. Make sure single leaders have close friends and safe places to share their burdens.
  • Care for the widowed and divorced. Stand by them in grief and help single parents practically, with meals, childcare and friendship.

And if you are a single leader, receive your life as a gift. Build deep friendships. Let others into your life. Rest. Give yourself fully to the Lord, “with nothing to draw you away”. You can say with the psalmist, “The LORD is the share I have been given and the cup I drink ... The measuring lines have marked out a lovely place for me” (Psalm 16:5-6).

A voice from the Church: Amy Carmichael and Mary Slessor

Amy Carmichael, whom we met in Chapter 10, Love: The Motive and the Mark, and in Chapter 35, Power, Abuse and Protecting the Vulnerable, never married. As a young missionary in Japan, in her twenties, she went alone to a cave in the hills to pray. She was afraid of the loneliness of a life without marriage. The biography Amy Carmichael: A Life, on Ochorus, tells how she brought that fear to God and received an assurance from the last verse of Psalm 34, which she knew in the old Authorised Version: “none of them that trust in him shall be desolate.” Modern translations, including the one used in this book, render that verse differently, because the Hebrew word can mean both being held guilty and being left desolate. But Amy took it as God’s promise that she would never be left alone. The biography adds honestly that she was often lonely afterwards. But she said that the promise held, and that she never again doubted that God would be enough for her.

Mary Slessor, the Scottish missionary to Calabar in what is now Nigeria, whom we met in Chapter 26, Men and Women in the Work of God, also served God single. But her story shows that singleness is not always chosen easily. In 1890, at about the age of forty-two, she became engaged to a younger missionary, Charles Morrison. She made one condition: she would not leave the people of Okoyong, where she was the only missionary. If they married, he would have to join her there. She wrote to a friend:

“I lay it all in God’s hands, and will take from Him whatever He sees best for His work in Okoyong. My life was laid on His altar for that people long ago, and I would not take one jot or tittle of it back.”

— Mary Slessor, letter, quoted in Mary Slessor: A Life

In plain words: I leave it all to God, and will accept whatever He thinks best for His work among these people. I gave my life to God for them long ago, and I will not take back even the smallest part of it. The mission board refused to let Morrison move. Mary said only, “What the Lord ordains is right.” Morrison’s health later broke down, and they never married. Mary served on in Okoyong and beyond, loved by the people as a mother, and adopting many children who had been abandoned.

A voice from the global Church: Sadhu Sundar Singh

Sundar Singh was born in 1889 into a Sikh family in the Punjab, in northern India. As a teenager, after the death of his mother, he was so troubled and angry that he burned a Bible. A few days later, in 1904, he prayed through the night and came to believe in Jesus Christ. His family turned against him and he was forced to leave home. He chose to live as a sadhu, a wandering holy man in the Indian tradition, wearing a simple robe and owning almost nothing, so that he could share Christ in a way his people would understand. He never married. For twenty-five years he travelled on foot through India, Nepal and into Tibet, often in great danger, preaching Christ. He also visited many countries, where people were moved by his humble and simple faith. In 1929 he set out once more for Tibet and was never seen again. His single life gave him the freedom to be, as he believed, an Indian follower of Jesus who belonged to everyone.

Complete in Christ

Marriage is a beautiful gift, and it is a picture of Christ and His Church. But it is not the final goal of human life. Jesus said that in the resurrection, “men no longer take wives and women are no longer given as brides” (Matthew 22:30). The one marriage that lasts for ever is the marriage of Christ and His people. Every believer, married or single, belongs to that.

So the single leader is not half a person or a person in waiting. In Christ they are complete, and in His Church they have a family. Honour them. Learn from them. And if you are single, serve with joy, knowing that the Lord is your share and your cup.

Questions for reflection

  • Read 1 Corinthians 7:7 and 7:32-35. What does Paul teach about singleness as a gift?
  • How does the fact that Jesus was single change the way you think about single people?
  • How are single people treated in your church and culture? Are they given leadership?
  • If you are single, what are the joys and the challenges of your calling? Who are your close friends?
  • If you are married, how could your family include a single person in its life?
  • What do you learn from Amy Carmichael’s prayer in the cave and Mary Slessor’s letter?
  • Read Mark 10:29-30. How is your church helping Jesus keep this promise to single believers?

A step for this week

If you are married, invite a single person from your church to share a meal with your family this week, and ask them how you can pray for them. If you are a leader, look at your church’s leaders and workers: are single people honoured and included, or overlooked and overloaded? If you are single, write down three ways your singleness has given you freedom to serve God, thank Him for them, and contact one friend this week to share honestly how you are.

study_questions.question: What does the Bible say about singleness?
study_questions.answer: That it is a gift, like marriage. Paul wrote, “God gives each person a gift of their own, to one this way and to another that” (1 Corinthians 7:7). Jesus Himself never married, and singleness gives freedom “to stay close beside the Lord with nothing to draw you away” (1 Corinthians 7:35).

study_questions.question: Can a single person be a church leader?
study_questions.answer: Yes. Jesus and Paul were single, as were Jeremiah, Philip’s four daughters who prophesied (Acts 21:9) and many great missionaries such as Amy Carmichael, Mary Slessor and Sadhu Sundar Singh. Singleness is a full and honoured calling, not a waiting room.

study_questions.question: How can the church care for single leaders?
study_questions.answer: By including them in family life, honouring their calling instead of asking “When will you marry?”, giving them leadership, protecting their rest, providing friendship, and caring for the widowed and divorced. Through the Church, Jesus keeps His promise of “homes, brothers, sisters, mothers, children” (Mark 10:30).

fields.title: Stewarding Yourself
fields.body_html:
“Teach us, then, to reckon our days rightly, so that our hearts may grow wise.”

— Psalm 90:12 (OWB)

A farmer has one ox to plough his field. If he never works the ox, it grows fat and lazy, and the field is never ploughed. If he works it day and night without food, water or rest, it will collapse in the middle of the season, and the field will not be ploughed either. A wise farmer feeds his ox, rests it, and works it steadily, season after season, for many years.

God has given every leader one life, one body, one mind and a limited number of days. These are not ours to waste. In Chapter 9, Keep Watch over Yourself, we saw that the leader’s own soul is the first field to tend. This chapter looks at the rest of the leader’s life: time, body, health and learning. It is about caring well for the one instrument God has given you.

You are a steward, not an owner

“Or do you not know that your body is a temple where the Holy Spirit lives, the Spirit who is in you and whom God has given you? You do not belong to yourselves. You were bought, and a price was paid for you. So bring glory to God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19-20).

In Chapter 33, Money and Greed, we heard John Wesley say that God placed us in the world “not as a proprietor, but a steward”. That is true of our money. It is also true of our time, our bodies, our minds and our gifts. They all belong to God. He has lent them to us, and one day He will ask what we did with them. In Jesus’ parable of the talents, the master did not blame the servant for having little. He blamed him for burying what he had: “You wicked, lazy servant!” (Matthew 25:26).

Paul urged the believers in Rome, “offer your bodies to God as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to him” (Romans 12:1). A living sacrifice is offered every day. It is not thrown away in one burst of zeal. It is given faithfully, over a lifetime.

Two opposite dangers

Leaders can waste the strength God has given them in two opposite ways.

The first is laziness. Some leaders have no one checking their work. They sleep late, waste hours and do little. They prepare their sermons on Saturday night. They visit no one. They call it “waiting on God”, but it is really idleness. Proverbs speaks sharply: “I walked past the field of someone lazy ... and I saw thorns had sprung up everywhere, weeds had covered the ground, and its stone wall lay in ruins ... a bit more sleep, a bit more dozing, a bit more lying with arms folded, and poverty will be on you” (Proverbs 24:30-31, 33-34). A lazy leader’s church will look like that field.

The second is overwork. Other leaders never stop. They work every day of the week, never sleep enough, never eat properly, never exercise and never take a holiday. They believe they are serving God. But they are slowly destroying the body He gave them, and often their families too. We looked at this in Chapter 15, Rest, Retreat and Rhythm, and Chapter 38, Discouragement and Burnout.

Both are failures of stewardship. One buries the talent. The other burns it up too soon. The wise leader asks God for the grace to work hard, and the grace to rest.

Stewarding time

“So take great care how you live, not as people without wisdom but as people who have it. Make good use of every opportunity, because the days are evil” (Ephesians 5:15-16). Moses prayed, “Teach us, then, to reckon our days rightly, so that our hearts may grow wise” (Psalm 90:12). Our days are numbered. Each one is a gift that will not come back.

Here are some ways leaders can use their time well.

  • Begin with God. Jesus, “Long before daylight, he got up and went out. He went off to a lonely place and spent time there in prayer” (Mark 1:35). Give the first and best part of the day to God, as we saw in Chapter 12, Prayer First.
  • Know your priorities. Write down the few things God has most clearly called you to do. Let them shape your week.
  • Plan your week. “The plans of the diligent bring nothing but gain” (Proverbs 21:5). Set aside time for prayer, study, people, family and rest before the week fills up.
  • Guard against time-wasters. Phones, social media, idle talk and endless meetings can steal hours each day. Be honest about where your time goes.
  • Say no. Not every good thing is your task. Share the work, as we saw in Chapter 22, No Lone Leaders.
  • Review your days. At the end of each week, look back. What did you do? What did you neglect? What will you change?

Stewarding the body

Many Christians, including many leaders, have treated the body as unimportant, as if only the soul matters. But God made our bodies. “I give you thanks, for the way I was made is awe-inspiring and marvelous” (Psalm 139:14). Jesus took a human body, and rose from the dead in a body. Our bodies will be raised too.

Paul cared about Timothy’s health. He told him, “take a little wine for your stomach and your frequent illnesses” (1 Timothy 5:23). He wrote, “Physical training has some value, but godliness is valuable in every way” (1 Timothy 4:8). Godliness matters more. But physical training still “has some value”. And John prayed for his friend Gaius “that you are doing well in every way and are in good health, just as your soul is doing well” (3 John 2).

When Elijah collapsed, God’s first answer was sleep and food (1 Kings 19:5-7). Sometimes the most spiritual thing a leader can do is go to bed.

  • Sleep. Most adults need seven to eight hours of sleep. A leader who never sleeps enough will make poor decisions, lose patience and become ill.
  • Eat wisely. Eat simple, healthy food where you can. Avoid too much sugar, fat and alcohol. Many leaders eat poorly because they are always rushing or always being fed at others’ homes.
  • Move. Walk, work, play or exercise regularly. Many leaders sit for most of the day.
  • See a doctor. Have your health checked when you can. Do not ignore warning signs.
  • Care for your mind. Anxiety and depression are real. Seek help when you need it.
  • Avoid what harms you. Tobacco, drunkenness, drugs and other habits that damage the body dishonour the temple of the Holy Spirit.

Stewarding the mind: keep learning

Jesus “advanced in wisdom and in stature” (Luke 2:52). Even the Son of God grew. “This is where wisdom starts: get wisdom. Spend all you have, if you must, to get understanding” (Proverbs 4:7).

Paul, at the end of his life, in a cold prison, asked Timothy to bring three things: “the cloak I left with Carpus at Troas, and my scrolls, especially the parchments” (2 Timothy 4:13). The cloak was for his body. The scrolls and parchments were for his mind. Paul was about to die, and he still wanted to read and study.

He told Timothy, “Put these things into practice and give yourself wholly to them, so that everyone may see your progress. Keep a close watch on yourself and on your teaching” (1 Timothy 4:15-16). A leader who stops learning will soon stop leading well.

  • Read the Bible as a whole, again and again, as we saw in Chapter 13, Living in the Word.
  • Read good books. Read the classics of the Christian faith. Many are free on Ochorus. Read history, biography and books about the world.
  • Learn from others. Ask questions of older leaders. Listen to people who disagree with you.
  • Develop your gifts. Work to become a better preacher, teacher, counsellor or administrator. Seek training where you can.
  • Learn from your mistakes. Each failure can be a teacher.

Many leaders in the world have little money for books or training. If that is you, do not lose heart. Many of the greatest leaders in history had only the Bible and a few books, and learned to read them deeply.

A voice from the Church: Jonathan Edwards and John Wesley

Jonathan Edwards, whom we met in Chapter 42, The Leader’s Home, wrote a list of seventy resolutions when he was still a young man, between the ages of about eighteen and twenty. He read them over every week. Two of them are about time and strength:

“Resolved, never to lose one moment of time; but improve it the most profitable way I possibly can.”

“Resolved, to live with all my might, while I do live.”

— Jonathan Edwards, Resolutions, 5 and 6

In plain words: I have decided never to waste a moment of time, but to use it in the most useful way I can. I have decided to live with all my strength for as long as I live. As the Ochorus book Key Teachings of Jonathan Edwards explains, Edwards knew he could not keep these resolutions by his own strength. He began them by asking God for grace. They were not a way to earn God’s favour, but a plan for how a person who has received grace will spend his time.

John Wesley lived to the age of eighty-seven, and was still travelling and preaching in his eighties. On his eighty-fifth birthday, in 1788, he wrote in his Journal, which is on Ochorus, about why he was still so strong. He gave the glory first to God, and then to the prayers of others. Then he listed some “inferior means”:

“1. To my constant exercise and change of air? 2. To my never having lost a night's sleep, sick or well, at land or at sea, since I was born? 3. To my having slept at command so that whenever I feel myself almost worn out I call it and it comes, day or night? 4. To my having constantly, for about sixty years, risen at four in the morning?”

— John Wesley, Journal, 28 June 1788

In plain words: Wesley thanked God for regular exercise and travel, for always sleeping well, for being able to sleep whenever he was very tired, and for the habit of getting up early. Few of us can sleep “at command”, and not every leader should rise at four. But Wesley shows us that good habits of sleep, exercise and discipline helped him to serve God for more than fifty years.

A warning from Dundee

Robert Murray M’Cheyne, the young Scottish pastor whom we met in Chapter 9, Keep Watch over Yourself, died in 1843 at the age of twenty-nine, after catching a fever while visiting the sick. He gave himself completely to his people. Some words are often attributed to him near the end of his life. We cannot be sure he said them, but they have been repeated for a long time because so many leaders recognise the truth in them: “God gave me a message to deliver and a horse to ride. Alas, I have killed the horse and can no longer deliver the message.”

M’Cheyne’s short life bore great fruit, and he died while serving the sick, as Jesus did. We should not judge him. But the words attributed to him are a warning to every leader. Your body is the horse God has given you to carry His message. Do not kill the horse.

Whatever your hand finds to do

“Whatever your hand finds to do, put all your strength into it” (Ecclesiastes 9:10). God calls His leaders to work hard, with all their might, while they live. He also calls them to sleep, eat, rest and learn, so that they can serve Him for many years. Both are part of offering your body as a living sacrifice.

One day, the Master will return and ask what we did with what He gave us. May each of us hear, “Well done.”

Questions for reflection

  • Read 1 Corinthians 6:19-20. What does it mean for you that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit?
  • Are you more tempted to laziness or to overwork? What would your family say?
  • Look back at last week. Where did your time go? What would you change?
  • How are you caring for your body: sleep, food, movement and health?
  • What are you learning at the moment? When did you last read a good book?
  • Edwards resolved “never to lose one moment of time.” How could this help you, without leading to overwork?
  • What do the words attributed to M’Cheyne say to you?

A step for this week

Keep a simple record of how you spend your time for one week. At the end, look at it honestly with God. Then choose one change for your body (for example, an earlier bedtime or a daily walk), one change for your mind (for example, reading a good book for twenty minutes a day) and one change for your time (for example, turning off your phone for the first hour of the day). Ask a friend to check on you in a month.

study_questions.question: What does it mean for a leader to steward themselves?
study_questions.answer: It means caring for our time, body and mind as gifts that belong to God. “Your body is a temple where the Holy Spirit lives” (1 Corinthians 6:19). We pray, “Teach us, then, to reckon our days rightly, so that our hearts may grow wise” (Psalm 90:12).

study_questions.question: How should a Christian leader use their time?
study_questions.answer: Wisely and with purpose: “Make good use of every opportunity” (Ephesians 5:16). The chapter warns against both laziness, like the field overgrown with weeds (Proverbs 24:30-31), and overwork that ruins health and family.

study_questions.question: Why should leaders keep learning?
study_questions.answer: Because a mind that stops growing grows stale. The chapter encourages reading, study and learning from others, and draws on Jonathan Edwards’s resolutions about using time and John Wesley’s disciplined habits into old age.

fields.title: Leaders at Work and in Society
fields.body_html:
“Seek the peace of the city where I have sent you as exiles, and pray to the LORD for it, since your own peace depends on its peace.”

— Jeremiah 29:7 (OWB)

In a small town, a pastor rises before dawn to work in the fields. By midday he is in the market, selling vegetables. In the evening he visits a sick family. On Sunday he preaches. He has never been to Bible college, and he receives no salary from the church. Some people think he is not a “real” pastor. But he has led this church faithfully for twenty years.

Across the world, most churches are led by people like him. They are farmers, teachers, nurses, traders, drivers and builders who also shepherd God’s people. And beyond the church, millions of believers lead in business, government, schools, hospitals and communities. This chapter is about leaders at work and in society. It is about the pastor who also works, and about the believer who leads in the world.

Work is God’s idea

Work is not a result of the fall. Before sin entered the world, “The LORD God took the man and settled him in the garden of Eden to work it and take care of it” (Genesis 2:15). Work is part of what it means to be made in God’s image. God Himself is a worker, who made the heavens and the earth.

Jesus spent most of His adult life working with His hands. People asked, “This is the carpenter’s son, is it not?” (Matthew 13:55). As we saw in Chapter 41, The Hidden Years, the Son of God spent many years making things in a workshop in Nazareth. This means that ordinary work is holy when it is done for God. “Whatever you are doing, put your whole self into the work, as for the Lord and not for people” (Colossians 3:23).

Some Christians think there are two kinds of work: “spiritual” work, like preaching and prayer, and “secular” work, like farming and business. They think the first is pleasing to God and the second is just for earning money. The Bible does not divide life like this. A Christian nurse caring for patients, a Christian teacher teaching children, and a Christian trader dealing honestly are all serving God.

Paul the tentmaker

In Chapter 33, Money and Greed, we saw that Paul often supported himself by working. When he came to Corinth, he met Aquila and Priscilla, “and because he and they worked at the same craft, he stayed in their home and worked with them. By trade they were tentmakers. Each Sabbath he debated in the synagogue” (Acts 18:3-4). He reminded the Thessalonians, “how hard we worked and toiled: we labored night and day so as not to be a burden to any of you while we preached the gospel of God to you” (1 Thessalonians 2:9).

Paul did this for several reasons. It meant he was not a burden on new churches. It protected him from the charge of preaching for money. It gave him contact with ordinary people in the marketplace. And it set an example of hard work for the believers (2 Thessalonians 3:8-9).

Today, leaders who work in another job as well as leading a church are often called “tentmakers” or “bi-vocational” leaders. They lead most of the world’s churches. If you are one of them, hear this clearly: your ministry is not second-class. You are following in the steps of the apostle Paul.

The joys and burdens of the tentmaker

Tentmaking leaders have great strengths.

  • They understand the daily lives of their people, because they live the same life.
  • They are free from financial pressure from the church.
  • They meet people who would never come to a church building.
  • They show that faith belongs in the whole of life, not only on Sunday.

But they also carry heavy burdens. They are often tired, with little time for study, prayer and family. They may feel guilty that they cannot do more for the church. Some churches expect them to do as much as a full-time pastor.

Here is some wisdom for tentmaking leaders and their churches.

  • Share the work widely. A tentmaking pastor cannot do everything. Raise up elders, deacons and others to carry the load, as we saw in Chapter 22, No Lone Leaders.
  • Protect time for God and family. Even if the time is short, guard it carefully.
  • Do your work well. “Do you see someone who is skilled at their work? They will serve kings” (Proverbs 22:29). Your work in the world is a witness.
  • Churches, support your leaders as you can. Even a small gift, help with their fields or meals for their family can ease the load.
  • Seek training that fits. Many good training programmes are designed for leaders who work, with evening classes, short courses or study by phone.

Joseph, Daniel and Nehemiah: leaders in the world

Some of the greatest leaders in the Bible led not in the temple but in government.

Joseph ran the whole economy of Egypt during seven years of plenty and seven years of famine. Pharaoh said, “Could we ever find another man like this one, a man who has the spirit of God in him?” (Genesis 41:38). Joseph’s wisdom saved the lives of millions, including the family of Israel.

Daniel served in the government of Babylon and then Persia for most of his long life. From the beginning, he set limits: “Daniel resolved not to make himself unclean with the royal food” (Daniel 1:8). He worked so honestly that his enemies “could find no grounds and no corruption, because he was trustworthy; no negligence or corruption could be found in him” (Daniel 6:4). When the king made praying to God a crime, Daniel “went home to his upstairs room, where the windows opened toward Jerusalem. Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had always done” (Daniel 6:10). He served the king faithfully, but he would not give the king what belonged to God.

Nehemiah was a servant in the Persian king’s palace who became governor of Judah. He led the rebuilding of Jerusalem’s walls. He refused to take the food allowance that other governors had demanded from the people: “The earlier governors before me had laid heavy burdens on the people ... But I did not act like that, because I feared God” (Nehemiah 5:15).

These three show us what a godly leader in society looks like: skilled, honest, prayerful, refusing corruption and serving the good of the whole community, including those who do not believe.

Salt and light in society

God told the exiles in Babylon to do something surprising. They were in a foreign land, ruled by an empire that had destroyed their city. But God said, “Seek the peace of the city where I have sent you as exiles, and pray to the LORD for it, since your own peace depends on its peace” (Jeremiah 29:7).

Jesus said, “You are the salt for the earth ... You are the light of the world ... your light must shine where people can see it, so that they will see your good deeds and give glory to your Father in heaven” (Matthew 5:13-14, 16). Salt does no good in the salt jar. Light does no good under a basket. Believers are meant to be present in every part of society.

Christian leaders in the world face particular tests.

  • Corruption. In many countries, bribes are expected in business and government. Daniel’s example shows that it is possible to serve faithfully without corruption, though it may be costly.
  • Divided loyalty. Leaders may be asked to put their company, party or tribe before what is right.
  • Pressure to hide their faith. Some workplaces mock or punish open faith.
  • Ambition. Success in the world can feed pride and the love of money, as we saw in Part Seven, Dangers on the Road.
  • Politics. Christians may serve in politics, and some are called to. But the Church must never become the servant of one political party. Its loyalty is to Christ.

Pastors should also equip their people for their work. Do you pray for the teachers, nurses, farmers, traders and officials in your church? Do you help them think about how to follow Christ at work? Most of your church’s ministry happens on Monday, not Sunday.

A voice from the Church: William Wilberforce and Lemuel Haynes

In Chapter 30, Justice, Mercy and the Poor, we met William Wilberforce. After his conversion in 1785, he wondered whether he should leave politics and become a minister. John Newton, whom we met in Chapter 39, Failure and Restoration, advised him to stay in Parliament and serve God there. Wilberforce stayed, and spent decades fighting against the slave trade and then slavery itself. His calling was in politics, not in the pulpit.

Lemuel Haynes was born in Connecticut, in America, in 1753. His father was African and his mother was white, and as a baby he was given away and grew up as an indentured servant, bound to work for a farming family. He taught himself to read and loved the Bible. As a young man he fought as a soldier in the American War of Independence. He also wrote against slavery, arguing that liberty was a gift from God to every person, of every colour. In 1785 he was ordained as a minister, one of the first Black Americans ordained by a major church in the United States. For about thirty years he pastored a white congregation in Rutland, Vermont, in a time when that was almost unheard of. He was a servant on a farm, a soldier, a writer and a pastor, and he served God in every one.

A voice from the global Church: Fanny Jackson Coppin and Kanzo Uchimura

Fanny Jackson Coppin was born into slavery in Washington, D.C., in 1837. Her aunt saved money and bought her freedom. She worked as a servant and studied whenever she could, and in 1865 she graduated from Oberlin College. She became the head of the Institute for Colored Youth in Philadelphia, a school for African American young people, and led it for nearly forty years. She trained hundreds of teachers, and she started a programme to teach young people trades so that they could find good work. She believed that education and honest work were ways to serve God and to lift her people. Late in life, she travelled with her husband, a bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal Church, to serve in South Africa.

Kanzo Uchimura was born in Japan in 1861. He came to faith in Christ as a student and became a teacher and writer. In 1891, at a school in Tokyo, the teachers were required to bow deeply before the Emperor’s signature on an official document. Uchimura believed this was an act of worship that he could not give. He did not bow fully. There was a public outcry, and he lost his job. Later he became a journalist and a Bible teacher, and his writings had a great influence on Japanese Christians. He loved his country deeply, and he spoke of loving “two Js”: Jesus and Japan. He is remembered for words that are now carved on his gravestone: “I for Japan; Japan for the World; the World for Christ; and All for God.”

All for God

Whether you are a pastor who farms, a teacher who leads a Bible study, a business owner who gives work to others, or an official who refuses a bribe, your work matters to God. “Serving the Lord and not people ... the Lord will repay each one for whatever good they do” (Ephesians 6:7-8).

Do not think that only the pulpit is holy ground. The field, the classroom, the clinic, the shop and the office can be holy ground too. Seek the peace of the city where God has placed you. Let your light shine there.

Questions for reflection

  • Read Genesis 2:15 and Colossians 3:23. How do these verses change the way you think about ordinary work?
  • Are you a tentmaking leader? What are the joys and burdens of your situation? How could your church help?
  • Read Daniel 6:1-10. What can leaders in government and business learn from Daniel?
  • What forms of corruption are common in your country? How can believers resist them?
  • Read Jeremiah 29:4-7. How can your church “seek the peace” of your town or city?
  • How does your church equip its people to serve Christ in their work?
  • Which of the voices in this chapter speaks most to you: Wilberforce, Haynes, Coppin or Uchimura?

A step for this week

If you are a pastor, find out this week what work the members of your church do. On Sunday, pray for them by name and by their work: farmers, teachers, nurses, traders, students and others. If you lead in the world, write down one way you can serve God more faithfully at work this week, perhaps by refusing a small dishonesty, encouraging a colleague or praying for your workplace. Then pray Jeremiah 29:7 for your town.

study_questions.question: Can a Christian serve God in ordinary work?
study_questions.answer: Yes. Work is God’s idea; He set Adam in the garden “to work it and take care of it” (Genesis 2:15). Jesus was “the carpenter’s son” (Matthew 13:55). “Whatever you are doing, put your whole self into the work, as for the Lord” (Colossians 3:23).

study_questions.question: What is a tentmaker in ministry?
study_questions.answer: A leader who earns a living through other work while serving the church, as Paul did when he worked with Aquila and Priscilla, “By trade they were tentmakers” (Acts 18:3), so as “not to be a burden” (1 Thessalonians 2:9).

study_questions.question: How can believers be salt and light in society?
study_questions.answer: By working with skill and honesty, seeking the good of their city, and standing for justice. “Seek the peace of the city where I have sent you” (Jeremiah 29:7). The chapter tells of Joseph, Daniel, Nehemiah, William Wilberforce, Lemuel Haynes, Fanny Jackson Coppin and Kanzo Uchimura.

fields.title: Faithful in Little: Accountability
fields.body_html:
“Someone who is faithful in the smallest matter is faithful in large matters too, and someone who is dishonest in the smallest matter is dishonest in large matters too.”

— Luke 16:10 (OWB)

A village builds a storehouse for its grain. One man is given the key. At first, everyone checks the grain each month. But the man is trusted, and after a while nobody bothers to check. Years later, in a time of famine, the village opens the storehouse and finds it half empty. The man did not plan to steal. It began with one small sack in a hard month. But nobody was watching, and one sack became many.

The problem in that village was not only one man’s sin. It was a system with no checks. This chapter, the last in Part Nine, The Leader’s Life, is about accountability. It is about the truth that leaders are stewards who will give an account, and about the wisdom of building accountability into our lives long before we think we need it.

Stewards of what belongs to another

Paul described leaders in this way: “So people should think of us in this way: as assistants of Christ and as household managers put in charge of the mysteries of God. Now what is looked for in household managers is this: that each one proves trustworthy” (1 Corinthians 4:1-2).

A household manager, or steward, looked after a rich man’s house while the master was away. He managed the money, the servants, the food and the land. None of it belonged to him. One day the master would come back and ask for a report. The one thing a master needed in a steward was faithfulness.

Leaders are stewards like this. The church is not ours. The people are not ours. The money is not ours. Our gifts, our time and our position are not ours. All belong to Christ, who has gone away and will come back. Jesus told the parable of the master who “summoned his own servants and handed his property over to them. He gave five bags of silver to one, two to another and one to a third, according to what each could manage” (Matthew 25:14-15). When he returned, he asked each one what they had done with what he had given. To the faithful, he said, “Well done! You are a good and faithful servant. You proved faithful in small matters; I will put you in charge of great ones” (Matthew 25:21).

Notice what the master praised. Not size. Not fame. Faithfulness. The servant with two bags received the same praise as the servant with five. God rewards faithfulness, not fame.

Faithful in little

“Someone who is faithful in the smallest matter is faithful in large matters too, and someone who is dishonest in the smallest matter is dishonest in large matters too” (Luke 16:10). Leaders rarely fall all at once. As we have seen in Part Seven, Dangers on the Road, great falls usually begin with small compromises: a little exaggeration, a little money borrowed, a little flirtation, a little pride.

The opposite is also true. Great faithfulness is built from small faithfulness. Keeping a small promise. Returning the change. Telling the truth when a lie would be easier. Being on time. Doing what you said you would do. These things may seem small, but they are the roots of a trustworthy life.

The Ochorus book Faithful with Little explores this for every believer, especially in the area of money. Its message applies with special force to leaders: the way we handle little shows how we will handle much.

Accountability in the early Church

Even the apostles were accountable. When Peter went to the house of Cornelius and ate with Gentiles, “Once Peter was back in Jerusalem, the circumcised believers took him to task ... Peter then explained everything to them step by step, from the beginning” (Acts 11:2, 4). Peter was the leading apostle, but he did not say, “Who are you to question me?” He explained himself.

When Paul and Barnabas returned from their first missionary journey, “they called the church together and told all that God had done” (Acts 14:27). They reported to the church that had sent them. Paul even went to Jerusalem to set his gospel before the other apostles. He wrote, “I did not want to find that I was running, or had run, for nothing” (Galatians 2:2).

When Paul carried a large gift of money for the poor in Jerusalem, he made sure other trusted believers travelled with it: “We are guarding against any charge that could be brought against us over this large sum we are handling. Our concern is for what is honorable, both before the Lord and before people” (2 Corinthians 8:20-21).

Paul also gave instructions for when an elder is accused: “Do not listen to an accusation against an elder unless it is supported by two or three witnesses. Those who keep on sinning should be rebuked in front of everyone” (1 Timothy 5:19-20). Leaders are protected from false accusation. But they are not above correction.

Why leaders avoid accountability

If accountability is so wise, why do so many leaders avoid it?

  • Pride. “I am the leader. I answer to God alone.” But God has placed us in a body, and He often speaks through others.
  • Fear. If someone knows the truth about me, they may think less of me.
  • Hidden sin. A leader who is hiding something will often resist anyone who might find it.
  • Culture. In some cultures, it is shameful to question an older person or a leader. The leader becomes untouchable.
  • Loneliness. Some leaders simply have no one close enough to ask them hard questions.
  • Busyness. Accountability takes time, and it is easy to let it slip.

But a leader without accountability is in great danger. “Two are better than one ... If one of them falls, the other can help that one up. But woe to anyone who falls alone, with no one else to help them up!” (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10). Hebrews says, “encourage one another day by day ... so that sin does not deceive any of you and make you hard” (Hebrews 3:13). Sin deceives. We cannot always see ourselves clearly. We need others to help us see.

Building accountability before you need it

The best time to build accountability is when everything is going well. Here are some forms it can take.

  • Personal accountability. Have one or two trusted, mature believers of the same sex who have permission to ask you hard questions about your walk with God, your marriage, your money, your purity and your use of power. Meet regularly. Tell them the truth. “So make it your practice to confess your sins to each other and to pray for each other, so that you may be healed” (James 5:16).
  • Accountability in leadership. Lead with a team of elders or other leaders, not alone, as we saw in Chapter 22, No Lone Leaders. Make important decisions together.
  • Accountability above you. Belong to a wider fellowship of churches, a denomination, or a group of trusted pastors who can speak into your life and, if necessary, act if something goes wrong. We saw this in Chapter 6, Authority Under Authority.
  • Financial accountability. At least two people count and record every offering. Accounts are checked independently. The leader’s pay is known to the church’s leaders. We saw this in Chapter 33, Money and Greed.
  • Accountability to the church. Report regularly to your church on what is happening, as Paul and Barnabas did. Be open about decisions and finances.
  • Accountability for safety. Have a clear plan for responding to any concern of abuse, including concerns about the senior leader, as we saw in Chapter 35, Power, Abuse and Protecting the Vulnerable.

Accountability is not only about catching sin. It is also about encouragement, prayer and growth. “As iron is sharpened against iron, so one person sharpens another” (Proverbs 27:17). A good accountability friend will rejoice with you, pray for you, and help you become more like Christ.

Receiving correction

Accountability only works if we are willing to hear hard things. “A friend’s wounds can be trusted, but an enemy’s kisses come in plenty” (Proverbs 27:6). “Fools think their own way is right, but the wise listen to advice” (Proverbs 12:15).

David prayed, “Let a righteous person strike me: that is loyal love. Let them reprove me: that is oil for my head, and may my head never refuse it” (Psalm 141:5). When Nathan said to David, “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7), David could have had him killed. Instead, he repented. That is the mark of a leader after God’s heart.

When someone corrects you, do not defend yourself at once. Listen. Ask questions. Pray about it. Even if the correction is only partly true, ask God to show you the part that is true. We looked at this in Chapter 25, Criticism, Opposition and Conflict.

A voice from the Church: John Wesley’s band meetings

In Chapter 22, No Lone Leaders, we saw how John Wesley organised his followers into classes of about twelve people. Wesley also formed smaller groups called “bands”, of a few people of the same sex and situation, for deeper honesty. In 1738 he wrote a set of rules for these bands. Every member was to answer questions like these at every meeting:

“What known sins have you committed since our last meeting? What temptations have you met with? How was you delivered? What have you thought, said, or done, of which you doubt whether it be sin or not? Have you nothing you desire to keep secret?”

— John Wesley, Rules of the Band Societies, 1738

In plain words: what sins do you know you have committed since we last met? What temptations have you faced? How did God help you? Is there anything you have thought, said or done that you are not sure was right? Is there anything you want to keep hidden?

These questions are hard. They were meant to be. The early Methodists believed that sin grows in the dark and dies in the light. Many of Wesley’s preachers and leaders met in bands like this. They were not perfect, but this habit of honest confession helped to keep a great movement of ordinary people from falling into scandal and hypocrisy.

Not every leader will use these exact questions, and they must be used with love, not as a way to control people. But every leader needs someone who can ask, “Have you nothing you desire to keep secret?” and to whom the leader will tell the truth.

In Chapter 34, Sexual Purity, we saw how Billy Graham and his team made commitments together in 1948 about money, honesty and purity. They kept each other to those commitments for decades. Accountability works best when it is shared.

Every one of us will give an account

“So each of us will have to give an account of ourselves” (Romans 14:12). Leaders carry a special weight. Hebrews describes them as “people who will have to answer for them”, the souls in their care (Hebrews 13:17). “Much will be asked of everyone who has been given much” (Luke 12:48). We will look at that final day in Chapter 50, Giving Account.

But the purpose of accountability now is to prepare us for that day with joy, not fear. If we let others help us to be faithful in little things today, we will be ready to hear our Master say, “Well done! You are a good and faithful servant.”

Questions for reflection

  • Read 1 Corinthians 4:1-2 and Matthew 25:14-30. What does it mean to be a steward rather than an owner?
  • Read Luke 16:10. What “small matters” in your life show whether you are faithful?
  • Who regularly asks you hard questions about your life? Do you tell them the truth?
  • Which of the reasons leaders avoid accountability is true of you?
  • Which forms of accountability does your church have? Which are missing?
  • Read Wesley’s band questions aloud. Which one is hardest for you to answer honestly?
  • How do you usually respond when someone corrects you?

A step for this week

Choose one or two mature, trusted believers of the same sex and ask them to be your accountability partners. Agree to meet regularly, perhaps once a month. Give them permission to ask you about your walk with God, your family, your money, your purity and your use of power. Write down the questions you want them to ask. At your first meeting, answer Wesley’s last question honestly: “Have you nothing you desire to keep secret?”

study_questions.question: Why do leaders need accountability?
study_questions.answer: Because leaders are stewards of what belongs to God, and “what is looked for in household managers is this: that each one proves trustworthy” (1 Corinthians 4:2). Even Peter explained his actions to the church in Jerusalem (Acts 11:2-4).

study_questions.question: What does it mean to be faithful in little?
study_questions.answer: “Someone who is faithful in the smallest matter is faithful in large matters too” (Luke 16:10). God watches how we handle small things. The master said, “Well done! You are a good and faithful servant. You proved faithful in small matters” (Matthew 25:21).

study_questions.question: How can a leader build accountability?
study_questions.answer: Before it is needed: by having one or two trusted friends who ask hard questions, being open about money and time, and welcoming correction. John Wesley’s band meetings asked members to answer five searching questions at every meeting.

fields.title: Passing the Baton
fields.body_html:
“And what you heard from me before many witnesses, pass on to trustworthy people who will be able to teach others as well.”

— 2 Timothy 2:2 (OWB)

In a relay race, four runners share one race. Each one runs as fast as they can. But the race is often won or lost not on the track but at the moment of the handover. If the baton is dropped, the whole team loses, however fast each runner is. A good runner does not stop running when the next runner begins. They run alongside for a few steps, until the baton is firmly in the other’s hand. Then they let go.

Every leader is running one part of a longer race. Nobody leads for ever. One day, by choice, by age, by illness or by death, we will hand on what we have carried. This chapter begins Part Ten, Finishing Well. It is about passing the baton: preparing others, letting go, and handing over well.

Moses and Joshua

Moses knew he would not enter the promised land.
