So he prayed for the people: “May the LORD ... appoint a man over the congregation, someone who will go out ahead of them and come in ahead of them ... so that the congregation of the LORD will not be like sheep with no shepherd” (Numbers 27:16-17). Moses was not thinking of his own name. He was thinking of the flock.

God answered: “Take Joshua son of Nun, a man with the spirit in him, and lay your hand on him, have him stand before Eleazar the priest and the whole congregation, and commission him in their sight, and give him some of your authority” (Numbers 27:18-20).

Notice several things about this handover.

  • It was prepared for many years. Joshua had been Moses’ assistant since his youth. He had fought Israel’s battles, gone up the mountain with Moses and stayed in the tent of meeting (Exodus 33:11).
  • God chose the successor. Moses did not simply choose his own son or his favourite.
  • It was public. Joshua was commissioned “in their sight”, before the priest and the whole people, so that everyone knew who would lead.
  • Authority was shared before it was handed over. Moses gave Joshua “some of your authority” while Moses was still alive.
  • The successor was encouraged. Moses said to Joshua, before all Israel, “Be strong and courageous ... The LORD himself goes ahead of you, and he will be with you. He will not let you go or abandon you. Do not be afraid or lose heart” (Deuteronomy 31:7-8).

The result: “Joshua son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom, since Moses had laid his hands on him. The Israelites obeyed him” (Deuteronomy 34:9).

A warning: the generation that did not know

But the story has a sad sequel. Joshua led Israel faithfully. But when he died, there is no record that he had prepared a successor as Moses had prepared him. “That whole generation also died and was gathered to their ancestors, and after them another generation grew up who did not know the LORD or what he had done for Israel” (Judges 2:10). The book of Judges follows, a time of confusion, sin and suffering.

Faith is always one generation from being lost. A leader who does great things but does not pass them on may see the work collapse within a few years. As we saw in Chapter 23, Making Leaders, Paul gave Timothy a chain of four generations: Paul, Timothy, “trustworthy people”, and “others as well” (2 Timothy 2:2). The task of every leader is not only to do the work, but to make sure the work goes on.

Elijah and Elisha

God told Elijah to anoint Elisha “to be prophet in your place” (1 Kings 19:16). Elijah found him ploughing in a field and threw his cloak over him. Elisha killed his oxen, cooked them for the people, and “got up, followed Elijah and became his attendant” (1 Kings 19:21). For years, Elisha served Elijah.

At the end, Elijah asked him, “Before I am taken from you, tell me what I can do for you.” Elisha asked for “a double portion of your spirit” (2 Kings 2:9). Then Elijah was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind. Elisha picked up the cloak that had fallen from him, went to the Jordan, struck the water and asked, “Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?” (2 Kings 2:14). The water divided. The prophets watching said, “The spirit of Elijah has come to rest on Elisha” (2 Kings 2:15).

Elisha’s question is important. He did not ask, “Where is Elijah?” He asked, “Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?” The great leader was gone. But the God of the great leader was still there. The work does not belong to the leader. It belongs to God, and He will carry it on.

Paul’s farewell

Paul’s farewell to the elders of Ephesus, in Acts 20, is one of the most moving scenes in the Bible. He knew he would not see them again. He reminded them of how he had lived among them. He told them what mattered most to him: “All I want is to run my course to the end and carry out the ministry I received from the Lord Jesus” (Acts 20:24). Then he handed the flock over to them: “Be on your guard, for yourselves and for the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers to shepherd the church of God” (Acts 20:28). He warned them of dangers ahead. And finally, he handed them over to God: “And now I place you in the care of God and of the message of his grace” (Acts 20:32).

“After saying this, he knelt down and prayed with them all. They all wept freely” (Acts 20:36-37).

In his very last letter, Paul handed the baton to Timothy: “I solemnly charge you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus ... Preach the word ... carry out your ministry fully. For I am already being poured out like a drink offering, and the time for my departure has come” (2 Timothy 4:1-2, 5-6).

Even Jesus prepared His disciples for His going. “My going away is to your advantage. For if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you at all; but if I go, I will send him to you” (John 16:7). Sometimes the greatest thing a leader can do is step aside, so that others can grow.

Why leaders find it hard to let go

Many leaders hold on too long. Some never prepare anyone at all. Why?

  • Identity. If my identity is in my role, giving it up feels like losing myself.
  • Fear for the work. “Nobody else can do it as well as I can.” This is often pride disguised as concern.
  • Money and security. Some leaders have nowhere to live and nothing to live on if they step down. Churches must care for retiring leaders.
  • Insecurity. Some leaders feel threatened by gifted younger people, like Saul with David, as we saw in Chapter 36, Envy, Rivalry and Favouritism.
  • Family pressure. Some want to hand the church to a son or daughter, whether or not God has called them.
  • Founder’s grip. Leaders who started a work often find it hardest to let go of it.

John the Baptist had the right spirit: “He must grow greater, but I must grow less” (John 3:30). The leader who has truly served Christ will be glad to see the work go on without them.

Handing over well

Here is some wisdom for passing the baton.

  • Start early. Begin preparing successors years before you expect to leave. Every leader should be training several people.
  • Pray for God’s choice. As Moses did, ask God to show who should lead next. Seek the wisdom of other leaders and the church.
  • Share authority before you leave. Give younger leaders real responsibility while you are still there to help them.
  • Make it public and clear. Let the church know who will lead, and bless that person publicly.
  • Prepare for the unexpected. Illness, arrest or death can come suddenly. Make sure someone could lead tomorrow if needed. We saw this in Chapter 40, Persecution and the Cost.
  • Leave well. Do not leave debts, secrets or unfinished conflicts for your successor. David gathered materials for the temple so that Solomon could build it (1 Chronicles 22:5).
  • Let go. Once you have handed over, step back. Do not keep interfering, criticising or undermining. Do not let people come to you to complain about your successor.
  • Stay as a blessing. If you stay in the church, be the new leader’s greatest supporter. Pray for them. Encourage them. Offer advice only when it is asked for.

And if you are the successor: honour the one who went before you. Learn from them. Do not rush to change everything. And remember that you too will one day pass the baton.

A voice from the Church: Henry Venn and Hudson Taylor

In Chapter 23, Making Leaders, we met Henry Venn, the leader of the Church Missionary Society in London in the nineteenth century. Venn taught that the aim of mission was to plant churches that would be self-governing, self-supporting and self-spreading. He believed that missionaries should plan from the beginning to hand over the leadership to local believers, and then move on. He even spoke of the “euthanasia” of a mission, a word that means a gentle and good death. By this he meant that a mission should happily come to an end in a place once the local church was strong enough to stand on its own. A missionary who is still in charge after fifty years, he believed, has not finished the work, however much he has done.

Not every mission followed Venn’s vision. As we saw in Chapter 36, Envy, Rivalry and Favouritism, the African leadership he had hoped for on the Niger was badly damaged after Crowther’s time. But his principle has shaped the global Church ever since. Today the great majority of the world’s Christians are led by their own people.

Hudson Taylor founded the China Inland Mission in 1865 and led it for over thirty-five years. By the end of the century it had become one of the largest missions in the world. In 1900, during the Boxer uprising in China, the mission lost fifty-eight missionaries and twenty-one children, as well as many Chinese believers. Taylor, old and ill in Switzerland, was almost broken by the news. As the Ochorus book Key Teachings of Hudson Taylor records, he then handed the leadership of the mission to a younger man, Dixon Hoste.

It was not easy for a founder to let go of the work he had carried for so long. But Taylor did it, and the mission continued and grew. In 1905, he travelled to China one last time, and he died quietly there, in Changsha. He had run his part of the race, and he had placed the baton firmly in another’s hand.

The work is God’s

When Moses died, God said to Joshua, “My servant Moses is dead. Now get up and cross this Jordan” (Joshua 1:2). The work did not stop. It went on, because it was God’s work, not Moses’.

David said to his son Solomon, “Be strong and courageous, and do the work. Do not be afraid or lose heart, for the LORD God, my God, is with you. He will not let go of you or abandon you until you have finished all the work” (1 Chronicles 28:20). Paul wrote, “the one who started a good work in you will keep working at it until it is finished” (Philippians 1:6).

Run your part of the race well. Then place the baton in another’s hand, and let go. The God of Elijah is still here.

Questions for reflection

  • Read Numbers 27:15-23 and Deuteronomy 31:7-8. What can you learn from the way Moses handed over to Joshua?
  • Read Judges 2:7-10. Why do you think the next generation “did not know the LORD”?
  • Read 2 Kings 2:9-15. What does Elisha’s question, “Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?”, teach you?
  • Who are you preparing to lead after you? If you left tomorrow, who would lead?
  • Which of the reasons leaders find it hard to let go is true of you?
  • If you have taken over from another leader, how have you honoured them?
  • What do you learn from Venn’s idea of the “euthanasia” of a mission?

A step for this week

Write down the names of the people you are preparing to lead after you. If there are none, ask God to show you one or two, and begin to meet with them this month. Then ask yourself, “If I could no longer lead from tomorrow, what would the church need to know?” Write it down, and share it with your fellow leaders. If you are near the end of your time in a role, talk with your leaders this week about a plan for handing over well.

study_questions.question: How should a leader pass on leadership?
study_questions.answer: Early and deliberately. Moses prayed for a successor, laid hands on Joshua and encouraged him: “Be strong and courageous ... The LORD himself goes ahead of you” (Deuteronomy 31:7-8). Paul passed the work to Timothy and told him to pass it on again (2 Timothy 2:2).

study_questions.question: Why do leaders find it hard to let go?
study_questions.answer: Because their identity is tied to the role, because they fear the work will fail without them, or because no one has been trained. The chapter reminds leaders that the work belongs to God, not to them.

study_questions.question: What happens when the next generation is not prepared?
study_questions.answer: Judges warns that after Joshua’s generation died, “another generation grew up” that did not know the LORD (Judges 2:10). The chapter tells how Henry Venn planned for the “euthanasia” of a mission and how Hudson Taylor handed over to Dixon Hoste.

fields.title: Legacy: What Lasts
fields.body_html:
“Those who are wise will shine like the brightness of the sky, and those who lead many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever.”

— Daniel 12:3 (OWB)

In a certain town there is a fine stone building with a name carved over the door. It was built many years ago by a wealthy man, as a monument to himself. Today the building is empty, the roof leaks, and nobody in the town remembers who the man was. But in the same town, an old woman who never had money taught children in her home to read the Bible. Some of those children became pastors, teachers and doctors. Their children and grandchildren follow Christ today. Her name is carved nowhere. But her work is still alive.

Every leader leaves something behind. The question is what. This chapter is about legacy: what will remain when we are gone. The Bible’s answer is clear. What lasts is not buildings, programmes or names. What lasts is people formed in Christ, and work done for Him.

“So that we may make a name for ourselves”

Long ago, people gathered on the plain of Shinar and said, “Come, let us build ourselves a city, with a tower that reaches to the heavens, so that we may make a name for ourselves” (Genesis 11:4). It is one of the oldest human desires: to be remembered, to leave a monument, to make our name great. God scattered them, and the tower was left unfinished.

Leaders face the same temptation. We want to build the biggest church, the finest building, the best-known ministry. We want our name on the door. As we saw in Chapter 32, Pride and the Love of Praise, this desire can quietly take the place of the desire for God’s glory.

The Teacher in Ecclesiastes saw the emptiness of building for ourselves: “I hated all the hard work I had done under the sun, because I must leave what it earned to the one who comes after me. And who knows whether that one will be wise or a fool?” (Ecclesiastes 2:18-19). Everything we build for our own name, we will leave to someone else, and it will pass away.

Gold or straw

Paul gives a picture of what lasts: “For there is no other foundation anyone can lay; the one already in place is Jesus Christ. If anyone builds on this foundation with gold, silver, costly stones, wood, hay or straw, each builder’s work will come out into the open. The Day will make it plain, since that Day arrives in fire, and the fire itself will prove what kind of work each one has done. If what someone has built on the foundation survives, that builder will receive a reward. If someone’s work burns up, that person will suffer loss. The builder will still be saved, but only as one who comes out through the fire” (1 Corinthians 3:11-15).

Paul was writing to leaders, those who build the church. Two leaders may both build on Christ. But one builds with gold and silver, and the other with wood and straw. From the outside, the straw building may look bigger and may go up faster. But on the last Day, fire will test every leader’s work. Only what is real will remain.

What is gold, and what is straw? Gold is work done in Christ, by His Spirit, with true motives, according to His Word. It is people truly brought to faith and truly built up in Him. Straw is work done for our own name, in our own strength, with wrong motives, or by methods that do not honour Him. It may draw crowds. But it will not stand the fire.

People are the lasting legacy

When Paul thought about what he would present to Christ at His coming, he did not think of buildings or numbers. He thought of people: “When our Lord Jesus comes, what will be our hope and joy, the crown we will be proud of before him? Surely it will be you, too. Yes, you are our glory and our joy” (1 Thessalonians 2:19-20). To the Corinthians he wrote, “Our letter is you yourselves ... Plainly you are a letter from Christ, produced through our service. It was written not in ink but by the Spirit of the living God ... on human hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:2-3).

John the elder wrote, “No joy of mine is greater than this: to hear that my children are walking in the truth” (3 John 4). Jesus told His disciples, “I appointed you for this: to go and bear fruit, and for your fruit to remain” (John 15:16).

Daniel saw the reward of those who give their lives to this work: “those who lead many to righteousness” will shine “like the stars forever and ever” (Daniel 12:3). Buildings crumble. Stars shine on.

Passing on faith to generations not yet born

The psalmist saw his work stretching across generations: “we will pass on to those who come after us the deeds for which the LORD is praised ... so that those born later, children not yet born, would know them, and would grow up and tell them to their own children, so that they would rest their hope on God” (Psalm 78:4, 6-7).

Notice the four generations here: “we”, “those who come after us”, “those born later” and “their own children”. The greatest legacy a leader can leave is a chain of faith that reaches people they will never meet. As we saw in Chapter 47, Passing the Baton, Paul gave Timothy the same vision: “pass on to trustworthy people who will be able to teach others as well” (2 Timothy 2:2).

Hebrews tells us that Abel, the first person to die, “though he died, he is still speaking” (Hebrews 11:4). The faith of those who have gone before still speaks to us. Their legacy lives on in the people they shaped, and in the example they left. “Keep in mind those who led you, who brought you the word of God. Look closely at where their way of life led them, and follow the example of their faith” (Hebrews 13:7).

The grain of wheat

Jesus taught the deepest secret of legacy: “Truly, truly, I tell you, if a grain of wheat does not fall into the ground and die, it stays just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). Jesus spoke first of His own death. But He went on to say that the same is true of everyone who follows Him.

A leader who tries to save their own life, protect their own name and build their own kingdom will remain alone, “a single grain”. A leader who gives their life away, in love, for Christ and for others, will bear much fruit. Many of the leaders whose work has lasted longest died poor, unknown or young. But their lives, buried like seed, became a harvest.

What will you leave?

Here are some questions to help a leader think about legacy.

  • Who am I investing in? Which people will carry the faith on after me?
  • What am I building on? Is my work built on Christ and His Word, or on my personality and gifts?
  • Why am I building? For His name or for mine?
  • What will my family remember? “A good person leaves an inheritance to their grandchildren” (Proverbs 13:22). The best inheritance is a living faith.
  • What will remain if my name is forgotten? If nobody remembers me in fifty years, will the work still go on?
  • What am I writing? Not only in books, but in the lives of the people I lead.

Moses prayed, “Give lasting worth to the work of our hands; yes, give the work of our hands lasting worth” (Psalm 90:17). That is a good prayer for every leader.

A voice from the Church: Francke, Müller and Brainerd

In the 1690s, a German professor named August Hermann Francke founded an orphanage in the city of Halle, trusting God in prayer to provide for the children. Francke died in 1727. A hundred years later, a young German student named George Müller came to Halle and stayed for two months in the very buildings Francke had built. The biography George Müller of Bristol, on Ochorus, describes how those buildings were to him “a visible, veritable, tangible proof that the Living God hears prayer.” That lesson, it says, was never lost.

Müller, whom we met in Chapter 13, Living in the Word, and Chapter 28, Wisdom and Planning, went on to found the orphan houses at Ashley Down in Bristol, England. For more than sixty years he cared for orphans without ever asking anyone for money, telling his needs to God alone. In time the homes housed more than two thousand children at once. Francke never knew Müller. But Francke’s faith, built in stone and prayer, spoke to Müller a hundred years later. And Müller’s story has since encouraged millions of believers around the world to trust God.

David Brainerd, whom we met in Chapter 19, Seeking the Lost, and Chapter 37, Loneliness and Hidden Burdens, died in 1747 at the age of twenty-nine. His mission among the Native Americans lasted only a few years, and he was often ill and discouraged. By the world’s standards, his life was short and small. But after his death, Jonathan Edwards published his diary, which is on Ochorus. That diary has been read by generations of missionaries. William Carey, whom we met in Chapter 27, Vision: Seeing What God Sees, and his fellow workers in India later wrote into their own covenant that they should often look at Brainerd’s example. Henry Martyn, a brilliant young English scholar, read Brainerd’s life and gave up a promising career to go as a missionary to India and Persia, where he translated the New Testament before dying at the age of thirty-one. Brainerd, like a grain of wheat, fell into the ground and died. But his life bore much fruit.

A voice from the global Church: the Dohnavur Fellowship

In Chapter 35, Power, Abuse and Protecting the Vulnerable, we saw how a little girl called Preena ran to Amy Carmichael in 1901. From that one child grew the Dohnavur Fellowship in South India, a large family that cared for hundreds of children over the following decades. Amy herself died in 1951, after many years as an invalid. But she had trained Indian co-workers to lead, and the work continued after her. Many of the children who grew up at Dohnavur became nurses, teachers and Christian workers themselves. Amy never wanted anyone to make a monument to her. She asked that there should be no stone with her name and achievements on her grave. As Amy Carmichael: A Life, on Ochorus, tells, the Fellowship placed a bird bath over it instead, and wrote on it a single word: Amma, the Tamil word for “mother” that the children had called her. Her legacy is not stone, but lives.

Stars, not monuments

“A voice from heaven spoke to me: ‘Write: From now on, how blessed are the dead who die in the Lord!’ ‘Indeed,’ the Spirit says, ‘let them rest from their toil, for what they have done goes with them’” (Revelation 14:13).

What we do in Christ goes with us. Nothing done for Him in love is ever wasted. Do not spend your life building a tower for your name. Spend it building people, on the foundation of Christ, with gold and not straw. One day, your name may be forgotten on earth. But those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars, for ever and ever.

Questions for reflection

  • Read Genesis 11:1-9. In what ways are leaders tempted to “make a name for ourselves”?
  • Read 1 Corinthians 3:10-15. What in your ministry is gold, and what might be straw?
  • Read 1 Thessalonians 2:19-20. Who will be your “joy and crown” when Christ comes?
  • Read Psalm 78:4-7. How are you passing on faith to generations not yet born?
  • What do you learn from the story of Francke and Müller?
  • Brainerd’s life was short, but its fruit was great. How does that encourage you?
  • If your name were forgotten in fifty years, what would remain of your work?

A step for this week

Write a short letter to someone you are investing in, perhaps a younger leader, a child or a new believer. Tell them what you have learned about following Christ, and what you hope and pray for them. Then write down, in one or two sentences, the legacy you want to leave. Pray Psalm 90:17 over it: “Give lasting worth to the work of our hands.”

study_questions.question: What kind of legacy lasts forever?
study_questions.answer: Not buildings or a name, but people brought to Christ and grown in Him. “Those who lead many to righteousness” will shine “like the stars forever” (Daniel 12:3). Paul said of the believers he had served, “Surely it will be you” who are his joy and crown (1 Thessalonians 2:19-20).

study_questions.question: What does Paul mean by building with gold or straw?
study_questions.answer: Every leader builds on the foundation of Jesus Christ, but some build with lasting materials and some with things that burn. On the last Day the fire will test each one’s work (1 Corinthians 3:11-15).

study_questions.question: How can a leader leave a legacy for generations not yet born?
study_questions.answer: By investing in people, training leaders and passing on the faith. The chapter tells of August Francke and George Müller, the influence of David Brainerd’s diary on later missionaries, and the Dohnavur Fellowship.

fields.title: Growing Old in the Work
fields.body_html:
“Even when they are old they will still bear fruit; they will stay rich with sap and green.”

— Psalm 92:14 (OWB)

In many parts of the world there are old trees in the centre of the village. Their trunks are wide and twisted with age. Their branches are not growing as fast as they once did. But under their shade the elders meet, the children play, and travellers rest. The young trees around them are taller in some places and grow faster. But no young tree can give the shade of the old one.

Leaders grow old. Their bodies weaken. They can no longer work the long hours they once did. But God does not throw away His old servants. Old age has its own gifts and its own fruit. It also has its own dangers. This chapter is about growing old in the work: the wisdom of older leaders, the blessing they can give to the young, and the danger of clinging on.

Still bearing fruit

The psalmist sang, “The righteous will thrive like the palm tree and rise tall as a cedar on Lebanon. Rooted in the LORD’s house, they will bloom in the courtyards of our God. Even when they are old they will still bear fruit; they will stay rich with sap and green” (Psalm 92:12-14).

The world often says that old people are finished, that their time is past. The Bible says something different. “Gray hair is a glorious crown, won by living a righteous life” (Proverbs 16:31). “Young men take pride in their strength; the old wear gray hair as their honor” (Proverbs 20:29). “Wisdom is with the aged, and long life brings understanding” (Job 12:12). God commanded His people, “Rise to your feet in the presence of the gray-haired, and give honor to the old” (Leviticus 19:32).

And God promises to carry His servants all the way: “Until you are old I am he, and until your hair turns gray I am the one who will carry you. I made you, and I will lift you; I will carry you and bring you to safety” (Isaiah 46:4). Paul said, “Our outer self may be decaying, but our inner self is being made new day after day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). The body grows weaker. The spirit can grow stronger.

Caleb at eighty-five

Caleb was one of the twelve spies Moses sent into the promised land. Only he and Joshua trusted God. Forty-five years later, when Israel had entered the land, Caleb came to Joshua with a request: “And here I am today, eighty-five years old. Today I am just as strong as on the day Moses sent me ... So now give me this hill country, the one the LORD promised me on that day. You yourself heard then that the Anakim were there, with large fortified cities. Perhaps the LORD will be with me, and I will drive them out” (Joshua 14:10-12).

Caleb did not ask for an easy place to retire. At eighty-five he asked for the hardest task, the hill country where the giants lived. He was still trusting God, still ready for a challenge, still looking forward. Not every older leader will have Caleb’s strength of body. But every older leader can have Caleb’s strength of faith.

Simeon and Anna

When Mary and Joseph brought the baby Jesus to the temple, two old people were waiting. Simeon was “upright and reverent, who longed for the day God would comfort Israel. The Holy Spirit was on him” (Luke 2:25). He took the child in his arms and said, “Master, now you are letting your servant go in peace, as you promised, because my eyes have seen the salvation that comes from you” (Luke 2:29-30).

Anna was “very old ... she was now eighty-four. She never left the temple, but served God night and day with fasting and prayer. She came up just then, gave thanks to God, and went on speaking about him to everyone who was waiting for God to set Jerusalem free” (Luke 2:36-38).

These two old people had no official position. But they had spent many years in prayer and waiting on God. Because of that, they recognised the Messiah when others did not. And they spoke about Him to others. The ministry of older believers is often a ministry of prayer, of spiritual discernment and of witness, and it is precious to God.

The gifts of older leaders

The psalmist prayed in his old age, “Now that I am old and gray, God, do not abandon me, not until I have told the generation after me what your arm has done, and made your power known to all who are yet to be born” (Psalm 71:18). This is the great task of older leaders: to pass on to the next generation what God has done.

Older leaders have special gifts to offer.

  • Wisdom. Years of walking with God, making mistakes and learning from them, give a depth of understanding that cannot be learned from books.
  • Memory. They remember God’s faithfulness in past trials. They can tell the young, “I have seen God do this before.”
  • Prayer. Many older believers have more time to pray. Like Anna, they can become the hidden strength of a church.
  • Blessing. In the Bible, the old blessed the young. Jacob blessed his grandsons. Moses blessed the tribes. An older leader’s blessing and encouragement can mean a great deal to a young leader.
  • Mentoring. Paul told Titus that the older men and women should teach and train the younger (Titus 2:2-4). Older leaders can walk alongside younger ones as Paul did with Timothy.
  • Example. A life that has stayed faithful to the end is itself a sermon.

Churches should honour their older leaders and make use of their gifts. Do not push them aside. Ask their advice. Rehoboam lost most of his kingdom because “he rejected the advice the elders had given him and consulted the young men who had grown up with him” (1 Kings 12:8).

The dangers of old age

Old age also has its dangers. Some of the saddest stories in the Bible are about leaders who began well and ended badly.

  • Turning away. “When Solomon was old, his wives turned his heart to follow other gods, and his heart was not wholly devoted to the LORD his God” (1 Kings 11:4). The wisest man in the world drifted from God in his old age.
  • Selfishness about the future. When Isaiah told King Hezekiah that disaster would come on his descendants, Hezekiah thought, “Is it not good, if there will be peace and stability as long as I live?” (2 Kings 20:19). He cared only about his own lifetime.
  • Pride. King Uzziah was greatly blessed, but “when he had become strong, his heart grew proud, to his own ruin” (2 Chronicles 26:16), and he ended his life as an outcast.
  • Clinging to power. Some older leaders will not let go. They block younger leaders, insist on their own way and stay long after they should have stepped aside. We looked at this in Chapter 47, Passing the Baton.
  • Bitterness. Some grow bitter about past hurts, or about changes in the church they do not like.
  • Stopping learning. Some older leaders stop growing. They live on old experiences and old sermons. Their faith becomes a memory rather than a living walk with God.

In some cultures, the danger is that older leaders are honoured so much that no one can ever correct them, and the young are never given room to lead. In other cultures, the danger is the opposite: older people are pushed aside and forgotten. The Church must do better than both. It must honour the old and make room for the young. “Never speak harshly to an older man, but appeal to him as you would to a father. Treat younger men as brothers, older women as mothers” (1 Timothy 5:1-2).

Ending well

How can older leaders end well?

  • Keep your walk with God fresh. Keep reading, praying and learning. Ask God to keep your heart “wholly devoted” to Him.
  • Make room for the young. Be glad when younger leaders rise. Step back from positions at the right time, and give them space.
  • Stay available. Be ready to pray, advise and encourage, without insisting on your own way.
  • Bless the next generation. Speak words of blessing over younger leaders. Tell them what God has done.
  • Accept your weakness. Your body will slow down. Accept help with grace.
  • Deal with old wounds. Forgive those who hurt you. Do not carry bitterness to the grave.
  • Prepare to die well. Put your affairs in order. Speak to your family about your faith and your hope. Look forward to seeing Christ.

A voice from the Church: John Wesley and George Müller

John Wesley, whom we have met many times in this book, kept travelling and preaching into his late eighties. In Chapter 44, Stewarding Yourself, we read what he wrote on his eighty-fifth birthday. Even then he was still riding, preaching early in the morning and caring for the societies. His Journal, on Ochorus, shows him still visiting Sunday schools, still noticing children who “truly fear God”, and still rejoicing in the work of God among the young.

A few days before he died in 1791, at the age of eighty-seven, Wesley wrote a letter to the young William Wilberforce, encouraging him to keep fighting the slave trade. He was still blessing the next generation. As he lay dying in London, those around him recorded, in an account that is included with his Journal, that he gathered all his remaining strength and cried out:

“The best of all is, God is with us.”

— John Wesley, as recorded by those present at his death, 1791

He said it twice. After a long life of service, his greatest joy was not in what he had done, but in the presence of God.

George Müller, whom we met in Chapter 48, Legacy: What Lasts, was born in 1805. In 1875, when he was about seventy, he began a new ministry. For the next seventeen years, until 1892, he travelled the world on preaching journeys. The biography George Müller of Bristol, on Ochorus, describes how these tours reached across Europe, America, Asia, Africa and Australia, and says that they “would of themselves have sufficed for the work of an ordinary life.” In his seventies and eighties, Müller was still telling the world about the God who hears prayer. He died at Ashley Down in 1898, at the age of ninety-two.

A crown of glory

Not every old leader will travel the world like Müller or preach like Wesley. Some will spend their last years in a small room, in weakness and pain. But their prayers, their example and their faith can still bear fruit. “Even when they are old they will still bear fruit.”

If you are growing old in the work, take heart. God has not finished with you. Keep growing. Keep praying. Bless the young. Make room for them. And look forward. Your best days are not behind you. They are ahead, in the presence of the One you have served.

Questions for reflection

  • Read Psalm 92:12-15 and Psalm 71:17-18. What kind of fruit can older leaders bear?
  • Read Joshua 14:6-12. What do you admire about Caleb at eighty-five?
  • Read Luke 2:25-38. What do Simeon and Anna teach you about the ministry of older believers?
  • Which of the dangers of old age do you see in older leaders around you? Which do you fear for yourself?
  • How does your church honour its older members? How does it make room for the young?
  • If you are older, who are you blessing and encouraging among the young?
  • If you are younger, which older leader could you ask for advice and blessing?

A step for this week

If you are an older leader, write a letter or record a message for a younger leader, telling them what God has done in your life and blessing them in their work. Then ask yourself honestly: is there any position I am holding that I should be preparing to hand on? If you are a younger leader, visit an older believer this week. Ask them to tell you their story of God’s faithfulness, and ask them to pray for you.

study_questions.question: Can older leaders still bear fruit?
study_questions.answer: Yes. “Even when they are old they will still bear fruit; they will stay rich with sap and green” (Psalm 92:14). At eighty-five Caleb asked for the hardest task, the hill country where the giants lived, and Simeon and Anna served God in old age.

study_questions.question: What gifts do older leaders bring to the church?
study_questions.answer: Wisdom, experience, prayer and perspective. “Wisdom is with the aged, and long life brings understanding” (Job 12:12). Scripture calls the church to “give honor to the old” (Leviticus 19:32).

study_questions.question: What are the dangers for older leaders?
study_questions.answer: Holding on too long, growing bitter or stale, and failing to make room for younger leaders. God promises, “until your hair turns gray I am the one who will carry you” (Isaiah 46:4). John Wesley and George Müller kept serving into old age.

fields.title: Giving Account
fields.body_html:
“For all of us must be laid open before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what matches the things done in the body, whether good or worthless.”

— 2 Corinthians 5:10 (OWB)

A shepherd in the hills is hired to look after a rich man’s flock for a season. Every evening he counts the sheep. When one is missing, he goes out to look for it, even in the dark. He knows that at the end of the season, the owner will come and count the flock himself. The shepherd will have to give an account of every sheep that was put in his care.

Every leader will one day stand before the Chief Shepherd and give an account. In Chapter 46, Faithful in Little: Accountability, we looked at accountability in this life. This chapter looks at the final account, on the day when we stand before Christ. It is a sobering subject. But it is also full of grace. The One before whom we will stand is the One who died for us.

We will all stand before Christ

Paul wrote, “That is why we set our hearts on pleasing him, whether we are still at home in the body or have left it. For all of us must be laid open before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what matches the things done in the body, whether good or worthless” (2 Corinthians 5:9-10). “We will all stand before God’s judgment seat” (Romans 14:10). “No created thing is concealed from him. All things are stripped bare and open to the eyes of the one we must answer to” (Hebrews 4:13).

For those who are in Christ, this judgment is not about whether we will be saved. That was settled at the cross. “Who is going to condemn them? Christ is the one who died; still more, he was raised, and he is at the right hand of God, where he pleads on our behalf” (Romans 8:34). But it is about what we did with the life, the gifts and the people He gave us. As we saw in Chapter 48, Legacy: What Lasts, the fire will test each builder’s work. Some work will remain and be rewarded. Some will be burned up, and “that person will suffer loss. The builder will still be saved, but only as one who comes out through the fire” (1 Corinthians 3:15).

The special weight on leaders

Every believer will give an account. But Scripture says leaders carry a special weight. “Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers and sisters, for you know that we who teach will be judged more strictly” (James 3:1). Hebrews describes leaders as those who “stay awake watching over your souls, as people who will have to answer for them” (Hebrews 13:17).

God told Ezekiel, “Son of man, I have appointed you a watchman for the house of Israel. When you hear a word from my mouth, you must warn them for me. If I say to a wicked person, ‘You will surely die,’ and you do not warn them or speak out to turn them from their wicked way and save their life, that wicked person will die for their sin, but I will hold you responsible for their death” (Ezekiel 3:17-18).

This is why Paul could say to the Ephesian elders, “I am free from guilt for anyone’s blood. I never drew back from making known to you God’s whole plan” (Acts 20:26-27). He had taught them everything God had given him to teach. He had not held back the hard parts. He had done his work as a watchman.

What will leaders give account for? Scripture suggests many things.

  • The people in our care. Did we feed, protect, seek and love them?
  • Our teaching. Did we teach the truth, all of it, without twisting it or holding back?
  • Our example. Did we live what we taught?
  • Our motives. Why did we lead? For His glory or for ours? God will “bring the purposes of all hearts out into the open” (1 Corinthians 4:5).
  • Our words. “Every idle word people speak is a word they will have to answer for on judgment day” (Matthew 12:36).
  • Our use of power and money. Did we serve, or did we take?
  • Our hidden life. “For God will bring every deed into judgment, including everything hidden, whether it is good or evil” (Ecclesiastes 12:14).

A sobering warning

Jesus gave one of the most frightening warnings in the Bible, and He gave it to people who had done great things in His name: “On that day many will say to me, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, drive out demons in your name, and do many miracles in your name?’ And then I will say to them openly, ‘I never knew you. Go away from me, you who break God’s law’” (Matthew 7:22-23).

These people had preached, cast out demons and done miracles. They had what looked like great ministries. But they did not know Christ, and they did not do the Father’s will. It is possible to lead in Christ’s name and not belong to Him. That is why Paul told Timothy, “Keep a close watch on yourself and on your teaching” (1 Timothy 4:16). We saw this in Chapter 9, Keep Watch over Yourself. The most important question a leader can ask is not, “How big is my ministry?” but, “Do I know Christ, and does He know me?”

Not judged by others, nor by ourselves

Paul had a freeing perspective on judgment: “For my part, it counts for very little if you put me on trial, or if any human court does. I do not even put myself on trial. I know of nothing I have done wrong, yet that is not what acquits me. The one who examines my case is the Lord. So do not pass sentence on anything ahead of time, before the Lord comes. He will shine light on what darkness now hides and bring the purposes of all hearts out into the open. Then each one will have from God whatever praise is due” (1 Corinthians 4:3-5).

This is a great relief for leaders. The opinions of our critics do not decide our worth. The praise of our admirers does not decide it either. Even our own judgment of ourselves is not final. Only Christ’s judgment counts. Some leaders who were praised on earth will receive little praise from Him. Some who were criticised or forgotten will be honoured. And notice how Paul ends: “Then each one will have from God whatever praise is due.” Paul expected the Lord to find something to praise.

Grace on the day of judgment

The day of account is serious. But for those who belong to Christ, it is not a day of terror. John wrote, “In this way love has been brought to completion among us, so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment ... Love has no room for fear; instead, complete love throws fear out” (1 John 4:17-18). “And now, dear children, remain in him. Then, when he appears, we will be able to face him boldly at his coming, instead of turning away from him in shame” (1 John 2:28).

The judge on that day is not a stranger. He is the Good Shepherd who laid down His life for the sheep, and for the shepherds too. He knows that we are dust. He has been praying for us all along. “God is not so unfair as to forget your work and the love you have shown for his name by serving his holy people” (Hebrews 6:10).

And He will finish what He began. “Of this I am convinced: the one who started a good work in you will keep working at it until it is finished on the day of Christ Jesus” (Philippians 1:6). Paul could say, “I know the one I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard what I have entrusted to him until that day” (2 Timothy 1:12).

Living now in the light of that day

How should the day of account shape the way we lead now?

  • Lead for an audience of One. Seek His “Well done” more than the praise of people.
  • Watch your heart. Ask God regularly to show you your true motives.
  • Teach the whole truth. Do not hold back what is hard. Be a faithful watchman.
  • Care for each one. You will give an account of people, not only programmes.
  • Deal with sin now. What is confessed and forgiven now will not be held against you then.
  • Do hidden good. The Lord sees what nobody else sees, and He will reward it.
  • Remember grace. Do not lead in fear, but in the confidence of those who are loved.

A voice from the Church: John Chrysostom and Richard Baxter

John Chrysostom, whom we met briefly in Chapter 4, The Call of God, was a great preacher in the city of Antioch, in what is now Turkey, in the late 300s, and later the bishop of Constantinople. His name means “golden mouth”, because of his preaching. As a young man, he hid to avoid being ordained, because he felt the weight of the office so deeply. He later wrote a book called On the Priesthood, which is on Ochorus, explaining why. He kept returning to the words of Hebrews 13:17 about leaders who must give account:

“But our condition hereafter how shall we endure, when we are compelled to give our account for each of those who have been entrusted to us? ... ‘Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit to them, for they watch in behalf of your souls as they that shall give account;’ though I have mentioned it once already, yet I will break silence about it now, for the fear of its warning is continually agitating my soul.”

— John Chrysostom, On the Priesthood, Book VI

In plain words: how will we bear the day when we must give an account for each person who was put in our care? I have spoken about this verse already, but I must speak of it again, because its warning keeps troubling my soul. Chrysostom did not take leadership lightly. He knew it would be judged. In the end, he did accept the call to lead, and he served faithfully, even to exile and death. But he never forgot the weight of the account.

Richard Baxter, the English pastor whom we met in Chapter 9, Keep Watch over Yourself, and Chapter 18, Knowing the Sheep, wrote The Saints’ Everlasting Rest when he was seriously ill and expected to die. It is on Ochorus. Baxter knew the weight of judgment as well as Chrysostom. But he also knew who the Judge would be. He wrote about the day when believers stand before Christ:

“If our Judge condemn us not, who shall? He that said to the adulterous woman, Hath no man condemned thee? Neither do I ... will say to us, more faithfully than Peter to him, though all men deny thee, or condemn thee, I will not.”

— Richard Baxter, The Saints’ Everlasting Rest

In plain words: if our Judge does not condemn us, who can? The same Jesus who said to the woman caught in adultery, “Neither do I condemn you,” will say to us that even if everyone else rejects or condemns us, He will not. And He will be more faithful to His word than Peter was to his. Chrysostom shows us the weight of the account. Baxter shows us the grace of the Judge. Every leader needs both.

Ready for that day

The shepherd in the hills counts the sheep every evening, because he knows the owner will come. He does not wait until the last day to start caring for the flock. He cares for them every day, so that when the owner comes, he is ready.

Jesus asked, “Who, then, is the manager who can be trusted and who acts wisely? ... Blessed is that servant if his master finds him doing just that when he comes home” (Luke 12:42-43). May each of us be found faithful when He comes. And may we hear, by His grace, the words every true servant longs to hear: “Well done! You are a good and faithful servant ... Come in and share the joy of your master” (Matthew 25:23).

Questions for reflection

  • Read 2 Corinthians 5:9-10 and 1 Corinthians 3:10-15. What will be tested on the day of judgment?
  • Read James 3:1 and Hebrews 13:17. Why are leaders “judged more strictly”?
  • Read Ezekiel 3:17-19. In what ways are you a watchman? Have you been faithful to warn?
  • Read Matthew 7:21-23. How can a leader be sure that they truly know Christ?
  • Read 1 Corinthians 4:3-5. How does this passage free you from the judgment of others and of yourself?
  • Chrysostom shows the weight of the account. Baxter shows the grace of the Judge. Which do you most need to hear today?
  • If your work were tested today, what would remain?

A step for this week

Set aside an hour this week to sit quietly before God. Imagine that you are giving Him an account of your leadership so far. Go through the list in this chapter: the people in your care, your teaching, your example, your motives, your words, your use of power and money, and your hidden life. Thank Him for His grace in each. Confess what needs confessing. Then read Philippians 1:6 aloud, and trust Him to finish the good work He began in you.

study_questions.question: Will Christian leaders give an account to God?
study_questions.answer: Yes. “All of us must be laid open before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what matches” what we have done (2 Corinthians 5:10). Teachers will be judged more strictly (James 3:1).

study_questions.question: Should believers fear the day of judgment?
study_questions.answer: Not with terror, because Christ has died for us and pleads for us: “Who is going to condemn them? Christ is the one who died” (Romans 8:34). Yet some will “suffer loss” though saved “as one who comes out through the fire” (1 Corinthians 3:15).

study_questions.question: How should the coming judgment shape a leader’s life today?
study_questions.answer: It should make us live to please Christ: “we set our hearts on pleasing him” (2 Corinthians 5:9). The chapter draws on John Chrysostom’s sober words about the weight of the priesthood and Richard Baxter’s Saints’ Rest.

fields.title: When the Chief Shepherd Appears
fields.body_html:
“Then when the Chief Shepherd is revealed, you will be given a crown of glory that will never wither.”

— 1 Peter 5:4 (OWB)

In some places, when a runner wins a race, the people put a crown of leaves on their head. It is a great honour. But within a few days the leaves turn brown and dry, and the crown crumbles. Within a few years, most people have forgotten who won.

Peter promised the elders of the churches a different kind of crown: “a crown of glory that will never wither.” It will not turn brown. It will not be forgotten. And the One who gives it is not a king or a crowd, but the Chief Shepherd Himself. This is the last chapter of Part Ten, Finishing Well. It is about the hope that keeps leaders going through every hardship: the day when the Chief Shepherd appears.

The Chief Shepherd

Peter wrote to elders as “an elder with you, a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and one who will also share in the glory that is about to be revealed” (1 Peter 5:1). He had seen Jesus suffer. He looked forward to seeing Jesus in glory. And he reminded the elders who they were: under-shepherds of a greater Shepherd. “Tend God’s flock among you as shepherds do ... Then when the Chief Shepherd is revealed, you will be given a crown of glory that will never wither” (1 Peter 5:2, 4).

All through this book we have seen that the flock is not ours. It belongs to Christ. He is the Good Shepherd, who “lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). He is “the great shepherd of the sheep”, whom God raised from the dead (Hebrews 13:20). We are His helpers. We feed His lambs, seek His lost sheep and protect His flock, until He comes.

And He is coming. “Look, I come soon, and I bring my reward with me, to pay back each person for what they have done” (Revelation 22:12). Every leader who has served Him faithfully, however small their flock and however hidden their work, will see Him face to face.

“Well done”

In Chapter 46, Faithful in Little: Accountability, and Chapter 50, Giving Account, we heard Jesus’ parable of the talents. The master returned and said to his faithful servants, “Well done! You are a good and faithful servant. You proved faithful in small matters; I will put you in charge of great ones. Come in and share the joy of your master” (Matthew 25:21).

Think of what those words will mean. The pastor of a village church of thirty people, who served for forty years and was never noticed by the wider world. The mother who taught her children to pray. The evangelist who was imprisoned and never released. The missionary who buried a spouse and children in a foreign land. The tentmaker who worked all week and preached on Sunday. The leader who failed, was restored and served again with humility. To each of them, the Lord of all the earth will say, “Well done.”

Notice that the master praised the servant for faithfulness, not for size. And notice what he invites them into: “Come in and share the joy of your master.” The greatest reward is not a position or a possession. It is to enter into the joy of Christ Himself.

Every hidden thing will be seen

Much of a leader’s work is hidden. Prayers in the night. Tears over people who wander. Visits nobody knows about. Sermons prepared with great care and heard by a few. Gifts given in secret. Insults received without reply. Faithfulness in the hidden years. Nobody sees most of it.

But He sees. “Your Father, who sees what is hidden, will repay you” (Matthew 6:4). Jesus said that even “a cup of cold water” given to one of His little ones will not lose its reward (Matthew 10:42). And on the last day, the King will say, “Truly I tell you, each time you did it for one of these my brothers and sisters, even the least of them, you did it for me” (Matthew 25:40). The things you thought were forgotten will be remembered. The things you thought were small will be honoured.

Paul wrote, “Now there is waiting for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day, and not only to me but also to all who have longed for his appearing” (2 Timothy 4:8). The crown is not only for apostles and martyrs. It is for “all who have longed for his appearing”.

Crowns thrown down

What will we do with our crowns? The book of Revelation gives us a picture of heaven. The twenty-four elders, representing the whole people of God, worship before the throne: “They throw down their crowns in front of the throne, saying: ‘Our Lord and God, you are worthy to receive the glory, the honor, and the power’” (Revelation 4:10-11).

This is the right end of every leader’s story. We will not keep our crowns to admire them. We will throw them down at His feet, because all that we did, we did by His grace. Every good thing in our ministry came from Him. As we saw in Chapter 7, Humility, and Chapter 32, Pride and the Love of Praise, the glory belongs to Him alone. On that day, at last, every leader will be completely free from the love of praise. We will be lost in praising Him.

The flock gathered home

And the flock will be there. John saw “those from every tribe and language and people and nation” whom Christ had bought with His blood (Revelation 5:9). The people we led, prayed for, taught, corrected and comforted will be there, if they belonged to Christ. Paul looked forward to that day: “When our Lord Jesus comes, what will be our hope and joy, the crown we will be proud of before him? Surely it will be you, too” (1 Thessalonians 2:19).

The great Shepherd will care for His flock for ever: “For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will shepherd them and guide them to springs of the water of life, and every tear God will wipe from their eyes” (Revelation 7:17). “Death will be no more, and no more mourning, no crying, no pain” (Revelation 21:4). The leader’s burdens will be over. There will be no more conflicts, no more failures, no more hidden sorrows, no more loneliness.

And best of all, “his servants will offer him worship; they will look upon his face” (Revelation 22:3-4). We will see the One we have served. “When he is revealed, we will be like him, for we will see him as he truly is” (1 John 3:2).

Living for that day

How should this hope shape the way we lead now?

  • It gives us courage. If the crown is certain, we can endure the cost. “For the sake of the joy that lay ahead of him, he endured a cross” (Hebrews 12:2).
  • It purifies our motives. If His “Well done” is what matters, we need not live for the praise of people.
  • It keeps us going. “Be firm and unshakable, always doing more and more in the work of the Lord, since you know that in the Lord your hard work is never wasted” (1 Corinthians 15:58).
  • It comforts us in loss. The believers we bury are not lost. We will see them again.
  • It humbles us. Our crowns will be thrown at His feet. Our work was always His.
  • It makes us long for Him. “Yes, I am coming soon!” Jesus says. And the Church answers, “Amen! Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20).

A voice from the Church: Polycarp and Valiant-for-Truth

In Chapter 8, Integrity: The Same in Secret, and Chapter 23, Making Leaders, we met Polycarp, the old bishop of Smyrna who had learned from the apostle John. When he refused to curse Christ, he was sentenced to be burned. The Martyrdom of Polycarp, on Ochorus, records that he asked not to be nailed to the stake, because God would give him strength to stand still in the fire. Then, his hands tied behind him, he looked up to heaven and prayed:

“O Lord God Almighty, the Father of thy beloved and blessed Son Jesus Christ, by whom we have received the knowledge of Thee ... I give Thee thanks that Thou hast counted me worthy of this day and this hour, that I should have a part in the number of Thy martyrs, in the cup of thy Christ, to the resurrection of eternal life.”

— Polycarp of Smyrna, as recorded in The Martyrdom of Polycarp

In plain words: Lord God Almighty, Father of Jesus Christ, through whom we have come to know You, I thank You that You have counted me worthy of this day and this hour, to share in the sufferings of Christ and to rise to eternal life. An old leader at the end of his race did not curse his enemies or fear the fire. He gave thanks, because he was looking beyond the fire to the resurrection.

Fifteen centuries later, John Bunyan, the English preacher whom we met in Chapter 39, Failure and Restoration, wrote the second part of The Pilgrim’s Progress, which is on Ochorus. Near the end, the pilgrims come to the river that every traveller must cross to reach the Celestial City, the city of God. One of them is an old soldier called Mr Valiant-for-Truth, who has fought many battles for his Lord. When his call comes, he gathers his friends and says:

“I am going to my Father’s; and though with great difficulty I have got hither, yet now I do not repent me of all the trouble I have been at to arrive where I am. My sword I give to him that shall succeed me in my pilgrimage, and my courage and skill to him that can get it. My marks and scars I carry with me, to be a witness for me that I have fought His battles who will now be my rewarder.”

— John Bunyan, The Pilgrim’s Progress, Part Two

In plain words: I am going home to my Father. It has been very hard to get here, but I do not regret any of the trouble it has cost me. I give my sword to the one who will follow me on the journey, and my courage and skill to anyone who can receive them. I take my wounds and scars with me, as proof that I have fought for the One who will now reward me. Then, as he went down into the river, he said, “Death, where is thy sting?” And Bunyan writes: “So he passed over, and all the trumpets sounded for him on the other side.”

Notice what Valiant-for-Truth does at the end. He passes on his sword to the one who comes after him, as we saw in Chapter 47, Passing the Baton. He carries his scars to the One who will reward him. And he does not regret the cost.

A voice from the global Church: Amma

Amy Carmichael, whom we have met many times in this book, spent the last nineteen years of her life mostly confined to her room at Dohnavur, after a fall in 1931. She could no longer go out to rescue children or travel to preach. But from her room she prayed, wrote books and letters, and loved the large family she had built. When she died on 18 January 1951, aged eighty-three, she was surrounded by Indian and British men and women who had grown up at Dohnavur or come to join the work, and who had learned from her how to give their lives for others. Over her grave there is no list of her achievements. There is only one word, the name the children had given her: Amma, “mother”. That is a crown that will not wither.

Until He comes

So, fellow shepherd, keep going. Feed His sheep. Seek the lost. Guard your heart. Pray. Love. Endure. Pass on the baton. And look up. The Chief Shepherd is coming. When He appears, every tear will be wiped away, every hidden faithfulness will be seen, and every true servant will hear, “Well done.”

“Goodness and loyal love will surely chase after me every day I live, and I will come home to the house of the LORD for all my days to come” (Psalm 23:6).

Questions for reflection

  • Read 1 Peter 5:1-4. How does the promise of “a crown of glory that will never wither” encourage you in your work?
  • Read Matthew 25:14-30. What would it mean for you to hear “Well done”?
  • What hidden acts of service in your life are known only to God? How does Matthew 6:4 encourage you?
  • Read Revelation 4:10-11. Why do the elders throw down their crowns? What does this teach you about your own work?
  • Read Revelation 7:9-17. Who do you hope will be there with you?
  • What do you learn from Polycarp’s prayer and Valiant-for-Truth’s farewell?
  • Are you living for that day, or for this one?

A step for this week

Read Revelation 21 and 22 slowly this week, perhaps aloud with your family or fellow leaders. Then write down the names of the people you have led, taught or cared for, and pray for each one, that you will see them on that day. Finally, write a short prayer of your own, giving your crown back to Christ in advance, and ending with the last prayer of the Bible: “Amen! Come, Lord Jesus!”

study_questions.question: What is the crown of glory for faithful shepherds?
study_questions.answer: Peter promised elders who tend God’s flock, “when the Chief Shepherd is revealed, you will be given a crown of glory that will never wither” (1 Peter 5:4). The reward comes from Christ, who says, “Well done! You are a good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25:21).

study_questions.question: Will hidden service be rewarded?
study_questions.answer: Yes. Jesus said, “Your Father, who sees what is hidden, will repay you” (Matthew 6:4). On that day every hidden thing will be seen, and the leaders who served unseen will be honoured.

study_questions.question: How should leaders live while waiting for Christ’s return?
study_questions.answer: Faithfully and with hope, living for His “Well done” rather than the praise of people. Jesus says, “Look, I come soon, and I bring my reward with me” (Revelation 22:12). The chapter draws on Polycarp, Bunyan’s Valiant-for-Truth and Amy Carmichael.

fields.title: Conclusion: Shepherds After His Heart
fields.body_html:
“I will give you shepherds who are after my own heart, and they will shepherd you with knowledge and insight.”

— Jeremiah 3:15 (OWB)

We began this book with a promise. Long ago, when God’s people had been led badly for many years, God spoke through Jeremiah: “I will give you shepherds who are after my own heart.” We have now walked a long road together, through fifty chapters, ten parts and many voices from Scripture and from the Church across the centuries and around the world. Before we close, let us look back at the road, and then look forward.

The road we have walked

In Part One, The Call, we saw that spiritual leadership begins with God. He calls, He equips, and He sends. True leaders are servants who take up the towel and the basin, and who lead under the authority of Christ.

In Part Two, The Leader’s Heart, we looked inside. God looks at the heart. We saw the need for humility, integrity, watchfulness over our own souls, love as the motive of everything, and courage to obey God rather than our fear.

In Part Three, The Leader with God, we saw that a leader’s strength comes from time with God: prayer first, life in the Word, the filling of the Spirit, rhythms of rest, and seeking His guidance.

In Part Four, Shepherding the Flock, we learned the work of the shepherd: feeding the sheep, knowing them by name, seeking the lost, correcting and restoring with gentleness, and comforting those who suffer.

In Part Five, Leading Together, we saw that God never meant leaders to work alone. We share the work, make new leaders, keep the unity of the Spirit, face conflict with grace, and honour the gifts God has given to both men and women.

In Part Six, Vision and Mission, we lifted our eyes to see what God sees: a lost world, the nations, the poor, and the possibility of revival. We learned to plan with wisdom and to work for justice and mercy.

In Part Seven, Dangers on the Road, we looked honestly at the ways leaders fall: pride, money, sexual sin, the abuse of power, and envy.

In Part Eight, Leading Through Hardship, we walked through loneliness, discouragement, failure, persecution and the hidden years, and found God faithful in each.

In Part Nine, The Leader’s Life, we looked at the leader’s home, at singleness, at the care of body, mind and time, at work in the world, and at accountability.

And in Part Ten, Finishing Well, we looked to the end: passing the baton, leaving a legacy that lasts, growing old in the work, giving account, and the day when the Chief Shepherd appears.

A portrait of a shepherd after God’s heart

If we gather together all that we have seen, what does a shepherd after God’s heart look like? Not one of us matches this picture fully. But it is the picture God is painting in His servants.

  • They have been called by God, and they know it.
  • They serve, and do not lord it over others.
  • They are humble, and the same in secret as in public.
  • They love God first, and love people for His sake.
  • They pray, and they live in the Word.
  • They depend on the Spirit, not on their own strength.
  • They know their sheep, feed them, seek the lost and bind up the broken.
  • They lead with others, and they raise up new leaders.
  • They see the nations and the poor with the eyes of Christ.
  • They guard their hearts against pride, greed, lust, the abuse of power and envy.
  • They endure hardship, and get up again when they fall.
  • They care for their homes, their bodies and their minds.
  • They are accountable, and faithful in little things.
  • They finish well, pass on the work, and live for the day of Christ’s appearing.

The psalmist described David in a single sentence: “He cared for them as a shepherd with an honest heart and led them with skillful hands” (Psalm 78:72). An honest heart and skilful hands. That is the whole of this book in one line. The heart comes first. The skill grows out of it.

Serving God’s purpose in your generation

Paul, preaching in a synagogue in Antioch, said something simple about King David: “For David, after serving God’s purpose in his own generation, fell asleep in death” (Acts 13:36).

David did not serve every generation. He served his own. You too have been given one generation, one place and one group of people to serve. You cannot do everything. You are not called to do everything. You are called to serve God’s purpose in your own generation, in the place where He has put you, with the people He has given you. Then you, too, will fall asleep and pass the work to others.

That should free you. Your task is not to save the world. Christ has already done that. Your task is to be faithful with what He has placed in your hands, today.

The Shepherd behind every shepherd

Most of all, remember this. The promise in Jeremiah was not finally about us. God said, “I will give you shepherds.” He is the giver. He makes leaders. And in the end, He kept His promise in the most wonderful way. He came Himself. Ezekiel heard God say, “I myself will search for my flock and look after them” (Ezekiel 34:11). Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11).

Every faithful shepherd in this book, from Moses to Polycarp, from Gregory to Crowther, from Brainerd to Bakhita, was a small picture of the Good Shepherd. They were imperfect pictures, and some were badly flawed. But in each of them, something of Christ could be seen. That is the goal of every Christian leader: not that people will see us, but that through us they will see Him.

So do not lead in your own strength. Lead as one who is led. Follow the Shepherd, and you will learn to shepherd.

A voice from the Church: Gregory the Great

The first voice from church history in this book, in Chapter 2, What Makes Leadership Spiritual, was Gregory the Great, the bishop of Rome who wrote The Book of Pastoral Rule around the year 590. It seems right to let him have the last word. At the very end of his book, after describing at great length what a pastor ought to be, Gregory turned to the friend who had asked him to write it and said:

“See now, good man, how, compelled by the necessity laid upon me by thy reproof, being intent on shewing what a Pastor ought to be, I have been as an ill-favoured painter pourtraying a handsome man; and how I direct others to the shore of perfection, while myself still tossed among the waves of transgressions. But in the shipwreck of this present life sustain me, I beseech thee, by the plank of thy prayer.”

— Gregory the Great, The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part IV

In plain words: you see, my friend, that in trying to show what a pastor should be, I am like an ugly painter painting a beautiful man. I point others towards the shore of perfection, while I myself am still being thrown about by the waves of my own sins. So in the shipwreck of this life, please hold me up by your prayers, as a drowning man is held up by a plank.

Those who have written this book can only say the same. We have tried to paint a picture of a shepherd after God’s heart. We have not painted ourselves. We are still tossed by the waves. Pray for us, as we pray for you.

A blessing

And so we send you back to your flock, whoever and wherever they are: a congregation, a house church, a class of children, a family, a team at work, a village, a city. Go with this blessing:

“May the God of peace, who led our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, up from the dead through the blood of an eternal covenant, make you ready in every good thing for doing his will. May he bring about in us whatever pleases him, through Jesus Christ. To him be the glory for all the ages. Amen” (Hebrews 13:20-21).

Questions for reflection

  • Which part of this book has spoken to you most deeply? Why?
  • Look at the portrait of a shepherd after God’s heart. Which marks do you see growing in your life? Which do you most need to ask God for?
  • Read Psalm 78:70-72. What does it mean to lead with “an honest heart” and “skillful hands”?
  • Read Acts 13:36. What is God’s purpose for you in your own generation?
  • Gregory called himself “an ill-favoured painter pourtraying a handsome man.” How does his humility encourage you?
  • Who will you pray for, and who will you ask to pray for you, as you go on leading?

A step for this week

Go back to the piece of paper you wrote at the end of Chapter 1, Introduction: After His Heart, with the names of the people you lead. If you did not write it then, write it now. Read the names aloud before God, and thank Him for each one. Then choose one chapter of this book that you most need to read again, and read it again this week, with a friend or fellow leader if you can. Finally, ask one person to pray for you regularly, as Gregory asked his friend, and promise to pray for them too.

study_questions.question: What does a shepherd after God’s heart look like?
study_questions.answer: Called by God, serving and humble, loving God first, prayerful and full of the Spirit, knowing and feeding the flock, leading with others, caring for the nations and the poor, guarding against sin, enduring hardship and finishing well. David “cared for them as a shepherd with an honest heart and led them with skillful hands” (Psalm 78:72).

study_questions.question: What does it mean to serve God’s purpose in your generation?
study_questions.answer: Each leader is given one generation, one place and one people. “For David, after serving God’s purpose in his own generation, fell asleep in death” (Acts 13:36). We are called to be faithful with what God has put in our hands, not to do everything.

study_questions.question: Who is the Shepherd behind every shepherd?
study_questions.answer: Jesus Christ. God promised shepherds after His heart, and then came Himself: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). Every faithful leader is a small picture of Him.

fields.title: Appendix A: How Churches Are Led
fields.body_html:
“He is also the head of the body, the church.”

— Colossians 1:18 (OWB)

Churches around the world are led in different ways. In one town, a bishop oversees many congregations and ordains their priests. In the next town, a church is led by a group of elders who meet with elders from other churches in a regional assembly. Down the road, a congregation gathers its members to vote on who its pastor will be. In a city far away, a network of house churches is led by a founding apostle and the leaders he or she has trained.

Faithful Christians have disagreed about church government for many centuries. This appendix sets out the main forms as fairly as we can, with the reasons their supporters give from Scripture and history, and the strengths and dangers of each. It does not pick a side. Its aim is to help leaders understand their own tradition better, to respect others, and to hold on to what all agree on. Chapter 6, Authority Under Authority, Chapter 22, No Lone Leaders, and Chapter 26, Men and Women in the Work of God, touch on these questions too.

What the New Testament shows

The New Testament does not give one detailed rulebook for church government. But it does show some clear patterns.

  • Elders. Paul and Barnabas “appointed elders” in each new church (Acts 14:23). Paul told Titus to “appoint elders in every town” (Titus 1:5). Elders were usually more than one in each church.
  • Overseers. The Greek word episkopos means “overseer”, and is the root of the English word “bishop”. Paul called the Ephesian elders to him (Acts 20:17) and then told them that the Holy Spirit had made them “overseers to shepherd the church of God” (Acts 20:28). In Titus 1:5-7 the two words also seem to describe the same people. Many therefore believe that in the New Testament, “elder” and “overseer” were two names for one office. Others believe the two were already beginning to be distinguished.
  • Deacons. Paul greeted the church in Philippi “together with the overseers and deacons” (Philippians 1:1). Deacons served the practical needs of the church. Many see the seven chosen in Acts 6 as the first deacons.
  • Apostles and their helpers. Apostles such as Paul had authority over many churches. Their helpers, such as Timothy and Titus, were sent to put churches in order and appoint leaders in a whole region (Titus 1:5).
  • Councils. When a great question arose about Gentile believers, “The apostles and the elders came together to consider this matter” (Acts 15:6). Their decision was then made “together with the whole church” (Acts 15:22).
  • The whole congregation. The church as a whole chose the seven (Acts 6:3). Jesus said that unresolved sin should be brought “before the church” (Matthew 18:17). Paul expected the church to act when “gathered together in the name of our Lord Jesus” (1 Corinthians 5:4).
  • Laying on of hands. Leaders were set apart with prayer, fasting and the laying on of hands (Acts 13:2-3; 1 Timothy 4:14).

Notice that each of the main forms of church government below can point to some of these patterns. That is one reason why the debate has lasted so long.

Episcopal government: led by bishops

What it is. In episcopal churches (from episkopos, “overseer”), there are usually three orders of ministry: bishops, priests (or presbyters) and deacons. A bishop oversees the churches of a region, called a diocese. Only bishops ordain new clergy. Some episcopal churches also have archbishops or patriarchs over many bishops.

Who uses it. The Orthodox churches, the Roman Catholic Church, the Anglican Communion, the ancient churches of the East, many Lutheran churches, and some Methodist churches. Many African, Asian and Latin American churches are episcopal.

The case for it. Supporters point to the apostles and to Timothy and Titus as overseers of many churches. They point to the very early Church. Ignatius of Antioch, writing around AD 110, said, “Wheresoever the bishop shall appear, there let the people be.” By the late second century, bishops were found in churches across the Roman world. Many in this tradition believe in apostolic succession: that bishops have been ordained in an unbroken line from the apostles, as a sign and guard of the Church’s unity and its faithfulness to the apostles’ teaching.

Its strengths. It gives clear oversight, care for pastors, and a strong sense of unity across many churches. Small and weak congregations are not left alone. Discipline of leaders can be clear.

Its dangers. Power can gather in a few hands, far from the local church. A bishop who is unfaithful can harm many churches. Ordinary believers may feel they have no voice.

Presbyterian government: led by elders

What it is. In presbyterian churches (from presbyteros, “elder”), each local church is led by a group of elders, usually including one or more teaching elders or ministers. Elders from a group of churches meet together in a regional body, often called a presbytery. Larger assemblies, sometimes called synods or general assemblies, make decisions for the wider church.

Who uses it. Presbyterian and Reformed churches around the world, including many large churches in Korea, Africa and Latin America. Many other churches use elder-led patterns in their local congregations.

The case for it. Supporters point out that the New Testament seems to use “elder” and “overseer” for the same office, and that elders were always plural. They point to the council of Acts 15, where apostles and elders met together, as a model for assemblies. They believe that authority should be shared among a body of qualified leaders, not held by one person.

Its strengths. Leadership is shared, and no single person holds all the power. Churches are connected and accountable to one another. Decisions are made carefully by groups of experienced leaders.

Its dangers. Decisions can be slow. Meetings and procedures can become more important than mission. Elders can become a closed group that does not listen to the congregation.

Congregational government: led by the congregation

What it is. In congregational churches, each local church governs itself.
