The members together have the final say on important matters, such as calling a pastor, appointing elders or deacons, accepting new members and church discipline. Churches may join together in associations or unions for fellowship and mission, but these do not have authority over the local church.

Who uses it. Most Baptist churches, Congregational churches, many independent churches, and many Pentecostal and evangelical churches.

The case for it. Supporters point to the passages where the whole church acts together: choosing the seven (Acts 6:3), hearing matters of discipline (Matthew 18:17; 1 Corinthians 5:4), and joining in the decision of Acts 15:22. They stress that every believer has the Holy Spirit and that Christ is the head of each local church.

Its strengths. Every member shares responsibility. Leaders are known and chosen by the people they serve. Churches can respond quickly to local needs.

Its dangers. Churches can become isolated, with no one outside to help in a crisis or to correct a failing leader. Church meetings can become places of conflict and politics. Strong personalities or wealthy members can control the vote.

Other patterns

Many churches today do not fit neatly into these three forms.

  • Apostolic networks. Many Pentecostal and charismatic churches, and many African and Asian churches, are led by a founder or senior leader, sometimes called an apostle or bishop, who oversees a network of churches he or she has planted or adopted. Supporters see this as a return to the apostolic pattern of the New Testament. The danger is that such leaders may answer to no one, as we saw in Chapter 35, Power, Abuse and Protecting the Vulnerable.
  • House church networks. In places where churches cannot meet openly, such as parts of China, many small groups are linked in networks led by trusted, often travelling, leaders. Leadership is often informal but deeply tested by suffering.
  • Mixed forms. Many churches combine elements. Some Methodist churches are led by an annual conference of ministers and lay people. Many local churches have elders and a pastor, but also hold members’ meetings for major decisions.

How churches recognise and appoint leaders

As we saw in Chapter 4, The Call of God, churches also differ in how they recognise and set apart leaders. But most include some form of these steps.

  • An inner call. A sense from God that He is calling a person to serve.
  • Testing. Deacons “too should first be tested; then, if no charge can be brought against them, let them serve” (1 Timothy 3:10). Their character, gifts and teaching are examined, often over years.
  • Recognition by the church. Through bishops, elders, the congregation, or a combination, the church confirms the call.
  • Setting apart. With prayer, and often fasting and the laying on of hands, the person is commissioned. Paul warned, “Do not be in a hurry to lay hands on anyone” (1 Timothy 5:22).

Churches also understand ordination differently. Some see it as a sacrament that gives grace and a lasting character to the one ordained. Others see it as the church’s public recognition of a gift God has already given. Churches also differ on whether women may be ordained to some or all offices, as we saw in Chapter 26, Men and Women in the Work of God.

What all agree on

Whatever form of government your church has, these truths are shared across the traditions.

  • Christ is the head. “He is also the head of the body, the church” (Colossians 1:18). Every bishop, elder, pastor and congregation is under Him.
  • Character matters most. All traditions use the qualifications of 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1. A leader’s life must match the gospel.
  • Leaders serve. Authority is given for the good of the flock, not for the benefit of the leader (Mark 10:42-45; 1 Peter 5:2-3).
  • No leader is beyond correction. Every form of government needs ways to correct and, if necessary, remove an unfaithful leader.
  • Leaders should be honoured. “Recognize those who work hard among you, who lead you in the Lord and correct you. Think of them with the highest respect and love because of the work they do” (1 Thessalonians 5:12-13).
  • Order and unity matter. “Let everything be done properly and in good order” (1 Corinthians 14:40). “Spare no effort to keep the unity the Spirit gives” (Ephesians 4:3).

No form of government can make a church holy. A church with the best structure in the world will fail if its leaders are proud, greedy or prayerless. A church with a weak structure can flourish if its leaders are humble, faithful and full of the Spirit. Structure matters. But the heart matters more.

Questions for discussion

  • Which form of church government does your church follow? What reasons does your tradition give for it?
  • What are the strengths of your church’s form of government? What are its dangers, and how does your church guard against them?
  • What can you learn from the strengths of other traditions?
  • If a senior leader in your church were unfaithful, how would they be corrected? Is there a clear way?
  • How does your church recognise and appoint new leaders? Is it careful enough?
  • How can you keep “the unity the Spirit gives” with believers whose churches are governed differently from yours?

study_questions.question: What are the main forms of church government?
study_questions.answer: Episcopal (led by bishops), presbyterian (led by elders meeting together in presbyteries and assemblies) and congregational (the members together have the final say). Many churches also follow apostolic networks, house-church networks or mixed forms.

study_questions.question: What does the New Testament show about church leadership?
study_questions.answer: It shows plural elders in each church (Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5), overseers and deacons (Philippians 1:1), apostles and their helpers, councils such as Acts 15, and the whole congregation acting together. Each form of government can point to some of these patterns.

study_questions.question: What do all churches agree on about leadership?
study_questions.answer: That Christ is the head: “He is also the head of the body, the church” (Colossians 1:18). Character matters most, leaders serve, no leader is beyond correction, leaders should be honoured, and order and unity matter.

fields.title: Appendix B: A Leader’s Self-Examination
fields.body_html:
“God, look deep into me and know my heart; put me to the test and know my restless thoughts. Look and see whether I am on a path that brings harm, and guide me along the road that never ends.”

— Psalm 139:23-24 (OWB)

A wise farmer walks around his fields regularly, looking for weeds, broken fences and signs of disease. He does not wait until the harvest has failed. In the same way, a wise leader regularly examines their own life before God.

Paul told Timothy, “Keep a close watch on yourself and on your teaching” (1 Timothy 4:16). He told the Corinthians, “Look closely at yourselves: are you holding to the faith? Put yourselves to the test” (2 Corinthians 13:5). And David prayed, “God, look deep into me and know my heart” (Psalm 139:23).

This appendix offers questions for a leader’s self-examination. They follow the ten parts of this book, and they draw on three voices from church history that we have met along the way: Richard Baxter’s The Reformed Pastor, John Wesley’s band meetings, and the East African Revival’s practice of “walking in the light”.

How to use these questions

  • Do not try to answer them all at once. Choose one section at a time. You might take one section each week for ten weeks, and then begin again.
  • Answer before God. Begin with prayer. Ask the Holy Spirit to show you the truth. Read Psalm 139:23-24 aloud.
  • Be honest. Nobody else needs to see your answers unless you choose to share them.
  • Remember grace. These questions are not meant to crush you. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous: he will forgive our sins and cleanse us from every kind of wrongdoing” (1 John 1:9). The purpose of examination is not condemnation but cleansing and growth.
  • Share with a trusted friend. Consider going through some questions with your accountability partner, as we saw in Chapter 46, Faithful in Little: Accountability.
  • Write down one step. At the end of each section, write down one thing you will do differently.

Three voices to begin with

Richard Baxter, the seventeenth-century English pastor whom we met in Chapter 9, Keep Watch over Yourself, and Chapter 18, Knowing the Sheep, wrote this warning to his fellow pastors in The Reformed Pastor, which is on Ochorus:

“Take heed to yourselves, lest your example contradict your doctrine ... lest you unsay with your lives, what you say with your tongues; and be the greatest hinderers of the success of your own labors.”

— Richard Baxter, The Reformed Pastor

In plain words: be careful that the way you live does not deny what you teach, so that you take back with your life what you said with your mouth, and become the greatest obstacle to your own work.

John Wesley, as we saw in Chapter 46, Faithful in Little: Accountability, asked the members of his bands to answer five questions at every meeting:

“What known sins have you committed since our last meeting? What temptations have you met with? How was you delivered? What have you thought, said, or done, of which you doubt whether it be sin or not? Have you nothing you desire to keep secret?”

— John Wesley, Rules of the Band Societies, 1738

The East African Revival, which we met in Chapter 20, Correction and Restoration, taught believers to “walk in the light”, from 1 John 1:7: “if we walk in the light, just as he is in the light, we share fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus, his Son, goes on cleansing us from every sin.” Brothers and sisters in the revival would often ask one another simple questions such as: Is there anything between you and the Lord? Is there anything between you and your brother or sister? Are you walking in the light?

Part One: The Call

  • Do I still have a clear sense that God has called me to this work? When did I last thank Him for it?
  • Am I leading because God called me, or because of position, money, family expectation or the praise of people?
  • Do I lead as a servant, or do I expect to be served?
  • Do I see myself as under Christ’s authority, under His Word, and under the authority of others in His Church?
  • Who can say no to me? Do I listen when they do?

Part Two: The Leader’s Heart

  • Am I growing in humility, or do I need to be noticed and thanked?
  • Am I the same person in secret as in public? Is there anything in my life I would be ashamed for my church to know?
  • Am I keeping watch over my own soul, or only over others?
  • Do I truly love the people I lead, including the difficult ones?
  • Is there anything God has told me to do or say that I have avoided out of fear?

Part Three: The Leader with God

  • How much time did I spend alone with God this week? Is prayer first in my life, or last?
  • Am I reading the Bible to know God, or only to prepare sermons?
  • Am I depending on the Holy Spirit, or on my own gifts and experience?
  • Do I keep a weekly day of rest? When did I last take a real break?
  • How do I make decisions? Do I seek God’s guidance and the counsel of others?

Part Four: Shepherding the Flock

  • Am I feeding my people with the Word of God, or with my own opinions?
  • Do I know the people in my care by name? Whom have I not visited or contacted for a long time?
  • When did I last share the gospel with someone who does not know Christ?
  • Do I correct people with gentleness, or with anger? Do I avoid correcting when I should?
  • Who in my care is suffering or grieving right now? Have I been with them?

Part Five: Leading Together

  • Am I trying to do everything myself? What could I share with others?
  • Whom am I training to lead? How much time do I give them?
  • Am I at peace with my fellow leaders? Is there anyone I need to forgive, or ask for forgiveness?
  • How do I respond to criticism? Do I listen, or defend myself at once?
  • Am I honouring and making room for the gifts God has given to everyone in the church, both men and women, young and old?

Part Six: Vision and Mission

  • Do I see my community as God sees it? When did I last weep or pray over the lost?
  • Are my plans made in prayer and with wisdom, or in haste and pride?
  • Is my church concerned for the nations, or only for itself?
  • How are we caring for the poor, the widow, the orphan and the stranger?
  • Am I longing and praying for God to do a new work in our day?

Part Seven: Dangers on the Road

  • Do I enjoy praise too much? Am I hurt when others are praised instead of me?
  • Is my handling of money open and honest? Would my accounts bear an independent check? Am I content?
  • Am I keeping my walls of protection in sexual purity? Is there anything I am looking at, thinking about, or doing in secret that I need to confess?
  • Do people feel safe to disagree with me and to tell me the truth? Have I ever used my position to control, frighten or take from anyone?
  • Is there a leader or church I envy? Do I treat some people as more important than others because of tribe, class, wealth or family?

Part Eight: Leading Through Hardship

  • What burdens am I carrying alone? Who could I share them with?
  • How full or empty is my lamp right now, in body, mind and spirit?
  • Is there a failure in my life that I am still hiding?
  • Am I ready to pay a price for faithfulness to Christ? Is there anything I would deny Him to keep?
  • Am I faithful in the small, hidden tasks that nobody else sees?

Part Nine: The Leader’s Life

  • Does my family get my best, or only what is left? What would my spouse or children say?
  • If I am single, am I receiving my life as a gift, and do I have close friends? If I am married, how am I helping single people feel part of God’s family?
  • How am I caring for my body: sleep, food, exercise and health? Am I lazy, or overworking?
  • Am I serving Christ in my daily work, and helping others to do the same?
  • Who regularly asks me hard questions? Do I tell them the whole truth?

Part Ten: Finishing Well

  • If I could no longer lead tomorrow, who would carry on the work?
  • What am I building that will last? What might burn up on the last Day?
  • Am I still learning and growing? Am I making room for those who are younger?
  • If Christ asked me today to give account of my leadership, what would I say?
  • Am I living for His “Well done”, or for the praise of people today?

A prayer after self-examination

When you have finished a section, pray in your own words, or use this prayer, based on Psalm 51 and Psalm 139:

Lord, You have searched me and You know me. You see what I cannot see. Thank You for Your grace in every part of my life. Forgive me where I have failed You and the people You have given me. Create a pure heart in me, and make my spirit new and steady. Give me back the joy of Your salvation. Help me to walk in the light with You and with my brothers and sisters. Make me a shepherd after Your own heart, for the sake of Jesus Christ, the Good Shepherd. Amen.

study_questions.question: Why should leaders examine themselves?
study_questions.answer: Because Scripture tells us to: “Look closely at yourselves: are you holding to the faith? Put yourselves to the test” (2 Corinthians 13:5). David prayed, “God, look deep into me and know my heart” (Psalm 139:23).

study_questions.question: How should I use self-examination questions without being crushed?
study_questions.answer: Take one section at a time, begin with prayer, answer honestly before God, and remember grace: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous: he will forgive our sins” (1 John 1:9). The purpose is cleansing and growth, not condemnation.

study_questions.question: What questions did John Wesley ask in his band meetings?
study_questions.answer: He asked what known sins had been committed since the last meeting, what temptations had been met, how the person was delivered, what they had done that they doubted was sin, and whether they had anything they wanted to keep secret.

fields.title: Appendix C: Using This Book to Train Leaders
fields.body_html:
“And what you heard from me before many witnesses, pass on to trustworthy people who will be able to teach others as well.”

— 2 Timothy 2:2 (OWB)

Jesus did not train His disciples in a classroom only. “He appointed twelve to be with him, and to be sent out to proclaim the message” (Mark 3:14). They learned by being with Him, by listening, by asking questions, by watching Him work, by trying for themselves and by coming back to talk about it. Paul trained leaders in the same way, teaching them for two years in a hall in Ephesus and taking them with him on his journeys (Acts 19:9-10).

This book was written to be used in the same way: not only read alone, but read and discussed by groups of leaders, prayed over and put into practice. This appendix gives two plans. The first is a short course of ten sessions, one for each part of the book. The second is a full year of fifty weeks, one chapter a week. A church, a group of churches, a Bible school or a mentor with one or two people can use either plan.

Who this is for

  • Church leaders training their elders, deacons, group leaders and youth leaders.
  • Groups of pastors from different churches in one town or district, meeting to learn and pray together.
  • Bible schools and training centres that want a course on the character and life of the leader.
  • Mentors meeting with one or two younger leaders.
  • Couples in leadership who want to read and pray together.

How to lead a session

A session of about ninety minutes might follow this pattern. Adjust it to suit your group and your culture.

  1. Welcome and prayer (10 minutes). Greet one another. Pray for God’s help.
  2. Review the last step (15 minutes). Ask each person how they did with the “step for this week” from the last session. Celebrate progress. Do not shame anyone who did not manage it.
  3. Read the Scripture (15 minutes). Read the main Bible passage aloud, slowly. Ask: what do we notice? What does it teach us about God, and about leadership?
  4. Discuss the chapter (25 minutes). Use the “Questions for reflection” at the end of the chapter. Choose two or three; you do not need to use them all. Let everyone speak.
  5. The voice from the Church (10 minutes). Read the story or letter aloud. Ask: what does this person teach us?
  6. Choose a step and pray (15 minutes). Each person chooses a step for the coming week, using the “step for this week”. Pray for one another in pairs or as a group.

Tips for the leader of the group

  • Read the chapter yourself first, and pray for each member of the group by name.
  • Read aloud. If some members do not read easily, or do not have their own copy, read the main parts of the chapter aloud together. Many of the world’s best leaders learned by listening.
  • Use your own language. If the book is not yet in your language, a member who reads English well can explain each section in the group’s language. Use the Glossary (Chapter 56, Glossary: Words Used in This Book) to agree on the words you will use.
  • Keep it practical. The aim is not only to understand but to change. Always end with a step.
  • Keep confidences. What people share honestly in the group must not be repeated outside it, except where someone is in danger or a child is at risk, as Chapter 35, Power, Abuse and Protecting the Vulnerable, explains.
  • Be honest yourself. If you share your own struggles, others will feel free to share theirs.
  • Add local voices. Each chapter has a voice from the Church. Invite members to tell stories of faithful leaders from your own church, people and country.
  • Pray more than you plan. The Holy Spirit is the true teacher.

Plan one: a ten-session course

This plan covers the whole book in ten sessions, one for each part. Before the first session, ask everyone to read Chapter 1, Introduction: After His Heart. Before each session, members read the five chapters of that part, or at least the focus chapter. In the session, discuss the focus chapter in depth and touch on the others. Sessions can be weekly, every two weeks or monthly.

Session 1: Part One: The Call

  • Read beforehand: Chapters 2 (What Makes Leadership Spiritual), 3 (Jesus, the Chief Shepherd), 4 (The Call of God), 5 (The Towel and the Basin), 6 (Authority Under Authority).
  • Focus chapter: Chapter 5, The Towel and the Basin.
  • Main Scripture: John 13:1-17.
  • Activity: Wash one another’s feet, or do another simple act of service for each other, as Jesus did. Then talk about how it felt to serve and to be served.

Session 2: Part Two: The Leader’s Heart

  • Read beforehand: Chapters 7 (Humility), 8 (Integrity: The Same in Secret), 9 (Keep Watch over Yourself), 10 (Love: The Motive and the Mark), 11 (Courage).
  • Focus chapter: Chapter 8, Integrity: The Same in Secret.
  • Main Scripture: 1 Samuel 16:1-13.
  • Activity: Each person writes down privately one area where their public and private life do not match, and prays about it. Pair up and pray for each other without sharing details unless they wish to.

Session 3: Part Three: The Leader with God

  • Read beforehand: Chapters 12 (Prayer First), 13 (Living in the Word), 14 (Filled with the Spirit), 15 (Rest, Retreat and Rhythm), 16 (Guidance and Decisions).
  • Focus chapter: Chapter 12, Prayer First.
  • Main Scripture: Mark 1:32-39.
  • Activity: Spend thirty minutes of the session in prayer together. Then each person plans a daily time with God for the coming week and shares it with a partner.

Session 4: Part Four: Shepherding the Flock

  • Read beforehand: Chapters 17 (Feed My Sheep), 18 (Knowing the Sheep), 19 (Seeking the Lost), 20 (Correction and Restoration), 21 (Comfort in Suffering and Grief).
  • Focus chapter: Chapter 18, Knowing the Sheep.
  • Main Scripture: John 10:1-18.
  • Activity: Each person writes the names of the people in their care and marks those they have not contacted for a month. Agree to visit or call two of them before the next session.

Session 5: Part Five: Leading Together

  • Read beforehand: Chapters 22 (No Lone Leaders), 23 (Making Leaders), 24 (Unity and Peacemaking), 25 (Criticism, Opposition and Conflict), 26 (Men and Women in the Work of God).
  • Focus chapter: Chapter 22, No Lone Leaders.
  • Main Scripture: Exodus 18:13-27.
  • Activity: Each leader lists their regular tasks and marks one they could hand to someone else. Name the person, and agree when you will ask them.

Session 6: Part Six: Vision and Mission

  • Read beforehand: Chapters 27 (Vision: Seeing What God Sees), 28 (Wisdom and Planning), 29 (To the Nations), 30 (Justice, Mercy and the Poor), 31 (Leading in Revival and Change).
  • Focus chapter: Chapter 27, Vision: Seeing What God Sees.
  • Main Scripture: Matthew 9:35-38.
  • Activity: Walk or drive around your community together, or draw a simple map of it. Pray for each area, and ask: who is not being reached? Who is poor or forgotten?

Session 7: Part Seven: Dangers on the Road

  • Read beforehand: Chapters 32 (Pride and the Love of Praise), 33 (Money and Greed), 34 (Sexual Purity), 35 (Power, Abuse and Protecting the Vulnerable), 36 (Envy, Rivalry and Favouritism).
  • Focus chapter: Chapter 35, Power, Abuse and Protecting the Vulnerable.
  • Main Scripture: Ezekiel 34:1-16.
  • Activity: Review together how your church handles money and how it protects children. Write down one change you will make in each.

Session 8: Part Eight: Leading Through Hardship

  • Read beforehand: Chapters 37 (Loneliness and Hidden Burdens), 38 (Discouragement and Burnout), 39 (Failure and Restoration), 40 (Persecution and the Cost), 41 (The Hidden Years).
  • Focus chapter: Chapter 38, Discouragement and Burnout.
  • Main Scripture: 1 Kings 19:1-18.
  • Activity: Each person rates how tired they are, from one to ten, in body, mind and spirit, and shares it with the group. Pray for one another, especially for those who are most tired.

Session 9: Part Nine: The Leader’s Life

  • Read beforehand: Chapters 42 (The Leader’s Home), 43 (Single and Serving), 44 (Stewarding Yourself), 45 (Leaders at Work and in Society), 46 (Faithful in Little: Accountability).
  • Focus chapter: Chapter 46, Faithful in Little: Accountability.
  • Main Scripture: Luke 16:10-12.
  • Activity: Form pairs or threes of the same sex as accountability partners. Agree on the questions you will ask each other and when you will meet.

Session 10: Part Ten: Finishing Well

  • Read beforehand: Chapters 47 (Passing the Baton), 48 (Legacy: What Lasts), 49 (Growing Old in the Work), 50 (Giving Account), 51 (When the Chief Shepherd Appears).
  • Focus chapter: Chapter 47, Passing the Baton.
  • Main Scripture: 2 Timothy 4:1-8.
  • Activity: Each person names one or two people they will prepare to lead after them. Close the course by laying hands on one another and praying a blessing, using Hebrews 13:20-21.

After the tenth session, you might hold a final meeting to read together Chapter 52, Conclusion: Shepherds After His Heart, share what God has taught each person, and celebrate with a meal.

Plan two: a year of fifty weeks

This plan takes one chapter a week for a year. It suits a group that wants to go deeper, or a mentor and a younger leader meeting regularly. It leaves a week in the year for holidays or special events.

Week 0 (first meeting): Chapter 1, Introduction: After His Heart. Get to know one another. Each person writes the names of the people they lead, as the chapter suggests.

Part One: The Call

  • Week 1: Chapter 2, What Makes Leadership Spiritual
  • Week 2: Chapter 3, Jesus, the Chief Shepherd
  • Week 3: Chapter 4, The Call of God
  • Week 4: Chapter 5, The Towel and the Basin
  • Week 5: Chapter 6, Authority Under Authority

Part Two: The Leader’s Heart

  • Week 6: Chapter 7, Humility
  • Week 7: Chapter 8, Integrity: The Same in Secret
  • Week 8: Chapter 9, Keep Watch over Yourself
  • Week 9: Chapter 10, Love: The Motive and the Mark
  • Week 10: Chapter 11, Courage

Part Three: The Leader with God

  • Week 11: Chapter 12, Prayer First
  • Week 12: Chapter 13, Living in the Word
  • Week 13: Chapter 14, Filled with the Spirit
  • Week 14: Chapter 15, Rest, Retreat and Rhythm
  • Week 15: Chapter 16, Guidance and Decisions

Part Four: Shepherding the Flock

  • Week 16: Chapter 17, Feed My Sheep
  • Week 17: Chapter 18, Knowing the Sheep
  • Week 18: Chapter 19, Seeking the Lost
  • Week 19: Chapter 20, Correction and Restoration
  • Week 20: Chapter 21, Comfort in Suffering and Grief

Part Five: Leading Together

  • Week 21: Chapter 22, No Lone Leaders
  • Week 22: Chapter 23, Making Leaders
  • Week 23: Chapter 24, Unity and Peacemaking
  • Week 24: Chapter 25, Criticism, Opposition and Conflict
  • Week 25: Chapter 26, Men and Women in the Work of God

Part Six: Vision and Mission

  • Week 26: Chapter 27, Vision: Seeing What God Sees
  • Week 27: Chapter 28, Wisdom and Planning
  • Week 28: Chapter 29, To the Nations
  • Week 29: Chapter 30, Justice, Mercy and the Poor
  • Week 30: Chapter 31, Leading in Revival and Change

Part Seven: Dangers on the Road

  • Week 31: Chapter 32, Pride and the Love of Praise
  • Week 32: Chapter 33, Money and Greed
  • Week 33: Chapter 34, Sexual Purity
  • Week 34: Chapter 35, Power, Abuse and Protecting the Vulnerable
  • Week 35: Chapter 36, Envy, Rivalry and Favouritism

Part Eight: Leading Through Hardship

  • Week 36: Chapter 37, Loneliness and Hidden Burdens
  • Week 37: Chapter 38, Discouragement and Burnout
  • Week 38: Chapter 39, Failure and Restoration
  • Week 39: Chapter 40, Persecution and the Cost
  • Week 40: Chapter 41, The Hidden Years

Part Nine: The Leader’s Life

  • Week 41: Chapter 42, The Leader’s Home
  • Week 42: Chapter 43, Single and Serving
  • Week 43: Chapter 44, Stewarding Yourself
  • Week 44: Chapter 45, Leaders at Work and in Society
  • Week 45: Chapter 46, Faithful in Little: Accountability

Part Ten: Finishing Well

  • Week 46: Chapter 47, Passing the Baton
  • Week 47: Chapter 48, Legacy: What Lasts
  • Week 48: Chapter 49, Growing Old in the Work
  • Week 49: Chapter 50, Giving Account
  • Week 50: Chapter 51, When the Chief Shepherd Appears

Final meeting: Chapter 52, Conclusion: Shepherds After His Heart. Share what has changed in each person’s life and leadership during the year. Pray for one another and commission one another for the work ahead.

Throughout the year, use Chapter 54, Appendix B: A Leader’s Self-Examination. At the end of each part, take ten minutes in the session for each person to answer that part’s questions privately before God. If your group is from different churches, Chapter 53, Appendix A: How Churches Are Led, will help you understand and respect one another’s traditions.

Training the next trainers

Paul’s instruction to Timothy had four generations: Paul, Timothy, “trustworthy people”, and “others as well” (2 Timothy 2:2). The best use of this course is not only to train leaders, but to train leaders who will train others.

  • After a group has finished the course, invite one or two members to lead a new group of their own, with you helping them at first.
  • Meet with these new group leaders regularly to pray, plan and encourage them.
  • Over time, a single group can become many, spreading across a church, a district or a nation.

“As iron is sharpened against iron, so one person sharpens another” (Proverbs 27:17). May God use this book, and the groups that read it, to raise up shepherds after His own heart in every nation.

study_questions.question: How can I use this book to train leaders?
study_questions.answer: Appendix C gives two plans: a ten-session course on key chapters, and a fifty-week plan through the whole book, with guidance on leading a session, using the questions, and training others to lead groups in turn.

study_questions.question: Why train leaders in a group?
study_questions.answer: Because leaders grow together: “As iron is sharpened against iron, so one person sharpens another” (Proverbs 27:17). Jesus trained His disciples together; “He appointed twelve to be with him” (Mark 3:14).

study_questions.question: What is the goal of training leaders?
study_questions.answer: That those trained will train others, as Paul told Timothy: “pass on to trustworthy people who will be able to teach others as well” (2 Timothy 2:2). The appendix ends with training the next trainers.

fields.title: Glossary: Words Used in This Book
fields.body_html:
Many of the words in this book have special meanings in the Bible and in the life of the Church. Some of them are translated in different ways in different languages and different churches. This glossary explains the most important ones in plain words. Where a chapter gives more teaching on a word, its number is shown.

  • Accountability. Being answerable to others, so that they can question and correct you.
  • Accountability partner. A trusted believer of the same sex who has permission to ask you hard questions and pray with you (Chapter 46).
  • Anointed. Set apart by God for a task, in the Old Testament by pouring oil on the head (1 Samuel 24:6).
  • Apostle. One of the twelve chosen by Jesus, or another early leader sent out with the gospel, such as Paul.
  • Apostolic succession. The belief that bishops have been ordained in an unbroken line from the apostles.
  • Atonement. God’s way of removing sin and bringing people back to Himself, fulfilled in the death of Jesus.
  • Authority. The right to lead or decide, given by God and to be used for building people up.
  • Benefactor. A title rulers liked, meaning one who does good to others (Luke 22:25).
  • Bi-vocational. Working two jobs: a paid job and an unpaid or part-paid ministry.
  • Bishop. In many churches, a senior leader who oversees several congregations or a region.
  • Burnout. Deep exhaustion of body, mind and spirit after long overwork or stress (Chapter 38).
  • Call, calling. God’s invitation and appointment of a person, first to follow Jesus and then to a particular task.
  • Centurion. A Roman army officer in charge of about a hundred soldiers.
  • Chief Shepherd. Jesus, the shepherd over all other shepherds (1 Peter 5:4).
  • Church. God’s people. With a capital letter, all believers everywhere; with a small letter, a local gathering.
  • Class meeting, band. Small groups John Wesley used: classes of about twelve for care, and smaller bands for deeper confession (Chapters 22 and 46).
  • Congregation. The people who gather as a local church.
  • Covenant. A solemn promise or agreement, especially between God and His people.
  • Crown of glory. The reward Christ will give faithful leaders when He appears (1 Peter 5:4).
  • Deacon. A servant appointed to care for practical needs in the church (Acts 6; 1 Timothy 3:8-13).
  • Denomination. A family or group of churches that share a name, beliefs and form of government.
  • Depression. An illness of deep and lasting sadness or emptiness, which may need medical help. It is not simply a lack of faith.
  • Diocese. The area of churches overseen by one bishop.
  • Disciple. A follower and learner of Jesus.
  • Elder. A mature believer appointed to lead and care for a church. In the New Testament, elders led each church together.
  • Episcopal, presbyterian, congregational. Three main ways churches are governed: by bishops, by elders, or by the congregation (Chapter 53).
  • Evangelist. A person gifted to share the good news of Jesus with those who do not yet believe.
  • Exile. Being forced to live away from one’s home or country.
  • Fasting. Going without food for a time in order to seek God in prayer.
  • Favouritism. Treating some people as more important than others because of tribe, class, wealth, family or race (Chapter 36).
  • Flock. A group of sheep. In the Bible, God’s people in a place.
  • Gentile. Someone who is not Jewish.
  • Gospel. The good news of what God has done in Jesus Christ to save sinners.
  • Grace. God’s free, undeserved kindness to sinners.
  • Holiness. Being set apart for God and made pure by Him.
  • Judgment seat of Christ. The place where every believer will give account to Christ for their life (2 Corinthians 5:10; Chapter 50).
  • Lament. A prayer or song that pours out grief or complaint honestly to God, as in many psalms.
  • Lay preacher. A believer who preaches without being ordained, such as John Wesley’s helpers (Chapter 22).
  • Laying on of hands. Placing hands on a person’s head or shoulders while praying, to bless, commission or set them apart (Acts 13:3).
  • Leader. Anyone whose words, choices and example move other people, with or without a title.
  • Legacy. What a person leaves behind after they die, especially in the lives of others (Chapter 48).
  • Martyr. A person who is killed because they will not deny Christ.
  • Mentor. An older or more experienced believer who walks alongside a younger one to help them grow.
  • Minister. A person who serves God’s people, often a pastor. The word means “servant”.
  • Ministry. Service done for God among His people.
  • Mission, missionary. Being sent to share the gospel; a person sent, often to another people.
  • Office. A recognised role or position of responsibility in the church, such as elder or deacon.
  • Ordination. The act by which a church sets a person apart for ministry, usually with prayer and the laying on of hands.
  • Overseer. A leader who watches over a church; in the New Testament the same people are called elders and overseers.
  • Parable. A short story Jesus told to teach a truth about God’s kingdom.
  • Pastor. A leader who teaches and cares for a congregation. The word comes from the Latin for “shepherd”.
  • Pentecost. The Jewish festival fifty days after Passover, when the Holy Spirit came on the first disciples (Acts 2).
  • Persecution. Hostility, harm or punishment suffered because of faith in Christ.
  • Presbyter. An old word for an elder, used in early Christian writings such as 1 Clement.
  • Presbytery. In presbyterian churches, a regional gathering of elders from several churches.
  • Prophet. A person who speaks a message from God. In the Old Testament, people such as Elijah and Jeremiah.
  • Prosperity gospel. A false teaching that God always wants believers to be rich and healthy, and that giving money to the preacher guarantees wealth (Chapter 33).
  • Puritans. English pastors and believers of the 1500s and 1600s who sought a purer, Bible-shaped church and life.
  • Ransom. A price paid to set someone free (Mark 10:45).
  • Reformation. The movement of the 1500s, led by Martin Luther and others, that called the Church back to the Bible.
  • Repentance. Turning away from sin and back to God, with a change of heart and life.
  • Restoration. Bringing a person who has fallen back into fellowship with God and the church; sometimes, after long testing, back into leadership (Chapter 39).
  • Revival. A time when the Holy Spirit wakes up the Church and many people turn to God.
  • Sabbath. The seventh day of rest God gave Israel; for leaders, a regular day of rest from work (Chapter 15).
  • Sacrament. A holy act given by Christ, such as baptism and the Lord’s Supper, through which many churches believe God gives grace.
  • Sadhu. In India, a holy man who gives up possessions to wander and pray. Sundar Singh lived as a Christian sadhu (Chapter 43).
  • Safeguarding. Steps a church takes to keep children and vulnerable adults safe from harm and abuse.
  • Sedition. Rebellion against rightful leaders. The word comes from old translations of 1 Clement.
  • Seraphim. Heavenly beings around God’s throne in Isaiah 6.
  • Servant leadership. Leading as Jesus did, by serving others and using power for their good.
  • Shepherd. A person who looks after sheep. In the Bible, a picture of God, of Jesus and of the leaders of His people.
  • Simony. Trying to buy or sell spiritual things or church positions, named after Simon in Acts 8.
  • Spiritual abuse. Using spiritual position or religious language to control, frighten or harm people (Chapter 35).
  • Spiritual leadership. Leading people toward God’s purposes, by God’s means, as someone who will answer to God.
  • Steward. Someone who manages what belongs to another.
  • Succession. Passing leadership on from one person to the next (Chapter 47).
  • Talents. In Jesus’ parable (Matthew 25), large sums of money entrusted to servants; a picture of all that God gives us to use for Him.
  • Tentmaker. A leader who earns their living by another job, as Paul made tents (Acts 18:3).
  • Under-shepherd. A human leader who cares for God’s people on behalf of Jesus, the Chief Shepherd.
  • Walking in the light. Living openly before God and other believers, quickly confessing sin; a phrase of the East African Revival from 1 John 1:7.

How this book is arranged

  • Going deeper. A section heading in this book for questions on which faithful Christians disagree. New readers may skip it.
  • A voice from the Church. A section heading in this book introducing a letter or story from church history or the global Church.
  • In plain words. After a quotation in old or difficult English, this book gives its meaning in simple modern words.
  • OWB. The Open Word Bible, the English translation quoted in this book. It is free for anyone to use. Where other English Bibles translate a verse differently, the book says so.

study_questions.question: Why does this book have a glossary?
study_questions.answer: So that new believers, new leaders and readers in other languages can understand words they may not know, such as elder, overseer, deacon, revival, ordination and grace, each explained in plain words.

study_questions.question: How is this book arranged?
study_questions.answer: An introduction, ten parts of five chapters each (The Call; The Leader’s Heart; The Leader with God; Shepherding the Flock; Leading Together; Vision and Mission; Dangers on the Road; Leading Through Hardship; The Leader’s Life; Finishing Well), a conclusion, three appendices and this glossary.
